sections.heading: 0.1 The maggot red herring
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Florence, summer 1668

Open an old tin of rice or *atta* that has sat at the back of a warm Mumbai kitchen cupboard through the monsoon, and you may find tiny brown beetles crawling through the grain. Leave a piece of raw fish on a plate in July heat, and within two days pale, legless maggots are wriggling over it. Where did they come from?

For centuries, the answer seemed too obvious to question: they grew out of the food itself. Aristotle taught that frogs and eels form out of pond mud, fleas out of dust, and maggots out of decaying meat. Even Jan Baptista van Helmont—a brilliant seventeenth-century doctor whom we will meet again in Chapter 5—wrote down a recipe for making mice: stuff a dirty shirt into a pot of wheat grains, wait twenty-one days, and mice will appear. The idea was called ==spontaneous generation==: the belief that living creatures can arise directly and regularly from non-living muck or food.

:::note Spontaneous generation
The old, mistaken belief that living organisms (such as maggots, beetles or microbes) regularly spring to life out of non-living matter like rotting meat, mud or broth.
:::

sections.heading: 0.2 The cloth merchant’s glass bead
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Delft, the Netherlands, September 1674

Redi settled the question for flies and maggots. Seven years later, however, a cloth merchant in the Dutch town of Delft opened a trapdoor beneath everyone's feet—and made the spontaneous generation mystery ten times harder.

Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was not a university professor. He sold linen and cloth, and to check the thread count of his fabrics he learned to make his own magnifying lenses. In London, a few years earlier (1665), Robert Hooke had used a compound microscope—a leather tube with two lenses—to look at a razor-thin slice of bottle cork. Hooke saw rows of tiny empty boxes separated by thin walls; they reminded him of the bare rooms (*cellae*) where monks slept in a monastery, so he called them ==cells==. What Hooke was actually looking at were the dead, empty wooden walls left behind after the tree bark cells had died.

:::note Cell
The smallest unit of life that can carry out all the processes of a living thing, bounded by a membrane and containing genetic instructions and molecular machinery. Coined by Robert Hooke in 1665 after looking at dead cork chambers.
:::

sections.heading: 0.3 The swan-neck trap
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Paris, 1859

For nearly two centuries after Leeuwenhoek, naturalists fought over where the microbes in spoiled broth came from. If you boiled meat broth in a flask to kill everything inside and left the flask open, it turned cloudy and teamed with swimming bacteria within forty-eight hours. If you boiled the broth and melted the glass neck shut, it stayed crystal clear—but critics gave the exact same reply they had given Redi: *"By sealing the glass, you ruined the fresh air that spontaneous generation needs!"*

In 1859, the French Academy of Sciences offered the Alhumbert Prize to anyone who could settle the question with a clean, decisive experiment. The chemist Louis Pasteur took up the challenge. Pasteur suspected that ordinary room air is full of invisible floating dust, and riding on those dust specks are dormantly waiting bacterial spores and yeast cells. What he needed was a flask that stayed wide open to fresh air, yet trapped every speck of dust before it could reach the boiled broth.

sections.heading: 0.4 The ladder of biological size
sections.excerpt:
Once Hooke and Leeuwenhoek opened the microscopic world, biologists needed a new set of rulers. Everything you hold in your hands—a pencil, a *moong* bean, your own thumb—is measured in metres ($\text{m}$) or millimetres ($\text{mm}$), where $1\text{ mm}$ is one thousandth of a metre ($10^{-3}\text{ m}$). Look at the finest millimetre ticks on your geometry-box ruler. Your naked eye can just make out an object about $0.1\text{ mm}$ across—roughly the width of a human hair or a large human egg cell.

To step down into the world of cells, bacteria, viruses and molecules, biologists divide the millimetre by a thousand, and then by a thousand again:

- **1 millimetre ($\text{mm}$) $= 10^{-3}\text{ m}$:** A small mustard seed (*rai*) is about $1\text{–}2\text{ mm}$ across; a dry *moong* bean is about $4\text{ mm}$ long.
- **1 micrometre ($\mu\text{m}$) $= 10^{-3}\text{ mm} = 10^{-6}\text{ m}$:** Divide a single $1\text{ mm}$ gap on your ruler into **one thousand** equal slices. That is the scale of **cells**. sections.heading: Case file: Looking at the evidence
sections.excerpt:
:::case The cloudy soup in the monsoon kitchen
On a warm July afternoon in Mumbai, two identical bowls of clear vegetable broth are boiled for five minutes. **Bowl 1** is placed inside a clean plastic box whose lid has a tiny, long S-shaped drinking straw glued through a hole in the top (open to the air at both ends). **Bowl 2** is placed in an identical plastic box with a wide, straight $2\text{ cm}$ hole in the top lid. After three days on the kitchen counter, Bowl 2 is cloudy and sour, while Bowl 1 is still clear. On Day 4, someone picks up Box 1, shakes it vigorously so the broth splashes against the inside of the lid and straw, and puts it back down. By Day 6, Bowl 1 is cloudy too.

Use the clues from this chapter to explain: (a) why Bowl 2 turned cloudy while Bowl 1 stayed clear for the first three days even though both boxes were open to the air, and (b) why shaking Box 1 on Day 4 made it turn cloudy by Day 6.
???
(a) Boiling killed the existing microbes in both bowls. In Box 2, dust particles carrying airborne bacteria and fungal spores fell straight down through the wide hole into the broth. In Box 1, the long S-shaped straw acted just like Louis Pasteur's 1859 swan-neck f

callouts.title: A critic looks at Redi's sealed jars—where no maggots grew—and says: "Your experiment is unfair! You didn't just block the flies; you also blocked something else that rotting meat needs to generate life." What did the sealed lid block?
callouts.body:
- Fresh air
- Gravity
- Room warmth
???
Fresh air. A sealed jar blocks both flies *and* the free circulation of air. As long as Redi changed two things at once (flies and air), critics could claim that fresh air was the missing ingredient for spontaneous generation. To clinch the case, Redi needed a third jar that let fresh air flow freely while still keeping flies out.

callouts.title: > "Weevils appear inside a sealed plastic packet of rice or besan that came straight from the shop, so they must have grown out of the grain!"
callouts.body: Look closely with a hand lens at grains of rice or wheat before they are packed. Female rice weevils (*Sitophilus oryzae*) chew a microscopic pinhole into a grain, lay a single egg inside, and seal the hole with a gelatinous plug you cannot see with the naked eye. Weeks later, in your warm kitchen cupboard, the larva finishes eating the inside of the grain and chews its way out as an adult beetle. The egg was already inside the packet before it was sealed.

callouts.title: Cambridge Lower Secondary and IGCSE Biology (Paper 6, Alternative to Practical) test three variable names on almost every paper: the **independent variable** (what the investigator changes, plotted on the horizontal x-axis), the **dependent variable** (what is measured, plotted on the vertical y-axis), and **controlled variables** (conditions kept constant so the test is fair).

Pasteur pours nutrient broth into a glass flask, heats the glass neck in a flame, and pulls it out into a long, downward-curving S-bend—like a swan's neck—leaving the tip of the neck completely open to the room. He boils the broth until steam shoots out of the open tip, then lets it cool slowly. What will happen to the broth over the next month?
callouts.body:
- It will turn cloudy within days, because fresh outside air can still flow freely down the open tube
- It will stay crystal clear, because heavy dust and microbes settle in the bottom dip of the curved neck while clean air passes over them
- It will stay clear only for a day, then grow mould from the oxygen in the air
???
It stays crystal clear—for months, and in fact for more than a century! As the flask cools, outside air is drawn gently in through the open tip, but dust particles and the microbes riding on them settle by gravity onto the damp glass walls at the bottom of the U-bend. Air reaches the broth; dust does not.

callouts.title: The two-glass broth test (with an adult)
callouts.body: Dissolve half a spoon of *dal* water (the clear starchy liquid from boiling *toor* or *moong dal*) or a pinch of sugar and a drop of milk in half a cup of water. With an adult's help, boil it in a small steel pan for 3 minutes to sterilise it, then pour equal amounts into two clean glasses rinsed with boiling water. Cover **Glass A** tightly with cling-film or aluminium foil right away while it is still steaming; leave **Glass B** uncovered on the kitchen counter, or stir it once with an unwashed finger. Put both glasses in a warm corner for 48 hours and look at them sideways against a torch beam (do not taste or smell close up; pour both down the sink with dish soap when done). Glass B turns cloudy as airborne microbes multiply; Glass A stays much clearer.

callouts.title: > "Atoms, molecules, viruses, bacteria and human cells are all just 'microscopic specks' of roughly the same size."
callouts.body: In surveys of twelve- and thirteen-year-olds, more than half guess that a protein molecule is bigger than or the same size as a cell! In reality, the gap between a water molecule ($0.28\text{ nm}$) and a human cell ($20\text{ }\mu\text{m}$) is a factor of nearly **100,000** in width—the same ratio as a $2\text{ cm}$ marble compared with a $2\text{ km}$ stretch of Marine Drive. A cell can hold *trillions* of molecules because molecules are tens of thousands of times smaller than cells.

callouts.title: On Cambridge IGCSE Biology exams, always convert ruler measurements from millimetres ($\text{mm}$) to micrometres ($\mu\text{m}$) by **multiplying by $1,000$** before using $M = I \div A$ (or $A = I \div M$), and write a multiplication sign in front of a magnification ($\times 270$), never a unit like $\text{mm}$.
The cloudy soup in the monsoon kitchen
callouts.body:
On a warm July afternoon in Mumbai, two identical bowls of clear vegetable broth are boiled for five minutes. **Bowl 1** is placed inside a clean plastic box whose lid has a tiny, long S-shaped drinking straw glued through a hole in the top (open to the air at both ends). **Bowl 2** is placed in an identical plastic box with a wide, straight $2\text{ cm}$ hole in the top lid. After three days on the kitchen counter, Bowl 2 is cloudy and sour, while Bowl 1 is still clear. On Day 4, someone picks up Box 1, shakes it vigorously so the broth splashes against the inside of the lid and straw, and puts it back down. By Day 6, Bowl 1 is cloudy too.

Use the clues from this chapter to explain: (a) why Bowl 2 turned cloudy while Bowl 1 stayed clear for the first three days even though both boxes were open to the air, and (b) why shaking Box 1 on Day 4 made it turn cloudy by Day 6.
???
(a) Boiling killed the existing microbes in both bowls. In Box 2, dust particles carrying airborne bacteria and fungal spores fell straight down through the wide hole into the broth. In Box 1, the long S-shaped straw acted just like Louis Pasteur's 1859 swan-neck flask: air could move in and out, but airborne dust and microbes settled on the inner walls of the curved straw and could not fall into the soup.
(b) When Box 1 was shaken on Day 4, liquid broth splashed against the trapped dust inside the straw and lid, picking up dormant bacterial cells and carrying them back into the bowl, where they multiplied over the next 48 hours.

sections.heading: 1.1 The first rains in June
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Sanjay Gandhi National Park, Mumbai, early June

Walk up the basalt trail towards Kanheri Caves in the last week of May, before the monsoon arrives. The hillsides look dead. The grass is brittle straw; the earth is baked into cracked brown brick; the rock pools are bone-dry dust. If an alien landed on those hills in late May, it might conclude that almost nothing on the ground was alive.

After the first heavy rains, brown hillsides begin turning green. Shoots emerge and pools refill. Different organisms return in different ways: seeds germinate, some tiny aquatic animals hatch from resistant resting eggs, and frogs breed in the new water. Tadpoles develop from frog eggs, not from dry mud cysts. There is no single timetable or survival mechanism for the whole hillside.

Where was the next generation of grass hiding through the dry weeks? Much of it was inside seeds. Pick up a dry green *moong* bean (*Vigna radiata*), a chickpea or a mustard seed. A viable seed contains a living embryo, stored materials and machinery that can resume development when conditions permit.

sections.heading: 1.2 The flame and the bean
sections.excerpt:
Now that you have watched a dry bean wake up, let us put it side by side with our rival suspect: a burning candle flame.

Look at why the candle flame fools so many people at first glance. A candle is made of solid hydrocarbon wax—chains of carbon and hydrogen atoms storing chemical potential energy, very much like the starch and fat stored inside a seed. When you touch a match to the wick:

- The flame **consumes fuel** (melted wax drawn up the wick).
- It **takes in oxygen** ($\text{O}_2$) from the room air and **releases carbon dioxide** ($\text{CO}_2$) and water vapour ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$)—the exact same gases a sprouting bean or a running human exchanges!
- It **moves and responds** to a draught of air, bending away from a breeze.
- It **grows** larger if you feed it more wick, and can **start new flames** if touched to another candle.

So why is the candle flame *not* alive, while the bean is?

To see the real difference, we have to zoom down to the nanometre scale—where chemistry and physics meet biology.

In the candle flame, vaporised wax reacts with oxygen through a network of reactions called **combustion**. Chemical changes transfer energy to the surroundings as heat

sections.heading: 1.3 Paying for repairs, and SubbaRow’s ₹10 coin
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Boston & Bhimavaram, 1929

A cell can build an organised structure while releasing heat and changing its surroundings. That fits the second law of thermodynamics: the total entropy of an isolated system does not decrease. A cell is an **open system**, exchanging matter and energy with its surroundings. Looking only at its internal organisation leaves part of the account out.

In his 1943 Dublin lectures, Erwin Schrödinger asked how living things maintain organisation. The useful question for our bean is concrete: how do reactions using stored nutrients help build and maintain its cells? A temporarily inactive dry seed can retain the machinery to resume. Irreversible loss of that capacity is different from a pause in activity.

All the hundreds of chemical reactions running inside a cell in growth, maintenance and energy transfer have a single name: ==metabolism== (from the Greek *metabolē*, "change"). Metabolism has two halves that work like a demolition crew and a construction crew:
- **Breaking down fuel** (like oxidising glucose in cellular respiration) to release stored chemical energy; and
- **Building up parts** (like stitching amino acids into proteins, or glucose u

sections.heading: 1.4 Seven processes in a living system
sections.excerpt:
Once you understand what a living organism actually is—**a cell-based machine that uses energy to maintain internal order and copy its genetic instructions**—you no longer need to memorise a school textbook's list of "seven characteristics of living things" as arbitrary rules. These processes describe living systems across their lives. They need not all be visible at once, and an individual can be alive without reproducing. A dry seed retains a capacity to resume development; it need not display rapid metabolism while dry.

In Cambridge IGCSE and British schools, the seven processes are remembered by the initials **MRS GREN**. Follow how these processes contribute to a living system:

:::fig c1_mrs_gren_engine() | The seven MRS GREN processes as a single connected engineering diagram of a living organism. Nutrition brings in matter and fuel; Respiration transfers chemical energy from nutrients into forms including ATP; Excretion removes toxic chemical wastes made by metabolism (CO₂, urea); Sensitivity and Movement let the organism find resources and dodge danger; Growth builds new cellular structure; and Reproduction passes the DNA blueprint across generations.

sections.heading: 1.5 The outlaw at the border
sections.excerpt:
Our working account of cellular life is this: living systems are made of one or more **cells**, use an internal **metabolism** with energy carriers such as **ATP** for maintenance and development, and inherit **DNA** instructions. The seven processes describe these systems across their lives.

And then a microscopic outlaw walks up to the border checkpoint and breaks our neat categories in half.

In 1892, the Russian botanist Dmitri Ivanovsky crushed up diseased tobacco leaves that were blotched with yellow-and-green spots (tobacco mosaic disease) and forced the sap through an ultra-fine porcelain filter whose pores were small enough to trap every known bacterium. To his astonishment, the crystal-clear liquid that dripped through the filter was still completely infectious! Six years later, the Dutch microbiologist Martinus Beijerinck repeated the test, showed that the invisible agent multiplied in living plant tissue, and named it a *contagium vivum fluidum*—a ==virus== (from the Latin word for "slimy liquid" or "poison").

sections.heading: Case file: Looking at the evidence
sections.excerpt:
:::case The Viking Mars soil puzzle (1976)
NASA's Viking landers investigated Martian soil in 1976. In the labelled-release experiment, adding nutrients containing radioactive carbon produced labelled gas. Heating a comparison sample strongly reduced the response. A later nutrient addition did not produce a renewed burst like the first.

Those observations raised a difficult question: metabolism or non-living soil chemistry? Heating can damage organisms, but it can also change chemical reactants. A second feeding is informative, but its result depends on the organisms and conditions assumed. It cannot alone settle every possible biological explanation.

The organic-chemical analyses were also difficult to interpret. Small chlorinated organic compounds were initially treated as contamination. Later experiments suggested that perchlorates, discovered on Mars by Phoenix in 2008, could destroy organics during heated analysis and produce such compounds. That interpretation does not establish life either. Viking provided no clear evidence of living microorganisms.

Which observations could fit both explanations? What further independent evidence would make a biological interpretation str

callouts.title: Two batches of viable moong beans are kept in darkness, one dry and one moist with access to air. Which observation would best support resumed metabolism rather than water absorption alone?
callouts.body:
- Increased wet mass immediately after soaking
- Sustained oxygen uptake accompanied by carbon dioxide release
- Droplets on the glass beside wet cotton
???
The second observation. Absorbed water increases wet mass, and wet cotton can supply water vapour without respiration. Sustained gas exchange under suitable controlled conditions supports metabolic activity. Our home activity observes swelling and germination; it does not measure those gas rates.

callouts.title: Kitchen forensics: The waking bean
callouts.body:
Use two clean small jars, cotton wool and whole moong beans sold for sprouting. Put two tablespoons of dry beans on dry cotton in Jar A. Soak another batch for about six hours, drain it, and place it on damp, not flooded, cotton in Jar B. Cover loosely so air can enter. Keep both together out of direct sunlight; inspect after a night and again the following day.

If you have a kitchen scale, weigh the same batch before and after soaking, draining and blotting consistently. Record the actual gain. Sketch any white embryonic roots, called *radicles*. Different seeds take different times, and some will not germinate. Swelling alone does not establish that a seed is alive. Droplets do not establish respiration, and a small batch need not feel warm.

Do not eat these experimental sprouts. Clear them away within two days, sooner if mould appears; do not sniff mouldy material. Wash hands, jars and surfaces. This comparison tests the effect of water availability on visible germination, not the rate of respiration.

callouts.title: A seed gains wet mass before a root appears. Does that prove it has built new living material? What later observation strengthens the evidence that it was viable?
callouts.body:
???
No. Absorbed water can explain the first gain. Continued root and shoot development supports viability and organised growth. Wet mass alone neither measures new dry material nor proves metabolism.

callouts.title: A germinating seed in darkness develops a longer root while its total dry mass falls. Which account reconciles those observations?
callouts.body:
- The growing root gains material transferred from reserves, while some reserve material leaves as respiration products
- Growth creates matter, so the dry-mass measurement must be wrong
- A longer root must mean the entire seed has gained dry mass
???
The first. Stored materials supply the developing root. Some fuel is also oxidised, and carbon dioxide leaves. A growing part can gain material while the whole seed loses dry mass. There is no claim here about equal gas quantities from wax and carbohydrate, or a fixed four-hour growth result.

callouts.title: Could a non-living chemical reaction release heat and carbon dioxide? Which additional features distinguish the viable seed from the flame?
callouts.body:
???
Yes. Gas and heat alone do not establish life. The seed contains a cellular system with inherited instructions and machinery capable of maintaining and developing it under suitable conditions. The flame lacks that system.

callouts.title: > "Snapping ATP's end bond releases energy by itself."
callouts.body: Bond breaking requires energy. Consider the full reaction, including the new interactions formed and the surrounding conditions. Also identify the coupling: an ATP reaction occurring separately cannot automatically drive another reaction elsewhere.

callouts.title: ATP is hydrolysed in a container beside an isolated motor protein. Must the motor move? Explain the missing connection.
callouts.body:
???
No. ATP's reaction must be coupled to the motor's binding and shape-changing cycle. Releasing heat nearby is not equivalent to supplying that organised reaction cycle.

callouts.title: After you eat a bowl of sweetcorn or leafy greens, tough cellulose plant fibres pass all the way through your digestive tract without being broken down and leave your body in faeces. In biology, does passing faeces count as **excretion**?
callouts.body:
- Yes, because faeces are waste leaving the body
- No—it is **egestion**, because those cellulose fibres never crossed into your body's cells or took part in any metabolic chemical reaction inside a cell
- Yes, for animals, though not for plants
???
The second choice. Think of your digestive canal as a hollow tunnel running right through the middle of your body. A cellulose fibre that enters your mouth and leaves in faeces never crossed the gut wall into your bloodstream or entered a single cell's metabolism. Passing undigested leftovers out of the gut tunnel is **egestion**. True **excretion** is getting rid of molecules that were produced by chemical reactions *inside* your cells (like $\text{CO}_2$ exhaled from your lungs, or urea filtered out of your blood into urine by your kidneys)—plus water and salts in excess.

callouts.title: > "Animals breathe and respire, while plants only photosynthesise."
callouts.body: Plants have no lungs, but their active cells carry out **cellular respiration** in both light and darkness. In a lit leaf, photosynthesis and respiration can occur together. Net gas exchange depends on their rates: bright light can produce net oxygen release; darkness removes the photosynthetic contribution. A dormant seed is a different state, with greatly restricted metabolic activity.

callouts.title: For Cambridge IGCSE 0610 Topic 1.1:
callouts.body:
1. If an exam question asks *"Name the characteristic of living organisms shown when carbon dioxide leaves the lungs"* or *"when sweat/urine leaves the body"*, the answer is **excretion** (never egestion).
2. If asked to define **growth**, always include **"permanent increase in dry mass"** (weighing an organism after all water has been removed, since temporary water intake is not growth).

callouts.title: A dry sponge dropped into a bucket of water swells to twice its size. A crystal of alum hung in a saturated alum solution slowly grows larger over a week. Using the biological definitions of growth and metabolism, explain why neither the sponge nor the alum crystal is carrying out biological growth.
callouts.body:
???
The sponge only absorbs liquid water into existing spaces; its **dry mass** does not increase at all, and the expansion is reversible when dried. The alum crystal increases in dry mass as ions from the solution stack onto its outer surface (**accretion**), but it has no cells, no internal metabolism, no ATP, and no genetic code directing the synthesis of new molecules from within. Biological growth builds new cells and protoplasm from the inside using metabolic energy.

callouts.title: A child comes down with a runny nose and fever caused by an influenza **virus**. Someone suggests taking an **antibiotic** (such as amoxicillin, which interferes with bacterial cell-wall construction; other antibiotics target bacterial ribosomes). Will the antibiotic cure the viral flu?
callouts.body:
- Yes, because antibiotics kill all microscopic germs including viruses
- No, because a virus has no bacterial cell wall and no ribosomes of its own for the antibiotic to attack; unnecessary antibiotic use can select resistant bacteria
- Only if the virus has a fatty envelope
???
No. Antibiotics target specific bacterial machinery—such as bacterial cell-wall synthesis or bacterial ribosomes. Because a virus has no cell wall, no metabolism, and uses *your own human ribosomes* inside your cells to make its proteins, an antibiotic has nothing to attack in a virus. These antibiotics do not treat influenza. Unnecessary use can affect helpful bacteria and select resistant bacteria (Chapter 14).

callouts.title: In Cambridge IGCSE Biology (Topic 1.2 & 1.3), remember two exact exam rules:
callouts.body:
1. **Viruses are not in any of the Five Kingdoms** (*Prokaryote, Protoctist, Fungus, Plant, Animal*). If an exam diagram shows a particle with only a **protein coat** and **genetic material (DNA/RNA)**, identify it as a **virus** and state that it is **non-living** because it cannot reproduce or carry out metabolic processes outside a host cell.
2. In a two-part scientific name (**binomial**), the first word is the **Genus** (always written with a **capital letter**, e.g. *Panthera*) and the second word is the **specific name** (always written with a **small letter**, e.g. *pardus*), printed in *italics* (or underlined when handwritten). The two words together identify the species.

callouts.title: Compare three tiny objects: (1) a dry *moong* seed, (2) a rod-shaped bacterium (*E. coli*), and (3) a coronavirus particle. Which of the three contain ribosomes and can make their own ATP when given water and nutrients?
callouts.body:
???
Only **(1) the *moong* seed** (whose cells contain ribosomes and mitochondria, with greatly restricted metabolism while dry; viable seeds can resume development when conditions permit) and **(2) the bacterium** (a single prokaryotic cell containing its own ribosomes and ATP-making enzymes). **(3) The coronavirus** has no ribosomes, no cytoplasm, and no ATP machinery even when placed in water and nutrients; it can only be copied by hijacking a living host cell.

callouts.title: The Viking Mars soil puzzle (1976)
callouts.body:
NASA's Viking landers investigated Martian soil in 1976. In the labelled-release experiment, adding nutrients containing radioactive carbon produced labelled gas. Heating a comparison sample strongly reduced the response. A later nutrient addition did not produce a renewed burst like the first.

Those observations raised a difficult question: metabolism or non-living soil chemistry? Heating can damage organisms, but it can also change chemical reactants. A second feeding is informative, but its result depends on the organisms and conditions assumed. It cannot alone settle every possible biological explanation.

The organic-chemical analyses were also difficult to interpret. Small chlorinated organic compounds were initially treated as contamination. Later experiments suggested that perchlorates, discovered on Mars by Phoenix in 2008, could destroy organics during heated analysis and produce such compounds. That interpretation does not establish life either. Viking provided no clear evidence of living microorganisms.

Which observations could fit both explanations? What further independent evidence would make a biological interpretation stronger?
???
Gas release and sensitivity to heating can occur in either biological or non-biological systems. Failure to respond to another feeding challenges a simple growth model, but does not identify the cause by itself. Seek independent evidence: reproducible activity under varied conditions, chemical analysis that accounts for reactive soil and instrument effects, and signs of a coordinated biological system. Organic molecules alone can also have non-biological origins. The lesson is to compare explanations and combine evidence, rather than turn one suggestive response into a verdict.

sections.heading: 2.1 Inside the walled city
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, an onion on the kitchen board

Peel a white onion bulb. Beside it, put a green leaf. Both came from plants. If every plant cell follows the same school drawing, both should be packed with green bodies. Yet the thin skin inside the onion is almost transparent. Where did its green parts go?

A drawing of “the plant cell” is a useful collection of features. It can tempt you into treating every real cell as a copy of that drawing.

:::predict
A white onion bulb cell has no developed green bodies for capturing light. What else must be missing?
- Its mitochondria, because plants use light instead of respiration
- Its cell membrane, because the wall does that job
- Neither: it can have mitochondria and a membrane without chloroplasts
???
The third choice. An ordinary white bulb cell has mitochondria and a cell membrane. It can use stored nutrients to supply ATP without capturing light itself.
:::

sections.heading: 2.2 The stowaways that became power stations
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Boston, 1967

You have just separated the nucleus from the rest of a cell in your mental picture. Now comes an awkward clue: some of the cell's DNA is elsewhere. Mitochondria have their own inherited DNA. Chloroplasts do too.

Lynn Margulis, publishing as Lynn Sagan, brought evidence for a remarkable explanation together in a 1967 paper. Perhaps these structures descended from bacteria that once lived inside other cells. The idea had earlier advocates; she made a powerful case for taking it seriously again.

An internal working structure such as a mitochondrion or chloroplast is called an **organelle**: a “little organ”. Before accepting the ancestry idea, ask what evidence could distinguish an internal bacterial descendant from a compartment assembled entirely by its host.

:::predict
Which finding would give the stronger reason to investigate bacterial ancestry?
- A mitochondrion looks roughly oval, like some bacteria
- Mitochondria have their own DNA and bacterial-related protein-making machinery, and gene comparisons connect them to bacteria
- Mitochondria are too small to see clearly with unaided eyes
???

sections.heading: 2.3 The geometry trap
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, cubes on the kitchen plate

Put a small potato cube beside a larger one. The larger cube has more outside surface. That seems helpful if its interior has to receive substances from the surrounding liquid. Perhaps a larger cell could feed itself more easily because its boundary is larger too.

There is a second quantity to count: how much interior that boundary serves. Keep shape and chemical demand per unit volume the same, and enlarge the cube. The outside and the inside do not grow at the same rate.

:::predict
A cube's side doubles from 1 cm to 2 cm. What happens to its surface and volume?
- Both double
- Surface becomes four times as large; volume becomes eight times as large
- Surface becomes eight times as large; volume becomes four times as large
???
The second choice. Each face has two dimensions to double; the interior has three. The bigger cube has more surface in total but less surface for each cubic centimetre of interior.
:::

:::scene Mumbai, a breath on a dusty afternoon

Air entering your breathing passages carries tiny particles. A sticky layer traps many of them. Under a microscope, the surface beneath that layer is busy: rows of tiny hairs beat and move the mucus towards your throat.

Now compare one of those cells with a red blood cell or a root hair cell. A single standard “cell” outline would hide the feature that explains each job. We have reached the next reason a body contains many cells: different arrangements of the shared machinery support different work.

- A long, thin extension that increases exposed contact area and keeps routes short
- A compact sphere because reducing its surface always speeds absorption
- The same volume guarantees the same absorption rate, whatever the shape
???

sections.heading: The cell that seems to break the rule
sections.excerpt:
:::case The pearl in the coastal mud
In 1997, researchers collected sediment from the continental shelf off Namibia. The bacterium described in 1999, *Thiomargarita namibiensis*, formed pale beads. Some cells reached **750 µm** across, large enough to see without a microscope.

Three clues sit in the file: it really is a bacterium; a huge nitrate-storing vacuole occupies much of its interior; most active cytoplasm forms a thin layer around that store. Does this overturn the geometry argument? Explain which distance and which volume matter.
???
It changes how the argument applies. Most of the large cell's volume is storage, so it is misleading to treat all of it as equally active cytoplasm. The thin active layer keeps much of the working machinery close to an exchange surface. Area, active volume, transport and chemical demand still matter. This coastal-sediment bacterium is a counterexample to “all bacteria are tiny”, not a suspension of geometry.
:::

:::next
A boundary creates a new puzzle. A cell must keep its internal chemistry separate while continually exchanging materials. How can anything cross without the cell simply mixing into the world outside? Next, we follow the rando

callouts.title: A white onion bulb cell has no developed green bodies for capturing light. What else must be missing?
callouts.body:
- Its mitochondria, because plants use light instead of respiration
- Its cell membrane, because the wall does that job
- Neither: it can have mitochondria and a membrane without chloroplasts
???
The third choice. An ordinary white bulb cell has mitochondria and a cell membrane. It can use stored nutrients to supply ATP without capturing light itself.

callouts.title: > “Plant cells have chloroplasts instead of mitochondria.”
callouts.body: Ordinary green leaf cells have both. Chloroplasts build carbohydrates using light; mitochondria help supply ATP through respiration. Onion bulb and root cells can respire using nutrients without developed chloroplasts. Respiration continues in light and darkness.

callouts.title: A white peel and a green leaf
callouts.body: With an adult handling any knife, put a white onion peel beside a green leaf on a white plate. Look with your eyes or a hand lens. Record what you can see, and separately what would require a microscope. You can compare colour and texture; a phone photograph alone does not establish whether an individual cell contains a nucleus or mitochondria. If your school has slides, compare them with your teacher. Wash your hands and clear the plate afterwards.

callouts.title: For IGCSE 0610 Topic 2.1, identify each structure and give its function in animal, plant and bacterial cells; bacteria have circular DNA in the cytoplasm and may have plasmids, rather than a nucleus. Topic 2.2 uses **magnification = image size ÷ actual size**, with both sizes in the same units.
A cell has a wall, a membrane, ribosomes and DNA, but no membrane-enclosed nucleus. Is the wall enough to identify it as a plant cell? Explain.
callouts.body:
???
No. Bacteria also usually have walls. The combination described fits a typical bacterial cell: it has DNA and ribosomes, but no enclosed nucleus. Plant walls contain cellulose; typical bacterial walls contain a different material. One feature alone is not enough.

callouts.title: Which finding would give the stronger reason to investigate bacterial ancestry?
callouts.body:
- A mitochondrion looks roughly oval, like some bacteria
- Mitochondria have their own DNA and bacterial-related protein-making machinery, and gene comparisons connect them to bacteria
- Mitochondria are too small to see clearly with unaided eyes
???
The second choice. Many unrelated things are oval or tiny. Several independent inherited similarities provide a much stronger test of ancestry.

callouts.title: > “Margulis proved that mitochondria are ordinary bacteria living in us today.”
callouts.body: Their ancestry is bacterial. Their present dependence on host-cell machinery makes them integrated parts of the cell. The evidence accumulated through many researchers; the 1967 paper was a major contribution to that investigation.

callouts.title: For 0610, give the present-day functions of mitochondria, chloroplasts and ribosomes precisely; “powerhouse” alone does not explain a function. This ancestry account explains why a cell can contain DNA outside its nucleus.
An unknown compartment has two membranes. Is that enough to conclude that it descended from a bacterium? Name two further tests.
callouts.body:
???
No. Membrane number alone does not establish ancestry. Look for its own inherited DNA and compare relevant gene sequences with bacterial sequences; investigate whether its ribosomes are bacterial-related and whether it divides from existing compartments. Several independent clues make the explanation stronger.

callouts.title: A cube's side doubles from 1 cm to 2 cm. What happens to its surface and volume?
callouts.body:
- Both double
- Surface becomes four times as large; volume becomes eight times as large
- Surface becomes eight times as large; volume becomes four times as large
???
The second choice. Each face has two dimensions to double; the interior has three. The bigger cube has more surface in total but less surface for each cubic centimetre of interior.

callouts.title: > “The large cube has more surface, so it must exchange substances more easily.”
callouts.body: It has more surface in total, but less per unit of volume. Compare both quantities. A dyed surface also does not show that every living cell inside the potato has received the same amount of a substance.

callouts.title: Investigation 2.3: Keep the material, change the shape
callouts.body:
Use one clean piece of soft roti dough. First shape a compact lump; then flatten the same piece into a thin disc, without adding or removing dough. Before flattening, predict what happens to the shortest route from the centre to a surface. Compare that route with your eyes or a ruler. The disc's centre is much closer to its nearest surface. The amount of material has stayed approximately the same while the shape has changed.

This is a geometry model: dough does not test a living cell membrane. Keep it separate from food being served, and wash your hands before and after. The cube arithmetic and this shape comparison are the main investigation; the optional staining activity below asks a less predictable question about real tissue.

callouts.title: Optional exploration: How far does the colour go?
callouts.body:
An adult must cut the potato and make every later centre cut. Use raw potato cubes with sides about **0.5 cm, 1 cm and 2 cm**, three small cups, a ruler, and cool beetroot juice or water with food colouring. Put each cube in enough of the same liquid to cover it fully. Keep the cups together, record the starting time, and predict which cube will have the largest fraction visibly coloured.

Inspect after **15 minutes**. Rinse and blot the outside briefly; have the adult cut each cube through its centre. Record any visible penetration depth and untouched centre. If there is no clear boundary, write that down: do not invent a depth. You can compare another set after a longer recorded time. Dye binding, tissue permeability and damaged cut cells can make the result patchy or faint; this activity may not produce a neat coloured layer.

Use the live model to explore a chosen or measured depth, keeping its geometric assumption separate from your observations. Never eat the used pieces. Clear them away the same day, and wash hands and surfaces. No heating or microbial growing is involved.

callouts.title: For 0610, relate efficient exchange to a **large surface area** and a **short diffusion distance**, and distinguish total area from area relative to volume; Topic 3.1 also asks how surface area and distance affect diffusion. Give units when calculating: cm² ÷ cm³ gives cm⁻¹.
Eight separate 1 cm cubes have the same total volume as one 2 cm cube. Which arrangement has more exposed surface when all faces touch the surrounding liquid, and by what factor?
callouts.body:
???
The eight separate cubes: each has 6 cm², so together they have 48 cm². The 2 cm cube has 24 cm². Exposed area doubles while total volume stays 8 cm³. If pieces are pressed together, their touching faces are not fully exposed; separation matters.

callouts.title: Two root cells contain similar amounts of active material and have equally permeable membranes. Which feature gives the stronger reason to predict faster absorption under the same surrounding conditions?
callouts.body:
- A long, thin extension that increases exposed contact area and keeps routes short
- A compact sphere because reducing its surface always speeds absorption
- The same volume guarantees the same absorption rate, whatever the shape
???
The extension increases exposed contact area while keeping routes short. Equal volume does not guarantee equal absorption: shape changes the exchange surface and distances even when the amount of active material stays similar.

callouts.title: > “A bigger animal is made by making all its cells bigger.”
callouts.body: Larger bodies generally contain more cells. Their different cell types also have different shapes and sizes. A long neurone is compatible with the geometry argument because it remains thin; a mature human red blood cell is compatible with cell theory despite having lost its nucleus.

callouts.title: For 0610 Topic 2.1, connect each specialised cell to its function, including sperm and egg cells for reproduction; use **cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism** with an example at every level. Cambridge commonly spells the nerve cell **neurone**.
The pearl in the coastal mud

Three clues sit in the file: it really is a bacterium; a huge nitrate-storing vacuole occupies much of its interior; most active cytoplasm forms a thin layer around that store. Does this overturn the geometry argument? Explain which distance and which volume matter.
???

The thin active layer keeps much of the working machinery close to an exchange surface. Area, active volume, transport and chemical demand still matter. This coastal-sediment bacterium is a counterexample to “all bacteria are tiny”, not a suspension of geometry.

sections.heading: 3.1 Blind bounces, not wishes
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, a crowded local train doorway

At a station, people pass through a train doorway in both directions. Counting only the people getting off gives you a poor account of how the carriage population changes. You must subtract those getting on. That difference is the **net** change.

Keep the two-way counting. Leave people's decisions behind. A molecule has no destination in mind, and it cannot inspect the other side of a membrane for an empty seat.

:::predict
Two equal-sized chambers contain the same gas at the same temperature. One begins with more molecules than the other. An opening connects them. Which account best predicts the change after the opening is made?
- Crossings occur only from the more crowded chamber until concentrations match
- Crossings occur both ways, with more expected from the more concentrated side
- Equal temperature means the expected numbers crossing each way must already be equal
???
The second account follows from random motion. More molecules near one side of the opening give more opportunities to cross from that side. Individual molecules need no instruction about the other chamber.
:::

:::evidence A spreading colour, then a stricter tes

sections.heading: 3.2 Water potential and the selective gate
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Baltimore, a water-channel experiment published in 1992

Two frog egg cells sit in very dilute water. They look much alike at first. One soon swells much faster than the other. The important difference is a protein placed in its membrane.

The surprise concerns the boundary. A cell is surrounded by water, and filled with water. Why should changing a protein alter how fast water crosses?

:::predict
Researchers arrange for some frog egg cells to make a suspected water-channel protein. Control eggs do not receive the instructions for that protein. What result would support the channel idea?
- The two groups always swell at exactly the same rate
- Eggs making the protein take up water much faster in dilute surroundings
- Only salt can enter eggs making the protein
???
The second result supports a water pathway. The control comparison matters: swelling by itself would not identify which protein changed water permeability.
:::

:::evidence The protein that changed the boundary | 1992 publication
Gregory Preston, Peter Agre and their colleagues tested a protein originally found in red blood cells. They arranged for frog egg cells to make it, then compared those eggs with control

sections.heading: 3.3 Balloons inside boxes
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, two cups and a raw potato

A raw potato strip can become firmer in plain water and limper in salty water. The water outside is visible; the changing water inside its cells is hidden. A potato gives you a way to feel a consequence of a microscopic boundary.

Before cutting anything, compare two kinds of boundary. An animal cell has a cell membrane. A plant cell also has a supporting wall outside that membrane. The difference changes what happens after water enters.

:::predict
An animal cell and a plant cell are placed in very dilute surroundings. Water can enter both. Which outcome is most plausible?
- Both must burst because water enters both
- The plant wall can support rising pressure, while an animal cell may swell and burst
- The plant wall completely blocks water, leaving the cell dry
???
The second outcome. The wall allows pressure to build as water enters. That pressure raises internal water potential and can balance further net entry. A red blood cell lacks that supporting wall.
:::

:::evidence The outline that stays, and the contents that retreat | Repeatable microscopy
At school, compare a suitable plant epidermis under a microscope before and after add

sections.heading: 3.4 Pushing uphill: roots and the salty sea
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Aarhus, crab nerve membranes, 1957

A membrane can provide a route for an ion. That leaves another puzzle. How can cells maintain more of an ion on the side where it is already concentrated? If electrical effects do not oppose it, passive spreading through an open route would tend to undo the concentration difference.

Jens Christian Skou investigated an enzyme in crab nerve membranes that broke down ATP. Its activity depended on the ions present. The link between chemical reactions and an uneven distribution of ions was becoming something experimenters could test.

:::predict
A root hair cell contains more nitrate ions per volume than the surrounding soil solution. Which explanation could sustain further nitrate uptake against that concentration gradient?
- A nitrate pathway alone guarantees further accumulation, regardless of electrical conditions
- Increasing membrane area alone can sustain uptake against an unfavourable combined gradient
- A transporter couples nitrate entry to an energy source, such as another ion gradient
???
The third explanation supplies the missing account. A root can use ATP to establish another gradient, then couple nitrate entry to movement dow

sections.heading: The thirsty sailor's case
sections.excerpt:
:::case Surrounded by water, losing water
A sailor has run out of fresh water. Seawater surrounds the boat. The sailor argues that a drink must help: it contains far more water than salt.

Clue one: dissolved substances can change the distribution of water between body fluids and cells. Clue two: absorbed excess salt must be removed, and the kidneys use water to excrete it. Clue three: humans do not have a mangrove's salt-handling system.

Why can drinking seawater make the sailor more dehydrated, despite the water swallowed?
???
The salt load matters along with the water intake. Human kidneys require water to remove that excess salt; dealing with seawater can cause a net loss of body water. Raised salt concentration in body fluids also favours water leaving cells. Osmosis explains those cell-level shifts, while salt excretion explains why the whole-body water account can worsen. Seawater is not safe drinking water. This is a reasoning case, never a drinking experiment.
:::

:::next
We can now follow molecules through a membrane, and we have seen proteins acting as channels, carriers and pumps. But how can a folded protein distinguish one molecule from another? In Chapter 4, a mole

callouts.title: Two equal-sized chambers contain the same gas at the same temperature. One begins with more molecules than the other. An opening connects them. Which account best predicts the change after the opening is made?
callouts.body:
- Crossings occur only from the more crowded chamber until concentrations match
- Crossings occur both ways, with more expected from the more concentrated side
- Equal temperature means the expected numbers crossing each way must already be equal
???
The second account follows from random motion. More molecules near one side of the opening give more opportunities to cross from that side. Individual molecules need no instruction about the other chamber.

callouts.title: > “Once it is evenly spread, the molecules have finished moving.”
callouts.body: They keep moving. Near equilibrium, crossings in opposite directions balance on average. Closing the opening stops transfer between chambers; it does not switch off motion within each chamber.

callouts.title: A drop with no spoon
callouts.body:
Use food colouring and a clear glass of cool tap water on a stable tray. Let the water settle, add one small drop gently, and watch without stirring. Sketch the coloured region at the start and after a few minutes. Keep the glass away from food and drinking cups afterwards.

If a coloured plume falls or swirls, record it. That is a clue that whole water parcels are moving, so you cannot use this glass to measure a pure diffusion rate. Compare your observation with the model's isolated random movement rule. Empty the glass, rinse it and wipe spills; do not taste the coloured water.

callouts.title: For 0610 Topic 3.1, include **net movement**, **higher to lower concentration**, and **random movement** in your explanation; the energy comes from the particles' kinetic energy. The four named rate factors are surface area, temperature, concentration gradient and distance.
Researchers arrange for some frog egg cells to make a suspected water-channel protein. Control eggs do not receive the instructions for that protein. What result would support the channel idea?
callouts.body:
- The two groups always swell at exactly the same rate
- Eggs making the protein take up water much faster in dilute surroundings
- Only salt can enter eggs making the protein
???
The second result supports a water pathway. The control comparison matters: swelling by itself would not identify which protein changed water permeability.

callouts.title: > “Salt sucks water through any barrier.”
callouts.body: A gradient cannot make an impermeable barrier pass water. Where passage is possible, net movement depends on water potential, including pressure. Salt ions may remain on their own side throughout.

callouts.title: In 0610 Extended Topic 3.2, connect **water molecules**, **higher to lower water potential**, and **a partially permeable membrane**. Use dilute-to-concentrated as the equal-pressure example; avoid the ambiguous phrase “concentration of solution”.
An animal cell and a plant cell are placed in very dilute surroundings. Water can enter both. Which outcome is most plausible?
callouts.body:
- Both must burst because water enters both
- The plant wall can support rising pressure, while an animal cell may swell and burst
- The plant wall completely blocks water, leaving the cell dry
???
The second outcome. The wall allows pressure to build as water enters. That pressure raises internal water potential and can balance further net entry. A red blood cell lacks that supporting wall.

callouts.title: > “The salty cup makes the potato limp because salt enters and bursts its cells.”
callouts.body: The initial explanation is net water loss from cells to lower-water-potential surroundings. Loss of turgor makes tissue less firm. Salt permeability and damage can matter during longer exposure, but they do not turn this into the dilute-water bursting of an animal cell.

callouts.title: Two cups, six strips, one fair comparison
callouts.body:
An adult should cut the potato and handle the knife. Use one raw potato to make six similar strips, about 60 mm long and 5 mm across. Prepare one cup with 100 mL of tap water. For the other, dissolve 5 g of table salt and add water to a **final volume of 100 mL**. This chosen 5% mass/volume solution is not a recipe for seawater. Without a suitable scale, a level teaspoon is an approximate alternative; label the concentration “approximate”.

Measure and label each strip. Put three in each cup, fully immersed, at the same room temperature and for the same time. Keep cups covered loosely against spills and dust. Predict changes in length and firmness. After 30 minutes, remove the strips, blot each gently in the same way, and measure again without squeezing. If the difference is unclear, note that and compare after a longer immersion, up to an hour. Never replace an awkward result with the expected one.

Record initial length, final length and firmness for each strip; compare the three-strip averages and their spread. Calculate percentage length change as **100 × (final − initial) ÷ initial**. A ruler with millimetre marks may miss a small change. A reliable mass measurement, if a sufficiently precise scale is available, gives another comparison; consistent blotting matters. A kitchen scale that reads only whole grams is too coarse for small changes in these strips. You can transfer the salty strips to fresh water to test possible recovery, without promising it.

Different potatoes, damaged cut surfaces and measurement uncertainty affect results. Do not eat the used potato or taste the liquids. Dispose of them the same day, wash hands and clean the cups and board.

callouts.title: For 0610 Topic 3.2, explain the water-potential direction and use **turgid**, **turgor pressure**, **flaccid**, or **plasmolysis** for the observed state. Reserve plasmolysis for contents separating from the wall; your kitchen strip tests tissue changes rather than showing that separation directly.
A plant cell's membrane-bound contents have visibly pulled away from an intact wall. Which way has net water movement occurred, and what would you need to know before predicting recovery?
callouts.body:
???
The cell has lost water overall and is plasmolysed. Fresh surroundings with higher water potential could favour re-entry, but recovery also depends on the cell remaining sufficiently undamaged. An intact-looking wall alone does not establish a living, functional membrane.

callouts.title: A root hair cell contains more nitrate ions per volume than the surrounding soil solution. Which explanation could sustain further nitrate uptake against that concentration gradient?
callouts.body:
- A nitrate pathway alone guarantees further accumulation, regardless of electrical conditions
- Increasing membrane area alone can sustain uptake against an unfavourable combined gradient
- A transporter couples nitrate entry to an energy source, such as another ion gradient
???
The third explanation supplies the missing account. A root can use ATP to establish another gradient, then couple nitrate entry to movement down that gradient. Concentration is part of the story for ions; electrical forces matter too.

callouts.title: > “Roots actively suck in water because the plant needs a drink.”
callouts.body: Name the transported substance and its route. Mineral-ion uptake can depend on energy-coupled transport; net water uptake follows water potential. A mangrove's salt barriers alone cannot explain intake unless its water-potential account also works.

callouts.title: For 0610 Topic 3.3, connect movement from **lower to higher concentration**, **against a concentration gradient**, **carrier proteins**, and **energy from respiration**. Root hair uptake of mineral ions is the key example; the proton relay explains how that energy can be supplied indirectly.

A mangrove excludes much salt at its roots. A second plant excludes the same amount, but its absorbing tissues have a higher water potential than the soil water. Will equal salt exclusion guarantee equal water uptake?
callouts.body:
???
No. Salt exclusion restricts one transfer; water uptake requires a favourable water-potential difference. If tissue water potential is higher than the surrounding soil water, that comparison favours net water loss rather than intake. Check the total water potential, not only the salt barrier.

A sailor has run out of fresh water. Seawater surrounds the boat. The sailor argues that a drink must help: it contains far more water than salt.

Seawater is not safe drinking water. This is a reasoning case, never a drinking experiment.

sections.heading: 4.1 Water's sticky geometry and carbon's four hands
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, rice, dal and a drop of oil

Stir sugar into water and it can disappear from sight. Add cooking oil and it gathers into droplets or a layer. Both are made of molecules. Why does water surround one so readily while separating from the other?

A tempting answer is that all tiny pieces should mix equally well. But smallness is only part of the story. The arrangement of electrical charge matters too.

:::predict
A water molecule has no overall electrical charge. Could it nevertheless attract another water molecule strongly in a particular orientation?
- No: neutral means there can be no electrical attraction
- Yes: its charge can be unevenly distributed even though the total is zero
- Only after an electron has moved completely from one water molecule to another
???
The second answer. Oxygen draws the shared electrons closer than hydrogen does. The oxygen end is partly negative and the hydrogen ends partly positive. The whole molecule remains neutral.
:::

sections.heading: 4.2 Folding the ribbon in Madras
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Madras, a collagen proposal in 1954

A ribbon can bend in many ways. A protein chain seems to offer an enormous number of possibilities too. Perhaps any arrangement that looks neat on paper will do. But paper lines have no thickness; atoms occupy space.

At the University of Madras, now Chennai, G. N. Ramachandran and Gopinath Kartha investigated collagen, a supporting protein in tissues such as skin and tendons. Their 1954 paper proposed three helical chains arranged together. Their 1955 revision coiled the chains around a common axis, with further refinements through later work. A plausible drawing had to satisfy chemical dimensions and experimental evidence together.

:::predict
Two drawings contain the same amino-acid sequence. In one, nonbonded atoms are forced almost into the same space. Can both be equally plausible protein structures?
- Yes: sequence is the only thing that matters
- No: a structure must also satisfy spatial and chemical restrictions
- Yes: if both drawings keep the same covalent bonds, the distances between other atoms do not matter
???
The second answer. Bonded atoms have particular arrangements, and nonbonded atoms strongly resist being pushed to

sections.heading: 4.3 The lock that bends the stick
sections.excerpt:
:::scene A watery cell, where chemistry happens

A molecule bumps against a protein. If suitable groups meet in a suitable arrangement, it may bind briefly. The surroundings of that pocket can then help chemical bonds rearrange. A different visitor, even one with a similar outline, may lack the right chemical groups.

A rigid key entering a rigid lock makes a useful first picture of selection. It gives a poor explanation of chemistry. A door lock does not normally help change the key into products.

:::predict
An enzyme speeds a reaction. Which explanation could preserve the same reactants, products and overall energy account?
- The enzyme supplies a fresh packet of net energy on every cycle
- The enzyme provides a route with a lower difficult hurdle between reactants and products
- The enzyme makes the forward reaction faster while leaving the reverse reaction completely unaffected
???
The second answer. A catalyst changes the route and its activation barrier. It does not change the net free-energy difference between the same starting and finishing states.
:::

sections.heading: 4.4 Why enzymes do not “die” when heated
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, the washing instructions

A packet of biological washing powder promises help with stains. It can contain enzymes that break larger stain molecules into smaller, more washable pieces. Would hotter water always make those helpers work better?

Chapter 3 gives one tempting argument: warmer molecules move faster, so more encounters should mean more reactions. That argument has a missing condition. The enzyme must still have a functional active site.

:::predict
An enzyme reaction runs slowly after strong heat exposure. Which comparison best tests whether the enzyme has persistently lost activity?
- Compare the heated sample while hot with a fresh sample while cold
- Cool the heated sample, then compare it with fresh enzyme at the same assay temperature and pH
- Call the enzyme dead because no reaction is visible
???
The second comparison. Matching the assay conditions separates continuing loss of activity from the immediate effect of different temperatures. The enzyme is a molecule, not an organism that can die.
:::

A teacher can prepare equal enzyme samples, expose them to di

sections.heading: 4.5 Forensic food tests
sections.excerpt:
:::scene A supervised school laboratory, five labelled portions

Return to lunch. “Rice contains starch” is a useful starting claim, but a detective should be able to ask what a particular sample reveals. A food may contain several kinds of molecules at once. Its natural colour can also confuse a test.

A tempting shortcut is to add something, notice any colour and announce a nutrient. First ask what the reagent detects, what counts as a positive observation and whether the comparison worked.

:::predict
An unknown food sample gives no positive result. The known positive tested alongside it also fails. What can you conclude about the unknown?
- The target substance is definitely absent
- The test has not shown that it can detect the target, so the unknown remains inconclusive
- The unknown is probably negative because it matched the known positive
???
The second answer. A failed positive control prevents a confident negative conclusion. Reagent quality, procedure or conditions may be wrong.
:::

:::evidence A result needs neighbours | The controlled comparison
Use separate portions of the sample for different tests. Beside each unknown, process a known target-containing sample in t

sections.heading: The washing-powder case
sections.excerpt:
:::case The hottest wash was not the best wash
Two matched stained cloth pieces are washed for the same time, with the same amount of biological washing powder and the same agitation. One wash follows the packet's recommended temperature range. The other uses excessively hot water. In this fictional comparison, the hotter wash leaves more of a protein-containing stain.

A second comparison provides a clue: equal enzyme samples from the two treatments are later tested with fresh substrate at the same suitable temperature and pH. The sample exposed to excessive heat has much less remaining activity. A no-enzyme washing comparison helps distinguish the detergent's other effects. Real washing also depends on the stain, fabric, formulation and time, so one cloth result alone would not identify the cause.

Explain why faster molecular motion did not guarantee better cleaning. Would adding “more energy” to the enzyme's name solve the problem?
???
The powder's protease can catalyse breakdown of protein in the stain. At a suitable temperature, encounters are frequent and the active site remains functional. Excessive heat can denature the enzyme and promote aggregation, leaving fewer functio

callouts.title: A water molecule has no overall electrical charge. Could it nevertheless attract another water molecule strongly in a particular orientation?
callouts.body:
- No: neutral means there can be no electrical attraction
- Yes: its charge can be unevenly distributed even though the total is zero
- Only after an electron has moved completely from one water molecule to another
???
The second answer. Oxygen draws the shared electrons closer than hydrogen does. The oxygen end is partly negative and the hydrogen ends partly positive. The whole molecule remains neutral.

callouts.title: > “If they contain the same atoms or building units, they must do the same job.”
callouts.body: Connections matter. Starch and cellulose contain glucose-derived units joined differently. Proteins add sequence and folding. A triglyceride has its own assembly pattern, not a glucose chain with three branches.

callouts.title: Water and oil: keep a comparison
callouts.body:
Use two small, clean, transparent containers with secure lids on a tray. Put the same small amount of cool tap water in each. Add about half a teaspoon of cooking oil to one; leave the other as the water-only control. These are chosen small quantities, not a calibrated solubility experiment.

Predict, then gently turn each closed container over a few times and stand it upright. Sketch immediately and again after settling. Droplets may remain for a while; record what you actually see rather than promising a fixed settling time. This comparison shows mixing behaviour, not individual hydrogen bonds. Do not taste either sample. Keep spills off the floor, wipe the little oil into absorbent waste, then wash the containers; do not pour oil down the drain. No heat or reagents are needed.

callouts.title: For 0610 Topic 4.1, connect carbohydrates and fats with **carbon, hydrogen and oxygen**, proteins also with **nitrogen**; know glucose → starch/glycogen/cellulose, amino acids → proteins, and fatty acids + glycerol → fats/oils. Some proteins also contain sulfur; our triglyceride example does not describe every lipid.
Two drawings contain the same amino-acid sequence. In one, nonbonded atoms are forced almost into the same space. Can both be equally plausible protein structures?
callouts.body:
- Yes: sequence is the only thing that matters
- No: a structure must also satisfy spatial and chemical restrictions
- Yes: if both drawings keep the same covalent bonds, the distances between other atoms do not matter
???
The second answer. Bonded atoms have particular arrangements, and nonbonded atoms strongly resist being pushed too close. A drawing can preserve the sequence while proposing a physically implausible shape.

callouts.title: > “Once the amino acids are in the right order, the shape cannot change.”
callouts.body: The sequence restricts possibilities, but water, temperature, pH and binding partners affect the interactions stabilising a shape. Those conditions can change while the peptide sequence remains intact.

callouts.title: For 0610, use the link between **protein shape and function** to explain an enzyme's **active site**; the backbone-angle map is our fuller explanation, not an extra phrase required in the school definition.
A proposed protein model has plausible local backbone angles. Has its full working structure been proved?
callouts.body:
???
No. It has passed one set of local spatial checks. The full arrangement must also fit experimental evidence and account for interactions across the whole molecule, its partners and its surroundings. Passing a restriction is different from proving a unique solution.

callouts.title: An enzyme speeds a reaction. Which explanation could preserve the same reactants, products and overall energy account?
callouts.body:
- The enzyme supplies a fresh packet of net energy on every cycle
- The enzyme provides a route with a lower difficult hurdle between reactants and products
- The enzyme makes the forward reaction faster while leaving the reverse reaction completely unaffected
???
The second answer. A catalyst changes the route and its activation barrier. It does not change the net free-energy difference between the same starting and finishing states.

callouts.title: > “The lock has used up its power after one reaction.”
callouts.body: During a catalytic cycle the enzyme can change temporarily, but it is regenerated when the cycle finishes. Products leave, allowing another cycle. Reuse does not make the enzyme indestructible: damage, inhibitors or unsuitable conditions can stop it working.

callouts.title: 0610 Topic 5.1 uses **biological catalyst**, **substrate**, **active site**, **complementary shape**, **enzyme–substrate complex** and **product**. Give that clear sequence, then remember that complementary chemistry and flexible molecules make the fuller mechanism work.
An enzyme reaction runs slowly after strong heat exposure. Which comparison best tests whether the enzyme has persistently lost activity?
callouts.body:
- Compare the heated sample while hot with a fresh sample while cold
- Cool the heated sample, then compare it with fresh enzyme at the same assay temperature and pH
- Call the enzyme dead because no reaction is visible
???
The second comparison. Matching the assay conditions separates continuing loss of activity from the immediate effect of different temperatures. The enzyme is a molecule, not an organism that can die.

callouts.title: > “All enzymes are fine below one fever temperature, then all of them die together.”
callouts.body: Different proteins have different stabilities, and exposure time matters. Enzymes were never alive. Use “activity changed” or “denatured” when the evidence supports it; do not turn a classroom curve into a medical rule.

callouts.title: For 0610 Extended Topic 5.1, explain temperature with **kinetic energy**, **frequency of effective collisions**, **shape and fit** and **denaturation**; explain pH through effects on the active site. State the **optimum temperature or pH** for the particular experiment, not for all enzymes.
Two samples react slowly: one is cold, the other has been strongly heated and then cooled. Why is testing both with fresh substrate at the same temperature and pH useful?
callouts.body:
???
It removes different immediate assay temperatures and pH as explanations for their rate difference. Recovery of the cold sample is consistent with reversible slowing. Continuing loss in the heat-treated sample supports persistent damage, though more evidence is needed to identify the exact structural change. Neither result is an enzyme dying.

callouts.title: An unknown food sample gives no positive result. The known positive tested alongside it also fails. What can you conclude about the unknown?
callouts.body:
- The target substance is definitely absent
- The test has not shown that it can detect the target, so the unknown remains inconclusive
- The unknown is probably negative because it matched the known positive
???
The second answer. A failed positive control prevents a confident negative conclusion. Reagent quality, procedure or conditions may be wrong.

callouts.title: > “No colour change proves there is none, and a stronger colour tells me the exact amount.”
callouts.body: First check the controls and the target. A valid negative means “not detected under these conditions”. Quantities require a calibrated method, standards and uncertainty; different sample colours or heating times can spoil a casual comparison.

callouts.title: 0610 Topic 4.1 requires all five tests: **Benedict's for reducing sugars, iodine for starch, biuret for proteins, ethanol emulsion for fats/oils and DCPIP for vitamin C**. Describe the observation and its inference separately; keep conditions and controls clear.
callouts.body:
:::

These are **school laboratory procedures, not home activities**. Follow the teacher's risk assessment and exact instructions. Wear eye protection, never taste samples or mouth-pipette, and use clean labelled equipment. A teacher manages hot water baths and reagent preparation. Ethanol is flammable: keep it away from flames and never heat it for this test. Biuret reagent is alkaline; its hazard depends on concentration. The teacher collects copper-containing and other reagent waste according to the laboratory's disposal rules. Wash hands afterwards. No household substitutes or mixtures are needed.

callouts.title: The hottest wash was not the best wash
callouts.body:
Two matched stained cloth pieces are washed for the same time, with the same amount of biological washing powder and the same agitation. One wash follows the packet's recommended temperature range. The other uses excessively hot water. In this fictional comparison, the hotter wash leaves more of a protein-containing stain.

A second comparison provides a clue: equal enzyme samples from the two treatments are later tested with fresh substrate at the same suitable temperature and pH. The sample exposed to excessive heat has much less remaining activity. A no-enzyme washing comparison helps distinguish the detergent's other effects. Real washing also depends on the stain, fabric, formulation and time, so one cloth result alone would not identify the cause.

Explain why faster molecular motion did not guarantee better cleaning. Would adding “more energy” to the enzyme's name solve the problem?
???
The powder's protease can catalyse breakdown of protein in the stain. At a suitable temperature, encounters are frequent and the active site remains functional. Excessive heat can denature the enzyme and promote aggregation, leaving fewer functional active sites. Faster encounters then cannot compensate for the lost catalytic machinery; the lower residual activity at a common assay temperature supports persistent damage.

The enzyme was not killed or used up as fuel. It normally lowers activation barriers and is regenerated. The detergent's other ingredients may still work, which is why both activity controls and washing controls help. Follow product instructions; this is a reasoning case, not a request to handle hot detergent or reproduce a wash experiment.
