sections.heading: 5.1 The five-year willow tree
sections.excerpt:
:::scene A willow experiment, reported in 1648

A seed has a little stored material. It can supply the beginning of a root and shoot; it cannot contain all the material of the eventual tree. Somewhere, matter must cross the growing plant's boundary.

Roots grip soil, so perhaps a tree eats the soil and turns it into wood. That is a respectable guess. It makes a prediction you could test with a balance: the earth should lose material as the tree gains it.

:::predict
Suppose a tree becomes much heavier while the dried soil loses very little mass. Which conclusion is justified?
- The missing material must all have come from water, because water was added
- Soil alone cannot account for the reported gain; both water and gas exchange need investigation
- The balance establishes the source if the tree and soil were weighed carefully enough
???
The second. A mismatch challenges the soil-only account. It does not identify every missing input or show that mineral nutrients are unnecessary.
:::

:::evidence A tree and its unbalanced ledger | Published posthumously, 1648
Jan Baptista van Helmont described putting 200 pounds of oven-dried earth into an earthen pot and planting a willow shoot

sections.heading: 5.2 Bubbles in the sunlight
sections.excerpt:
:::scene England, an experiment in 1771 and a book in 1779

If air contributes material, leaves should change the air around them. But “plants improve air” is too vague. What changes, under which conditions, and how could you tell?

A green leaf sitting quietly looks inactive. Put suitable green material under water in light, and gas may collect as bubbles. It is tempting to call every bubble a parcel of newly made oxygen, and every missing bubble proof that the chemistry stopped. First separate what you see from what you infer.

:::predict
A reliable gas measurement in weak light shows no net oxygen release. Which interpretation is justified?
- Photosynthesis has stopped, because every oxygen-producing reaction must give a surplus
- Photosynthesis and oxygen consumption may balance; the net measurement alone cannot separate them
- Respiration has stopped, because the oxygen concentration is not changing
???
The second. Photosynthesis can occur while respiration consumes oxygen. No net release does not by itself establish no production; invisible dissolved gas also complicates bubble observations.
:::

:::evidence The missing conditions | 1771, 1779 and 1804
Joseph Priestley report

sections.heading: 5.3 Inside the green solar panel
sections.excerpt:
### From absorbed light to building reactions

A leaf does not catch carbon atoms falling from sunlight. Its material and energy arrive by different routes. Carbon dioxide diffuses in from air; water arrives through the plant. Light transfers energy to machinery inside certain cells.

The tempting shortcut is “chlorophyll makes food”. A pigment name cannot do the explaining. What does absorbed light actually change?

:::predict
You could mark oxygen atoms in the supplied water and collect the released oxygen gas before later exchange obscures its origin. What result would distinguish water as the source from carbon dioxide as the source?
- The collected oxygen carries the water's mark
- The collected oxygen is unmarked, because its atoms came directly from carbon dioxide
- Marking water cannot help because the net equation alone identifies the source
???
The first result supports water as the source. A mark lets us follow atoms even when their chemical partners change. The net equation balances the atoms but does not identify every atom's route; tracing tests that route.
:::

:::evidence Follow the oxygen, not the shape of an equation | 1941
Samuel Ruben, Merle Randall, Martin Kame

sections.heading: 5.4 Engineering a flat solar factory
sections.excerpt:
Turn a familiar houseplant leaf edge-on. Much of the surface you saw face-on almost disappears. A broad, thin blade can intercept light over a large area while keeping diffusion distances short. But a broad wet surface also risks losing water. How can the same organ admit gas and conserve liquid?

One tempting design would seal the leaf completely. Water loss would fall, but carbon dioxide delivery would suffer too.

:::predict
If most gas-exchange pores close on a water-stressed leaf in daylight, what trade-off is likely?
- Water loss can decrease, but carbon dioxide entry can also decrease
- Water loss can decrease while carbon dioxide entry remains unchanged, because they always use separate routes
- Both rates must fall by the same fraction, whatever the gradients outside
???
The first. Restricting a shared gas route affects both water vapour leaving and carbon dioxide entering. Actual rates also depend on the surrounding conditions.
:::

:::evidence A section through a leaf | Microscopy, not a flat-cell model
Microscope sections reveal layers within a typical dicot leaf. A waxy cuticle lies outside the epidermis. Below the upper epidermis, elongated palisade cells contain many

sections.heading: 5.5 Pulling water upwards without a heart
sections.excerpt:
### Xylem: replacing water lost from leaves

The leaf now has an entrance for carbon dioxide. Water still has to reach it from roots below. If every part of a tree required a little heart to push water higher, where are the pumps?

The tempting answer is “roots suck it up”. That moves the mystery underground. Begin instead where liquid leaves the system.

:::predict
Which change can help drive the upward transpiration stream?
- Evaporation from moist leaf surfaces creates a pull transmitted through connected water
- Root pressure alone accounts for the supply to the tops of all tall trees
- Atmospheric pressure pushes the water column as it does in an open drinking straw
???
The first. Water molecules attract one another, so tension created near evaporating surfaces can be transmitted through liquid in xylem. Roots replace the water lost along the route.
:::

:::evidence A connected liquid can transmit a pull | The cohesion–tension account
Measurements of xylem pressure and leaf water loss support water transport under tension during transpiration. Water evaporates from moist mesophyll walls into internal air spaces, then water vapour diffuses through stomata to the surroundings. A

sections.heading: The sealed-garden case
sections.excerpt:
:::case A lid closes the matter account, not the energy account
This is a **fictional reasoning case**, not a report about a famous bottle with a verified sealing date. A transparent terrarium contains suitable plants, damp substrate and decomposers. Its lid stays closed, matter exchange is very limited, and suitable indirect light reaches it. Droplets sometimes condense on the glass and return to the substrate. For the period observed, the plants remain alive without added water.

Someone concludes: “It needs nothing from outside. Water, oxygen and energy all go round forever. The plants make oxygen by day, and only the decomposers respire.”

Find the mistakes. Where can water and carbon go inside? What must still cross the boundary? Does survival over the observed period guarantee survival indefinitely?
???
Water can enter roots, leave leaves as vapour, condense and return. Carbon can move from carbon dioxide into plant organic material and back through respiration by plants and decomposers. Decomposition can return mineral nutrients to available forms. These are material cycles, with finite supplies and biological constraints.

Light transfers energy through the glass. Photosynt

callouts.title: Suppose a tree becomes much heavier while the dried soil loses very little mass. Which conclusion is justified?
callouts.body:
- The missing material must all have come from water, because water was added
- Soil alone cannot account for the reported gain; both water and gas exchange need investigation
- The balance establishes the source if the tree and soil were weighed carefully enough
???
The second. A mismatch challenges the soil-only account. It does not identify every missing input or show that mineral nutrients are unnecessary.

callouts.title: > “Air weighs nothing, so solid wood cannot come from it.”
callouts.body: Gases consist of atoms and have mass. Incorporating carbon atoms from carbon dioxide into a solid changes their chemical partners and arrangement; it does not summon matter from nothing. Sunlight will supply energy, not those carbon atoms.

callouts.title: For 0610 (2026–2028), Topic 6.1, connect carbohydrate synthesis to carbon dioxide and water, and explain nitrate ions in amino-acid production and magnesium ions in chlorophyll production. A plant's food and its mineral nutrients are different parts of the account.
A reliable gas measurement in weak light shows no net oxygen release. Which interpretation is justified?
callouts.body:
- Photosynthesis has stopped, because every oxygen-producing reaction must give a surplus
- Photosynthesis and oxygen consumption may balance; the net measurement alone cannot separate them
- Respiration has stopped, because the oxygen concentration is not changing
???
The second. Photosynthesis can occur while respiration consumes oxygen. No net release does not by itself establish no production; invisible dissolved gas also complicates bubble observations.

callouts.title: > “Twice as many bubbles means exactly twice as much oxygen.”
callouts.body: Only if each bubble represented the same known amount, collection were reliable and the other conditions were controlled could such a conversion be justified. A bubble count is an imperfect proxy, not an automatic calibration.

callouts.title: 0610 Topic 6.1 includes controlled investigations of light, chlorophyll and carbon dioxide, and light/dark gas exchange with hydrogencarbonate indicator. Describe the observation before the inference; plant respiration continues in the light.

You could mark oxygen atoms in the supplied water and collect the released oxygen gas before later exchange obscures its origin. What result would distinguish water as the source from carbon dioxide as the source?
callouts.body:
- The collected oxygen carries the water's mark
- The collected oxygen is unmarked, because its atoms came directly from carbon dioxide
- Marking water cannot help because the net equation alone identifies the source
???
The first result supports water as the source. A mark lets us follow atoms even when their chemical partners change. The net equation balances the atoms but does not identify every atom's route; tracing tests that route.

If enzymes lower activation barriers, why does a leaf still require an energy input to synthesise carbohydrate from carbon dioxide and water?
???
A catalyst provides a lower-barrier route but does not supply the net energy needed for an unfavourable overall transformation. Light-supported processes provide that input; enzymes help the connected reactions proceed.

callouts.title: > “A leaf is a solar panel, so brighter and hotter must always be better.”
callouts.body: A leaf's chemistry also requires supplies, functional enzymes and water balance. More of one input cannot replace the others. The analogy concerns energy capture; a leaf also makes and transports material and continually respires.

callouts.title: For 0610 (2026–2028) 6.1, Core covers the word equation, pigment, carbohydrate uses and controlled investigations; Supplement adds the balanced chemical equation and explanations of limiting factors. State light and chlorophyll, and say energy is transferred into chemicals, never created.
If most gas-exchange pores close on a water-stressed leaf in daylight, what trade-off is likely?
callouts.body:
- Water loss can decrease, but carbon dioxide entry can also decrease
- Water loss can decrease while carbon dioxide entry remains unchanged, because they always use separate routes
- Both rates must fall by the same fraction, whatever the gradients outside
???
The first. Restricting a shared gas route affects both water vapour leaving and carbon dioxide entering. Actual rates also depend on the surrounding conditions.

callouts.title: > “All plant cells are green factories, and every pore closes only at night.”
callouts.body: Root hair cells and many other plant cells lack developed chloroplasts. Stomatal behaviour varies. Even a green leaf with open pores still requires suitable conditions and functioning chemistry to photosynthesise.

callouts.title: Read a leaf without taking it apart
callouts.body:
Use a familiar, safe houseplant already in your home. Leave the leaf attached. In diffuse daylight, look at its broad surface, thin edge, visible veins and both surfaces; gently move the pot only if an adult can do so safely. Do not climb, taste, pluck, cut or rub sap, and avoid unfamiliar or irritating plants. Keep it away from hot direct sun while inspecting it.

Sketch what you can actually see, then label which features would require magnification. Compare another attached leaf if available. You may notice different vein patterns or surface appearances; neither proves a stomatal count or a photosynthesis rate. Individual stomata and chloroplasts are not established by this unaided observation. There is no waste to dispose of; wash your hands after handling the pot. This is an observation activity, not a physical trial performed for this book.

callouts.title: 0610 6.2 asks you to identify the listed structures in a dicot leaf and explain how they support photosynthesis. Pair each structure with a job and a reason: “thin” shortens a diffusion path; “large surface area” intercepts more light under comparable exposure.
Which change can help drive the upward transpiration stream?
callouts.body:
- Evaporation from moist leaf surfaces creates a pull transmitted through connected water
- Root pressure alone accounts for the supply to the tops of all tall trees
- Atmospheric pressure pushes the water column as it does in an open drinking straw
???
The first. Water molecules attract one another, so tension created near evaporating surfaces can be transmitted through liquid in xylem. Roots replace the water lost along the route.

Does every step of water movement from soil to air count as osmosis? Where does active ion transport fit?
???
No. Osmosis describes water movement across a partially permeable membrane down a water-potential gradient. Flow through xylem and diffusion of water vapour are different steps. Active ion transport can alter solute conditions and requires energy; that does not make the whole xylem stream an ATP-driven pump.

callouts.title: > “Xylem is water going up; phloem is food going down. That is all.”
callouts.body: You have remembered two arrows and lost the mechanisms. Xylem carries water and mineral ions in the transpiration stream. Phloem carries assimilates from sources to sinks; those connections can run upwards or downwards. Explain the pull in one and the pressure difference in the other.

callouts.title: 0610 Topics 8.1–8.3 connect xylem structure, water uptake and transpiration; Extended includes cohesion-linked transpiration pull, humidity and wilting. Supplement 8.4 uses sources, sinks, sucrose and amino acids for translocation. The leaf plate is not a substitute for learning to identify xylem and phloem in school root and stem cross-sections.
A lid closes the matter account, not the energy account
callouts.body:
This is a **fictional reasoning case**, not a report about a famous bottle with a verified sealing date. A transparent terrarium contains suitable plants, damp substrate and decomposers. Its lid stays closed, matter exchange is very limited, and suitable indirect light reaches it. Droplets sometimes condense on the glass and return to the substrate. For the period observed, the plants remain alive without added water.

Someone concludes: “It needs nothing from outside. Water, oxygen and energy all go round forever. The plants make oxygen by day, and only the decomposers respire.”

Find the mistakes. Where can water and carbon go inside? What must still cross the boundary? Does survival over the observed period guarantee survival indefinitely?
???
Water can enter roots, leave leaves as vapour, condense and return. Carbon can move from carbon dioxide into plant organic material and back through respiration by plants and decomposers. Decomposition can return mineral nutrients to available forms. These are material cycles, with finite supplies and biological constraints.

Light transfers energy through the glass. Photosynthesis can store some of that input in chemical form; respiration supports cellular work and energy ultimately disperses as heat. Energy does not cycle indefinitely as a reusable supply. Plants as well as decomposers respire, including in the light. Net oxygen depends on the balance of production and consumption.

A closed lid does not guarantee adequate nutrients, gas balance, light or long-term stability. Darkness removes the photosynthetic input while respiration can continue to draw on finite stores. Do not put animals in such a container or open or sniff a mouldy jar. This case asks for reasoning, not a home sealed-culture experiment.

chapters.hookSummary: Your chest moves as you breathe. A root tip appears still. The tempting wrong idea is “My lungs do respiration; plants have no lungs, so they do something else.” It bundles a delivery system together with the chemistry it supplies.

sections.heading: 6.1 Breathing is only the delivery service
sections.excerpt:
Your chest moves as you breathe. A root tip appears still. The tempting wrong idea is “My lungs do respiration; plants have no lungs, so they do something else.” It bundles a delivery system together with the chemistry it supplies.

:::predict
A root cell underground is growing and actively taking up mineral ions. Must it have lungs to obtain usable energy from nutrients?
- Yes; oxygen must first pass through a lung before any cell can use it
- No; gas delivery and energy-transferring cell reactions are different processes
- No; the root can use sugar without any enzyme-controlled energy transfer
???
The second. A root can receive sugars from other parts of the plant and oxygen from its surroundings without having lungs. Its own enzymes carry out the chemical reactions. Soil is not a supply of finished ATP for the root.
:::

:::evidence A reaction system separated from an animal | From Chapter 4's evidence to this chapter's question
Eduard Buchner's 1897 yeast-juice experiments already gave us a useful clue. A preparation separated from intact yeast cells could still ferment suitable sugar. Neither lungs nor a chest movement were required for that chemical activity.

Enzyme prepara

sections.heading: 6.2 A membrane between the fuel and the work
sections.excerpt:
“Mitochondria make ATP” gives us an address. How can changing the chemical partners of carbon atoms drive a protein elsewhere?

The tempting picture is a miniature fire: oxygen hits sugar, heat flashes out, and a spinning part collects it. There is no flame. Enzymes control small chemical steps, with carriers and a membrane linking reactions.

First follow the whole relay without learning any new pathway names. Fuel reactions transfer electrons to reusable carriers. Further electron transfers help move hydrogen ions across a membrane. The membrane slows their return, so a difference in concentration and charge builds up. Their controlled return through a protein drives changes that help make ATP. We will now give each part an address and a name.

### First follow carbon, then the electrons


:::evidence The missing link was a membrane difference | 1961 and 1997
Peter Mitchell proposed in 1961 that fuel oxidation and ATP formation could be coupled indirectly. Electron transfers could establish a hydrogen-ion difference across a membrane; return through suitable machinery could then support ATP formation. The stored difference includes both concentration and electric potential. His c

sections.heading: 6.3 The atoms do not turn into heat
sections.excerpt:
Put a representative fat molecule into our chemical account. After complete oxidation, the original fat is no longer there. Where is its material?

One tempting answer is “It became energy.” Warm surroundings encourage that picture. But transferring energy is not an explanation for missing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms. In the chemistry being described, those atoms have new partners. They must appear in the products.

:::predict
A mathematical sample containing 1 kg of fat is completely oxidised. Can the total products weigh more than 1 kg?
- No; that would create matter
- Yes; incoming oxygen contributes mass to the products
- Yes; ATP turns heat into extra carbon atoms
???
The second. Compare every input with every output. Weighing the fuel alone leaves oxygen off the input side. The mass of all products can exceed the starting fuel mass while the complete account still balances.
:::

:::evidence Two different questions behind “where did it go?” | Meerman and Brown, 2014
Ruben Meerman and Andrew Brown examined this misconception in a 2014 BMJ article. They represented triglyceride fat by C₅₅H₁₀₄O₆ and balanced its complete oxidation. The products contain the fuel atoms plus s

sections.heading: 6.4 Keeping the carrier ready for another round
sections.excerpt:
Suppose the aerobic electron route cannot keep pace with glycolysis, or oxygen is unavailable. Why should that affect sugar-splitting enzymes elsewhere?

The tempting answer is “There is still sugar, so splitting can continue forever.” But glycolysis also transfers electrons to NAD⁺. A finite supply cannot keep accepting electrons if it remains in the NADH form.

:::predict
A cell has glucose and functioning glycolytic enzymes, but NADH cannot pass its electrons onwards. What eventually restricts continued glycolysis?
- The available NAD⁺ form becomes too scarce
- Sugar alone keeps the pathway running even if every carrier remains NADH
- Extra oxygen could restore NAD⁺ without any working electron-transfer machinery
???
The first. Electron collection converts NAD⁺ to NADH. Passing electrons onwards regenerates NAD⁺. A pathway using a reusable participant depends on its return, just as a delivery route depends on containers becoming available again.
:::

:::evidence Bubbles are one clue; tracing carbon gives another | Idli studies and a lactate tracer
A 1965 study by Mukherjee and colleagues investigated the microbes in idli batter and identified Leuconostoc mesenteroides as a princ

sections.heading: The waterlogged-root case
sections.excerpt:
:::fig c6_roots() | Flooded soil can restrict oxygen delivery to roots, despite abundant water. Rice provides a contrasting example of internal gas routes; these are representative schematics, not a prediction of survival time or a universal plant design.

:::case Water everywhere, oxygen in short supply
This is a fictional reasoning case. After prolonged rain, a potted plant stands in waterlogged soil. Its leaves remain above water in daylight. A pupil says: “The roots have sugar from the leaves and plenty of H₂O. Each water molecule contains oxygen, so aerobic respiration cannot be short of oxygen.” Another says: “Then fermentation will supply exactly the same ATP and the plant will be fine indefinitely.”

Identify the missing distinction in each claim. Why might waterlogging impair ATP-supported root functions? Why should a comparison with rice make you cautious about predicting the same outcome for every plant?
???
Roots require a route for **molecular oxygen, O₂**, to reach the reactions that use it. Oxygen chemically bound within H₂O is not free O₂ for the aerobic chain. O₂ diffuses much more slowly through water-filled paths than through connected air spaces. When water fill

callouts.title: A root cell underground is growing and actively taking up mineral ions. Must it have lungs to obtain usable energy from nutrients?
callouts.body:
- Yes; oxygen must first pass through a lung before any cell can use it
- No; gas delivery and energy-transferring cell reactions are different processes
- No; the root can use sugar without any enzyme-controlled energy transfer
???
The second. A root can receive sugars from other parts of the plant and oxygen from its surroundings without having lungs. Its own enzymes carry out the chemical reactions. Soil is not a supply of finished ATP for the root.

A lit green leaf releases oxygen overall. Does that mean its respiration has stopped?
???
No. Photosynthesis can produce oxygen faster than respiration consumes it, leaving a net release. The leaf can carry out both processes at once. Roots supplied by the leaf also continue their metabolism without receiving light.

callouts.title: > “Plants make food by day and only start respiration at night.”
callouts.body: Living plant cells require a continuing usable energy supply in light and darkness. Photosynthesis adds another process in suitable illuminated tissues; it does not switch respiration off. Root cells can use carbohydrates delivered from those tissues.

callouts.title: 0610 Topic 12 distinguishes cellular respiration from breathing and asks for uses of released energy, including contraction, synthesis, division, active transport, growth, nerve impulses and temperature maintenance. Use “releases energy” with its source understood: chemical reactions transfer energy; they do not create it.
Suppose the inner mitochondrial membrane becomes freely leaky to hydrogen ions. Proteins still transfer electrons and pump those ions. What happens to the useful difference across the membrane?
callouts.body:
- The same pumping can maintain the original difference even when the return leak becomes much larger
- The difference becomes harder to maintain, so normal ATP production through that relay is impaired
- ATP synthase works faster because every returning ion must still pass through it
???
The second. Pumping separates ions; unrestricted return undoes the separation. Electron transfer and normal ATP production need not remain coupled if the membrane cannot hold the difference.

Does an ATP-using enzyme obtain energy simply by breaking one special bond?
???
No. Breaking an isolated chemical bond requires energy. The whole ATP hydrolysis reaction can release free energy because the resulting products and their interactions in water are more stable under the relevant conditions. Coupling that overall change to another process can support work; the enzyme does not create the energy.

callouts.title: > “Oxygen meets sugar in the lungs, and all the energy comes out when a bond snaps.”
callouts.body: Fuel processing happens through cellular pathways. Carbon dioxide is released during carbon-processing reactions; oxygen accepts electrons and protons to form water at the chain's end. ATP-supported work depends on complete reaction and coupling accounts, not energy released by snapping an isolated bond.

callouts.title: 0610 Topic 12.2 uses oxygen-dependent nutrient breakdown and the aerobic word equation; Supplement adds the balanced glucose equation. The membrane relay explains how that overall account supports ATP formation, without assigning one fixed ATP yield to every cell.
A mathematical sample containing 1 kg of fat is completely oxidised. Can the total products weigh more than 1 kg?
callouts.body:
- No; that would create matter
- Yes; incoming oxygen contributes mass to the products
- Yes; ATP turns heat into extra carbon atoms
???
The second. Compare every input with every output. Weighing the fuel alone leaves oxygen off the input side. The mass of all products can exceed the starting fuel mass while the complete account still balances.

callouts.title: > “The fuel weighed 1 kg, so all its products together must weigh 1 kg.”
callouts.body: That leaves incoming oxygen off the input side. Balance every input against every output. The optional original-fuel account asks a different question and should never be substituted for total product mass.

callouts.title: The 0610 aerobic equation is a useful balanced starting point. Whenever a question asks where matter goes, account for gases as well as solids and liquids; energy release does not remove the requirement to balance the atoms.
A cell has glucose and functioning glycolytic enzymes, but NADH cannot pass its electrons onwards. What eventually restricts continued glycolysis?
callouts.body:
- The available NAD⁺ form becomes too scarce
- Sugar alone keeps the pathway running even if every carrier remains NADH
- Extra oxygen could restore NAD⁺ without any working electron-transfer machinery
???
The first. Electron collection converts NAD⁺ to NADH. Passing electrons onwards regenerates NAD⁺. A pathway using a reusable participant depends on its return, just as a delivery route depends on containers becoming available again.

callouts.title: Watch the batter, keep the inference small
callouts.body:
An adult must manage this observation during an ordinary preparation of familiar idli batter. Ask them to set aside a small observation portion in a clean transparent container with room above it and a loose cover. Put a clean mark outside at the initial batter level. Record the starting time and later observations during the adult's normal preparation schedule; look from outside for a level change or visible gas pockets.

The observation portion is not for eating. Do not taste raw batter, add experimental starter cultures, seal the container, sniff it closely or deliberately keep it beyond the adult's normal preparation period. Leave cooking equipment and the main food preparation to the adult. If there is unexpected colour, mould or another sign that concerns the adult, stop and let them discard it without further investigation. They should dispose of the observation portion and clean the container; wash your hands afterwards.

Record your observations in a table:

| Time | Batter level relative to the mark | Visible gas pockets | What remains uncertain? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Start | At the mark | Record what you see | Gas may be dissolved or escape |
| Later | Above, at or below the mark | Record what you see | Level also depends on batter structure |

Sketch the changes; no visible rise is a valid observation. Could gas have escaped or remained dissolved? The marked level helps compare expansion, without identifying an organism or calibrating a rate. This proposed observation was not physically trialled for the book.

callouts.title: > “Without oxygen, cells either stop instantly or produce the same gas and waste everywhere.”
callouts.body: Carrier-regenerating routes can support continued glycolysis. Yeast's taught route releases CO₂; the glucose-to-lactate route does not. Lactate can also form while oxygen is present and can be reused. Neither observation establishes a universal all-or-nothing oxygen switch.

callouts.title: The school term **anaerobic respiration** includes the yeast and muscle fermentation examples. Keep its equations alongside the carrier-recycling mechanism; the fuller terminology and oxygen-debt account are explained in the note above.
callouts.body:
:::

In wider biochemistry, **anaerobic respiration** can also mean electron transport using a final acceptor other than oxygen. Fermentation restores carriers through organic recipients without that respiratory electron chain. The distinction concerns the mechanism; the school's equations remain useful.

callouts.title: Water everywhere, oxygen in short supply
callouts.body:
This is a fictional reasoning case. After prolonged rain, a potted plant stands in waterlogged soil. Its leaves remain above water in daylight. A pupil says: “The roots have sugar from the leaves and plenty of H₂O. Each water molecule contains oxygen, so aerobic respiration cannot be short of oxygen.” Another says: “Then fermentation will supply exactly the same ATP and the plant will be fine indefinitely.”

Identify the missing distinction in each claim. Why might waterlogging impair ATP-supported root functions? Why should a comparison with rice make you cautious about predicting the same outcome for every plant?
???
Roots require a route for **molecular oxygen, O₂**, to reach the reactions that use it. Oxygen chemically bound within H₂O is not free O₂ for the aerobic chain. O₂ diffuses much more slowly through water-filled paths than through connected air spaces. When water fills soil pores, delivery can fall behind the continuing oxygen use by roots and microbes. Sugar alone cannot maintain the usual aerobic relay without its final electron recipient.

Fermentation can restore carriers and support continued glycolysis, but the taught glucose route gives a much smaller ATP return than complete aerobic processing. It does not guarantee that every root function or long-term survival can be maintained. Active ion transport and growth can suffer when the usable energy supply is restricted.

Plants differ. Rice has internal gas spaces and other root features that can improve oxygen movement towards submerged tissues. Such adaptations change the delivery problem; they do not abolish respiration's chemical requirements. Water depth, duration, temperature, plant condition and species matter. No fixed survival time follows from the drawing. This case is for reasoning, not a request to flood a houseplant or grow a sealed culture.

chapters.subtitle: Chapter 7 of The Living World
chapters.hookSummary: When you swallow food in an ordinary meal, it disappears from view. Has it therefore become part of your muscles? The tempting answer is “It is inside me, so my cells already have it.” But a coin inside a pocket has not crossed the cloth. Being enclosed and crossing a boundary are different facts.

sections.heading: 7.1 A tube through the body, and a barrier to cross
sections.excerpt:
When you swallow food in an ordinary meal, it disappears from view. Has it therefore become part of your muscles? The tempting answer is “It is inside me, so my cells already have it.” But a coin inside a pocket has not crossed the cloth. Being enclosed and crossing a boundary are different facts.

:::predict
Imagine a starch-containing food particle in the small intestine, surrounded by fluid but still in the gut's central space. Which event would establish absorption of material from it?
- It has passed below the stomach, so absorption is already complete
- Suitable substances cross the gut's epithelial lining into the internal tissues
- The particle leaves the body as faeces
???
The second. Position along the tube is not proof of crossing its lining. Digestion can produce absorbable substances in the central space; absorption then requires passage across the barrier. Unabsorbed remnants can continue along the tube and leave.
:::

:::evidence Follow connections rather than the body outline | Anatomy and transport
Anatomical examination reveals a continuous canal from mouth to anus, bounded by living tissue. A swallowed meal follows that canal. The liver, pancreas and gallbladder

sections.heading: 7.2 Moving, mixing and digesting without digesting the wall
sections.excerpt:
The bread in your buttered pav can become a paste while its starch molecules remain mostly joined in chains. What turns that paste into absorbable substances? One tempting answer is “The stomach grinds everything fine enough, and acid dissolves the rest.” That gives physical force and acid every job. We need a comparison that separates them from the chemistry of digestive juice.

:::predict
Gastric juice is collected and placed with food in a warm vessel outside the stomach. If food breaks down there too, which claim is challenged?
- Digestive juice can carry out chemical work apart from muscular grinding
- All stomach digestion must be caused by its muscular wall rubbing on food
- The whole intestinal absorption route has been reproduced in the vessel
???
The second claim is challenged. Chemical activity can occur without the stomach wall doing the grinding. This observation does not tell us that acid alone is responsible, nor does it show absorption into living tissues.
:::

:::evidence Gastric juice could act outside the stomach | Experiments in 1825; book in 1833
In 1822, Alexis St. Martin, a French Canadian voyageur, survived an accidental gunshot injury at Mackinac. William B

sections.heading: 7.3 What bile changes—and what lipase changes
sections.excerpt:
The butter from the pav supplies triglycerides. A layer of melted butter or oil tends to gather separately from water. Now imagine dispersing the same fat into many small droplets. Have you made smaller fat molecules? That is the tempting mistake. A droplet is an assembly containing many molecules, just as a crumb contains many starch molecules. Changing the size of the assembly need not change the molecules themselves.

:::predict
One spherical fat droplet is replaced by eight equal spheres with the same combined volume. Which claim follows from geometry alone?
- Each sphere has one-eighth the radius and the total area is eight times as large
- Each sphere has half the radius and the total area doubles
- Fatty acids and glycerol must have formed because the droplets are smaller
???
The second. Halving each radius reduces each sphere's volume to one-eighth and its area to one-quarter. Eight of those areas total twice the original area. That calculation changes the interface, not chemical identity; it does not establish a biological reaction-rate multiplier.
:::

:::evidence Hold the amount fixed and calculate the interface | A mathematical comparison
For a sphere of radius R, volum

sections.heading: 7.4 Crossing the intestinal wall
sections.excerpt:
Suppose digestion has supplied glucose from the pav beside the intestinal lining. The molecule has reached the correct address. Why doesn't that finish the journey? The tempting answer is “It is now small, so it can fall through little holes into blood.” But a living barrier is selective. More available surface helps only if substances can cross it through suitable routes.

:::predict
The intestine has a large folded surface, but a glucose transporter at its lumen-facing membrane stops functioning. Does extra surface alone guarantee the same glucose absorption?
- Yes; surface area overrides all membrane chemistry
- No; area and a functioning crossing mechanism are different requirements
- Yes; villi are holes straight into blood
???
The second. More surface can provide room for more transport machinery, but it cannot replace a missing transport mechanism. Villi are tissue projections lined with cells, not open funnels into vessels.
:::

:::evidence Measure a folded surface carefully | A reassessment published in 2014
Herbert Helander and Lars Fändriks combined a literature review with microscopic measurements of normal adult gut lining. Their abstract reports an estimated total muc

sections.heading: The missing reservoir
sections.excerpt:
:::case The patient whose gallbladder was removed
This is a fictional reasoning case, not advice about any individual patient. A person's gallbladder has been removed. The liver and pancreas still function, and the remaining bile ducts provide an open route to the duodenum.

One pupil says: “There can be no bile, because the gallbladder made it.” Another says: “Then fat cannot be chemically digested, because bile was the fat-digesting enzyme.” A third says: “Nothing at all has changed: production, storage and delivery are the same.”

Correct all three claims. What could continue, what has changed, and why would the drawing be insufficient to predict every person's experience after the operation?
???
The **liver makes bile**. Removing the gallbladder removes its storage and concentration function, not the liver's production. Bile can flow through the remaining ducts from liver to duodenum, without first waiting in that reservoir. The storage and meal-linked delivery pattern have therefore changed even though bile remains available.

Bile helps disperse fat and present its products; it is not lipase. Pancreatic lipase can still catalyse molecular hydrolysis when enzyme, water, substr

callouts.title: Imagine a starch-containing food particle in the small intestine, surrounded by fluid but still in the gut's central space. Which event would establish absorption of material from it?
callouts.body:
- It has passed below the stomach, so absorption is already complete
- Suitable substances cross the gut's epithelial lining into the internal tissues
- The particle leaves the body as faeces
???
The second. Position along the tube is not proof of crossing its lining. Digestion can produce absorbable substances in the central space; absorption then requires passage across the barrier. Unabsorbed remnants can continue along the tube and leave.

callouts.title: > “Digestion makes energy, and anything left over is excretion.”
callouts.body: Digestion changes food's physical form and chemical molecules. Respiration is a separate set of reactions transferring chemical energy for cellular metabolism, including ATP regeneration. Egestion removes undigested remnants; excretion concerns metabolic waste or excess substances. Neither process creates energy or makes atoms disappear.

callouts.title: 0610 (2026–2028) Topic 7.2 names ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion, and the canal and associated organs. Its absorption definition uses movement from intestines into blood; retain that exam wording alongside the fuller blood-or-lymph routes below. This chapter teaches food processing and some nutrient roles; it does not cover all of Topic 7.1's balanced-diet, dietary-source and deficiency objectives.
Gastric juice is collected and placed with food in a warm vessel outside the stomach. If food breaks down there too, which claim is challenged?
callouts.body:
- Digestive juice can carry out chemical work apart from muscular grinding
- All stomach digestion must be caused by its muscular wall rubbing on food
- The whole intestinal absorption route has been reproduced in the vessel
???
The second claim is challenged. Chemical activity can occur without the stomach wall doing the grinding. This observation does not tell us that acid alone is responsible, nor does it show absorption into living tissues.

If an enzyme helps a bond undergo hydrolysis, does the energy come simply from breaking that isolated bond?
???
No. Breaking an isolated chemical bond requires energy. The overall reaction also forms bonds and changes interactions with surrounding water. Its complete free-energy change and coupling determine available energy transfer. An enzyme lowers an activation barrier; it does not supply a fresh packet of net energy each time.

callouts.title: > “Acid does the digesting, so the right pH is the same everywhere.”
callouts.body: An enzyme supplies the catalytic mechanism; pH affects whether its active site and substrate are in suitable chemical states. Pepsin works in acidic stomach conditions; trypsin acts in the different conditions of the small intestine. Enzymes have particular substrates and conditions, and protection is actively maintained rather than guaranteed.

callouts.title: 0610 Topic 7.3 names physical digestion, tooth types and structures, and stomach mixing. Topic 7.4 distinguishes amylase, protease and lipase; Supplement makes the starch sequence **amylase → maltose, then maltase → glucose**, and contrasts pepsin's acidic conditions with trypsin's intestinal conditions. Protease names do not imply that pepsin alone completes protein digestion to amino acids.
One spherical fat droplet is replaced by eight equal spheres with the same combined volume. Which claim follows from geometry alone?
callouts.body:
- Each sphere has one-eighth the radius and the total area is eight times as large
- Each sphere has half the radius and the total area doubles
- Fatty acids and glycerol must have formed because the droplets are smaller
???
The second. Halving each radius reduces each sphere's volume to one-eighth and its area to one-quarter. Eight of those areas total twice the original area. That calculation changes the interface, not chemical identity; it does not establish a biological reaction-rate multiplier.

callouts.title: Divide the amount, not the molecule
callouts.body:
Use a small piece of familiar modelling clay or an adult-prepared piece of cool dough, a washable tray and a ruler. Keep it separate from food for eating; do not taste it. If flour irritates your skin, use suitable modelling clay instead. No knives, heating or chemicals are required.

Roll the material into one roughly spherical ball about 3 cm across, a chosen size large enough to compare with a ruler. Before dividing it, predict the change in radius and total surface area if the same amount becomes eight equal balls. Divide by hand and make eight balls as nearly equal as you can, without adding material. Compare their approximate diameters with the original diameter. Repeat the modelling with the same material; do the results vary?

The controlled quantity is the amount of material; the intended change is the number of approximately equal spheres. The model predicts about half the diameter and twice the total surface area. Your ruler does not directly measure all those surfaces: this is a geometric prediction supported only approximately by the shapes. Unequal balls, dents, cracks and material left on the tray limit the comparison. It shows neither bile chemistry nor lipase action nor intestinal absorption.

Return reusable clay to its container. Put used dough in ordinary household food waste, clean the tray and wash your hands. This proposed activity has been reviewed for feasibility, not physically trialled for the book.

callouts.title: > “Bile turns fat into tiny molecules, so lipase only has to absorb them.”
callouts.body: Bile helps disperse droplets and present digestion products. Lipase catalyses chemical hydrolysis; it does not perform the whole absorption route. A smaller droplet still contains many fat molecules, and a larger calculated interface does not fix the measured speed of digestion.

callouts.title: 0610 Supplement Topics 7.3–7.4 expects bile emulsification and its alkaline contribution to neutralisation; include pancreatic bicarbonate in the fuller mechanism. The Core lipase summary uses **fatty acids and glycerol**. Learn that net-breakdown convention while recognising that the main pancreatic products include **monoacylglycerols**, which retain glycerol attached to one fatty acid.
The intestine has a large folded surface, but a glucose transporter at its lumen-facing membrane stops functioning. Does extra surface alone guarantee the same glucose absorption?
callouts.body:
- Yes; surface area overrides all membrane chemistry
- No; area and a functioning crossing mechanism are different requirements
- Yes; villi are holes straight into blood
???
The second. More surface can provide room for more transport machinery, but it cannot replace a missing transport mechanism. Villi are tissue projections lined with cells, not open funnels into vessels.

If glucose moves from a low concentration in the lumen into a cell with a higher glucose concentration, can simple diffusion of glucose alone explain that net movement?
???
No. Simple diffusion alone gives net spreading down a concentration gradient when passage is possible. Glucose can enter by a coupled transporter using the downhill movement of sodium ions. An ATP-driven pump helps maintain the sodium electrochemical gradient. The glucose movement is therefore powered indirectly by ATP-supported ion transport, rather than by diffusion alone or the molecule wanting to enter.

callouts.title: > “Villi suck everything straight into blood, and the large intestine absorbs all the water.”
callouts.body: Villi provide a large, thinly lined surface, but particular transport mechanisms do the crossing. Much long-chain lipid material is packaged inside epithelial cells before entering lymph; some other lipid-derived substances use portal blood. Water is absorbed in both intestines, usually mainly in the small intestine. Names for structures cannot replace these routes and mechanisms.

callouts.title: 0610 Topic 7.5 Core places nutrient absorption and most water absorption in the small intestine, with some water absorption in the colon. Supplement asks for villi, microvilli, villus structure, capillaries and lacteals. Keep “one cell thick” attached to the absorptive epithelium, and distinguish absorption from later cellular assimilation.
The patient whose gallbladder was removed
callouts.body:
This is a fictional reasoning case, not advice about any individual patient. A person's gallbladder has been removed. The liver and pancreas still function, and the remaining bile ducts provide an open route to the duodenum.

One pupil says: “There can be no bile, because the gallbladder made it.” Another says: “Then fat cannot be chemically digested, because bile was the fat-digesting enzyme.” A third says: “Nothing at all has changed: production, storage and delivery are the same.”

Correct all three claims. What could continue, what has changed, and why would the drawing be insufficient to predict every person's experience after the operation?
???
The **liver makes bile**. Removing the gallbladder removes its storage and concentration function, not the liver's production. Bile can flow through the remaining ducts from liver to duodenum, without first waiting in that reservoir. The storage and meal-linked delivery pattern have therefore changed even though bile remains available.

Bile helps disperse fat and present its products; it is not lipase. Pancreatic lipase can still catalyse molecular hydrolysis when enzyme, water, substrate and suitable conditions are available. Pancreatic bicarbonate also contributes to neutralising incoming acid. Separating production, storage, delivery, physical dispersion and chemical reaction avoids all three mistakes.

The arrangement explains why gallbladder removal need not abolish fat digestion. It does not promise identical digestion or symptoms for everyone. Duct condition, other organs and individual circumstances matter; the model supplies no personal diagnosis, diet prescription or universal prediction.

sections.heading: 8.1 Moving air to an exchange surface
sections.excerpt:
Take a quiet breath through your nose. Air enters because pressure inside the alveoli briefly falls below pressure outside. Your respiratory muscles create that difference by expanding the chest. Follow the movement first, then ask how chest movement reaches the lungs.
:::predict
During quiet inhalation, your diaphragm contracts and flattens downward while your ribcage swings upward and outward. Which sequence explains why outside air enters the alveoli?
- Alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric pressure and drives air inward
- Thoracic volume increases, lowering alveolar gas pressure slightly below atmospheric pressure so outside air is pushed in
- Incoming air forces the passive chest wall and diaphragm to expand like someone blowing up a party balloon
???
The second. In normal breathing, respiratory muscles expand the thoracic cavity first. Increasing the enclosed gas volume lowers alveolar pressure slightly below outside atmospheric pressure (about −1 mmHg gauge), and the higher outside air pressure pushes air down the airway into the lungs.
:::

:::evidence Stereology across two lungs, not a fixed universal count | Ochs et al., 2004
Textbooks often repeat that a human has “3

sections.heading: 8.2 Harvey’s circulation question and quantitative evidence
sections.excerpt:
Once oxygen crosses the alveolar wall into pulmonary capillaries, blood must carry it—along with the nutrients absorbed in Chapter 7—to every organ in the body. Today the word “circulation” is so familiar that we forget it had to be proved. For centuries before 1628, European and Islamic physicians debated how blood moved. In the dominant tradition descending from **Galen** of Pergamon (second century CE), chyle from the gut was turned by the liver into dark nutritive blood that drifted outward through the veins to nourish the organs, while a separate vital stream moved in the arteries; most of that blood was thought to be **consumed by the tissues** rather than returning in a continuous loop.

:::predict
Suppose a physician calculates that the left ventricle ejects at least several kilograms of blood into the aorta every half hour—far more than the total blood in the body or the mass of food and drink taken in. What does that arithmetic establish by itself, and what does it still need mechanical experiments to show?
- The arithmetic alone proves the exact microscopic shape of capillaries and the role of oxygen in mitochondria
- The arithmetic rules out one-way manufacture and comp

sections.heading: 8.3 The heart and two connected circuits
sections.excerpt:
Why do mammals and birds have a **four-chambered heart** divided down the middle by a solid muscular wall, rather than a single two-chambered pump like a bony fish?

Compare the two designs honestly—without treating a fish as a defective human. In a fish's ==single circulation==, the heart has one main atrium and one ventricle that pumps deoxygenated blood forward to the **gill capillaries**. Blood picks up oxygen across the thin gill lamellae, and then flows **directly on** into the systemic capillaries of the body before returning to the heart, passing through the heart **once** for each complete circuit of the body. Because the narrow gill capillaries offer resistance, blood pressure drops sharply across the gills (`Heart → Gills (P drops) → Body tissues (low P) → Heart`). That lower systemic pressure suits a buoyant aquatic ectotherm whose body is supported by water and whose metabolic oxygen demand is lower than a mammal's.

:::note Single circulation
A circulatory plan (as in bony fish) in which blood passes through the heart once for each complete circuit of the body, flowing from heart to gill capillaries and directly on to body capillaries before returning to the heart.
::

sections.heading: 8.4 Vessels, capillaries, tissue fluid and blood as a multi-job tissue
sections.excerpt:
Once the left ventricle ejects blood into the aorta, the blood travels through a branching tree of vessels—**arteries → arterioles → capillaries → venules → veins**—before returning to the heart. Why doesn't the body use the same kind of pipe everywhere? Because three different mechanical jobs require three different wall designs.

:::predict
A single capillary is microscopic (about 8 µm in internal diameter, barely wide enough for one red blood cell), whereas the aorta is about 2.5 cm wide. When blood leaves the aorta and branches into the body's capillary beds, does the blood speed up like water squirting out of a pinched garden hose, or slow down to a crawl?
- It speeds up dramatically because each capillary is much narrower than the aorta
- It slows down ~1,000-fold because billions of capillaries in parallel have a combined cross-sectional area roughly 1,000 times larger than the single aorta
- It keeps the exact same linear speed (in mm/s) in every vessel because cardiac output is constant
???
The second. Pinched-hose intuition applies only when the **entire flow** is forced through **one** narrow nozzle. In the body, the single aorta (A ≈ 4.5 cm²) branches into billions of c

sections.heading: A hole between the ventricles
sections.excerpt:
:::fig c8_septal_defect_case() | Compare an intact ventricular septum (left) with an uncomplicated post-natal ventricular septal defect (right). Because left ventricular systolic pressure (~115–120 mmHg) is much higher than right ventricular pressure (~25–35 mmHg), oxygenated blood jets left-to-right into the right ventricle and recycles through the lungs.

:::case The child with a hole in the septum
This is a fictional reasoning case, not clinical advice about any individual patient. A paediatric cardiologist uses echocardiography to examine a child who becomes breathless during playground games and has a loud harsh sound (a **systolic murmur**) between the normal “lub” and “dub” heart sounds. The scan shows an opening large enough to produce the stipulated extra pulmonary flow and symptoms in the muscular wall between the left and right ventricles—an uncomplicated post-natal **ventricular septal defect (VSD)**—while all four heart valves are normal.

One pupil says: “Because the right ventricle holds deoxygenated blood, a hole in the septum must send dark deoxygenated blood straight from the right ventricle into the left ventricle and aorta, turning the child's lips blue immediat

callouts.title: During quiet inhalation, your diaphragm contracts and flattens downward while your ribcage swings upward and outward. Which sequence explains why outside air enters the alveoli?
callouts.body:
- Alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric pressure and drives air inward
- Thoracic volume increases, lowering alveolar gas pressure slightly below atmospheric pressure so outside air is pushed in
- Incoming air forces the passive chest wall and diaphragm to expand like someone blowing up a party balloon
???
The second. In normal breathing, respiratory muscles expand the thoracic cavity first. Increasing the enclosed gas volume lowers alveolar pressure slightly below outside atmospheric pressure (about −1 mmHg gauge), and the higher outside air pressure pushes air down the airway into the lungs.

callouts.title: Time your resting breaths and test the dead-space arithmetic
callouts.body:
Use a wristwatch or wall clock with a second hand, a notebook and a pencil, sitting quietly in a chair. Do not hold your breath, hyperventilate or exercise to exhaustion.

Sit quietly for two minutes, then count how many normal breaths you take in one full minute (or ask a family member to count while you read so you do not consciously alter your rhythm). Write down your resting breathing rate f in breaths per minute. Now use a chosen illustrative tidal volume—say 400 mL per breath and an assumed conducting airway dead space of 120 mL—to calculate both your **total minute ventilation** (f × 400 mL) and your **fresh alveolar ventilation** (f × (400 − 120) mL). Next, calculate what would happen if your total minute ventilation stayed identical, but you took twice as many breaths at half the depth (2f × 200 mL).

The controlled quantity in the second calculation is total air moved per minute; the changed variable is breath depth versus rate. Your watch measures breathing frequency, not actual lung volumes or gas partial pressures; the volumes are chosen model assumptions to reveal why every breath pays the dead-space tax first.

Put your pencil and notebook away. This proposed activity has been reviewed for feasibility, not physically trialled for the book.

Why does blood returning from working leg muscles to the lungs have a lower oxygen partial pressure and a higher carbon dioxide partial pressure than alveolar air?
???
In Chapter 6, aerobic cellular respiration inside working muscle cells uses oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor (forming water) and releases carbon dioxide as carbon compounds are oxidised to regenerate ATP. Tissue blood therefore loses oxygen to the muscle cells and picks up carbon dioxide before returning to the right side of the heart and lungs.

callouts.title: > “We breathe in pure oxygen and breathe out pure carbon dioxide, and the diaphragm sucks the air into our lungs.”
callouts.body: Inspired air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen; expired air still contains about 16% oxygen alongside 4% carbon dioxide and 78% nitrogen. And muscles cannot pull on gas molecules from afar: contracting the diaphragm and external intercostals expands thoracic volume, lowering alveolar pressure slightly below atmospheric pressure so outside air is pushed in.

callouts.title: Cambridge 0610 links increased breathing during activity with CO₂ production and detection by the brain. Retain that school account alongside the fuller distinction: increased production is not the same as increased arterial concentration, and exercise also recruits neural control.

Suppose a physician calculates that the left ventricle ejects at least several kilograms of blood into the aorta every half hour—far more than the total blood in the body or the mass of food and drink taken in. What does that arithmetic establish by itself, and what does it still need mechanical experiments to show?
callouts.body:
- The arithmetic alone proves the exact microscopic shape of capillaries and the role of oxygen in mitochondria
- The arithmetic rules out one-way manufacture and complete consumption of blood by tissues, requiring blood to return and recirculate, while ligature and valve experiments establish the one-way direction of flow in arteries and veins
- The arithmetic proves that Galen thought the liver made a person's entire body weight of blood every hour
???
The second. A conservative lower-bound multiplication rules out continuous one-way production from food and complete tissue consumption unless the vessels burst or run dry. Mechanical experiments with vessel pinching, arm bandages and venous valves then demonstrate that arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins return it towards the heart.

callouts.title: > “Harvey discovered capillaries and oxygen in London in 1628 by calculating 70 beats per minute times 60 mL.”
callouts.body: Harvey lectured in London from 1616, but *De Motu Cordis* was published in **Frankfurt** in 1628. His Chapter IX calculation used deliberately tiny apothecaries' weights (such as 1 drachm or half an ounce per beat over 1,000 beats in half an hour), not modern metric millilitres. He never saw capillaries—**Marcello Malpighi** observed them in frog lungs with a microscope in **1661**—and oxygen was not identified until the 1770s.

callouts.title: When an exam question gives heart rate and stroke volume, use Cardiac output = Heart rate × Stroke volume and watch units carefully (1 L = 1,000 mL). Keep one-way flow linked to **valves** preventing backflow and **pressure differences** generated by muscular contraction.

In a healthy resting person with an intact septum, the left ventricular muscular wall is about three times thicker than the right ventricular wall. Which statement correctly compares what the two ventricles pump each minute?
callouts.body:
- The left ventricle pumps three times as many litres per minute as the right ventricle because its wall is three times thicker
- Both ventricles pump the same volume per minute in series, but the left ventricle generates ~5 times higher systolic pressure to overcome the resistance of the whole-body systemic circuit
- The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood because its thick muscular wall adds oxygen molecules to the blood
???
The second. Because the pulmonary and systemic circuits are connected in series in a closed loop, both ventricles must pump the same steady volume per minute (Q_p = Q_s, e.g. 4.2 L min⁻¹); otherwise blood would pile up in one circuit. The left ventricle's thicker muscle generates much higher pressure (~120 mmHg vs ~25 mmHg), while oxygenation happens in the lungs, never in the heart wall.

callouts.title: > “The left ventricle has a thicker wall because it contains more blood, and the heart muscle absorbs its oxygen straight from the blood inside the left ventricle.”
callouts.body: Both ventricles pump the same stroke volume (~60–70 mL) and the same cardiac output per minute in series; the left ventricular wall is thicker because it must generate ~5 times higher **pressure** (~120 mmHg vs ~25 mmHg) to drive blood through the whole body. And the ventricular wall is far too thick for oxygen to diffuse from the chamber lumen: cardiac muscle depends on the **coronary arteries** branching from the aorta.

callouts.title: Cambridge 0610 asks you to connect heart structures, valves and wall thickness with their functions, compare single and double circulation, and describe monitoring and coronary heart disease. Explain pressure differences and flow direction before learning the structure names.

A single capillary is microscopic (about 8 µm in internal diameter, barely wide enough for one red blood cell), whereas the aorta is about 2.5 cm wide. When blood leaves the aorta and branches into the body's capillary beds, does the blood speed up like water squirting out of a pinched garden hose, or slow down to a crawl?
callouts.body:
- It speeds up dramatically because each capillary is much narrower than the aorta
- It slows down ~1,000-fold because billions of capillaries in parallel have a combined cross-sectional area roughly 1,000 times larger than the single aorta
- It keeps the exact same linear speed (in mm/s) in every vessel because cardiac output is constant
???
The second. Pinched-hose intuition applies only when the **entire flow** is forced through **one** narrow nozzle. In the body, the single aorta (A ≈ 4.5 cm²) branches into billions of capillaries arranged in parallel whose **combined cross-sectional area** is roughly 4,500 cm². By conservation of volume flow (v = Q / A_total), a ~1,000-fold increase in total area reduces average linear speed ~1,000-fold (from ~180 mm s⁻¹ to ~0.2 mm s⁻¹), giving time for diffusion across the capillary wall.

In Chapter 2 we saw that a mature mammalian red blood cell has a biconcave disc shape and lacks a nucleus. How do both features suit its job in a capillary?
???
The biconcave disc shape (thinner in the centre than at the rim) provides a larger surface-area-to-volume ratio than a sphere of the same volume, shortening the diffusion distance for oxygen entering and leaving every part of the cell, and lets the cell flex through narrow 8 µm capillaries. Lacking a nucleus (and mitochondria) leaves more internal room for millions of **haemoglobin** molecules and ensures the red blood cell does not consume the oxygen it is transporting.

callouts.title: > “Tissue fluid is just whole blood that leaked out of broken capillaries, and blood clots because red blood cells dry up in the air.”
callouts.body: Healthy capillaries are not torn open: water and small solutes filter through microscopic gaps between endothelial cells, while **red blood cells and large plasma proteins stay inside the capillary**. And clotting is an enzyme-controlled chemical cascade triggered by **platelets**, converting **soluble fibrinogen** into an **insoluble fibrin mesh** that traps red blood cells even while wet.

callouts.title: Cambridge 0610 uses phagocytes and lymphocytes as useful blood-cell categories. A lobed neutrophil is one phagocyte; B lymphocytes can develop into antibody-secreting cells, while other lymphocytes have other roles. Keep clotting linked to soluble fibrinogen becoming an insoluble fibrin mesh.
The child with a hole in the septum
callouts.body:
This is a fictional reasoning case, not clinical advice about any individual patient. A paediatric cardiologist uses echocardiography to examine a child who becomes breathless during playground games and has a loud harsh sound (a **systolic murmur**) between the normal “lub” and “dub” heart sounds. The scan shows an opening large enough to produce the stipulated extra pulmonary flow and symptoms in the muscular wall between the left and right ventricles—an uncomplicated post-natal **ventricular septal defect (VSD)**—while all four heart valves are normal.

One pupil says: “Because the right ventricle holds deoxygenated blood, a hole in the septum must send dark deoxygenated blood straight from the right ventricle into the left ventricle and aorta, turning the child's lips blue immediately.”

A second pupil says: “No blood will cross the hole at all, because both ventricles contract at the exact same moment and cancel each other out.”

A third pupil says: “Only the systemic circuit is affected; the lungs receive the exact same blood flow per minute as before (Q_p = Q_s).”

Use the pressures of the two ventricles to correct all three claims. Which way does blood actually shunt across the defect during ventricular systole, what happens to pulmonary blood flow (Q_p) relative to systemic blood flow (Q_s), and why does the child feel breathless on exertion?
???
Fluid flows from **higher pressure to lower pressure**, even when two chambers contract at the same time. During post-natal ventricular systole, the thick-walled **left ventricle** generates roughly **115–120 mmHg**, whereas the thinner-walled **right ventricle** generates only about **25–35 mmHg**.

1. **Why the first and second pupils are wrong:** Because left ventricular pressure is more than three times right ventricular pressure during systole, the pressure difference drives a **left-to-right shunt**: already-oxygenated blood from the left ventricle jets across the septal defect **into the right ventricle**, not from right to left into the aorta. (This case assumes lower right-sided pressure. Other haemodynamic situations can change shunt direction.) The turbulent high-velocity jet from left to right during contraction produces the **systolic murmur** heard between “lub” and “dub”.
2. **Why the third pupil is wrong (Q_p > Q_s):** The right ventricle now receives both the normal venous return from the venae cavae **plus** the shunted oxygenated blood from the left ventricle. It therefore pumps an abnormally large volume into the **pulmonary artery and lungs** (Q_p > Q_s, for the explorer’s chosen example, 6.72 L min⁻¹ through the lungs while 4.2 L min⁻¹ enters the aorta; this assumed ratio is not predicted from every defect’s diameter).
3. **Why exertion causes breathlessness:** Recycling extra blood through the pulmonary circuit overloads the pulmonary capillaries and increases the work of the ventricles, while leaving less reserve capacity to boost systemic oxygen delivery to working muscles during exercise.

sections.heading: 9.1 Two ways to coordinate a 30-trillion-cell body: nerves and hormones
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, a pavement startle and a hot kitchen tawa

Compare two moments from an ordinary day. First, your fingertips accidentally brush the edge of a hot steel tawa on the stove. Only the muscles of that arm need to contract, and they need to act rapidly to limit further heat exposure. Second, as you walk past a parked autorickshaw at dusk, a dog barks inches from your leg. Now a single muscle twitch is not enough: your heart, lungs, pupils, liver and leg arterioles all need to shift into emergency readiness together and stay ready for several minutes.

Every coordination pathway in a living organism begins with a detectable change in the internal or external environment: a ==stimulus== (plural: **stimuli**), such as heat, light, sound, gravity or a change in blood glucose concentration. Specialised cells or nerve endings called **receptors** detect a particular stimulus. A **coordinator** (such as the brain, spinal cord or an endocrine gland) integrates the incoming information and sends a signal to an ==effector==—a **muscle** that contracts or a **gland** that secretes a chemical—producing the organism's **response**.

:::note Stimulus
A detectable change in the internal

sections.heading: 9.2 Fast electrical wiring: neurones, the reflex arc, and the synapse
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Plymouth, 1939 & TIFR Colaba, Mumbai, 1976

Look closely at the wiring that pulls your hand off a hot pan. In Chapter 2 we saw why a cell cannot grow into a thick, metre-wide sphere without starving its interior of diffusion surface. Yet a single **motor neurone** running from the lower spinal cord in your back to the muscles of your big toe can be **one metre long**. It solves the geometry trap by keeping its conducting fibre—the **axon**—microscopically thin (typically 1 to 20 µm across), while wrapping that fibre in insulating layers so electrical impulses race along it at up to **70 to 120 m/s**.

### Three specialist neurones: sensory, relay and motor

In Cambridge 0610 diagrams and photomicrographs (Topic 14.1.4), you can tell the three classes of neurone apart immediately by the position of the **cell body** (containing the nucleus, cytoplasm, ribosomes and mitochondria) and the length of the fibres:

1. **Sensory neurone:** carries electrical impulses **from a receptor to the CNS**. Its receptor endings join a long fibre (**dendron**) leading towards the spinal cord, and its **cell body sits out on a side branch** (in a swelling called the dorsal root ganglion just

sections.heading: 9.3 Sense organs and the human eye: catching and focusing light
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai, stepping from midday marine glare into a shaded lobby

Step out of midday sunlight along Marine Drive into a dimly lit building hallway. At first the hallway looks nearly black; within seconds your **pupils** widen automatically, and over the next few minutes your **rod** cells take over from your **cone** cells so you can make out the stairs in monochrome. Glance down at your watch (25 cm away) and then out through the doorway at a ship on the horizon (kilometres away): without your having to turn a focusing ring with your fingers, a circular muscle inside your eye adjusts the curvature of your **lens** so both images land sharply on your **retina**. Meanwhile, on a windowsill beside the stairs, a potted moong seedling with no eyes, nerves or muscles has bent its growing stem steadily towards the sunlit glass.

### Sense organs and the architecture of the mammalian eye (0610 14.2.1–14.2.3)

A ==sense organ== is a group of receptor cells responding to a specific stimulus, together with the tissues that deliver or focus that stimulus (0610 14.2.1):

- **Eye:** photoreceptor cells (rods and cones in the retina) respond to **light**.
- **Ear:** mechanoreceptor hair ce

sections.heading: 9.4 Slow chemical steering in plants: phototropism, gravitropism, and auxin
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Calcutta, 1901, Utrecht, 1926 & a potted seedling on a Mumbai windowsill

Plants have no brain, no spinal cord and no muscles. Yet as **Jagadish Chandra Bose** showed in Calcutta at the turn of the twentieth century with his optical-lever **crescograph** (magnifying plant growth ten thousand times) and fine galvanometers, plants are far from passive: wounded or touched leaves such as *Mimosa pudica* (*chui-mui*) can transmit rapid **electrical action potentials** along their vascular bundles to trigger turgor folding within a second, while growing shoots and roots steer their architecture over hours by regulating cell elongation.

:::story p-bose

In Cambridge 0610 Topic 14.5, a **tropic response (tropism)** is a growth movement of a plant part in response to the direction of an external stimulus:

- ==Phototropism== is a response in which parts of a plant grow **towards or away from the direction of a light source**. Plant **shoots** show **positive phototropism** (growing towards light so leaves intercept sunlight for photosynthesis, Chapter 5), whereas most **roots** show either no response or **negative phototropism** (growing away from light).
