sections.heading: The pufferfish molecule that silences sodium gates
sections.excerpt:
:::case The pufferfish molecule that silences sodium gates
In 1964, the neurophysiologists Toshio Narahashi, John W. Moore and William R. Scott used a voltage clamp on giant axons to solve a famous marine mystery: how **tetrodotoxin (TTX)**—a small positively charged guanidinium molecule produced by marine bacteria and accumulated in the liver and ovaries of pufferfish (*Takifugu*)—causes rapid skeletal-muscle paralysis at nanomolar concentrations. *(This is a molecular reasoning case from laboratory neurophysiology, never a substance for experiment.)*

Three experimental clues sit in the laboratory file when nanomolar TTX is added to the saline bathing a motor nerve–muscle preparation:

1. **Clue 1 (Resting membrane check):** The axon's **resting potential stays steady at −70 mV**, and when the membrane is held depolarised under voltage clamp, outward **potassium (`K⁺`) current** through voltage-gated `K⁺` channels flows at its normal size.
2. **Clue 2 (Axonal spike check):** Stimulating the motor axon electrically fails to produce the inward **sodium (`Na⁺`) current**: the +30 mV action potential vanishes completely, just as warming to 32 °C silenced Obaid Siddiqi's `para^ts` fru

callouts.title: A signal must activate particular arm muscles rapidly. Which feature most directly gives a nervous pathway that precision?
callouts.body:
- The route of connected neurones delivers signals to selected muscles
- Every cell reached by a hormone must respond to it
- A stronger stimulus makes an impulse travel to every muscle
???
The first. Connections route neural signals, while receptors determine which cells respond to a circulating hormone. Both systems can coordinate several organs; their typical speed and routing differ.

callouts.title: > “The pancreas sends insulin straight to the liver because the hormone knows where it is needed.”
callouts.body: A hormone molecule has no map or destination. A hormone enters circulating blood; its route depends on where it was released. Pancreatic venous blood reaches the liver through the portal circulation before joining the wider circulation. Blood can distribute a hormone broadly, rather than delivering it only to cells that respond. Only **target organs** whose cells display **complementary receptor proteins** bind the hormone and change their activity.

callouts.title: School uses the typical comparison of fast, short-lived nervous responses and slower, longer-lasting hormonal responses. Keep the qualification: both systems can act together, and receptors determine which cells respond to a hormone.
In an axon firing an action potential from left to right, which way do the sodium ions (`Na⁺`) that generate the +30 mV spike primarily move when the voltage-gated `Na⁺` channels open?
callouts.body:
- From left to right for the entire 1-metre length of the axon, like electrons in a wire
- Sideways across the cell membrane from the outside fluid into the cytoplasm, down their electrochemical gradient
- Out of the cytoplasm into the extracellular fluid, pumped by ATP during the spike
???
The second choice. Each patch of membrane opens its voltage-gated `Na⁺` channels so `Na⁺` ions cross **sideways** (inward across the 7 nm lipid membrane), and a tiny local spread of that inward current triggers the next patch's channels to open. The wave travels down the axon, while the ions move across the boundary.

callouts.title: > “A stronger stimulus, like a hotter pan, makes each nerve impulse taller (more millivolts).”
callouts.body: Action potentials are **all-or-nothing**: once a stimulus depolarises the membrane past threshold (−55 mV), the voltage-gated `Na⁺` channels open fully and fire the same ~+30 mV spike every time. A stronger stimulus signals its intensity by firing **more impulses per second** (higher frequency) and by recruiting **more neurones**, never by sending a taller voltage spike.

callouts.title: > “Catching a dropped 30 cm ruler between your thumb and forefinger measures your spinal reflex time.”
callouts.body: Catching a falling ruler is a **conscious voluntary reaction** (~150 to 250 ms), **not** a simple spinal reflex arc. To catch the ruler, light from the moving ruler must stimulate photoreceptors in your **retina** → impulses travel along the **optic nerve** to the **visual cortex** at the back of your brain → relay neurones pass the signal to your **decision and motor cortex** → impulses travel down the **spinal cord** and **motor neurones** to your finger muscles. Its measured time includes visual processing, response selection and finger movement; it is not a measurement of one spinal pathway. (Never attempt to test a withdrawal reflex using heat or sharp objects.)

callouts.title: Investigation 9.2: Measure your voluntary visual reaction time with a 30 cm ruler
callouts.body:
You can measure the total time required for a **conscious voluntary reaction pathway** (eye → optic nerve → brain visual and motor cortex → spinal cord → motor neurone → finger muscles) using a rigid **30 cm plastic or wooden ruler**, a notebook, and a partner sitting across a table in a well-lit room.

1. **Setup and controls:** Sit comfortably with your dominant forearm resting flat on the table and your hand extending just beyond the table edge, thumb and index finger held **4 cm apart** (check the gap with a spare ruler or mark so every trial starts with the same finger separation). Your partner holds the top of the 30 cm ruler vertically so the **0 cm mark** sits exactly level with the top of your thumb, without touching your fingers.
2. **Procedure:** Without giving a verbal countdown or moving their hand upward first, your partner releases the ruler at an unannounced moment within a 5-second window. As soon as you **see** the ruler move, pinch your thumb and index finger shut to catch it. Record the centimetre mark (`d`, in cm) at the top of your thumb across **5 repeat trials** (discarding any false start where you pinched before release).
3. **Convert fall distance `d` into voluntary reaction time `t`:** Under free fall from rest with gravitational acceleration `g ≈ 9.8 m/s² = 980 cm/s²`, distance and time are linked by `d = ½gt²`, so `t = √(2d ÷ g)`:
   - Caught at **10 cm** (`0.10 m`): `t = √(0.20 ÷ 9.8) ≈ 0.143 s =` **143 ms**.
   - Caught at **18 cm** (`0.18 m`): `t = √(0.36 ÷ 9.8) ≈ 0.192 s =` **192 ms**.
   - Caught at **25 cm** (`0.25 m`): `t = √(0.50 ÷ 9.8) ≈ 0.226 s =` **226 ms**.
4. **Controlled comparison:** Keep the same hand, posture, 4 cm starting finger gap and room lighting, and compare 5 trials when **focused solely on the ruler** versus 5 trials while **counting backwards aloud by sevens from 100** (cognitive distraction in the brain's cortex).
5. **What is measured vs model limits:** You directly measure the **catch distance `d` in cm**; the millisecond value is calculated assuming zero air resistance, release from exact rest (`v₀ = 0`), and a consistent 4 cm pinch travel. Notice why distraction in the brain lengthens this **voluntary reaction time**, whereas a true spinal reflex arc is automatic. Pack the ruler away when finished. *This proposed activity has been reviewed for feasibility, not physically trialled for the book.*

callouts.title: For 0610, identify sensory, relay and motor neurones and trace the simple reflex arc. Its synapse sequence describes the excitatory chemical relay taught here; use release, diffusion, receptor binding and stimulation of the receiving cell in that order.
When you look up from reading a book held 25 cm from your eyes to watch a boat on the horizon 2 km away, what happens to your ciliary muscles, suspensory ligaments and lens?
callouts.body:
- Ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments slacken, and the lens becomes thicker and more convex
- Ciliary muscles relax, suspensory ligaments are pulled tight, and the lens is pulled thinner and less convex
- Ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments are pulled tight, and the lens becomes thinner
???
The second choice. Because the ciliary muscle is a circular sphincter ring around the lens, **relaxing** it restores tension in the surrounding fibres, which pulls the **suspensory ligaments tight** and stretches the **lens thinner and less convex** so nearly parallel rays from the distant boat are refracted less and focus sharply on the retina.

callouts.title: > “When you focus on a distant object, your ciliary muscles have to contract hard to pull the suspensory ligaments tight and flatten the lens.”
callouts.body: It is the exact opposite—and that is why looking at a distant horizon rests your eyes, whereas reading small print close up makes your ciliary muscles tired. Because the ciliary muscle is a **circular ring** around the lens, **contracting** it makes the ring *smaller*, which **slackens** the suspensory ligaments so the elastic lens bulges thicker for **near** vision. **Relaxing** the ciliary muscle restores tension in the surrounding fibres, pulling the suspensory ligaments **tight** to flatten the lens for **distant** vision.

callouts.title: Investigation 9.3: Map your own blind spot and observe the pupil reflex in ordinary room light
callouts.body:
You can test two structural features of the human eye—the receptor-free **blind spot** (where the optic nerve exits the retina) and the **pupil reflex**—using an index card, a black pen, a 30 cm ruler and ordinary indoor room lighting. **Eye safety rule:** never look at the Sun and never shine a torch, phone LED or laser into anyone's eye; ordinary desk or window lighting is completely sufficient.

1. **Part A — Mapping the blind spot:** On a plain white card, draw a bold `+` cross on the left and a solid 4 mm black dot `●` exactly **8 cm to the right** of the `+`. Hold the card at arm's length (~50 cm) in front of your face with the `+` directly in front of your open **right eye** and the `●` to the right.
2. **Procedure:** Close your **left eye** and stare steadily at the `+` with your **right eye** (do not glance over at the dot). Slowly bring the card closer to your face while keeping your right eye fixed on the `+`. Search slowly over a comfortable range of distances for the dot to disappear; keep looking at the cross. The distance varies with the arrangement and your eye. Move closer or farther to see whether it reappears. Record the position, or record that it did not disappear.
3. **Why it vanishes:** At that exact distance, light rays from the `●` land on the **blind spot** (optic disc) of your right retina—where over a million ganglion axons exit into the **optic nerve** and **zero rods or cones** are present.
4. **Part B — Partner pupil check:** With an adult, compare a partner's pupils in two ordinary indoor lighting conditions, keeping their viewing distance and direction steady. Move between a dimmer part of the room and a brighter part lit indirectly by a window. Allow time for adjustment and observe without shining a light into the eye. Both pupils respond together, so covering one eye while the other stays lit does not isolate dark adaptation. Record what you can see; a subtle or absent visible change is a valid observation. *This proposed activity has not been physically trialled for the book.*

callouts.title: For 0610, distinguish the pupil reflex from accommodation. Near focus: ciliary muscle contracts, ligaments slacken and the lens becomes more convex; distant focus reverses those changes.

In Frits Went's 1926 experiment, a small agar block soaked in auxin from a coleoptile tip is placed on the **left** side of a decapitated coleoptile stump kept in **complete darkness**. Which way does the coleoptile stump grow, and why?
callouts.body:
- It grows straight upward because there is no unilateral light in darkness
- It bends to the left (towards the agar block) because auxin pulls the tip towards itself
- It bends to the right (away from the agar block) because auxin diffuses down the left side and stimulates those shoot cells to elongate faster than the right side
???
The third choice. Auxin from the agar block diffuses downward along the **left** side of the shoot and **stimulates cell elongation** on that side; because the left side elongates faster than the right side, the stem curves to the **right** even in complete darkness.

callouts.title: > “Sunlight destroys auxin on the sunny side of a shoot, or warms the sunny side so it grows towards the window.”
callouts.body: Two classic traps sit in that sentence. First, if the sunny side elongated faster, the shoot would bend *away* from the window; a shoot bends towards light only because the **shaded side elongates faster**. Second, Frits Went's split-agar measurements showed that total auxin leaving a coleoptile tip stays the same in unilateral light as in darkness: light triggers **unequal lateral distribution** of auxin towards the shaded side rather than destroying it.

callouts.title: For 0610, describe auxin production, transport, unequal distribution and its effect on shoot elongation. The syllabus calls transport diffusion; directed cellular transport supplies the fuller mechanism.
The pufferfish molecule that silences sodium gates
callouts.body:
In 1964, the neurophysiologists Toshio Narahashi, John W. Moore and William R. Scott used a voltage clamp on giant axons to solve a famous marine mystery: how **tetrodotoxin (TTX)**—a small positively charged guanidinium molecule produced by marine bacteria and accumulated in the liver and ovaries of pufferfish (*Takifugu*)—causes rapid skeletal-muscle paralysis at nanomolar concentrations. *(This is a molecular reasoning case from laboratory neurophysiology, never a substance for experiment.)*

Three experimental clues sit in the laboratory file when nanomolar TTX is added to the saline bathing a motor nerve–muscle preparation:

1. **Clue 1 (Resting membrane check):** The axon's **resting potential stays steady at −70 mV**, and when the membrane is held depolarised under voltage clamp, outward **potassium (`K⁺`) current** through voltage-gated `K⁺` channels flows at its normal size.
2. **Clue 2 (Axonal spike check):** Stimulating the motor axon electrically fails to produce the inward **sodium (`Na⁺`) current**: the +30 mV action potential vanishes completely, just as warming to 32 °C silenced Obaid Siddiqi's `para^ts` fruit-fly axon.
3. **Clue 3 (Synapse check):** Applying acetylcholine directly onto the muscle's postsynaptic membrane still produces a **local endplate depolarisation**. This does not establish normal propagated muscle action potentials or whole-muscle contraction.

Using these three clues, answer three questions:
- Which specific membrane protein does tetrodotoxin block, and why does the resting potential remain at −70 mV?
- Why does action-potential-evoked acetylcholine release fail when the motor nerve is stimulated in the presence of TTX, while the postsynaptic response to directly supplied acetylcholine remains?
- How does TTX blockade differ from curare blockade (Section 9.2)?
???
- **Target protein & resting potential:** Tetrodotoxin plugs the outer pore of **voltage-gated sodium (`Na⁺`) channels** (its positively charged guanidinium group binds the selectivity mouth of the `Na⁺` pore while its bulky cage blocks hydrated `Na⁺` ions from entering). Because TTX does not block **potassium (`K⁺`) leak channels**, voltage-gated `K⁺` channels or Skou's **`Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase` pump**, the resting potassium gradient and **−70 mV resting potential** remain intact.
- **Why the synapse stays silent:** With voltage-gated `Na⁺` channels blocked along the axon, no action potential can propagate down the motor neurone to reach the **presynaptic knob**. Because the presynaptic membrane never depolarises, Step 1 of synaptic transmission (vesicle fusion and exocytosis) is never triggered, Clue 3 tests the receiving receptors, not presynaptic vesicle function. TTX can also affect skeletal-muscle sodium channels; a local endplate response is different from a propagated muscle spike. Spontaneous transmitter release is not excluded by failure of evoked release.
- **TTX versus curare:** **TTX** stops **axonal conduction** by blocking **voltage-gated `Na⁺` channels** *before* the impulse reaches the synapse (preventing neurotransmitter release), whereas **curare** leaves axonal conduction and presynaptic neurotransmitter release intact but blocks the **postsynaptic receptor proteins** (Step 3) across the synaptic gap.

sections.heading: 10.1 The thermostat and the pantry: homeostasis, negative feedback, and blood glucose
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Paris, 1859–1865, and Toronto, January 1922

Why do thirty-seven trillion human cells care so much about keeping the liquid around them steady? A single-celled amoeba in a huge pond can let the pond absorb its waste and buffer its temperature. Your brain neurones, heart muscle fibres and kidney cells do not live in an open pond; as the French physiologist Claude Bernard pointed out in Paris between 1859 and 1865, multicellular animals live inside an enclosed liquid **internal environment** (*milieu intérieur*)—the blood plasma and **tissue fluid** you traced in Chapter 8.

If the concentration of glucose, water or mineral ions in that internal bath drifts too far, or if its temperature shifts by more than a few degrees, cellular functions can be disrupted, with some tissues more vulnerable than others:

- If blood plasma and tissue fluid become **too concentrated** (too little water or too many dissolved solutes, lowering their **water potential**), water leaves your cells by **osmosis** (Chapter 3) and the cells shrink and dehydrate. If plasma becomes **too dilute** (too high a water potential), water enters cells by osmosis and brain cells swell inside the rigid skull.
-

sections.heading: 10.2 38 °C in Dadar: skin structure, evaporative cooling, and thermoregulation
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Outside Dadar railway station, Mumbai, 2:30 p.m. in May

Step out of the shade outside Dadar station at half past two in May. The weather screen reads **38 °C** with **65% relative humidity**. Your own heart, brain, liver and kidneys are sitting at a core temperature of **37.0 °C**.

Pause for a second and ask the question a physicist from Book 2 ([*The Moving World*](https://saxster.github.io/kym-physics/), Chapter 8) would ask. Whenever two objects are at different temperatures, thermal energy flows spontaneously by **conduction, convection and radiation** from the **hotter** one to the **colder** one—never the other way around. When you stood in a 22 °C room this morning, your 37 °C body was warmer than the room, so your skin steadily gave out thermal energy to the air.

Now, at 38 °C on the Dadar pavement, the outside air is **hotter than your body**, and meanwhile your own cells are continuously generating another **100 to 200 watts** of internal thermal energy through **aerobic respiration** (Chapter 6). Dry conduction and convection are now pushing thermal energy *into* you from the street, not taking it away. How can your body possibly stay at **37.0 °C** while pre

sections.heading: 10.3 The chemical cleanup crew: liver deamination, urea, and the kidney’s two-stage nephron ledger
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Philadelphia, 1924, and a Mumbai lunch table

At lunch after your walk in Dadar, you eat a bowl of *dal tadka* and *paneer*. In Chapter 7 you followed how stomach **pepsin** and intestinal **trypsin** and peptidases hydrolyse those dietary proteins into twenty kinds of **amino acids**, which cross the small-intestinal villi into capillaries and travel straight up the **hepatic portal vein** to the **liver**.

Now compare what your body can do with excess carbohydrate or fat versus excess amino acids:

- Extra **glucose** can be polymerised into **glycogen** in the liver and muscles, or converted into **fat** stored in adipose tissue.
- Extra **fatty acids and glycerol** are stored compactly in adipose tissue.
- **Excess amino acids, however, cannot be stored in a waiting tank** in the human body. Every day you eat protein, your cells take the exact amino acids they need right now for **assimilation**—building new cellular enzymes, structural proteins, and blood plasma proteins such as **albumin** and **fibrinogen** in the liver—and amino acids not used for synthesis can be broken down, with their nitrogen handled safely by the liver.

Before tracing how the liver and kidne

sections.heading: 10.4 The invisible border guard: pathogens, barriers, cholera, antibodies, and immunological memory
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Parel, Mumbai, 1958, Bongaon, 1971, and Vellore, 2014

Homeostasis and excretion keep your internal temperature, glucose, water and urea in balance. Yet a warm, nutrient-rich bath of blood plasma and tissue fluid held at 37.0 °C with 5.0 mmol/L glucose is also a five-star hotel for microscopic invaders.

Every time the June monsoon floods a street, or someone sneezes in a crowded carriage between Dadar and Churchgate, you encounter microorganisms seeking to enter that internal environment. In **Cambridge IGCSE (`0610 Topic 10.1`)**, keep two foundational definitions crisp:

- A ==pathogen== is a **disease-causing organism** (including disease-causing **bacteria**, **fungi**, **protoctists** such as the malaria parasite *Plasmodium*, and—by functional extension in medicine and exams—non-living **viruses**).
- A ==transmissible disease== is a **disease in which the pathogen can be passed from one host to another** (in contrast to non-transmissible diseases such as Type 1 diabetes, scurvy or coronary heart disease, which cannot be caught from another person).

:::note Pathogen and transmissible disease

callouts.title: Compare a homeostatic **negative feedback** loop with a **positive feedback** loop. After you eat a sweet mango and your blood glucose rises from 5.0 mmol/L to 8.5 mmol/L, what happens under negative feedback versus what would happen if blood glucose were controlled by positive feedback?
callouts.body:
- Under negative feedback, effectors push blood glucose higher to 12.0 mmol/L; under positive feedback, effectors bring it back to 5.0 mmol/L
- Under negative feedback, the pancreas and liver oppose the rise by storing glucose as glycogen so blood glucose returns toward 5.0 mmol/L; under positive feedback, a rise in blood glucose would trigger further glucose release into the blood, driving a runaway climb away from the set point
- Negative feedback means only decreases are allowed, whereas positive feedback means only increases are allowed
???
The second choice. In engineering and physiology, "negative" does not mean "bad" or "downward only"—it means the corrective action has the **opposite sign** (`−`) to the error from the set point. When blood glucose rises **above** 5.0 mmol/L, negative feedback pushes it **down**; when blood glucose falls **below** 5.0 mmol/L, negative feedback pushes it **up**. A **positive feedback** loop amplifies whatever change just happened (like a microphone held too close to a speaker), which drives a system further away from stability rather than maintaining homeostasis.

If glucose falls, must negative feedback make it fall further?
???
No. Negative feedback opposes the disturbance; low glucose calls for a response that raises it.

callouts.title: > "Glycogen and glucagon are just two spellings of the same word, and people with Type 1 diabetes can simply take insulin tablets after lunch."
callouts.body:
Look closely at the endings of the three words—the similar names describe different things:

- **Glucose** (`-ose` = sugar) is the **soluble monosaccharide** carried in blood plasma.
- **Glycogen** (`glyco-gen` = sugar-former) is the **insoluble storage polysaccharide** kept inside liver and muscle cells.
- **Glucagon** (`gluca-gon` = glucose-driver) is the **protein hormone** secreted by pancreatic alpha cells when blood glucose is low (`glucagon` tells the liver to turn `glycogen` back into `glucose`).
And **insulin** is a folded **protein** hormone: if swallowed as a pill, stomach acid and protease enzymes (**pepsin** and **trypsin**, Chapter 7) would digest it into amino acids in the gut before it could ever reach the bloodstream. That is why insulin must be **injected**.

callouts.title: Cambridge 0610 describes homeostasis as maintaining a constant internal environment and uses insulin, glucagon and liver glycogen to explain glucose regulation. Learn the opposing loops together: hormones signal cells to change reactions; they do not themselves turn into glucose or glycogen.

On two different afternoons, the dry-bulb air temperature in the shade is identical: **38 °C**. Afternoon A is in dry inland Nagpur (**20% relative humidity**, wet-bulb temperature **21 °C**). Afternoon B is on the humid Mumbai coast (**80% relative humidity**, wet-bulb temperature **34.8 °C**). A walker generates **180 W** of metabolic heat on both afternoons and secretes plenty of sweat. Why is the walker in far greater danger of overheating (heat exhaustion / heatstroke) in humid Mumbai than in dry Nagpur at the exact same 38 °C air temperature?
callouts.body:
- Because humid air has a higher temperature than dry air at 38 °C
- Because sweating cools the body only when the water in sweat **evaporates** (absorbing 2,420 J/g of latent heat); at 80% relative humidity the air is already nearly saturated with water vapour, so evaporation slows down and sweat merely drips off the skin without cooling it
- Because sweat glands stop secreting sweat whenever the air is humid
???
The second choice. Evaporation supplies the large cooling effect of sweat: escaping water vapour carries away about **2,420 J per gram** of latent heat. Liquid dripping from skin provides no evaporative latent-heat removal. With air hotter than skin, convection adds heat; radiation depends separately on surrounding surface temperatures (in fact, 38 °C air transfers heat *into* 35.6 °C skin). In the chosen dry-air example, sufficient sweat evaporation can remove over 220 W of heat. Humidity alone does not specify the rate: airflow, clothing and sweat supply matter too. In humid Mumbai (80% relative humidity), the air is already crowded with water vapour molecules returning to the liquid surface, so the air–skin conditions restrict net evaporation. If evaporation removes less heat than your body gains and produces, heat accumulates even while sweat drips from your skin.

callouts.title: > "When you get hot, your skin capillaries move closer to the surface of the skin and dilate; when you get cold, the capillaries move deeper down."
callouts.body:
The vessels remain in place. Explain the change in blood flow through them.

1. **Capillaries are fixed in place** in the dermis—they do not swim or migrate up and down through tissue.
2. **Capillary walls are only one endothelial cell thick** and contain **no muscle fibres**, so capillaries cannot actively constrict or dilate on their own.
3. What actually changes is the ring of **smooth muscle in the walls of the arterioles** that supply the skin surface capillaries: during **vasodilation**, the **arterioles** relax and widen so **more blood flows through the surface capillaries**; during **vasoconstriction**, the **arterioles** contract and narrow so **less blood flows through the surface capillaries**.

callouts.title: Two tumblers and a handkerchief: why dripping sweat does not cool
callouts.body:
*Note: This safe kitchen comparison is an educational design to illustrate evaporative cooling and relative humidity; it has not been classroom-trialled with pupils for this edition.*

Use three identical small stainless-steel tumblers, three cotton cloths, a kitchen thermometer and a transparent bag, with an adult supervising. Leave the water and tumblers in the same room until their starting temperatures are close to room temperature. Record the room temperature, then add equal water volumes and record each starting temperature. Wrap A in a damp, wrung-out cloth and B in a dry cloth. Wrap C in another damp cloth and enclose it in the bag without placing the bag near moving fan blades. Place them together in the same gentle airflow. Measure every 15 minutes for 45 minutes, using the same method and keeping A damp with room-temperature water.

Predict first: which tumbler will lose heat fastest? Compare temperature changes with the starting measurements. A may cool below room temperature as evaporation removes energy; the amount depends on humidity and airflow, so little measurable change is a valid result. B can approach room temperature through ordinary heat transfer. The bag around C restricts evaporation, but also changes airflow and insulation, so it is not a perfect one-variable comparison. Repeat if practical, note water added to A, and clean and put away the equipment afterwards. Do not taste experimental water.

callouts.title: Cambridge 0610 links sweating, insulation, shivering and brain coordination to temperature maintenance. For vasodilation and vasoconstriction, name the arterioles supplying fixed skin capillaries.

callouts.body:
Does every litre filtered become urine?
???
No. Most filtered water returns to blood; filtration and final excretion are different rates.

callouts.title: Your entire bloodstream contains only about **3 litres of liquid blood plasma**, yet your two kidneys filter **180 litres of fluid every single day** (60 times your total plasma volume) out of the blood into the nephron capsules. Look at the size of dissolved molecules in blood plasma:
callouts.body:
- **Plasma proteins (such as albumin):** relative molecular mass `M_r ≈ 66,500` (large folded chains)
- **Glucose:** `M_r = 180` (small six-carbon sugar)
- **Urea:** `M_r = 60` (tiny nitrogen waste)
- **Water & sodium/chloride ions:** `M_r = 18 to 35.5` (tiny)

Which explanation fits glucose in filtrate but ordinarily no glucose detected in urine?
- The glomerulus never admits glucose
- Glucose filters, then tubule transport recovers it
- Tubules turn every glucose molecule into urea
???
The second choice. The glomerular barrier admits glucose along with water, urea and ions. Tubule transporters normally recover nearly all that glucose. For our chosen adult illustration, 5.0 mmol/L equals 0.09 g/100 mL; filtering 180 L/day delivers about **162 g glucose per day** into tubules. That is a filtered load, not a daily loss. Insufficient recovery can cause glucose loss and increase urinary water loss; glucose reabsorption alone does not determine a dehydration timescale.

callouts.title: > "Urea is made in the kidneys, and its concentration is 67 times higher in urine than in blood because the kidney tubule actively pumps urea into the urine."
callouts.body:
Correct both parts:

1. **Where urea is made vs excreted:** **Urea is formed in the LIVER** from **excess amino acids** by **deamination** (removal of the nitrogen-containing part of amino acids). It travels dissolved in blood plasma to the **kidneys**, which **excrete** it.
2. **Why urea concentration rises ~67-fold from filtrate (`0.03 g/100 mL`) to urine (`2.00 g/100 mL`):** In this chosen adult account, when `180 L/day` of filtrate travels down the renal tubule and collecting duct, **more than 99% of the water (`178.5 L/day`) is reabsorbed back into the blood by osmosis**, shrinking the liquid volume ~120-fold down to `1.5 L/day` of urine while urea is partly reabsorbed and recycled. In this ledger, 54 g/day is filtered and 30 g/day leaves in urine: 24 g/day has returned from the tubular route.

callouts.title: Kitchen sieve and rescue: why a size filter alone cannot save your sugar
callouts.body:
*Note: This safe kitchen activity is an educational design to model glomerular size filtration and show why selective carrier reabsorption is required; it has not been classroom-trialled with pupils for this edition.*

In a clean mixing bowl, stir together half a cup of tap water, one tablespoon of whole **kidney beans (*rajma*)** (representing red blood cells and large plasma proteins), half a teaspoon of **sugar** (representing glucose, `M_r = 180`), and half a teaspoon of **table salt** (representing small dissolved ions and urea, `M_r = 58.5–60`) until the sugar and salt dissolve completely. Hold a kitchen tea strainer (or paper coffee filter) over a clear glass ("the renal capsule") and pour the mixture through.

Predict and observe: which materials does this particular strainer retain? The beans remain while dissolved sugar and salt pass through with water. This coarse model represents a barrier that admits both useful glucose and urea; it cannot establish what every molecular filter could separate. Add labelled counters for glucose and urea beside the collected filtrate, and move only the glucose counters to a second labelled “returned to blood” bowl. That selection models a separate recovery rule; hands and counters are not transport proteins. Wash utensils and do not taste experimental mixtures.

callouts.title: Cambridge 0610 separates excretion from egestion and the liver’s urea formation from kidney excretion. Its normal-nephron model reabsorbs all glucose, some ions and most water; read “all” as the ordinary-load school model, with physiological limits explained here.

callouts.body:
Does receiving ready-made antibody automatically build immune memory?
???
No. Passive antibody protection does not itself create the recipient’s specific memory response.

callouts.title: Look at the antibody concentration graph in Figure 10.7C. On **Day 0**, a child receives a **vaccine** containing a weakened form of **Pathogen A** (carrying **Antigen A**). On **Day 28**, the child is accidentally exposed at school to *both* live **Pathogen A** and a completely different live **Pathogen B** (carrying differently shaped **Antigen B**, assumed in this model not to be recognised by the anti-A response). What happens to the child's antibody production and symptoms against Pathogen A versus Pathogen B after Day 28?
callouts.body:
- The memory cells made after the vaccine immediately destroy both Pathogen A and Pathogen B, because memory cells attack all germs
- Against **Pathogen A**, the child's **memory cells** recognise **Antigen A** immediately and trigger a **very fast, massive secondary surge of complementary anti-A antibodies** that can reduce the chance or severity of illness; against **Pathogen B**, the anti-A memory cells and antibodies do **not recognise the stipulated model Antigen B**, so a slow **primary response** must start from scratch
- Vaccines already contain ready-made antibodies from a factory, so no lymphocytes are needed on Day 0 or Day 28
???
The second choice. Antibody binding depends on molecular features of an antigen. In our chosen example, the memory cells and antibodies formed against Antigen A do not recognise Antigen B in this deliberately simplified comparison; real antigens may share features and cross-react. Against Pathogen A, the memory cells divide and flood the blood with anti-A antibodies in 1–2 days (**secondary response**), often reducing illness, with protection depending on the pathogen, vaccine and person. Against Pathogen B, a brand-new set of lymphocytes with receptors complementary to Antigen B must be found and multiplied over 5–14 days (**primary response**).

callouts.title: > "A vaccine works by injecting ready-made antibodies so your white blood cells learn how to copy them, and breast milk gives a baby permanent active immunity."
callouts.body:
Correct both parts—this is a classic Cambridge 0610 Supplement contrast:

1. **What is inside a vaccine:** A vaccine contains **weakened or dead pathogens, or their antigens** (Gives **active immunity**). Your own **lymphocytes** must bind those antigens, divide, and produce the **antibodies** and **memory cells** themselves.
2. **What is inside breast milk (and crosses the placenta):** Ready-made **antibodies** made by the mother's body (Gives **passive immunity**). They protect the infant **immediately**, antibody transfer itself does not create the baby’s specific memory response, and the protection is **short-term** because the borrowed antibody proteins are gradually broken down.

callouts.title: Cambridge 0610 distinguishes active and passive immunity and asks how cholera-driven chloride secretion causes osmotic water loss. Antibody transfer supplies temporary protection; vaccination stimulates the recipient’s response and memory, with effectiveness and duration varying.
The sweet urine and the innocent filter
callouts.body:
A fictional patient has thirst, fatigue and increased urination. Tests find high plasma glucose, very low insulin and no abnormal protein detected by an ordinary urine test. For this reasoning case, independent measurements establish functioning tubule transporters with a **chosen simplified maximum glucose recovery rate of 330 mg/min** and GFR **125 mL/min**. These are model inputs, not universal clinical limits.

| Quantity | Comparison state | High-glucose state |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plasma glucose | 5.0 mmol/L = 0.90 mg/mL | 16.0 mmol/L = 2.88 mg/mL |
| GFR | 125 mL/min | 125 mL/min |
| Filtered glucose | 112.5 mg/min | 360 mg/min |
| Model recovery capacity | 330 mg/min | 330 mg/min |
| Glucose excreted | 0 in this model | 30 mg/min = 43.2 g/day |
| Observed urine volume | 1.5 L/day | 3.8 L/day |

One pupil says glucose in urine requires a torn glomerular filter. Another says the transporters must be destroyed. A third suggests that excess glucose delivery can overwhelm functioning transporters. Which explanation fits these stipulated measurements? Calculate the glucose loss, explain the extra water loss, and identify what the negative protein test cannot prove.
???
Glucose normally enters filtrate, so it needs no tear to reach the tubule. No abnormal protein detected gives no evidence for a major protein leak, but is not proof that every kidney structure is normal. The independent transport measurements, rather than that negative test, establish the functioning carriers assumed here.

Filtered glucose is concentration × filtration rate: **2.88 mg/mL × 125 mL/min = 360 mg/min**. With the chosen recovery maximum of **330 mg/min**, excretion is **30 mg/min**, or **43.2 g/day**. In the comparison state the filtered load is below capacity. This sharp-capacity model omits differences between nephrons and the gradual onset of glucose spillage in real kidneys. A plasma concentration threshold is not the same quantity as a maximum transport rate.

Glucose remaining in tubular fluid lowers its water potential and reduces water recovery by osmosis. This can increase urine volume and promote thirst. **3.8 L/day is an observation supplied in the case**, not a volume calculated from glucose alone; water intake, ADH and other solutes matter. Glucose concentration also changes as water is recovered, so we cannot subtract plasma concentrations and carry the difference unchanged down the tubule.

Restoring an appropriate insulin signal improves muscle glucose uptake and liver glucose handling, including reducing excessive liver glucose production. Lower plasma glucose reduces the filtered load and can end the glucose loss without repairing a tear that was never required by the explanation. This case illustrates mechanisms, not a personal treatment or diagnostic rule.

sections.heading: 11.1 The hidden instruction book: chromosomes, DNA and genes
sections.excerpt:
:::scene A pathology bench in London, 1928, a biochemical laboratory in New York, 1944, and a Mumbai kitchen counter

Look inside the **nucleus** of a plant or animal cell under a microscope (Chapter 2). When the cell is about to divide, the grainy tangle inside the nucleus condenses into dark, thread-like structures called ==chromosomes== (from Greek *chroma*, "colour", and *soma*, "body", because nineteenth-century microscopists noticed how strongly they soaked up coloured aniline dyes). Chemical analysis of isolated cell nuclei soon showed that chromosomes contain two main classes of giant molecules: **proteins** (built from 20 different amino acids) and **deoxyribonucleic acid** (**DNA**, built from just 4 different nucleotide building blocks).

For more than forty years, almost every biologist in the world bet on the wrong molecule. Because proteins are built from a rich twenty-letter alphabet of amino acids that fold into countless shapes, while DNA uses only a four-letter alphabet, most researchers assumed that **chromosomal proteins** must carry the cell's hereditary instructions (**genes**), while DNA was merely a dull wooden frame holding the proteins in place.

How do yo

sections.heading: 11.2 The twisted ladder: Photo 51, Chargaff's ratios and the double helix
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Columbia University, New York, 1950, King's College London, May 1952, and the Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge, April 1953

Once Avery's team proved that genes are made of **DNA**, a fierce race began to solve a physical puzzle: **how are the atoms inside a DNA molecule arranged in three-dimensional space, and how can a molecule built from just four kinds of bases store thousands of different protein recipes?**

Start with what chemists already knew about the building blocks of DNA. DNA is a long biological polymer (macromolecule, Chapter 4) assembled from repeating monomer units called **nucleotides**. Each DNA nucleotide consists of three parts joined together:

1. A **phosphate group** (which gives DNA its acidic nature and negative electrical charge),
2. A five-carbon sugar called **deoxyribose** (which joins with alternating phosphate groups to form the strong outer **sugar–phosphate backbone** of each strand), and
3. One of four nitrogen-containing organic **bases** projecting inward from the sugar:
   - **Adenine (`A`)** — a larger, **two-ring** base (a **purine**),
   - **Guanine (`G`)** — a larger, **two-ring** base (also a **purine**),
   - **Thymine (`T`)** — a s

sections.heading: 11.3 Cracking the triplet cipher and printing the protein: from mRNA to the ribosome
sections.excerpt:
:::scene The Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge, 1961, Bethesda, Maryland, May 1961, and Madison, Wisconsin, 1964–1968

Solving the double helix in 1953 revealed how the master instruction book is bound, but it immediately exposed two new puzzles:

- **The coding puzzle:** DNA has an alphabet of only **four bases** (`A`, `T`, `C`, `G`), whereas proteins are built from **twenty different amino acids** (Chapter 4). How can a four-letter alphabet spell out twenty different amino-acid names?
- **The location puzzle:** In every eukaryotic plant, animal and fungal cell, the chromosomes and their **genes stay locked inside the nucleus** (`11.1`), whereas the **ribosomes**—the tiny molecular machines that actually link amino acids together into proteins (Chapter 2)—sit **outside the nucleus in the cytoplasm** (and on the rough endoplasmic reticulum). If the DNA gene never leaves the nucleus, how does the instruction reach the ribosome?

Take the coding puzzle first. Imagine trying to write a code for **20 different amino acids** using an alphabet of **4 letters**:

- If each code word is **1 base long (a singlet code)**, there are only **`4¹ = 4`** possible words (`A`, `T`, `C`, `G`)—leaving

sections.heading: 11.4 One letter changed: beta-globin, silent triplets and why sequence controls shape
sections.excerpt:
:::scene The Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge, 1956–1957, and a haematology laboratory in Mumbai

Now put the entire causal spine of Chapter 11—**DNA base sequence → mRNA codon sequence → amino-acid sequence → 3D folded protein shape → cellular function**—to a quantitative test on a single human protein you already know from Chapter 8: **haemoglobin**.

Each red blood cell in your bloodstream is packed with roughly 280 million molecules of **adult haemoglobin (`HbA`)**. Each haemoglobin molecule is a four-subunit protein tetramer made of two **alpha-globin (`α`)** polypeptide chains (141 amino acids each) and two **beta-globin (`β`)** polypeptide chains (**146 amino acids** each, specified by `146 × 3 = 438` coding bases for the **mature beta-globin sequence**, excluding the removable initiator methionine and stop codon, in the **`HBB` gene** on human chromosome 11), with each subunit cradling an iron-containing **haem** group (`Fe²⁺`) that reversibly binds oxygen (`O₂`).

In **sickle-cell anaemia**, a person's red blood cells produce an altered version of haemoglobin called **sickle-cell haemoglobin (`HbS`)**. When `HbS` carries oxygen in the lungs and arteries, it stays dissolved.

callouts.title: In 1944 at the Rockefeller Institute in New York, **Oswald Avery**, **Colin MacLeod**, and **Maclyn McCarty** broke open heat-killed Smooth (S) bacteria, removed the lipids and polysaccharide coats, and divided the active cell-free transforming extract into three test tubes before adding live Rough (R) bacteria:
callouts.body:
**Tube 1** was treated with **protease enzymes** (trypsin and chymotrypsin, Chapter 7), which digest **proteins**.
**Tube 2** was treated with **ribonuclease (RNase)**, an enzyme that digests **RNA**.
**Tube 3** was treated with **deoxyribonuclease (DNase)**, an enzyme that digests **DNA**.

If **DNA**—and not protein or RNA—is the molecule that carries genes, which tubes will still transform harmless Rough (R) bacteria into capsulated Smooth (S) bacteria, and which tube will fail?
- Tube 1 (protease-treated) will fail to transform R bacteria, while Tubes 2 and 3 will still produce live S bacteria
- Tubes 1 and 2 will still transform R bacteria into live Smooth (S) bacteria because destroying protein or RNA leaves the DNA intact, whereas Tube 3 (DNase-treated) will produce only Rough (R) bacteria because destroying DNA destroys the gene
- All three tubes will fail because genes require protein, RNA and DNA to stay glued together at all times
???
The second choice. Because enzymes have complementary active sites that are strictly specific to their substrates (Chapter 4), **proteases** destroy only proteins, **RNase** destroys only RNA, and **DNase** destroys only DNA. When Avery, MacLeod and McCarty destroyed all the protein in Tube 1 or all the RNA in Tube 2, the extract transformed Rough (R) cells into Smooth (S) cells just as strongly as the untreated control. Only when **DNase** chopped up the **DNA** in Tube 3 did hereditary transformation vanish completely.

callouts.title: > "DNA is made of chromosomes, and each chromosome is inside a gene."
callouts.body:
Reverse that hierarchy completely. Think of a **multi-volume recipe encyclopaedia** locked inside a library reading room:

- **The library room = the cell nucleus.**
- **Each bound volume = one chromosome** (made of one continuous, tightly coiled **DNA** thread).
- **One recipe printed on a few pages of that volume = one gene** (a specific **length of DNA** that codes for one protein).
- **The paper and ink letters themselves = the DNA molecule and its bases.**

Therefore, from largest to smallest: **Cell → Nucleus → Chromosome → Gene → DNA nucleotide bases**. Chromosomes are made of DNA, and each chromosome contains many genes along its length.

A protein’s surface depends on the chemistry of its amino acids. Explain why changing a DNA base may change that surface, while another substitution may leave the amino-acid sequence unchanged.
???
A chemically different amino acid can change a surface. Synonymous codons specify the same amino acid; effects on RNA or production still need checking.

callouts.title: Spooling white threads of DNA from a mashed banana
callouts.body:
**Disclosure:** This is an optional kitchen-chemistry demonstration based on standard school and outreach nucleic-acid precipitation protocols (not a laboratory trial performed during the authoring of this chapter). If you try it at home, work with an adult and use **chilled rubbing alcohol (70–91% isopropyl alcohol or surgical spirit)** strictly as an external reagent in a glass—never taste or swallow rubbing alcohol, keep it away from stove flames, and wash your hands afterwards.

1. Place **half a ripe banana** in a resealable plastic bag with `100 mL` (about half a teacup) of warm water and mash it thoroughly with your fingers for two minutes until it forms a smooth porridge (**Step 1 in Figure 11.1:** mechanical mashing separates clumped cells and breaks open cellulose cell walls).
2. In a clear glass cup, gently stir together `10 mL` (two teaspoons) of **liquid dishwashing detergent** and `3 g` (half a teaspoon) of **table salt (`NaCl`)** in `50 mL` of water without whipping up foam. Pour this lysis mixture into the mashed banana bag, rock gently for five minutes, and filter the liquid through a fine tea strainer or coffee filter into a narrow glass (**Step 2:** detergent dissolves the fatty **lipid bilayers** of both the cell membrane and the **nuclear membrane**, releasing DNA into solution; **Step 3:** positively charged sodium ions **`Na⁺`** from the salt shield the negatively charged phosphate groups along the DNA backbones so the strands can come together instead of repelling each other).
3. Tilt the narrow glass and slowly pour an equal volume of **ice-cold rubbing alcohol** (chilled in the freezer for 30 minutes) down the inside wall of the glass so it floats as a clear top layer above the cloudy banana filtrate (**Step 4:** DNA is soluble in salty water but **insoluble in cold alcohol**).
4. Watch the boundary between the two layers for two minutes: millions of microscopic DNA molecules precipitate out of solution together as **cloudy white, mucus-like threads** rising into the cold alcohol layer, which you can spool around a wooden toothpick. Remember what you are looking at: a single DNA double helix is only **`2.0 nm` wide**—far too thin to see with the naked eye or a school light microscope—so the white thread on your toothpick is millions of DNA strands clumped together, mixed with other cellular material. This DNA-rich precipitate does not reveal the helix or prove that DNA carries genes.

callouts.title: **Cambridge Lower Secondary Science (`0893`)** requires you to describe how **chromosomes are found in the nucleus of a cell and are made of DNA** (`9Bs.01`), and how **genes are located on chromosomes and help to determine the characteristics of an organism** (`9Bs.02`). **Cambridge IGCSE Biology (`0610`, Topic 17.1 Core 1–2)** requires you to state that **chromosomes are made of DNA, which contains genetic information in the form of genes**, and to define a **gene** precisely as **a length of DNA that codes for a protein**.

Suppose a biochemist analyses a double-stranded DNA molecule from a newly discovered deep-sea fish and finds that **22% of all the bases in the DNA are cytosine (`C`)**. Using complementary base pairing and Chargaff's rules, what are the percentages of **guanine (`G`)**, **adenine (`A`)**, and **thymine (`T`)** in that DNA molecule?
callouts.body:
- 22% G, 22% A, and 34% T, because C, G and A are always equal
- 28% G, 25% A, and 25% T, because C and G always add up to 50%
- 22% G, 28% A, and 28% T, because C always pairs with G (so %G = %C = 22%, totalling 44%), and the remaining 56% of bases must be split equally between A and T pairs (%A = %T = 28%)
???
The third choice. Work through the two-step arithmetic:

1. Because every **cytosine (`C`)** on one strand is paired across the rung with a **guanine (`G`)** on the opposite strand (`C≡G`), `%G` must equal `%C = 22%`. Together, `C + G` account for `22% + 22% = 44%` of all bases.
2. That leaves `100% − 44% = 56%` of the bases for `A` and `T`. Because every **adenine (`A`)** pairs with a **thymine (`T`)** (`A=T`), `%A` must equal `%T = 56% ÷ 2 = 28%`. Check the total: `22% C + 22% G + 28% A + 28% T = 100%`.

callouts.title: > "Different organisms have different proteins because their DNA has different sugar–phosphate backbones or pairs A with G instead of A with T."
callouts.body: Neither is true. From a banana tree to an *E. coli* bacterium to your own neurones, **every DNA double helix uses the exact same deoxyribose sugar–phosphate backbone and the exact same complementary base-pairing rule (`A` with `T`, `C` with `G`)**. What makes a human insulin gene different from a human beta-globin gene—or a human different from a banana—is the **sequence (order) of bases (`A, T, C, G`) running lengthwise along the DNA strands** of each gene (`0610 17.1 Core 3`).

callouts.title: **Cambridge IGCSE Biology (`0610`, Topic 4.1)** requires every candidate to describe the structure of a DNA molecule as: **(a) two strands coiled together to form a double helix**, **(b) each strand contains chemicals called bases**, **(c) cross-links between the strands are formed by pairs of bases**, and **(d) the bases always pair up in the same way: `A` with `T`, and `C` with `G`**. Note that while knowing the full names **adenine, thymine, cytosine, and guanine** deepens your biochemical understanding, the `0610` syllabus notes that Core exam questions do not require you to recall the full names from memory as long as you use the letters **`A`, `T`, `C`, and `G`** accurately.

Because **`4³ = 64`** three-letter triplets are available to code for only **20 amino acids** (plus 3 stop signals), which description matches the experimentally established standard code’s relationship between triplets (codons) and amino acids?
callouts.body:
- 44 of the 64 triplets are unused blanks that pause the ribosome, while each of the 20 amino acids has only 1 triplet
- Each single triplet codes for 3 different amino acids at random, so the same gene makes many different proteins
- Most amino acids are coded for by more than one triplet (for example, 6 different triplets code for leucine), while every individual triplet specifies one unambiguous meaning (either one specific amino acid or STOP)
???
The third choice. Biologists call this property of the genetic code **degeneracy** (or **redundancy**):

- **Unambiguous in the forward direction (`codon → amino acid`):** Every one of the 61 sense codons specifies **one and only one amino acid** (for instance, `GAG` always specifies glutamic acid, never valine or leucine).
- **Degenerate / redundant in the reverse direction (`amino acid → codons`):** Because 61 sense codons share 20 amino acids, most amino acids have **2, 3, 4, or 6 synonymous codons** (usually differing at the third base of the triplet). As you will see in Section 11.4 and the end-of-chapter case, this degeneracy shields living cells against many single-base mutations.

callouts.title: > "To make a protein, the gene leaves the nucleus and goes to the ribosome, where the ribosome turns the mRNA bases into amino acids."
callouts.body:
Correct both parts—examiners penalise both phrasing slips heavily on **Cambridge IGCSE `0610 17.1`**:

1. **The gene never leaves the nucleus:** State clearly that **the gene coding for the protein remains in the nucleus**, and that a **messenger RNA (`mRNA`) copy of the gene is made in the nucleus and moves to the cytoplasm**.
2. **Bases are not turned into amino acids:** Nucleotides (`A, U, C, G`) and amino acids are completely different chemical monomers. As **mRNA passes through a ribosome**, the ribosome reads the **sequence of bases in the mRNA** and **assembles free amino acids into a protein molecule** in the corresponding order.

callouts.title: **Cambridge IGCSE Biology (`0610`, Topic 17.1 Core 3 & Supplement 4–5)** requires you to:
callouts.body:
- **Core (`17.1.3`):** Explain that the **sequence of bases in a gene** is the **genetic code** for putting together **amino acids in the correct order** to make a **specific protein** (note that Core exam papers do not test the detailed mechanism of triplet anticodons or nucleotide monomer chemistry, which belong to Supplement/enrichment).
- **Supplement (`17.1.4`):** Explain that **DNA controls cell function by controlling the production of proteins**, including **enzymes**, **membrane carriers**, and **receptors for neurotransmitters**.
- **Supplement (`17.1.5`):** Explain how a protein is made using the six-point spine: **(1) the gene coding for the protein remains in the nucleus**, **(2) messenger RNA (`mRNA`) is a copy of a gene**, **(3) mRNA molecules are made in the nucleus and move to the cytoplasm**, **(4) the mRNA passes through ribosomes**, **(5) the ribosome assembles amino acids into protein molecules**, and **(6) the specific sequence of amino acids is determined by the sequence of bases in the mRNA**.

callouts.title: A segment of the **coding strand** of a human gene inside the nucleus has the base sequence **`5'- G T G · C A C · C T G · A C T -3'`** (and its complementary **template strand** reads **`3'- C A C · G T G · G A C · T G A -5'`**).
callouts.body:
1. Write down the base sequence of the **mRNA** molecule transcribed from this segment, and state **where in the cell** this mRNA is made and **where it moves next**.
2. Using the genetic code (`GUG = Val`, `CAC = His`, `CUG = Leu`, `ACU = Thr`), write down the **four-amino-acid sequence** assembled when this mRNA passes through a **ribosome**, and explain how DNA controls the function of a **synapse** (Chapter 9) and **active transport** (Chapter 3).
???

1. **mRNA sequence and cellular pathway:**
   - The transcribed **mRNA** sequence is **`5'- G U G · C A C · C U G · A C U -3'`** (complementary to the `3'→5'` template strand `CAC GTG GAC TGA`, which is identical to the `5'→3'` coding strand with **Uracil `U` replacing Thymine `T`**).
   - The **gene remains in the nucleus**; the **mRNA copy is made in the nucleus** and **moves through a nuclear pore into the cytoplasm**, where it **passes through a ribosome**.
2. **Amino-acid sequence and control of cell function:**
   - The ribosome reads the mRNA triplets in order (`GUG → CAC → CUG → ACU`) and assembles the amino-acid sequence **`Val – His – Leu – Thr`** (`Valine – Histidine – Leucine – Threonine`).
   - DNA controls cell function by controlling the production of specific folded **proteins**: at a **synapse**, DNA codes for the postsynaptic **receptors for neurotransmitters** (whose 3D binding sites match the neurotransmitter); in **active transport**, DNA codes for the specific **membrane carrier proteins** embedded in the cell membrane.

callouts.title: When **Vernon Ingram** sequenced the 146 amino acids of the normal beta-globin chain (`HbA`) and the 146 amino acids of the sickle-cell beta-globin chain (`HbS`), how many of the 146 amino acids had changed, and what happened to the electrical charge and water solubility of that spot?
callouts.body:
- 42 out of the 146 amino acids were scrambled because a single-base insertion near the start shifted the entire reading frame
- The chain was cut in half at residue 73 by a premature stop codon, leaving a 72-amino-acid fragment
- Only 1 amino acid out of 146 changed—at position 6 (Codon 6), where a single base substitution (DNA `GAG → GTG`, mRNA `GAG → GUG`) replaced negatively charged, hydrophilic glutamic acid (`Glu⁶`) with neutral, hydrophobic valine (`Val⁶`)
???
The third choice. Out of the **438 bases** specifying the 146 residues of mature beta-globin (excluding the initiator methionine and stop codon), **437 bases are completely unchanged**. At **Codon 6**, the middle base of the triplet changes from **`A` to `T`** on the coding DNA strand (**`GAG → GTG`**, or `CTC → CAC` on the template strand), which changes the sixth **mRNA codon** from **`GAG` to `GUG`**. Instead of inserting **glutamic acid (`Glu⁶`)**—whose side chain carries a negative electrical charge (`−COO⁻`) and loves water (**hydrophilic**)—the ribosome inserts **valine (`Val⁶`)**, whose hydrocarbon side chain carries zero charge and repels water (**hydrophobic**).

callouts.title: > "Every mutation in a gene's DNA base sequence changes the amino-acid sequence and alters the 3D shape of the protein."
callouts.body: Not every single-base substitution changes the amino-acid sequence. Because **64 triplets (`4³`)** code for only **20 amino acids** (plus 3 stop signals), most amino acids are specified by several synonymous codons (for example, `CUU`, `CUC`, `CUA`, and `CUG` all code for **leucine**). If a single-base substitution changes one codon into another codon for the **same amino acid** (a **silent / synonymous** change), the **amino-acid sequence is completely unchanged**, but this alone does not establish how much protein is produced or exclude effects on RNA processing.

callouts.title: **Cambridge IGCSE Biology (`0610`, Topics 4.1 & 17.1, connecting to 17.4)** expects you to connect the **sequence of bases in a gene (`A, T, C, G`)** to the **sequence of bases in mRNA (`A, U, C, G`)**, the **sequence of amino acids in a protein**, and the **3D shape and function** of that protein (such as an enzyme active site, a membrane carrier, a neurotransmitter receptor, an antibody, or haemoglobin). Notice how Chapter 11 keeps our focus strictly at the **molecular sequence-to-protein level** (`DNA → mRNA → amino acid → 3D protein`); how alternative versions of a gene (**alleles**) are inherited from parents to children belongs to Chapter 13, and how natural selection acts on variation in malaria zones belongs to Chapter 14.
Two children, two single-base changes, one unchanged amino-acid sequence
callouts.body:
This is a fictional molecular-diagnostics reasoning case uniting Section 11.2 (complementary base pairing), Section 11.3 (transcription of mRNA and translation at the ribosome), and Section 11.4 (the degenerate 64-codon genetic code and beta-globin folding), not medical advice about any individual patient.

For this case, compare the protein encoded by the displayed HBB copy, rather than diagnosing a child from one sequence. A person normally has two HBB copies; actual red-cell behaviour depends on both and other factors. Assume the remaining sequence, RNA processing and production are unchanged. Synonymous means the amino acid is unchanged; it does not universally mean biologically harmless.

A paediatric haematology laboratory in Mumbai sequences the first seven codons (**Codons 1 to 7**, 21 bases) of the **beta-globin (`HBB`) gene** from a healthy reference standard and from two twelve-year-old patients, **Child X** and **Child Y**. Remarkably, **both Child X and Child Y have exactly 1 base out of the 21 bases changed** compared with the standard reference sequence:

| Sample | Coding DNA strand (`5' → 3'`, Codons 1–7) | Location of single-base change | Red blood cell & haemoglobin test result |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Reference (`HbA`)** | `GTG · CAC · CTG · ACT · CCT · GAG · GAG` | None (0 bases changed) | Normal soluble `HbA`; flexible biconcave red blood cells |
| **Child X** | `GTG · CAC · CTT · ACT · CCT · GAG · GAG` | **Codon 3:** `CTG → CTT` (1 base changed: `G → T`) | **Usual beta-globin sequence; normal function assumed here** |
| **Child Y** | `GTG · CAC · CTG · ACT · CCT · GTG · GAG` | **Codon 6:** `GAG → GTG` (1 base changed: `A → T`) | **Sticky `HbS` fibres at low `O₂`; sickled red blood cells** |

A relevant excerpt of the standard **mRNA genetic code dictionary** is provided alongside the sequencing report:

- `GUG`, `GUU`, `GUC`, `GUA` = **Valine (`Val`)** *(neutral, hydrophobic side chain)*
- `CAC`, `CAU` = **Histidine (`His`)**
- `CUG`, `CUU`, `CUC`, `CUA`, `UUA`, `UUG` = **Leucine (`Leu`)** *(hydrophobic interior residue)*
- `ACU`, `ACC`, `ACA`, `ACG` = **Threonine (`Thr`)**
- `CCU`, `CCC`, `CCA`, `CCG` = **Proline (`Pro`)**
- `GAG`, `GAA` = **Glutamic acid (`Glu`)** *(negatively charged, hydrophilic surface residue)*

A classmate looks at the table and says: *"The laboratory must have mixed up Child X's blood sample. Child X has a one-letter DNA mutation (`G → T`) in the beta-globin gene just like Child Y (`A → T`), so Child X's ribosomes must also be printing a mutated, abnormally folded beta-globin protein."*

Use the molecular mechanisms of Sections 11.2, 11.3, and 11.4 to prove why the laboratory did **not** mix up the samples:

1. For both **Child X** and **Child Y**, write down **(a)** the complementary **template DNA strand (`3' → 5'`)** inside the nucleus and **(b)** the **mRNA codon sequence (`5' → 3'`)** that moves through a nuclear pore to pass through the **ribosomes** in the cytoplasm.
2. Translate both **mRNA** sequences into their seven-amino-acid chains (`Residues 1–7`) using the codon table, and explain why **Child X's single-base DNA mutation leaves the amino-acid sequence unchanged** (with normal RNA processing, production and folding assumed in this case), whereas **Child Y's single-base DNA mutation alters the 3D surface behavior of haemoglobin**.
3. Suppose a third patient, **Child Z**, had a single base **deleted (`−1`)** from **Codon 3** (so Codon 3 lost its `G` and became `CT`, instead of `G` being substituted by `T`). Would Child Z's mutation also be silent like Child X's? Explain why or why not using **Francis Crick and Sydney Brenner's (1961)** discovery.
???

1. **Template DNA strands (`3' → 5'`) in the nucleus and transcribed mRNA codons (`5' → 3'`) in the cytoplasm:**
   Using DNA complementary pairing (`A ↔ T`, `C ↔ G`) for the template strand, and RNA transcription (`U` replacing `T` of the coding strand) for the **mRNA** copy that moves from the nucleus to the cytoplasmic ribosomes:
   - **Child X:**
     - Template DNA (`3' → 5'`): **`3'- CAC · GTG · GAA · TGA · GGA · CTC · CTC -5'`** *(Codon 3 template changed from `GAC` to `GAA`)*
     - Transcribed mRNA (`5' → 3'`): **`5'- GUG · CAC · CUU · ACU · CCU · GAG · GAG -3'`** *(mRNA Codon 3 changed from `CUG` to `CUU`)*
   - **Child Y:**
     - Template DNA (`3' → 5'`): **`3'- CAC · GTG · GAC · TGA · GGA · CAC · CTC -5'`** *(Codon 6 template changed from `CTC` to `CAC`)*
     - Transcribed mRNA (`5' → 3'`): **`5'- GUG · CAC · CUG · ACU · CCU · GUG · GAG -3'`** *(mRNA Codon 6 changed from `GAG` to `GUG`)*

2. **Translation at the ribosome and why Child X is silent while Child Y is missense:**
   - **Child X polypeptide (`Residues 1–7`):** Reading `GUG · CAC · CUU · ACU · CCU · GAG · GAG` at the ribosome gives **`Val¹ – His² – Leu³ – Thr⁴ – Pro⁵ – Glu⁶ – Glu⁷`**. Because the 64-codon genetic code is **degenerate**, both `CUG` (Reference) and `CUU` (Child X) code for the **exact same amino acid: Leucine (`Leu³`)**, and Codon 6 is still `GAG` (**hydrophilic `Glu⁶`**). The displayed change leaves the mature beta-globin amino-acid sequence unchanged (**synonymous substitution**). Under this case's stated assumptions about RNA processing, protein production and folding, the chain supplies normal beta-globin. Ramachandran's work explains constraints on possible backbone conformations; it does not prove that every synonymous DNA change has no biological effect.
   - **Child Y polypeptide (`Residues 1–7`):** Reading `GUG · CAC · CUG · ACU · CCU · GUG · GAG` at the ribosome gives **`Val¹ – His² – Leu³ – Thr⁴ – Pro⁵ – Val⁶ – Glu⁷`**. At **Codon 6**, changing `GAG` to `GUG` is a **missense substitution** that replaces negatively charged, water-loving **glutamic acid (`Glu⁶`)** with neutral, water-repelling **valine (`Val⁶`)**. That exposed **hydrophobic `Val⁶` patch** causes deoxygenated `HbS` molecules to stick together into rigid fibres that distort red blood cells into sickles.

3. **Why a single-base deletion (`−1`) at Codon 3 in Child Z would NOT be silent (Crick & Brenner 1961 frameshift):**
   Deleting the `G` at the end of Codon 3 leaves only 2 bases (`CT`), so the ribosome—which reads mRNA in **non-overlapping triplets without commas**—pulls the first base of Codon 4 into Codon 3 and shifts the **reading frame** of every single triplet downstream (`GTG · CAC · CTA · CTC · CTG · AGG · AG...` → `mRNA GUG · CAC · CUA · CUC · CUG · AGG...`). Instead of `Val–His–Leu–Thr–Pro–Glu–Glu`, Child Z's ribosome prints `Val–His–Leu–Leu–Leu–Arg...`, changing the reading frame and usually many subsequent amino acids, often introducing an early stop and destroying the 3D beta-globin protein (**frameshift mutation**).

sections.heading: 12.1 Unzipping the ladder: semi-conservative DNA replication
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge, April 1953, and Norman Church Laboratory, Caltech, Pasadena, 1957–1958

At the close of their April 1953 paper in *Nature*, **James Watson** and **Francis Crick** wrote one of the most famous single-sentence predictions in the history of science: *"It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material."*

Look back at the base-pairing rule you mastered in Chapter 11. Along the interior of a DNA double helix, purine and pyrimidine rungs fit together by strict hydrogen-bond geometry: **adenine (`A`) pairs only with thymine (`T`)** via two hydrogen bonds (`A=T`), and **cytosine (`C`) pairs only with guanine (`G`)** via three hydrogen bonds (`C≡G`). Because of that one-to-one lock, the two strands of a double helix are not identical copies of each other—they are **complementary partners**. If you know the base sequence along one strand (`3'-A T G C C G T A-5'`), the opposite strand is completely determined (`5'-T A C G G C A T-3'`).

Before any eukaryotic cell can divide by mitosis or meiosis, it must make an **exact copy of every chromosome** during

sections.heading: 12.2 The thread dance: mitosis, growth, repair and asexual cloning
sections.excerpt:
:::scene University of Kiel, Germany, 1879–1882, and a Mumbai kitchen windowsill

Once S-phase replication has duplicated every chromosome in a human somatic cell into a pair of identical sister chromatids (`46` chromosomes = `92` chromatids), the cell faces a mechanical sorting challenge. Imagine holding `46` pairs of shoelaces tangled inside a microscopic sphere `6 µm` across and needing to hand **one shoelace from every single pair** to the left side of the room and its twin to the right side—without dropping or doubling even one.

That precision sorting operation is ==mitosis==: **nuclear division giving rise to genetically identical cells** (**0610 `17.2 Core 1`**).

Although Cambridge IGCSE `0610` does not require you to memorise the Greek stage names (*prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase*), watching the four physical movements that **Walther Flemming** traced in aniline-stained salamander cells between 1879 and 1882 makes it crystal clear how mitosis normally distributes chromosomes accurately:

1. **Condensing the threads:** In a working interphase nucleus, DNA threads are uncoiled and spread out (**chromatin**) so RNA polymerase can read genes. As mitosis begins, each

sections.heading: 12.3 Same library, different bookmarks: stem cells and selective gene expression
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Department of Zoology, Oxford, 1962, Indian Cancer Research Centre, Parel, Mumbai, 1960s, and Kyoto University, 2006

Step back and notice a seeming paradox created by Section `12.2`. You began life as a **single diploid zygote (`2n = 46`)**, and every somatic cell in your body—except mature red blood cells and lens fibres that ejected their nuclei at the final step of maturation—was produced from that zygote by **mitosis**. Because mitosis deals an exact copy of all `46` chromosomes to both daughter cells at every division, a **beta cell** in your pancreas, an immature **erythroblast** in your bone marrow, a **cone photoreceptor cell** in your retina, and a **motor neurone** in your spinal cord all carry the **exact same 46 chromosomes and the exact same ~20,000 protein-coding genes**.

Why, then, doesn't your eyeball secrete digestive trypsin or insulin? Why doesn't a pancreatic beta cell fill itself with red oxygen-carrying haemoglobin or sprout a one-metre nerve axon?

The answer lies in a two-stage partnership between ==stem cells== (**0610 `17.2.5 Supplement`**) and ==selective gene expression== (**0610 `17.1.6 Supplement`**):

### 1. Stem cells: the unspecialised mi

:::scene Mediterranean marine stations and Liège, 1876–1887, and the Imperial Sugarcane Breeding Institute, Coimbatore, 1934–1939

We now arrive at the third puzzle from Chapter 11’s closing bridge—a puzzle of pure arithmetic first stated clearly by the German biologist **August Weismann** in `1887`, after **Oscar Hertwig** (`1876`, in transparent Mediterranean sea-urchin eggs) and **Edouard van Beneden** (`1883`, in *Ascaris* roundworms) watched sperm and egg nuclei fuse under the microscope.

A typical human body cell has a ==diploid== nucleus (`2n = 46`): **a nucleus containing two sets of chromosomes**, arranged as **23 chromosome pairs**. The 22 autosomal pairs contain matching ==homologous chromosomes==; the sex-chromosome pair can be `XX` or `XY` (**0610 `17.1 Core & Supplement`**). In each homologous pair—say, the two copies of Chromosome `11`—one chromosome came originally from the person’s mother (**maternal homologue**) and the matching partner came from the person’s father (**paternal homologue**). Homologous autosomes have broadly matching lengths, centromere positions, and gene loci (both carry `HBB` and `INS` at matching positions), though they may carry different ve
