This is an agricultural cytogenetics synthesis case uniting Section 12.1 (S-phase DNA replication), Section 12.2 (mitosis and asexual crop cloning), Section 12.3 (apical meristem stem cells and selective gene expression), and Section 12.4 (meiosis, homologous pairing, and sexual variation).

If you slice open a wild banana (*Musa acuminata*) growing in the forests of Assam or the Western Ghats, the pulp is packed with dozens of rock-hard black seeds the size of peppercorns. Yet when you

callouts.title: Suppose you grow *Escherichia coli* bacteria for fourteen generations in a nutrient broth containing only **heavy nitrogen (`¹⁵N`)**, so both strands of every bacterial DNA double helix are completely heavy (`¹⁵N/¹⁵N`). You then transfer the bacteria into broth containing only **light nitrogen (`¹⁴N`)** and allow them to divide **once** (Generation `1`) and then **a second time** (Generation `2`). If you spin the extracted DNA in a density gradient that separates heavy (`1.724 g/cm³`), intermediate-hybrid (`1.717 g/cm³`), and light (`1.710 g/cm³`) DNA into distinct bands, what band pattern will appear under **semi-conservative replication**?
callouts.body:
- At Generation 1, two equal bands (50% heavy and 50% light); at Generation 2, 25% heavy and 75% light
- At Generation 1, a single 100% hybrid band (1.717 g/cm³); at Generation 2, a single blended band halfway between hybrid and light (1.7135 g/cm³)
- At Generation 1, a single 100% hybrid band (1.717 g/cm³); at Generation 2, two equal bands—50% hybrid (1.717 g/cm³) and 50% light (1.710 g/cm³)
???
The third choice. Trace the two parental `¹⁵N` single strands step by step:

1. **Generation 1 (one doubling in `¹⁴N`):** The original `¹⁵N/¹⁵N` double helix unzips into two heavy `¹⁵N` single strands, and each templates a new light `¹⁴N` complementary partner. Both daughter molecules are **`¹⁵N/¹⁴N` hybrids (`100%` at `1.717 g/cm³`)**. This single intermediate band immediately falsifies the **conservative** hypothesis (the first choice), which predicted `50%` heavy + `50%` light and zero hybrid DNA.
2. **Generation 2 (two doublings in `¹⁴N`):** The two hybrid (`¹⁵N/¹⁴N`) molecules unzip into `2` heavy `¹⁵N` strands and `2` light `¹⁴N` strands. Each of those `4` template strands gets a new light `¹⁴N` partner, producing **`2` hybrid (`¹⁵N/¹⁴N`) duplexes (`50%` at `1.717 g/cm³`) and `2` pure light (`¹⁴N/¹⁴N`) duplexes (`50%` at `1.710 g/cm³`)**. This clean two-band split falsifies the **dispersive** hypothesis (the second choice), which predicted a single blended band at `1.7135 g/cm³`.

callouts.title: > "After DNA replication in S phase, a human diploid cell has 92 chromosomes (4n), and semi-conservative replication means one daughter cell gets all the original DNA while the other gets all the newly made DNA."
callouts.body:
Both halves of that statement are classic exam traps:

1. **Centromere counting (`46` chromosomes, `92` chromatids):** After S-phase replication, the two copies of each chromosome (**sister chromatids**) remain linked near their centromeres and count as **one replicated chromosome**. Thus a human cell entering mitosis still has **46 chromosomes (`2n = 46`)** made of **92 sister chromatids (`92` DNA molecules)**.
2. **Every daughter duplex is a `50:50` hybrid:** Under **semi-conservative** replication, **every** replicated DNA double helix (every sister chromatid) contains **one original parental strand and one newly synthesised strand**. Neither daughter cell receives `100%` old DNA.

callouts.title: **Cambridge IGCSE Biology (`0610`, Topic 17.2 Supplement 3)** requires you to state that **the exact replication of chromosomes occurs before mitosis**. Connect this directly to **Topic 4.1**: complementary base pairing (**`A` with `T`**, **`C` with `G`**) ensures that each new DNA strand is an exact copy of the partner strand it replaced, so the two **sister chromatids** of a chromosome carry identical genes and alleles.

A potato farmer in Maharashtra discovers a single potato plant in her field that produces unusually large, smooth, high-starch tubers. To fill her next two-hectare field with plants that all share that exact same large-tuber trait, should she plant **true seeds collected from the potato plant's small green berries** (formed after insect pollination of its flowers), or should she cut the plant's **underground stem tubers into pieces each containing an "eye" bud** and plant those—and what risk does her choice create if a new strain of late-blight pathogen (*Phytophthora infestans*) arrives next monsoon?
callouts.body:
- Plant berry seeds, because sexual seeds always produce 100% identical clones with high disease resistance
- Plant cut tuber pieces with "eye" buds (asexual reproduction by mitosis) so every daughter plant is a genetically identical clone keeping the large-tuber trait; however, little genetic variation apart from mutations means if one clone is susceptible to the new blight strain, the entire field can be wiped out
- Either method gives identical results, because potato flowers and potato tuber eyes both divide by meiosis
???
The second choice. Cutting and planting **stem tuber pieces containing "eye" buds** uses **asexual reproduction by mitosis**: every new potato plant (`2n = 48`) inherits an exact copy of the parent's chromosomes and preserves the elite high-starch, large-tuber phenotype. In contrast, seeds inside the green berries are produced by **sexual reproduction (meiosis + fertilisation)**, which reshuffles parental alleles so many seedlings lose the desirable trait combination. The trade-off (`0610 16.1.2`) is **monoculture vulnerability**: because all cloned plants in the field have **very little genetic variation apart from mutations**, a single pathogen strain able to infect one plant can destroy the entire crop (as happened in the `1845–1849` Irish Potato Famine).

callouts.title: Rooting an onion bulb in a water tumbler and sprouting a potato eye (clones by mitosis)
callouts.body:
**Disclosure:** This is an optional kitchen-botany observation based on standard school vegetative propagation demonstrations (not a laboratory trial performed during the authoring of this chapter). Handle wooden toothpicks carefully, wash your hands after touching raw potato sprouts, and **never eat raw potato sprouts or green-skinned potato tubers**—light-exposed potato sprouts synthesise bitter glycoalkaloids (**solanine**) that are toxic if swallowed. Dispose of the sprouted potato in the compost or household bin when finished.

1. **Onion root-tip meristem (`Allium cepa`, `2n = 16`):** Push three or four wooden toothpicks partway into the equator of a firm kitchen onion bulb so it rests on the rim of a glass tumbler of tap water with just its flat basal root disc touching the water surface. Within `3–5 days` on a bright windowsill, dozens of crisp white roots will emerge and lengthen by `3–5 mm` per day. Look closely at the tip of each white root: the translucent cap (`0.5 mm`) shields the creamy-white **apical meristem** immediately behind it, where cells are dividing by **mitosis (`2n = 16 → 2n = 16`)** around the clock.
2. **Potato stem-tuber clone (`Solanum tuberosum`, `2n = 48`):** Rest an old potato showing small dimpled buds ("eyes") on a damp paper towel in a saucer. Over `7–10 days`, watch a sturdy shoot with tiny scale leaves and root initials grow out of each eye. Because every cell in that new shoot was produced by **mitosis** from the single parent tuber without flowers, pollen, or seeds, the sprouting shoot is a **genetic clone apart from new mutations** of the parent potato plant.

callouts.title: > "When you train at high altitude, your mature red blood cells divide by mitosis in the bloodstream to carry more oxygen."
callouts.body: Mature mammalian red blood cells have **no nucleus** and **no chromosomes** (Chapter 2 and Chapter 8), so it is physically impossible for a mature red blood cell to perform DNA replication or mitosis. Instead, low blood oxygen stimulates the kidneys to release the hormone **erythropoietin (`EPO`)**, which travels in the blood to **red bone marrow** and accelerates **mitosis of nucleated haematopoietic stem cells**, producing more red blood cells to release into circulation.

callouts.title: **Cambridge IGCSE Biology (`0610`, Topics 17.2 & 16.1)** tests these exact phrases:
callouts.body:
- **Define mitosis (`17.2.1 Core`):** *"Nuclear division giving rise to genetically identical cells."* (Note that stage names—prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase—are *not* required.)
- **State the four roles of mitosis (`17.2.2 Core`):** **growth**, **repair of damaged tissues**, **replacement of cells**, and **asexual reproduction**.
- **State the Supplement chromosome rules (`17.2.3 & 17.2.4`):** **Exact replication of chromosomes occurs before mitosis**, and **during mitosis, the copies of chromosomes separate, maintaining the chromosome number in each daughter cell**.
- **Discuss asexual reproduction (`16.1.1 & 16.1.2`):** Always separate advantages/disadvantages **in the wild** (one parent, fast colonisation vs no variation for evolution/adaptation) from **in crop production** (uniform desirable traits/yield vs uniform susceptibility of monocultures to disease).

callouts.title: 1. Define **mitosis** (`0610 17.2.1`), state its **four biological roles** (`0610 17.2.2`), and explain how chromosome number is maintained from parent cell to daughter cells (`0610 17.2.3 & 17.2.4`).
callouts.body:
2. Strawberry plants can reproduce **both** asexually (by sending out horizontal stems called **runners** that grow roots by mitosis) and sexually (by producing insect-pollinated flowers that form seeds). Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of reproducing via **runners** (a) for a wild strawberry population in a forest clearing, and (b) for a commercial strawberry farmer.
???

1. **Mitosis** is **nuclear division giving rise to genetically identical cells**. Its four roles are **(1) growth**, **(2) repair of damaged tissues**, **(3) replacement of worn-out cells**, and **(4) asexual reproduction**. Chromosome number is maintained because **exact replication of chromosomes occurs before mitosis** (duplicating `2n = 46` chromosomes into `92` sister chromatids), and **during mitosis, the copies of chromosomes separate** to opposite poles so each daughter nucleus receives a complete diploid set (`2n = 46`).
2. (a) **In the wild:** An **advantage** of runners is that a single well-adapted strawberry plant can colonise the clearing rapidly without needing a mate or insect pollinators; a **disadvantage** is that all runner offspring are genetically identical clones with **little genetic variation apart from mutations**, so a new frost, drought, or fungal pathogen could wipe out the local population. (b) **In commercial crop production:** An **advantage** is that every runner daughter plant is a genetic clone apart from new mutations that preserves the exact sweet flavour, large fruit size, and uniform ripening time of the parent; a **disadvantage** is **monoculture disease vulnerability**—if one cloned plant is susceptible to a fungal wilt or virus, the entire field is equally vulnerable.

callouts.title: A molecular biologist isolates two pure nucleic-acid samples from the **pancreatic beta cells** and **immature bone-marrow red blood cells (erythroblasts)** of the same healthy person: **Sample Set A** contains total **nuclear genomic DNA**, and **Sample Set B** contains total **cytoplasmic messenger RNA (`mRNA`)**. She tests both sets with molecular probes for the **insulin sequence (`INS`)** and the **beta-globin haemoglobin sequence (`HBB`)**. What will she find?
callouts.body:
- In Sample Set A (DNA), beta cells contain only the INS gene and erythroblasts contain only the HBB gene, because unused genes are deleted during differentiation
- In Sample Set A (DNA), both cell types contain BOTH the INS gene and the HBB gene; in Sample Set B (cytoplasmic mRNA), beta cells contain INS mRNA (and zero HBB mRNA) while erythroblasts contain HBB mRNA (and zero INS mRNA)
- Both Sample Set A (DNA) and Sample Set B (mRNA) are identical in both cell types, because all genes are transcribed into mRNA in every cell
???
The second choice. Because both the pancreatic beta cell and the bone-marrow erythroblast descended from the same diploid zygote by **mitosis**, **both cells contain the exact same nuclear DNA (`2n = 46`)**, including **both** the `INS` gene and the `HBB` gene on Chromosome `11` (**Sample Set A**). However, **many genes in a particular cell are not expressed because the cell only makes the specific proteins it needs (`0610 17.1.6`)**: both cells express many housekeeping genes; among the specialist genes tested, the beta cell transcribes **`INS` mRNA** (`Sample Set B`) to translate insulin, whereas the erythroblast transcribes only **`HBB` mRNA** (`Sample Set B`) to translate haemoglobin.

callouts.title: > "A muscle cell and a salivary gland cell make different proteins because the muscle cell only inherited muscle genes during mitosis and deleted its digestive enzyme genes."
callouts.body: Never write that cells lose or delete genes when they specialise (`0610 17.1.6`). Because mitosis copies and separates all `46` chromosomes equally, both the muscle cell and the salivary gland cell contain the **exact same complete set of genes** (both carry the amylase gene and the myosin gene). They make different proteins because **myosin/contractile genes are strongly expressed (transcribed into mRNA and translated into protein) in the muscle cell**, while **amylase/secretory genes are strongly expressed in the salivary gland cell**.

callouts.title: **Cambridge IGCSE Biology (`0610`, Topics 17.1.6 & 17.2.5 Supplement)** frequently pairs these two questions on Paper 4:
callouts.body:
1. **Define stem cells (`17.2.5`):** *"Unspecialised cells that divide by mitosis to produce daughter cells that can become specialised for specific functions."*
2. **Explain how cells from the same embryo become specialised (`17.1.6`):** State three clear points: **(a)** all body cells descend from the zygote by mitosis and therefore **normally retain the same inherited gene set** (apart from changes such as new mutations; mature red blood cells later lose their nuclei); **(b)** in any particular specialised cell, **many genes are not expressed (switched off)** and **only specific genes are expressed (switched on)**; **(c)** the cell therefore transcribes specific **mRNA** and **only makes the specific proteins it needs** for its specialised structure and function.

callouts.title: 1. Define a **stem cell** (`0610 17.2.5`) and explain why a retinal cone cell in your eye and a beta cell in your pancreas contain the exact same genes on Chromosome `11`, yet only the pancreatic beta cell produces **insulin** (`0610 17.1.6`).
callouts.body:
2. Explain how **John Gurdon's (1962)** frog nuclear-transfer experiment and **Shinya Yamanaka's (2006)** induced pluripotent stem cell (`iPSC`) experiment prove that cell specialisation does not delete unused genes.
???

1. **Stem cells** are **unspecialised cells that divide by mitosis to produce daughter cells that can become specialised for specific functions**. Both the retinal cone cell and the pancreatic beta cell were formed by **mitosis** from the same diploid zygote, so **both contain the exact same 46 chromosomes and the same genes** (including the insulin gene `INS` on Chromosome `11`). However, **many genes in a particular cell are not expressed because the cell only makes the specific proteins it needs**: in the pancreatic beta cell the `INS` gene is **expressed** (transcribed into `INS` mRNA and translated at ribosomes into insulin), whereas in the retinal cone cell the `INS` gene is **not expressed (switched off)** and light-sensitive opsin genes are expressed instead.
2. In `1962`, **John Gurdon** transplanted the nucleus of a fully differentiated **tadpole intestinal epithelial cell** into a UV-enucleated frog egg, and that single gut nucleus directed the growth of a normal tadpole and frog with working heart muscle, brain neurones, and eyes. In `2006`, **Shinya Yamanaka** added four transcription factors (`Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc`) to differentiated adult **skin fibroblasts** and rewound them into **induced pluripotent stem cells (`iPSCs`)** that could differentiate into heart, nerve, or beta cells. If differentiation had deleted unused genes, neither an intestinal nucleus nor a skin fibroblast could ever build heart or nerve proteins again; their reprogramming shows that differentiation need not delete the genes needed to build other tissues. It does not mean that every specialised cell retains an entirely unchanged genome; mature red blood cells, for example, lose their nuclei.

A beta cell and an erythroblast both contain INS and HBB DNA. Predict which RNA probes distinguish them, and explain why neither cell makes just one protein.
???
Both cell types contain the genes, but their specialist RNA differs. Both also make many shared housekeeping proteins.

callouts.title: The domestic horse (*Equus caballus*) has a diploid chromosome number of **`2n = 64`** (`32` homologous pairs), whereas the domestic donkey (*Equus asinus*) has a diploid chromosome number of **`2n = 62`** (`31` homologous pairs). When a male donkey mates with a female horse, their offspring is a **mule**—a strong, healthy, long-lived animal that is almost always **sterile** (unable to produce functional gametes). How many chromosomes are in a horse egg (`n`), a donkey sperm (`n`), and a mule's body cells—and why can the mule grow from a zygote into a strong adult yet fail at meiosis?
callouts.body:
- Horse egg n = 64, donkey sperm n = 62, mule zygote = 126; the mule is sterile because 126 chromosomes cannot fit inside a sperm head
- Horse egg n = 32, donkey sperm n = 31, mule zygote = 63 chromosomes; the mule grows normally because mitosis copies and separates all 63 chromosomes individually without needing pairs, but is sterile because 63 chromosomes (an odd number from two different species) cannot pair up evenly two-by-two during Meiosis I
- Horse egg n = 32, donkey sperm n = 31, mule zygote = 63 chromosomes; the mule is sterile because its body cells cannot perform S-phase DNA replication
???
The second choice. Work through both divisions:

1. **Gamete counts and fertilisation:** Meiosis in the mother horse halves `2n = 64` to a haploid egg with **`n = 32` chromosomes**. Meiosis in the father donkey halves `2n = 62` to a haploid sperm with **`n = 31` chromosomes**. Fusion of gamete nuclei at fertilisation produces a mule zygote with `32 + 31 =` **`63` chromosomes**.
2. **Why mitosis succeeds (`growth to adulthood`):** In **mitosis**, homologous chromosomes **never need to pair up**: all `63` chromosomes replicate in S phase to `126` sister chromatids, line up individually at the spindle equator, and separate `63 + 63` into every daughter cell.
3. **Why meiosis jams (`sterility`):** In **Meiosis I**, chromosomes **must pair up side-by-side into homologous pairs** before separating. With an **odd number (`63` chromosomes)** from two different karyotypes, the chromosomes cannot pair evenly two-by-two, leading to chaotic segregation and non-viable gametes.

callouts.title: > "Meiosis halves the chromosome number because DNA does not replicate before meiosis, and a haploid human sperm simply gets any random 23 chromosomes out of the 46."
callouts.body:
Both parts of that statement are incorrect:

1. **DNA replicates once before meiosis:** Just like mitosis, meiosis is preceded by S-phase DNA replication (`46` chromosomes → `92` sister chromatids). Homologues separate in Meiosis I, halving the chromosome sets from `2n = 46` to `n = 23`. Overall meiosis performs **two consecutive nuclear divisions** (`Meiosis I` separates homologous pairs; `Meiosis II` separates sister chromatids) after that single replication.
2. **One complete set (`1` from each of the `23` pairs):** A normal haploid gamete (`n = 23`) never receives "any random 23 chromosomes" (such as two copies of Chromosome `1` and zero copies of Chromosome `2`). Because homologous pairs separate in Meiosis I, every normal gamete receives **one complete haploid set**—exactly **one chromosome from each of the 23 homologous pairs**.

callouts.title: **Cambridge Lower Secondary Science (`0893`, `7Bp.03` & `9Bs.03`)** and **Cambridge IGCSE Biology (`0610`, Topics 17.1, 17.3 & 16.2)** test these exact definitions and comparisons:
callouts.body:
- **Haploid vs diploid (`17.1 Core/Supplement & 16.2.3`):** A **haploid nucleus** contains a **single set of chromosomes** (e.g. **nuclei of gametes**, `n = 23` in humans); a **diploid nucleus** contains **two sets of chromosomes** (e.g. **nucleus of a zygote** and body cells, **`23` pairs = `46` chromosomes** in humans).
- **Meiosis (`17.3.1 Core & 17.3.2 Supplement`):** State that meiosis is involved in the **production of gametes**, and describe it as a **reduction division in which the chromosome number is halved from diploid to haploid resulting in genetically different cells**.
- **Fertilisation and sexual reproduction (`16.2.1 & 16.2.2 Core`):** Define **fertilisation** as the **fusion of the nuclei of gametes**, and **sexual reproduction** as **a process involving the fusion of the nuclei of two gametes to form a zygote and the production of offspring that are genetically different from each other**.

callouts.title: 1. Define (a) a **haploid nucleus**, (b) a **diploid nucleus**, (c) **meiosis** (`0610 17.3.2`), and (d) **fertilisation** (`0610 16.2.2`).
callouts.body:
2. A female Indian muntjac deer (*Muntiacus muntjak*) has a diploid chromosome number of **`2n = 6`** (`3` homologous pairs) in her body cells. State how many chromosomes are present in (a) a muntjac skin cell produced by mitosis, (b) a muntjac egg cell nucleus produced by meiosis, and (c) a muntjac zygote immediately after fertilisation—and explain why **both** meiosis and fertilisation are necessary in every generation.
???

1. (a) A **haploid nucleus** is a nucleus containing a **single set of unpaired chromosomes** (`n`, e.g. `23` in human gametes). (b) A **diploid nucleus** is a nucleus containing **two sets of chromosomes** (`2n`, e.g. `23` homologous pairs = `46` chromosomes in human body cells and the zygote). (c) **Meiosis** is a **reduction division in which the chromosome number is halved from diploid to haploid resulting in genetically different cells**. (d) **Fertilisation** is the **fusion of the nuclei of gametes**.
2. (a) Skin cell produced by mitosis: **`6` chromosomes (`2n = 6`)**. (b) Egg cell nucleus produced by meiosis: **`3` chromosomes (`n = 3`**, one from each of the `3` homologous pairs, with `2³ = 8` possible independent-assortment combinations). (c) Zygote immediately after fertilisation: **`6` chromosomes (`n + n = 3 + 3 = 2n = 6`)**. Both processes are required in every generation because **meiosis halves** the chromosome count (`2n → n`) while generating genetic variation, and **fertilisation fuses** two haploid gamete nuclei (`n + n → 2n`) to restore the species' diploid chromosome number instead of allowing it to double (`6 → 12 → 24`) every generation.

callouts.title: Why your Cavendish banana has no seeds—and why one fungus threatens it
callouts.body:
This is an agricultural cytogenetics synthesis case uniting Section 12.1 (S-phase DNA replication), Section 12.2 (mitosis and asexual crop cloning), Section 12.3 (apical meristem stem cells and selective gene expression), and Section 12.4 (meiosis, homologous pairing, and sexual variation).

If you slice open a wild banana (*Musa acuminata*) growing in the forests of Assam or the Western Ghats, the pulp is packed with dozens of rock-hard black seeds the size of peppercorns. Yet when you peel a sweet yellow **Cavendish banana** (such as the `'Grand Naine'` and `'Robusta'` cultivars grown across Maharashtra’s Jalgaon banana belt, Gujarat, and Tamil Nadu), you find only tiny brown specks along the centre and **zero hard seeds**.

A crop cytogenetics laboratory in Coimbatore compares the chromosome counts and division behaviour of three tropical crop plants:

| Crop | Ploidy (`x`) | Meiosis & Propagation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Wild Forest Banana** (*Musa acuminata*) | **Diploid (`2n = 22`)**, `11` homologous pairs (`x = 11`) | Balanced `11 + 11` Meiosis I → viable **`n = 11`** gametes & **sexual seeds** (`2n = 22`); **genetically diverse** |
| **2. Cavendish Banana** (*Musa acuminata* `'Cavendish'`) | **Triploid (`3n = 33`)**, `11` homologous triplets (`x = 11`) | Uneven `2-vs-1` Meiosis I split → gametes (`11–22` chr) abort; **asexual mitosis only** (suckers & meristem clones) |
| **3. Coimbatore Sugarcane** (*Saccharum* `'Co'`, **E. K. Janaki Ammal**) | **Even Polyploid (`2n = 80–112`)**, `40–56` pairs (`x = 10`) | Viable gametes allow **sexual crosses** (*S. officinarum* × *S. spontaneum*); **mitotic stem cuttings** clone the crop |

Today, banana farmers worldwide face an urgent crisis: a soil-borne fungus called **Panama disease Tropical Race 4 (`Fusarium oxysporum` f. sp. *cubense* `TR4`)** invades banana roots and blocks their water-conducting xylem vessels. In the 1950s, a related strain (`Race 1`) wiped out the world’s previous export banana clone (`'Gros Michel'`, also `3n = 33`), and `TR4` can now infect the Cavendish clone.

Use all four sections of Chapter 12 to answer three diagnostic questions:

1. **S-phase replication and mitosis (`12.1 & 12.2`) vs Meiosis (`12.4`):** Explain why a **triploid Cavendish banana cell (`3n = 33`)** can normally copy its DNA in S phase and dividing by **mitosis** to grow a huge leafy plant (stating the exact number of chromosomes and sister chromatids before and after S phase), yet usually fails to produce balanced, fertile gametes during **meiosis**. Its fruit can develop without fertilisation (**parthenocarpy**), while low fertility explains why normal viable seeds are usually absent.
2. **Stem cells and selective gene expression (`12.3`):** To supply millions of disease-free Cavendish plantlets to farmers in Jalgaon, a tissue-culture laboratory excises a `1 mm` dome of **apical meristem** from a single Cavendish shoot tip and places it on sterile nutrient agar. Explain why apical meristem cells can regenerate complete roots, stems, and leaves, and how **selective gene expression (`0610 17.1.6`)** allows cells with the exact same `33` chromosomes to become either root hair cells or photosynthetic palisade mesophyll cells.
3. **Asexual vs sexual reproduction in crop production (`0610 16.1.2 & 16.2.4`):** Explain why propagating Cavendish bananas exclusively by **mitosis** (suckers and tissue culture) is simultaneously a huge **commercial advantage** for fruit quality and a huge **biological disadvantage** against Panama disease `TR4`—and how breeders are using **wild diploid (`2n = 22`) bananas** and **E. K. Janaki Ammal’s** Coimbatore breeding strategy to rescue the crop.
???

1. **Why `3n = 33` succeeds in mitosis (`12.1 & 12.2`) but jams in meiosis (`12.4`):**
    - **In S phase and mitosis:** Before mitosis, **semi-conservative DNA replication** unzips and copies all **`33` chromosomes** into **`66` sister chromatids** linked as `33` replicated chromosome units. During **mitosis**, homologous chromosomes **do not pair up**: all `33` replicated chromosomes line up individually at the spindle equator, the links between sisters are released, and `33` identical daughter chromosomes move to each pole (`3n = 33 → 3n = 33`). Thus the banana plant grows leaves, roots, and suckers normally.
    - **In meiosis:** During **Meiosis I**, homologous chromosomes **must pair up side-by-side** before separating to halve the chromosome count. Because the triploid Cavendish nucleus has **`11` homologous triplets (`3` copies of each chromosome)**, three chromosomes cannot divide evenly into two poles: at each triplet, `2` chromosomes go to one pole and `1` goes to the other at random. Almost every resulting spore/gamete receives an unbalanced chromosome number (`between 12 and 21`) and aborts, so fertile seeds are rare. A separate inherited capacity called **parthenocarpy** allows fruit to develop without fertilisation.

2. **Apical meristem stem cells (`0610 17.2.5`) and selective gene expression (`0610 17.1.6`):**
    - The shoot-tip **apical meristem** consists of **plant stem cells**—**unspecialised cells that divide by mitosis to produce daughter cells that can become specialised for specific functions**.
    - Every daughter cell produced by mitosis inherits the **exact same `33` chromosomes and the exact same genes**. As plant hormones guide differentiation, **selective gene expression (`0610 17.1.6`)** switches ON root-hair membrane-carrier and cell-wall genes in basal cells (while silencing photosynthetic genes), and switches ON Rubisco and chlorophyll-synthesis genes in upper leaf palisade mesophyll cells (while silencing root-specific genes). Each cell **only expresses the genes coding for the specific proteins it needs**.

3. **The monoculture trap and the sexual-breeding rescue (`0610 16.1.2 & 16.2.4`):**
    - **Commercial advantage of asexual mitotic propagation:** Every sucker or tissue-cultured plantlet is a **genetically very similar clone (`3n = 33`)** that preserves the exact seedless, sweet, high-yield Cavendish phenotype across every farm.
    - **Biological disadvantage against `TR4`:** Because mitosis produces **very little genetic variation apart from mutations**, Cavendish plants have a narrow genetic base, although mutations and tissue-culture variation can occur. Once *Fusarium* `TR4` evolves the molecular keys to overcome the defences of one Cavendish plant, **every single Cavendish plant in the plantation is equally susceptible**.
    - **The Coimbatore breeding rescue:** Because sterile `3n = 33` Cavendish plants cannot be crossed directly, breeders return to **wild fertile diploid (`2n = 22`) bananas** that undergo normal **meiosis (`n = 11`)** and carry natural `TR4`-resistance alleles. Following **E. K. Janaki Ammal's** two-step sugarcane strategy, breeders use **sexual reproduction (meiosis + cross-pollination)** involving diploid/tetraploid parents to generate genetically diverse new **triploid (`3n = 33`)** hybrids that combine `TR4` resistance with seedless fruit, and then multiply the winning hybrid by **mitotic tissue culture**.

sections.heading: 13.1 The monk in the pea patch: why traits don't blend, and how genes come in alleles
sections.excerpt:
:::scene St Thomas's Abbey, Brno (Moravia), 1856–1866

Walk into the walled kitchen garden of St Thomas's Abbey in Brno in the spring of 1856, and you would find a thirty-three-year-old Augustinian friar named **Johann Gregor Mendel** kneeling beside rows of climbing garden peas (*Pisum sativum*) with a pair of jeweller's forceps, a camel-hair paintbrush, and a ruled ledger book.

Before Mendel began his eight-year pea investigation, scientists had no agreed explanation of inheritance. One tempting model was **blending inheritance**. According to the blending view, the hereditary material of the mother and the father mixed irreversibly inside the offspring like a pot of red paint stirred into a pot of white paint to make pink paint. Once mixed, red and white could never be separated again.

Trained in experimental physics and combinatorial probability at the University of Vienna, Mendel investigated how parental characters reappear in later generations. Garden peas offered a way to test whether inherited instructions blend or remain distinct:

- **Strict pollination control:** A pea flower's reproductive organs (pollen-making anthers and ovule-holding carpel) are sealed inside a bo

sections.heading: 13.2 The Punnett ledger: monohybrid crosses, test crosses, and family pedigrees
sections.excerpt:
:::scene University of Cambridge, 1900–1905, and Tata Memorial Centre, Parel, Mumbai, 1950s

When **Mendel**'s 1866 paper was rediscovered in the spring of 1900, Cambridge biologist **William Bateson** read it on the train to London to address the Royal Horticultural Society and realised that biology had found its atomic theory. Over the next five years in Cambridge, **William Bateson** coined the terms **genetics**, **allele**, **homozygote**, and **heterozygote**, while his collaborator **Reginald Punnett** introduced a simple visual matrix—the **`2 × 2` Punnett square**—that turns meiotic chromosome segregation and random fertilisation into a foolproof accounting grid.

Every **monohybrid cross** (a genetic cross tracking **one gene locus** with two alleles) follows the same **six-line genetic diagram protocol**:

1. **Parental phenotypes:** Write the observable feature of each parent (e.g. `Purple flower × Purple flower`).
2. **Parental genotypes (`2n`):** Write **two allele letters** for each diploid parent (e.g. `Bb × Bb`).
3. **Gametes (`n`):** Because **meiosis halves the chromosome number (`2n → n`)** by separating homologous chromosomes, each haploid gamete receives **onl

sections.heading: 13.3 When neither allele yields: codominance and the ABO blood group puzzle
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Institute of Pathological Anatomy, Vienna, 1900–1901, and Indian Cancer Research Centre, Parel, Mumbai, 1950s

In **Mendel**'s seven pea characters, one allele was always completely dominant over the other: a heterozygous `Rr` seed looked identical to an `RR` seed. Soon after 1900, however, geneticists discovered traits where **neither allele masks the other** inside a heterozygote.

In 1900–1901 in Vienna, physician **Karl Landsteiner** solved the mystery of why blood transfusions between some people succeeded while others caused fatal clumping (**agglutination**) of red blood cells. As you learned in Chapter 8 (`8.4`) and Chapter 10 (`10.4`), the cell membranes of human red blood cells carry carbohydrate identity tags (**antigens**), while blood plasma carries Y-shaped **antibodies** against whichever foreign ABO antigens the person lacks. In 1924, mathematician Felix Bernstein showed that the inheritance of the four ordinary ABO blood groups—**A**, **B**, **AB**, and **O**—fits **three alleles at one locus**. Researchers mapped this locus to **Chromosome `9`** decades later, and in the 1950s **L. D. Sanghvi** mapped the frequencies and family pedigrees of those alleles

sections.heading: 13.4 The twenty-third pair: XX, XY, and sex-linked inheritance
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Bryn Mawr College, Pennsylvania, 1905, and the Fly Room, Columbia University, New York, 1910

In Sections `13.1` to `13.3`, every gene we tracked—pea seed shape (`R/r`), stem height (`T/t`), and human `ABO` blood group on Chromosome `9` (`Iᴬ/Iᴮ/Iᴼ`)—behaved identically in males and females. That is because **22 of the 23 homologous chromosome pairs** in a human diploid cell (`2n = 46`) are **autosomes** (`Chromosomes 1` to `22`), which are present in two matched copies of equal length and equal gene content in both sexes.

What about the **twenty-third pair**—the **sex chromosomes** first linked to sex determination by **Nettie Stevens** in 1905?

1. **Human females are `XX` (`44` autosomes + `XX` = `46`):** In a female diploid cell, Pair `23` consists of **two large, homologous `X` chromosomes**. When a woman's ovaries produce haploid egg cells (**ova**, `n = 23`) by meiosis, every single ovum receives `22` autosomes plus **one `X` chromosome (`100%` `X` ova)**.
2. **Human males are `XY` (`44` autosomes + `XY` = `46`):** In a male diploid cell, Pair `23` consists of **one large `X` chromosome** and **one much smaller `Y` chromosome**. When a man's testes produce haploid *

sections.excerpt:
:::fig c13_mumbai_maternity_case() | Forensic synthesis plate for Case 13 resolving (Left) the Mumbai maternity ward ABO bracelet swap (Couple 1 IᴬIᴮ × IᴼIᴼ can only produce Group A or Group B children, proving Group O Baby 1 belongs to Couple 2 IᴬIᴼ × IᴮIᴼ and Group A Baby 2 belongs to Couple 1) and (Right) the X-linked clinic pedigree (showing why two normal-vision parents XᴮXᵇ × XᴮY have a 50% chance among sons—25% of all children—of an affected son XᵇY and how the allele passed from the affected maternal grandfather XᵇY through the carrier mother XᴮXᵇ).

:::case Solving the Mumbai maternity ward & genetic clinic case files
This clinical genetics synthesis case unites Section 13.1 (genes, loci, alleles, homozygosity vs heterozygosity, and sufficient protein activity), Section 13.2 (`2 × 2` Punnett squares, test crosses, and pedigree detective rules), Section 13.3 (Chromosome `9` `ABO` multiple alleles `Iᴬ, Iᴮ, Iᴼ` and codominance), and Section 13.4 (`XX` vs `XY` sex determination and X-linked recessive inheritance).

Return to the two hospital puzzles from the opening of Chapter 13 at our teaching hospital in Parel, Mumbai:

| Case File | Parents' Phenotypes | Offspring & Family

callouts.title: Suppose **Mendel** crosses a **pure-breeding round-seeded pea plant** with a **pure-breeding wrinkled-seeded pea plant** to produce first-generation (**`F₁`**) hybrid seeds, and then allows those `F₁` plants to self-pollinate to produce second-generation (**`F₂`**) seeds. If the **paint-pot blending hypothesis** were true, what should the `F₁` and `F₂` seeds look like—and what did **Mendel** actually observe?
callouts.body:
- Blending predicts 100% round F₁ seeds and 75% round : 25% wrinkled F₂ seeds; Mendel observed 100% half-wrinkled F₁ and F₂ seeds
- Blending predicts semi-wrinkled intermediate F₁ seeds that stay semi-wrinkled forever in F₂; Mendel observed 100% round F₁ seeds, and in F₂ the wrinkled trait returned completely unblemished in roughly 25% of the seeds (a 3 : 1 ratio of round to wrinkled)
- Blending predicts 50% round and 50% wrinkled seeds in both F₁ and F₂; Mendel observed 100% wrinkled seeds in F₁
???
The second choice. If maternal and paternal instructions blended like paint, crossing round with wrinkled would produce intermediate, mildly dimpled `F₁` seeds, and self-pollinating those `F₁` plants could never recover a purely wrinkled seed. Instead, **Mendel** observed that **100% of the `F₁` seeds were completely smooth and round**. Even more strikingly, when those round `F₁` plants self-pollinated to form `F₂` seeds, **roughly one quarter (`25.3%`) of the `F₂` seeds were completely wrinkled**, indistinguishable from the original wrinkled grandparent. The wrinkled instruction had lain hidden inside the `F₁` plants for an entire generation without being diluted away.

callouts.title: Two frequent traps to avoid when using `dominant` and `recessive`:
callouts.body:
1. **"Dominant" does NOT mean "more common in the population" or "stronger/healthier":** Dominance only describes which allele is expressed inside a **heterozygote (`Aa`)**. Whether an allele is common or rare in a population depends on natural selection and history (Chapter 14), not on whether it is dominant. For example, in humans, some forms of **polydactyly** (extra fingers or toes) and **Huntington's disease** can be caused by **dominant alleles**, yet those alleles are uncommon. Conversely, **Blood Group O (`IᴼIᴼ`)** is recessive, yet it is the single most common blood group in many human populations.
2. **Never write "a dominant gene" or "a recessive gene":** Everyone has the *same genes* (the seed-shape gene, the flower-colour gene, the beta-globin gene). Always write **"a dominant allele"** or **"a recessive allele"**.

callouts.title: **Cambridge Lower Secondary Science (`0893`)** and **Cambridge IGCSE Biology (`0610`, Topic 17.4 Core)** require word-accurate definitions of these nine terms:
callouts.body:
- **Inheritance (`17.4.1`):** The **transmission of genetic information from generation to generation**.
- **Gene (`17.1.2`) vs Allele (`17.1.3`):** A **gene** is a **length of DNA that codes for a protein**; an **allele** is an **alternative form of a gene**.
- **Dominant allele (`17.4.2`):** An **allele that is expressed if it is present in the genotype**.
- **Recessive allele (`17.4.3`):** An **allele that is only expressed when there is no dominant allele of the gene present in the genotype**.
- **Genotype (`17.4.4`) vs Phenotype (`17.4.5`):** **Genotype** is the **genetic make-up of an organism in terms of the alleles present**; **phenotype** is the **observable features of an organism**.
- **Homozygous (`17.4.6–17.4.7`) vs Heterozygous (`17.4.8–17.4.9`):** **Homozygous** means having **two identical alleles of a particular gene** (two identical homozygous individuals that breed together will be **pure-breeding**); **heterozygous** means having **two different alleles of a particular gene** (a heterozygous individual is **not pure-breeding**).

callouts.title: 1. Define (a) **allele**, (b) **genotype**, (c) **phenotype**, (d) **homozygous**, and (e) **heterozygous**, and state which of (d) or (e) is **pure-breeding**.
callouts.body:
2. In pea plants, the allele for **tall stems (`T`)** is dominant to the allele for **dwarf stems (`t`)**, where `T` codes for functional gibberellin `3β-hydroxylase` enzyme and `t` codes for an enzyme with greatly reduced activity. State the **genotype**, **zygosity**, **enzyme activity** (normal, much reduced, or sufficient for tall growth), and **stem-length phenotype** of (a) a pure-breeding tall plant, (b) a pure-breeding dwarf plant, and (c) an `F₁` hybrid produced by crossing (a) and (b).
???

1. (a) An **allele** is an **alternative form of a gene**. (b) **Genotype** is the **genetic make-up of an organism in terms of the alleles present**. (c) **Phenotype** is the **observable features of an organism**. (d) **Homozygous** means having **two identical alleles of a particular gene**; **two identical homozygous individuals that breed together will be pure-breeding**. (e) **Heterozygous** means having **two different alleles of a particular gene**; a heterozygous individual is **not pure-breeding**.
2. (a) Pure-breeding tall plant: genotype **`TT`**, **homozygous dominant**, **normal enzyme activity**, **tall stem phenotype**. (b) Pure-breeding dwarf plant: genotype **`tt`**, **homozygous recessive**, **much reduced enzyme activity**, **dwarf stem phenotype**. (c) `F₁` hybrid (`TT × tt`): genotype **`Tt`**, **heterozygous**, **sufficient enzyme activity for tall growth** (enough active growth hormone `GA₁`), **tall stem phenotype**.

callouts.title: A plant breeder in Pune has a prize **purple-flowered pea plant (`B_`)** and wants to know whether it is **pure-breeding (`BB`)** or a **heterozygous carrier (`Bb`)** of the white-flower allele. Which partner should she cross the mystery purple plant with to reveal a hidden recessive allele in the next generation—and what offspring ratios distinguish `BB` from `Bb`?
callouts.body:
- Cross the mystery plant with a homozygous recessive white-flowered tester plant (`bb`, a **test cross**); if the mystery plant is `BB`, 100% of the offspring will be purple (`Bb`), whereas if the mystery plant is `Bb`, the offspring will split in a **1 : 1 ratio** (`50%` purple `Bb` : `50%` white `bb`)
- Cross the mystery plant with a homozygous dominant purple plant (`BB`); if it is `Bb`, 25% of the offspring will have white flowers
- Cross the mystery plant with a known heterozygote (`Bb`); only a `3 : 1` ratio can reveal a hidden allele
???
The first choice. Crossing with `BB` (the second choice) is useless because `BB` gives a dominant `B` allele to every single gamete, making `100%` of the offspring purple regardless of whether the mystery plant is `BB` or `Bb`. By crossing the mystery plant (`B_`) with a **homozygous recessive tester (`bb`)**—a procedure now called a ==test cross==, of the kind Mendel used—every tester gamete contributes only the recessive allele `(b)`. Therefore the offspring phenotypes directly display the gametes of the mystery parent:

- **If the mystery parent is homozygous dominant (`BB × bb`):** All gametes from the mystery parent are `(B)`, so **100% of the offspring are heterozygous (`Bb`) and purple-flowered** (`0%` white).
- **If the mystery parent is heterozygous (`Bb × bb`):** Half of its gametes are `(B)` and half are `(b)`, producing **`50%` purple (`Bb`) and `50%` white (`bb`) offspring—an expected `1 : 1` ratio**. Even a **single white-flowered (`bb`) offspring** proves beyond doubt that the purple parent carried a hidden `b` allele. An all-purple sample supports `BB` but does not prove it: a `Bb` parent can also produce only purple offspring by chance. For four offspring, that chance is `(1/2)⁴ = 1/16`.

callouts.title: **The Two-Coin & Two-Dal Mendel Ledger (Mumbai Kitchen Investigation)**
callouts.body:
*Educational adaptation disclosure:* This safe household probability model is a non-trialled educational adaptation designed to demonstrate how independent gamete segregation (`50% : 50%`) generates `1 : 2 : 1` genotype ratios, `3 : 1` phenotype ratios, `1 : 1` test crosses, and convergence from small (`N = 16`) to larger (`N = 64`) samples. It uses only dry kitchen items or coins (`0` chemicals, `0` heat, `0` biological fluids).

**What you need:** Two identical Indian coins (`₹1`, `₹2`, or `₹5`, where **Heads = dominant allele `R`** and **Tails = recessive allele `r`**)—or two small bowls each holding `20` pale **kabuli chana (chickpeas = `R`)** and `20` dark **kala chana (dark chickpeas = `r`)** mixed thoroughly—plus a notebook and pen.

**Part A — Simulating a monohybrid `Rr × Rr` cross (`N = 16` vs `N = 64`):**

1. **Small-family run (`16` fertilisations):** Toss both coins together (or draw one bean blindfolded from Bowl 1 and one from Bowl 2, returning the beans and remixing after each draw) **16 times**. Coin 1 represents the **maternal egg (`R` or `r`)**; Coin 2 represents the **paternal sperm (`R` or `r`)**. Use the coins if the two kinds of chickpea feel different when you draw them. Tally each outcome in four columns: **`RR` (Heads–Heads, Round)**, **`Rr` (Heads–Tails or Tails–Heads, Round)**, **`rr` (Tails–Tails, Wrinkled)**, and **Total Round (`RR + Rr`) vs Wrinkled (`rr`)**.
2. **Check the small-sample bounce:** With only `16` trials, your theoretical expectation is `4 RR : 8 Rr : 4 rr` (`12` Round : `4` Wrinkled = `3 : 1`), but random luck often gives `10 : 6` (`1.67 : 1`) or `14 : 2` (`7 : 1`). That is why a single pea pod or a human family of four children rarely shows an exact `3 : 1` split.
3. **Full `64`-trial convergence run:** Continue tossing for `48` more trials to reach **`N = 64` total fertilisations** (expecting `16 RR : 32 Rr : 16 rr`, or `48` Round : `16` Wrinkled). Compare the combined `RR + Rr` percentage with **`75%`**. Did it move closer? It need not do so in every run; larger samples have smaller *typical* percentage fluctuations. There are two routes to `Rr` (`Heads–Tails` + `Tails–Heads`), so its expected probability (`50%`) is twice that of `RR` or `rr` (`25%` each).

**Part B — Simulating a `1 : 1` diagnostic test cross (`Rr × rr`):**

1. Lay Coin 2 flat on the table showing **Tails (`r`)** permanently—this is your **homozygous recessive tester (`rr`)**, which can only ever supply `(r)` gametes.
2. Toss only Coin 1 (`Rr` parent) **32 times**. Every Heads gives **`Rr` (Round)**; every Tails gives **`rr` (Wrinkled)**. Compare your result with the expected **`50% Rr : 50% rr` (`1 : 1`)**. Thirty-two tosses need not split exactly in half; record what happened rather than changing the counts to fit.

callouts.title: Watch out for three classic Punnett and pedigree mistakes:
callouts.body:
1. **Gametes carry 1 allele, never 2:** In a monohybrid cross of `Bb × Bb`, the gametes are **`(B)` and `(b)`**—never `(BB)` or `(Bb)`. Putting two letters of the same gene into one gamete means meiosis failed to separate homologous chromosomes.
2. **Probabilities do not "use up" squares across siblings:** A `1 in 4` (`25%`) chance of an `aa` child in `Aa × Aa` does **not** mean that if the first child is `aa`, the next three children are guaranteed to be unaffected. Every pregnancy draws fresh gametes from the `2 × 2` grid with the same `25%` probability.
3. **Always write ratios in simplest whole numbers:** Write **`3 : 1`** (not `75% : 25%` or `12 : 4` when a ratio is asked for) and **`1 : 1`** (not `2 : 2`), and always label which phenotype belongs to which number (e.g. **`3 round : 1 wrinkled`**).

callouts.title: **Cambridge IGCSE Biology (`0610`, Topic 17.4 Core & Supplement)** tests three core diagram skills here:
callouts.body:
- **Monohybrid Punnett squares (`17.4.10 & 17.4.12 Core`):** Construct and interpret genetic diagrams, including Punnett squares, to predict the results of monohybrid crosses and calculate phenotypic ratios (**`1 : 1`** and **`3 : 1`**) and probabilities (`100%`, `75%`, `50%`, `25%`, `0%`).
- **Pedigree diagrams (`17.4.11 Core`):** Use and interpret pedigree diagrams for the inheritance of a given characteristic (`Rule 1: Unaffected × Unaffected → Affected = recessive`; `Rule 2: Affected × Affected → Unaffected = dominant`).
- **Test crosses (`17.4.13–17.4.14 Supplement`):** Identify an unknown dominant genotype (`AA` vs `Aa`) by crossing with a **homozygous recessive individual (`aa`)** and interpreting the resulting **`100%` dominant** versus **`1 : 1`** offspring ratio.

callouts.title: 1. Use **cystic fibrosis** as an autosomal recessive example: let `f` represent a condition-causing allele and `F` a working allele. **Beta-thalassaemia involves a different gene**, but can follow the same recessive pattern. Two unaffected parents (`Ff × Ff`) are expecting a child. Construct the six-line genetic diagram (parental phenotypes, parental genotypes, gametes, `2 × 2` Punnett square, offspring genotypes/phenotypes, and ratios) and state the percentage probability that the child will (a) have the condition, (b) be an unaffected heterozygous carrier, and (c) be unaffected overall.
callouts.body:
2. A farmer in Nashik buys a black-coated ram. In this sheep breed, **black coat (`B`)** is dominant to **white coat (`b`)**. Explain how the farmer can use a **test cross** to determine whether the ram is pure-breeding (`BB`) or heterozygous (`Bb`).
???

1. **Genetic diagram for `Ff × Ff`:**
    - **Parental phenotypes:** Unaffected carrier mother × Unaffected carrier father
    - **Parental genotypes:** `Ff × Ff`
    - **Gametes:** Maternal `(F)` and `(f)` × Paternal `(F)` and `(f)`
    - **Punnett grid (`2 × 2`):** `(F) + (F) → FF` (`25%`); `(F) + (f) → Ff` (`25%`); `(f) + (F) → Ff` (`25%`); `(f) + (f) → ff` (`25%`).
    - **Offspring genotypes & ratio:** `1 FF : 2 Ff : 1 ff` (`25%` homozygous normal : `50%` heterozygous carrier : `25%` homozygous recessive affected).
    - **Offspring phenotypes & ratio:** `3 unaffected : 1 affected` (`75% : 25%`).
    - **Answers:** (a) Probability of having the condition (`ff`) = **`25%` (`1/4` or `0.25`)**. (b) Probability of being an unaffected carrier (`Ff`) = **`50%` (`1/2` or `0.50`)**. (c) Probability of being unaffected overall (`FF` + `Ff`) = **`75%` (`3/4` or `0.75`)**.
2. **Test cross protocol:** Mate the black ram (`B_`) with several **white-coated ewes**, which are guaranteed to be **homozygous recessive (`bb`)** and produce only `(b)` ova. If the ram is **homozygous dominant (`BB`)**, `100%` of the lambs will be black (`Bb`). If the ram is **heterozygous (`Bb`)**, approximately **`50%` of the lambs will be black (`Bb`) and `50%` will be white (`bb`)** (`1 : 1` ratio); the birth of even a single white lamb (`bb`) proves the ram is heterozygous (`Bb`). All-black offspring support `BB` but do not establish it with certainty; a `Bb` ram can produce an all-black sample by chance.

callouts.title: Suppose a mother with **Blood Group A** whose father was **Group O** marries a father with **Blood Group B** whose mother was **Group O**. What are the exact genotypes of the two parents, and which ABO blood groups can appear among their children?
callouts.body:
- The parents are `IᴬIᴬ` and `IᴮIᴮ`; 100% of their children will have Blood Group AB (`IᴬIᴮ`)
- Because each parent inherited an `Iᴼ` allele from a Group O (`IᴼIᴼ`) grandparent, the mother is **`IᴬIᴼ`** and the father is **`IᴮIᴼ`**; their children have an equal **25% (`1 in 4`) chance of each of the four blood groups—Group AB (`IᴬIᴮ`), Group A (`IᴬIᴼ`), Group B (`IᴮIᴼ`), and Group O (`IᴼIᴼ`)** (a `1 : 1 : 1 : 1` ratio)
- Their children can only be Group A (`50%`) or Group B (`50%`), because Group O and Group AB cannot appear in the same family
???
The second choice. A Group O grandparent has the genotype `IᴼIᴼ` and can pass only an `(Iᴼ)` gamete to every child. Therefore the Group A mother **must** be heterozygous **`IᴬIᴼ`** (producing `50%` `(Iᴬ)` and `50%` `(Iᴼ)` ova), and the Group B father **must** be heterozygous **`IᴮIᴼ`** (producing `50%` `(Iᴮ)` and `50%` `(Iᴼ)` sperm). Combining those gametes in a `2 × 2` Punnett square yields:

- `(Iᴬ) + (Iᴮ) → IᴬIᴮ` = **Group AB (`25%`)**
- `(Iᴬ) + (Iᴼ) → IᴬIᴼ` = **Group A (`25%`)**
- `(Iᴼ) + (Iᴮ) → IᴮIᴼ` = **Group B (`25%`)**
- `(Iᴼ) + (Iᴼ) → IᴼIᴼ` = **Group O (`25%`)**

Four siblings in the same family can legally and biologically have **all four human ABO blood groups (`1 AB : 1 A : 1 B : 1 O`)**.

callouts.title: Three high-frequency notation and conceptual rules for codominance and ABO blood groups:
callouts.body:
1. **Keep the base letter `I` on all three ABO alleles:** Always write **`Iᴬ`, `Iᴮ`, and `Iᴼ`**—never mix `Iᴬ` and `Iᴮ` with a bare lowercase `o` or `i` in Cambridge `0610` exams (`17.4.17`).
2. **Never write `IᴬIᴮIᴼ` for one person:** Three alleles exist in the *human population*, not inside one diploid cell. Every person's genotype has **exactly two alleles** (e.g. `IᴬIᴼ`, `IᴮIᴼ`, `IᴬIᴮ`, `IᴼIᴼ`), and every gamete has **exactly one** (`(Iᴬ)`, `(Iᴮ)`, or `(Iᴼ)`).
3. **Group O is recessive (`IᴼIᴼ`), not codominant:** Only **`Iᴬ` and `Iᴮ`** are codominant (`IᴬIᴮ` = Group AB). The `Iᴼ` allele is **recessive** to both `Iᴬ` (`IᴬIᴼ` = Group A) and `Iᴮ` (`IᴮIᴼ` = Group B).

callouts.title: **Cambridge IGCSE Biology (`0610`, Topic 17.4 Supplement)** specifies:
callouts.body:
- **Codominance (`17.4.15`):** Describe **codominance** as a situation in which **both alleles in heterozygous organisms contribute to the phenotype**.
- **ABO blood groups (`17.4.17`):** Explain the inheritance of **ABO blood groups**: phenotypes are **`A`, `B`, `AB` and `O` blood groups** and alleles are **`Iᴬ`, `Iᴮ` and `Iᴼ`**.
- **Codominant Punnett squares (`17.4.18`):** Construct and interpret genetic diagrams to predict the results of monohybrid crosses involving **codominance** and calculate phenotypic ratios (`1 : 2 : 1`, `1 : 1 : 1 : 1`, `1 : 1`) and probabilities.

callouts.title: 1. State all six possible diploid genotypes formed by the alleles **`Iᴬ`, `Iᴮ`, and `Iᴼ`**, and group them under the four blood group phenotypes (**Group A, Group B, Group AB, Group O**).
callouts.body:
2. A woman with **Blood Group AB (`IᴬIᴮ`)** marries a man with **Blood Group O (`IᴼIᴼ`)**. Construct the six-line genetic diagram (including gametes and a `2 × 2` Punnett square) and state the percentage probability that their child will have (a) Group A, (b) Group B, (c) Group AB, and (d) Group O.
???

1. **Group A:** **`IᴬIᴬ`** and **`IᴬIᴼ`**. **Group B:** **`IᴮIᴮ`** and **`IᴮIᴼ`**. **Group AB:** **`IᴬIᴮ`**. **Group O:** **`IᴼIᴼ`**.
2. **Genetic diagram for `IᴬIᴮ × IᴼIᴼ`:**
    - **Parental phenotypes:** Group AB mother × Group O father
    - **Parental genotypes:** `IᴬIᴮ × IᴼIᴼ`
    - **Gametes:** Maternal `(Iᴬ)` and `(Iᴮ)` × Paternal `(Iᴼ)` and `(Iᴼ)`
    - **Punnett grid (`2 × 2`):** Two boxes are **`IᴬIᴼ`** (`50%`, Group A) and two boxes are **`IᴮIᴼ`** (`50%`, Group B).
    - **Offspring ratio:** **`1 Group A : 1 Group B`** (`50% : 50%`).
    - **Probabilities:** (a) Group A = **`50%`**, (b) Group B = **`50%`**, (c) Group AB = **`0%`**, (d) Group O = **`0%`**.

callouts.title: Contrast two X-linked family crosses for red–green colour vision (`Xᴮ` = normal colour vision, `Xᵇ` = red–green colour vision deficiency):
callouts.body:
**Cross A:** An unaffected **carrier mother (`XᴮXᵇ`)** and a **normal-vision father (`XᴮY`)**.
**Cross B:** A **homozygous normal-vision mother (`XᴮXᴮ`)** and a **colour-blind father (`XᵇY`)**.

In which cross can a **son** inherit red–green colour vision deficiency (`XᵇY`), and why do `0%` of the sons in Cross B inherit their father's colour vision deficiency?
- In **Cross A (`XᴮXᵇ × XᴮY`)**, **50% of sons are affected (`XᵇY`)** (`25%` of all children) because sons inherit their single `X` chromosome from their carrier mother; in **Cross B (`XᴮXᴮ × XᵇY`)**, **0% of sons are affected (`100% XᴮY`)** because a father always passes his `Y` chromosome to his sons and passes his `Xᵇ` chromosome exclusively to his daughters (`100% XᴮXᵇ` carriers)
- In Cross B, 50% of sons are colour-blind because the father is affected (`XᵇY`); in Cross A, 0% of sons are colour-blind because both parents have normal vision
- In both Cross A and Cross B, 25% of daughters and 25% of sons are colour-blind
???
The first choice. Trace the sex chromosomes in each cross:

- **In Cross A (`XᴮXᵇ × XᴮY`):** Maternal ova are `(Xᴮ)` and `(Xᵇ)`; paternal sperm are `(Xᴮ)` and `(Y)`.
    - **Daughters (`XX`):** `50% XᴮXᴮ` (normal) and `50% XᴮXᵇ` (unaffected carrier) → **`0%` of daughters are affected**.
    - **Sons (`XY`):** `50% XᴮY` (normal) and **`50% XᵇY` (colour-blind)** → **`50%` of sons are affected** (which equals **`25%` of all children**).
- **In Cross B (`XᴮXᴮ × XᵇY`):** Maternal ova are all `(Xᴮ)`; paternal sperm are `(Xᵇ)` and `(Y)`.
    - **Sons (`XY`):** Every son receives his father's `(Y)` sperm and his mother's `(Xᴮ)` ovum → **`100% XᴮY` normal sons (`0%` affected sons)**. There is **zero father-to-son transmission** of an X-linked gene.
    - **Daughters (`XX`):** Every daughter receives her father's `(Xᵇ)` sperm and her mother's `(Xᴮ)` ovum → **`100% XᴮXᵇ` unaffected carrier daughters** (who can then pass `Xᵇ` to `50%` of their own sons in the next generation, explaining the famous "grandfather-to-carrier-mother-to-grandson" pedigree pattern).

callouts.title: Three essential exam rules for sex-linked genetic diagrams (`0610 17.4.19–17.4.20`):
callouts.body:
1. **Always write the `X` and `Y` chromosomes in genotypes and gametes:** For sex-linked traits, never write bare letters like `Bb` or `Hh` as if the gene were autosomal. Always write **`XᴮXᵇ`**, **`XᴮY`**, **`XᵇY`** (or **`XᴴXʰ`**, **`XᴴY`**, **`XʰY`**), and write gametes as **`(Xᴮ)`**, **`(Xᵇ)`**, and **`(Y)`**.
2. **Never attach an X-linked superscript to `Y`:** Write **`XᴮY`** and **`XᵇY`**—never `XᴮYᵇ` or `XYᵇ`. The `Y` chromosome lacks the non-homologous X-linked locus.
3. **Check the denominator ("of all children" vs "of sons" vs "of daughters"):** Always write both numbers clearly in your answer (e.g. *"25% of all children, which is 50% of the sons"*), so your answer is unambiguous under any mark scheme.

callouts.title: **Cambridge Lower Secondary Science (`0893`, `8Bp.01` & `9Bp.01`)** and **Cambridge IGCSE Biology (`0610`, Topics 17.1 & 17.4 Supplement)** require:
callouts.body:
- **Sex chromosomes (`0893` & `0610 17.1`):** State that human females have **`XX`** sex chromosomes and males have **`XY`** sex chromosomes, and use a Punnett square to show why sex is inherited in a **`1 : 1` (`50% : 50%`) ratio**.
- **Sex-linked characteristic (`0610 17.4.16`):** Describe a **sex-linked characteristic** as a **characteristic in which the gene responsible is located on a sex chromosome and that this makes it more common in one sex than in the other**.
- **Red–green colour blindness (`17.4.19`) & sex-linked Punnett squares (`17.4.20`):** Describe **red–green colour blindness** as an example of sex linkage, and construct/interpret genetic diagrams using `X`/`Y` superscripts (`Xᴮ, Xᵇ, Y` or `Xᴴ, Xʰ, Y`) to predict phenotypes, carrier status, ratios, and probabilities.

callouts.title: 1. Define a **sex-linked characteristic** (`0610 17.4.16`) and explain why X-linked recessive conditions such as **red–green colour blindness (`Xᵇ`)** and **haemophilia (`Xʰ`)** are much more common in males (`XY`) than in females (`XX`).
callouts.body:
2. A woman who is a **carrier for haemophilia (`XᴴXʰ`)** and a man with **normal blood clotting (`XᴴY`)** have children. Construct a six-line genetic diagram (including gametes and a `2 × 2` Punnett square) and state (a) the probability that a **son** has haemophilia, (b) the probability that a **daughter** is a carrier, and (c) the probability that **any child** born to the couple has haemophilia.
???

1. A **sex-linked characteristic** is a **characteristic in which the gene responsible is located on a sex chromosome and that this makes it more common in one sex than in the other**. X-linked recessive conditions are much more common in males because the gene locus sits on the non-homologous region of the **`X` chromosome** and is absent from the shorter **`Y` chromosome**. A male (`XY`) has only **one `X` chromosome**, so inheriting a single recessive allele (`XᵇY` or `XʰY`) from his mother causes the condition; a female (`XX`) has **two `X` chromosomes**, so a heterozygote (`XᴮXᵇ` or `XᴴXʰ`) is shown as an unaffected carrier in this diagram. A daughter inheriting altered copies from both parents has `XᵇXᵇ` or `XʰXʰ`. In real haemophilia, some women with only one altered copy also have symptoms because X-inactivation changes the balance of cells using each allele.
2. **Genetic diagram for `XᴴXʰ × XᴴY`:**
    - **Parental phenotypes:** Carrier mother (normal clotting) × Normal father (normal clotting)
    - **Parental genotypes:** `XᴴXʰ × XᴴY`
    - **Gametes:** Maternal `(Xᴴ)` and `(Xʰ)` × Paternal `(Xᴴ)` and `(Y)`
    - **Punnett grid (`2 × 2`):**
        - `XᴴXᴴ` (`25%`): Homozygous normal daughter (normal clotting, non-carrier)
        - `XᴴXʰ` (`25%`): Heterozygous carrier daughter (normal clotting, carrier)
        - `XᴴY` (`25%`): Normal son (normal clotting)
        - `XʰY` (`25%`): Affected son (haemophilia)
    - **Probabilities:** (a) Probability that a **son** has haemophilia = **`50%` (`1 in 2` sons)**. (b) Probability that a **daughter** is a carrier (`XᴴXʰ`) = **`50%` (`1 in 2` daughters)**. (c) Probability that **any child** has haemophilia = **`25%` (`1 in 4` of all children)**.

callouts.title: Solving the Mumbai maternity ward & genetic clinic case files
callouts.body:
This clinical genetics synthesis case unites Section 13.1 (genes, loci, alleles, homozygosity vs heterozygosity, and sufficient protein activity), Section 13.2 (`2 × 2` Punnett squares, test crosses, and pedigree detective rules), Section 13.3 (Chromosome `9` `ABO` multiple alleles `Iᴬ, Iᴮ, Iᴼ` and codominance), and Section 13.4 (`XX` vs `XY` sex determination and X-linked recessive inheritance).

Return to the two hospital puzzles from the opening of Chapter 13 at our teaching hospital in Parel, Mumbai:

| Case File | Parents' Phenotypes | Offspring & Family Data |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Case A1 — Couple 1 (Desai)** | Mother = **Group AB**; Father = **Group O** | Assigned Either **Baby 1 (Group O)** or **Baby 2 (Group A)** |
| **Case A2 — Couple 2 (Kulkarni)** | Mother = **Group A**; Father = **Group B** | Both Kulkarnis had one **Group O** parent in Generation I |
| **Case B — Paediatric Clinic** | Mother = **Normal colour vision**; Father = **Normal colour vision** | **Son (age 6) = Red–green colour-blind**; **Daughter (age 8) = Normal**; Maternal grandfather = **Colour-blind** |

Use all four sections of Chapter 13 to answer three forensic diagnostic questions:

1. **Case A — Resolving the maternity ward bracelet swap (`13.1–13.3`):** Using the standard ABO model, state the diploid `ABO` genotypes (`Iᴬ`, `Iᴮ`, `Iᴼ`) of **Couple 1 (Desai)**, **Couple 2 (Kulkarni)**, **Baby 1 (Group O)**, and **Baby 2 (Group A)**. Construct the Punnett squares showing which assignment fits. First explain the result using gametes and alleles. Then connect it to the molecular mechanism: how do the Chromosome `9` enzymes `GTA` and `GTB`, and a non-functional `Iᴼ` allele, produce the predicted blood groups?
2. **Case B — Tracing the X-linked colour-vision pedigree (`13.2 & 13.4`):** Using the alleles **`Xᴮ`** (normal retinal cone opsin photopigment) and **`Xᵇ`** (red–green colour vision deficiency) and **`Y`**, state the exact genotypes of the **maternal grandfather**, the **mother**, the **father**, the **six-year-old son**, and the **possible genotypes of the eight-year-old daughter**. Explain why the son did **not** inherit his condition from his father, and why his mother has normal colour vision despite inheriting `Xᵇ` from her father.
3. **Comparing inheritance patterns (`13.1–13.4`):** The clinic couple (`XᴮXᵇ × XᴮY`) is now expecting a **third child**. Calculate (a) the probability that the new baby will be a **boy (`XY`)**, (b) the probability **among sons** versus **among all children** that the baby will have red–green colour vision deficiency, and (c) how that probability would change if the condition were instead **autosomal recessive (`Aa × Aa`)** like beta-thalassaemia or sickle-cell anaemia (`HbᴬHbˢ × HbᴬHbˢ`) studied by **L. D. Sanghvi** in Mumbai.
???

1. **Case A — Maternity ward ABO proof (`13.1–13.3`):**
    - **Genotypes of Couple 1 (Desai):** Mother is Group AB = **`IᴬIᴮ`** (codominant heterozygote); Father is Group O = **`IᴼIᴼ`** (homozygous recessive).
    - **Punnett proof for Couple 1 (`IᴬIᴮ × IᴼIᴼ`):** The mother's ova carry `(Iᴬ)` (`50%`) or `(Iᴮ)` (`50%`)—never `(Iᴼ)`. The father's sperm carry only `(Iᴼ)` (`100%`). Therefore `100%` of Couple 1's biological children must be either **`IᴬIᴼ` (Group A, `50%`)** or **`IᴮIᴼ` (Group B, `50%`)**. At the molecular level on Chromosome `9`, every child of Couple 1 inherits either a functional `GTA` allele (`Iᴬ`, adding GalNAc = Antigen A) or a functional `GTB` allele (`Iᴮ`, adding D-Gal = Antigen B) from the mother paired with a non-functional `Iᴼ` allele from the father (the common `ΔG261` deletion is one example), so **Group O (`IᴼIᴼ`, `0%`) and Group AB (`IᴬIᴮ`, `0%`) are impossible for Couple 1**.
    - **Genotypes & Punnett proof for Couple 2 (Kulkarni, `IᴬIᴼ × IᴮIᴼ`):** Because both Kulkarnis had a Group O (`IᴼIᴼ`) parent, the Group A mother is **`IᴬIᴼ`** and the Group B father is **`IᴮIᴼ`**. Their `2 × 2` Punnett grid yields **`25% IᴬIᴮ` (Group AB), `25% IᴬIᴼ` (Group A), `25% IᴮIᴼ` (Group B), and `25% IᴼIᴼ` (Group O)**.
    - **Verdict within our standard ABO model:** Because **only Couple 2** can contribute two `(Iᴼ)` gametes to form **`Baby 1 (Group O, IᴼIᴼ)`**, **Baby 1 belongs to Couple 2 (Kulkarni)** and **Baby 2 (`Group A, IᴬIᴼ`) fits Couple 1 (Desai)**. The hospital would confirm the assignment with records and DNA identity testing.

2. **Case B — X-linked pedigree deduction (`13.2 & 13.4`):**
    - **Maternal grandfather:** **`XᵇY`** (affected hemizygous male). He passed his single `(Xᵇ)` chromosome to his daughter.
    - **Mother:** **`XᴮXᵇ`** (unaffected heterozygous carrier female). She inherited `Xᵇ` from her father and `Xᴮ` from her mother; her single `Xᴮ` allele synthesises functional red/green opsin photopigment in her retinal cone cells (`9.4`), giving her normal trichromatic colour vision.
    - **Father:** **`XᴮY`** (normal hemizygous male). He gave his son his **`(Y)` chromosome** (which carries no colour-vision locus), so the son could **not** inherit `Xᵇ` from his father.
    - **Six-year-old son:** **`XᵇY`** (affected male), having inherited `(Xᵇ)` from his carrier mother's ovum and `(Y)` from his father's sperm.
    - **Eight-year-old daughter:** Either **`XᴮXᴮ` (`50%` chance among daughters, homozygous normal)** or **`XᴮXᵇ` (`50%` chance among daughters, unaffected carrier)**, because she definitely received `(Xᴮ)` from her father's X-sperm and had an equal chance of receiving `(Xᴮ)` or `(Xᵇ)` from her mother's ovum.

3. **Next-pregnancy probabilities & autosomal comparison (`13.1–13.4`):**
    - **(a) Probability of a boy (`XY`):** **`50%` (`1 : 1`)**, independent of the two older children, because paternal meiosis produces `50%` `(X)` sperm and `50%` `(Y)` sperm.
    - **(b) X-linked recessive probability (`XᴮXᵇ × XᴮY`):** Among **sons (`XY`)**, the probability of red–green colour vision deficiency (`XᵇY`) is **`50%` (`1 in 2` sons)**; among **daughters (`XX`)**, the probability of being affected is **`0%`** (`50%` are `XᴮXᵇ` carriers); among **all children**, the probability of an affected child is **`25%` (`1 in 4`)**, and `100%` of affected children in this cross are male.
    - **(c) Contrast with autosomal recessive (`Aa × Aa`):** If two unaffected carrier parents (`Aa × Aa`, e.g. `HbᴬHbˢ × HbᴬHbˢ` on Chromosome `11`) have a child, the `25%` (`1 in 4`) probability of an affected child (`aa` / `HbˢHbˢ`) applies **equally to daughters (`25%`) and sons (`25%`)**, and **both** parents must be heterozygous carriers (`Aa`), whereas in X-linked recessive inheritance (`XᴮXᵇ × XᴮY`) **only the mother** is a carrier and **only sons** (`50%` of sons) can be affected.
