sections.heading: 14.1 The glitch engine: continuous vs discontinuous variation, mutations and mutagens
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Mumbai School Biology Laboratory & University of Wisconsin, Madison, 1952

Imagine measuring the heights of two hundred 12-year-old students in Mumbai, then grouping the measurements into `5 cm` intervals. You might find many students near the middle and fewer near either end, though a real class need not make a perfect bell curve. Now sort their recorded `ABO` blood groups into `O`, `B`, `A`, and `AB`. These make separate categories: there is no blood group "A-and-a-quarter". These are an imagined classroom comparison, not measurements from a survey.

Look closely at those two classroom charts before we name a single technical term. All two hundred students belong to the same species, *Homo sapiens*, yet no two classmates (except identical twins) are genetic copies. In biology, any difference between individuals of the same species is called ==variation==. Why does one human characteristic spread out into an unbroken rainbow of measurements while another snaps into four rigid, non-overlapping boxes?

The height chart illustrates ==continuous variation==: a characteristic can take intermediate numerical values rather than falling into a few separate categories. Height, mas

sections.heading: 14.2 The six-step filter: natural selection, peppered moths and antibiotic resistance
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Birmingham & Dorset Woodlands, 1953–1955, and KEM Hospital Ward, Mumbai

First, stand beside **Bernard Kettlewell** in a soot-darkened woodland near Birmingham in `1953`. A pale and a dark peppered moth (*Biston betularia*) face different risks because birds can more easily spot the one contrasting with its resting background. Now imagine a laboratory culture containing susceptible and resistant bacteria. An antibiotic may kill susceptible cells more readily, changing the composition of the survivors. This laboratory comparison explains selection without pretending to forecast a child's infection or prescribe a treatment duration.

In Section 14.1 we saw how random DNA mutations continuously inject new alleles into populations, and how meiosis and fertilisation shuffle them. Left to itself, mutation is blind: it produces alleles that darken moth wings, thin plant cuticles, or alter bacterial enzymes without anticipating which changes will help. How does a blind glitch engine produce organisms that become better suited to particular environments?

The answer is the mechanism independently discovered by **Charles Robert Darwin** and **Wallace in Ternate** (Alfred Russel Wall

sections.heading: 14.3 Built for the extremes: adaptive features of xerophytes, hydrophytes and animals
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Thar Desert Dunes, Rajasthan & Mumbai Botanical Pond

Hold two contrasting leaves in a Mumbai teaching garden. A marram grass (*Ammophila arenaria*) blade from dry coastal dunes rolls inward, enclosing grooves and hairs that shelter its stomata. A floating water-lily (*Nymphaea*) leaf spreads a broad pad across a pond; its upper surface meets air, and air chambers run through its tissues. A third plant, fully submerged *Elodea*, has thin leaves with no stomata. Floating and submerged leaves share an aquatic habitat but do not solve gas exchange in the same way.

Why do leaves in these environments have different structures? In Chapters 3 and 5, we discovered the central dilemma of every photosynthesising plant: to make glucose (`6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂`), an air-exposed leaf generally opens stomatal pores so carbon dioxide (`CO₂`) can diffuse in—yet the moment stomata open, water vapour (`H₂O`) diffuses out down a steep water potential gradient (`ΔΨ`) from the moist spongy mesophyll air spaces into the drier outside air (transpiration).

Over millions of generations, natural selection has shaped inherited features that solve this dilemma in radically different habitats

sections.heading: 14.4 Guided evolution and deep time: selective breeding, fossils and DNA clocks
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Imperial Sugarcane Station, Coimbatore, 1930s & Institute of Palaeobotany, Lucknow, 1948

Visit two Indian laboratories working at different scales of evolutionary time. At Coimbatore in the `1930s`, cytogeneticist **E. K. Janaki Ammal** studied sugarcane chromosomes and hybrids between sugarcane and related grasses. Her studies of inheritance and chromosome behaviour helped strengthen the scientific basis for crop breeding. Now travel to Lucknow in `1948`, where **Birbal Sahni** described *Pentoxyleae*, an unusual extinct group of seed plants from the Rajmahal Hills. He called these fossils Jurassic; later work assigned the relevant Rajmahal material an **Early Cretaceous** age. Their anatomy helps researchers compare ancient seed plants, but does not by itself prove that they were direct ancestors of modern conifers.

In Section 14.2 we saw how the natural environment—predators, drought, cold, and disease—filters heritable variation across generations. Ten thousand years ago, human farmers realised they could replace the environment as the filter. Instead of waiting for nature to select which plants or animals bred, humans chose the parents themselves. This human-directe

sections.heading: Why the sickle-cell allele stays common in malaria belts
sections.excerpt:
:::fig c14_sickle_cell_malaria_case() | Balancing selection of the sickle-cell allele (Hbˢ) in Plasmodium falciparum malaria belts across East Africa (Anthony Allison 1954) and Central/Western India (L. D. Sanghvi): opposing selection pressures against HbᴬHbᴬ (malaria mortality) and HbˢHbˢ (sickle-cell anaemia) illustrate heterozygote advantage using assumed relative fitness values.

:::case Why the sickle-cell allele stays common in malaria belts
We are now ready to solve the chapter's central mystery—and tie together the entire four-chapter arc of Volume IV (*Chapters 11, 12, 13, and 14*).

Consider two **hypothetical populations**, inspired by the malaria and sickle-cell studies of **Anthony Allison** in East Africa and **L. D. Sanghvi** and colleagues in India. Population H has no malaria exposure; Population M has persistent *P. falciparum* exposure. To isolate selection, assume random mating, a large population, no migration or new mutation, and constant relative reproductive contributions (`w`). The numbers below are **teaching assumptions**, not measured fitness values for named districts or modern patients. In M, let `wAA = 0.85`, `wAS = 1.00` and `wSS = 0.20`.

| Genotype

callouts.title: Suppose an Olympic sprinter in Mumbai trains for ten years, building large leg muscles and a deep sun tan, and also eats a calcium-rich childhood diet that helped her grow `4 cm` taller than her poorly nourished cousins. Which of these features—her muscle bulk, her sun tan, her extra `4 cm` of diet-boosted height, or her `Group AB` blood alleles (`IᴬIᴮ`) and polygenic height alleles—can be passed on to her baby at fertilisation?
callouts.body:
- All four features are passed on equally because the baby develops inside the mother's body
- Her gametes pass inherited height alleles and **one** ABO allele (`Iᴬ` or `Iᴮ` in each egg); these acquired body changes are not transmitted as new DNA alleles
- Only continuous traits like height and muscle mass are inherited, whereas discontinuous traits like `ABO` blood group reset every generation
???
The second choice. Environmental variations—muscle hypertrophy in somatic muscle fibres, melanin pigment induced by ultraviolet light in skin cells, or extra bone growth from childhood nutrition—do not alter the base sequence of DNA inside her haploid egg cells (gametes). These acquired features are not inherited as changed DNA alleles. Parental environments can affect offspring in other ways, including maternal effects and, in some circumstances, inherited epigenetic marks; that is different from inheriting a trained muscle or a suntan.

callouts.title: - **Misconception: "Mutations are always harmful and turn organisms into monsters."**
callouts.body:
*Correction:* Most DNA base substitutions are **neutral** (occurring in non-coding DNA or producing a synonymous codon that codes for the same amino acid). Some are harmful (such as `HbˢHbˢ` in non-malarial regions), and a small fraction are **beneficial** in a specific environment (such as a bacterial enzyme that breaks down penicillin or `HbᴬHbˢ` in a malaria belt).
- **Misconception: "Meiosis and fertilisation create new alleles."**
  *Correction:* Crossing over, independent assortment, and random fertilisation create **new combinations of existing alleles** (new genotypes), but **only mutation** creates brand-new alleles by altering the DNA base sequence.
- **Misconception: "Good nutrition or climate can shift discontinuous traits just a little bit."**
  *Correction:* Diet can affect height and mass but does not change inherited ABO alleles. Other categorical traits can respond to the environment, so category shape alone does not establish its cause.

callouts.title: **How school exams phrase 14.1 (Cambridge `0893` & `0610` Topic `18.1`):**
callouts.body:
- **Variation (Core `18.1.1`):** Describe variation as *differences between individuals of the same species*.
- **Continuous vs Discontinuous (Core `18.1.2–18.1.4`):** Continuous variation results in a *range of phenotypes between two extremes* (e.g. body length, body mass) and is caused by *both genes and the environment*; discontinuous variation results in a *limited number of phenotypes with no intermediates* (e.g. `ABO` blood groups, seed shape in peas, seed colour in peas) and, for the standard ABO and Mendelian examples, is described as caused by *genes only*. This is the school model for those examples, not a universal claim about every categorical trait.
- **Mutation & Mutagens (Core & Supplement `18.1.6–18.1.10`):** Define mutation as *genetic change* and gene mutation as *a random change in the base sequence of DNA*. State that mutation is the *way in which new alleles are formed*, that *ionising radiation and some chemicals increase the rate of mutation*, and that *mutation, meiosis, random mating and random fertilisation are sources of genetic variation in populations*.

callouts.title: 1. **Classifying classroom measurements:** A botanist in Pune measures two traits across `300` pea plants (*Pisum sativum*): (A) the mass of each dry seed in milligrams (`120 mg` to `310 mg`), and (B) flower colour (`224` purple flowers and `76` white flowers, with zero pale-lilac flowers). Identify which trait shows continuous variation and which shows discontinuous variation, state the genetic and environmental basis of each, and state which graph type the botanist should draw for each.
callouts.body:
2. **Evaluating a student's statement on X-rays and new alleles:** A student writes: *"When bacteria are exposed to X-rays and penicillin at the same time, the X-rays and penicillin force the bacteria to undergo meiosis and invent a penicillin-resistance allele."* Identify **three** biological errors in this sentence and rewrite it accurately.
???

1. **Trait A (seed mass)** shows **continuous variation** because measurements span an unbroken range (`120–310 mg`) with intermediates; it is controlled by **many genes (polygenic) plus environmental factors** (water, soil nitrates, sunlight) and should be plotted as a **histogram of touching intervals**. **Trait B (flower colour)** shows **discontinuous variation** because plants fall into two distinct categories (purple vs white, `~3 : 1`) with no intermediates; it is controlled by the inherited flower-colour locus in this Mendelian example and should be plotted as a **categorical bar chart with spaces between bars**.
2. **Error 1:** Bacteria are prokaryotes that reproduce asexually by **binary fission**, never meiosis. **Error 2:** Even in eukaryotes, meiosis only reshuffles existing alleles; **mutation** (a random change in DNA base sequence) is the only process that forms new alleles. **Error 3:** Neither X-rays nor penicillin "force" a directed resistance mutation; **X-rays (ionising radiation) are a mutagen that increases the rate of random mutations at susceptible DNA sites**, while **penicillin can act as a selection pressure**, favouring resistant variants; some antibiotics can also raise mutation rates, without specifying a useful change.

callouts.title: A hypothetical culture starts with `990` susceptible bacteria and `10` resistant bacteria. During one exposure, suppose `90%` of susceptible cells die but every resistant cell survives. Does resistance become more common even before any cell divides?
callouts.body:
- No: a population changes only when new mutations appear
- Yes: `99` susceptible and `10` resistant cells remain, so the resistant fraction rises from `1%` to about `9.2%`
- The antibiotic must have changed all `99` survivors into resistant bacteria
???
The second choice. The resistant **number** stayed at `10`, but its **fraction** increased because susceptible cells were removed. If resistance is inherited, reproduction by survivors can carry that difference forward. The numbers are model assumptions, not measurements from a patient.

callouts.title: **The forceps-and-newspaper camouflage hunt (Mumbai Desk Investigation)**
callouts.body:
*Educational adaptation disclosure:* This safe household and classroom simulation is a non-trialled educational adaptation designed to demonstrate how visual predation on a patterned background produces differential survival and shifts morph frequencies across generations. It uses only dry paper dots and blunt tweezers (`0` chemicals, `0` heat, `0` live animals).

You can measure differential survival and changes in **morph frequency** on your desk. This is an asexual paper model: colour is copied exactly, unlike dominance and mating in real moths.

1. Prepare `30` white dots and `30` newspaper-print dots, plus at least `100` spare dots of each kind. Scatter the starting `60` across a newspaper sheet while your partner looks away. These are contrasting paper morphs, not literal pale and dark moths.
2. Give your partner blunt tweezers. They pick the first dot they notice, looking away between picks, until they have removed **exactly `30` dots**. Record the elapsed time and both colours caught.
3. Count each surviving colour. Add one matching daughter dot per survivor, then scatter all `60` again. For example, if `8` white and `22` printed dots survive, reproduction gives `16` white and `44` printed dots: `73.3%` printed. These are worked-example numbers, not a promised result.
4. Repeat for two more generations and calculate each percentage from your counts. Run at least two fresh trials: chance affects which dots are caught.
5. Repeat on plain white paper. If both colours remain, the favoured colour may reverse. If one has disappeared, changing the background cannot recreate it: restart with both colours to compare the environments.

callouts.title: - **Misconception: "Organisms mutate or adapt because they 'need to', 'try to', or 'want to' survive."**
callouts.body:
*Correction:* Need does not specify the helpful DNA change. Variants can arise before or during an environmental change; selection favours those that lead to more descendants under the new conditions.
- **Misconception: "A moth evolves darker wings during its own lifetime."**
  *Correction:* Cells can acquire mutations during an individual's life. In this example, **populations** evolve as inherited variants change in frequency across generations; an individual moth does not choose a new inherited wing colour.
- **Misconception: "Humans become resistant to antibiotics if they take them too often."**
  *Correction:* It is the **populations of bacteria** living inside or on humans that become resistant to antibiotics by natural selection, not the human patient's own body cells.

callouts.title: **How school exams phrase 14.2 (Cambridge `0893` & `0610` Topic `18.3`):**
callouts.body:
- **Natural Selection (Core `18.3.1`):** Every mark scheme looks for the linked chain: *genetic variation within populations → production of many offspring → struggle for survival / competition for resources → greater chance of reproduction by individuals that are better adapted to the environment than others → these individuals pass on their alleles to the next generation*.
- **Adaptation as Process (Supplement `18.3.3`):** Describe adaptation as *the process, resulting from natural selection, by which populations become more suited to their environment over many generations*.
- **Antibiotic Resistance (Supplement `18.3.4`):** Describe the development of strains of antibiotic-resistant bacteria (such as **MRSA**) as an example of evolution by natural selection: *random mutation produces a resistance allele → antibiotic acts as a selection pressure killing sensitive bacteria → resistant bacteria survive and reproduce (reduced competition) → pass the resistance allele to offspring → frequency of resistance allele increases in the population*.

callouts.title: 1. **Six-mark exam question — Rat resistance to warfarin:** In the `1950s`, the poison warfarin was introduced to control brown rat (*Rattus norvegicus*) populations on farms. Initially, warfarin killed over `98%` of rats by blocking vitamin K recycling in blood clotting. Within ten years, farm rat populations were thriving and unaffected by standard doses of warfarin. Using the six steps of natural selection, explain how warfarin resistance evolved in the rat population.
callouts.body:
2. **Viral coughs and antibiotic stewardship:** A patient visits a Mumbai clinic with a `2-day` runny nose and cough caused by a rhinovirus (common cold) and asks the doctor for amoxicillin *"just in case"*. Give **two** biological reasons why the doctor must refuse to prescribe an antibiotic.
???

1. (1) **Genetic variation:** Due to pre-existing **random gene mutation**, a tiny fraction of rats in the original population already carried an allele conferring resistance to warfarin (an altered vitamin K epoxide reductase enzyme). (2) **Overproduction:** Rats produce large litters (many more offspring than farm food and shelter can support). (3) **Selection pressure / struggle for existence:** When farmers applied warfarin, the poison acted as an intense **environmental selection pressure**. (4) **Differential survival:** Sensitive wild-type rats died of internal bleeding, whereas rats carrying the warfarin-resistance allele survived (and experienced less competition for food). (5) **Reproduction and inheritance:** The surviving resistant rats bred and **passed the resistance allele** to their offspring. (6) **Allele frequency increase:** Repeated over many generations of warfarin application, the frequency of the resistance allele increased until almost the entire farm rat population was warfarin-resistant.
2. (1) **Zero effect on viruses:** Rhinoviruses are acellular particles (protein capsid + nucleic acid) with no peptidoglycan cell wall, no cell membrane, and no `70S` ribosomes; amoxicillin targets bacterial cell-wall synthesis and therefore cannot kill or inhibit viruses. (2) **Selection for antibiotic resistance:** Taking amoxicillin unnecessarily exposes the patient's normal commensal bacteria (in the gut and respiratory tract) to an antibiotic **selection pressure**, killing sensitive bacteria and selecting for pre-existing **antibiotic-resistant mutants**, which can multiply and transfer resistance plasmids to pathogenic bacteria.

callouts.title: Suppose you smear a thin film of waterproof petroleum jelly (Vaseline) over (A) the **lower** surface only of a floating water lily leaf (*Nymphaea*), and (B) the **upper** surface only of a second floating water lily leaf on a sunny afternoon. Which leaf's rate of gaseous exchange and photosynthesis will be most strongly reduced—and how does this contrast with performing the same Vaseline test on a terrestrial garden bean leaf?
callouts.body:
- Coating the lower surface (Leaf A) stops gas exchange in both the water lily and the bean leaf because all plant stomata sit on the underside
- In the floating water lily, coating the **upper surface (Leaf B)** blocks almost `100%` of its stomata and greatly restricts atmospheric `CO₂` entry, whereas coating the lower surface (Leaf A) has much less direct effect on stomatal exchange (`0` lower stomata); in a terrestrial bean leaf, the opposite occurs because most stomata  sit on the shaded lower epidermis
- Petroleum jelly has no effect on either leaf because `CO₂` diffuses straight through thick wax cuticles
???
The second choice. In the floating water lily (*Nymphaea*), smearing petroleum jelly on the **upper surface (Leaf B)** blocks almost `100%` of its stomata, greatly restricting atmospheric `CO₂` entry and therefore photosynthesis, whereas smearing the lower surface (Leaf A) does not directly block stomata because the water-contacting underside has `0` stomata. In a terrestrial garden bean leaf, the exact opposite occurs: most stomata  sit on the cooler, shaded **lower epidermis** to reduce solar evaporation, so coating the lower surface blocks gas exchange far more severely than coating the upper surface.

callouts.title: - **Misconception: "Cacti have zero stomata and never transpire."**
callouts.body:
*Correction:* Cacti have stomata on their green stems; fully submerged vascular plants can take up dissolved gases without leaf stomata. Cacti have **fewer, sunken stomata** located on their green stems, and they typically open them **at night** when air temperatures are cool and relative humidity is higher.
- **Misconception: "Water lilies need a thick waxy cuticle to stop pond water from flooding into their leaves."**
  *Correction:* Plant cells have rigid cellulose cell walls that withstand turgor pressure (recall Chapter 3), so water lilies do not burst in freshwater. Floating upper surfaces can have water-repellent wax; submerged surfaces often have much thinner barriers for dissolved-gas exchange. Turgor resistance and keeping an air-facing leaf dry are different problems.
- **Misconception: "When a person climbs to Leh in Ladakh and makes more red blood cells over two weeks, that is an evolutionary adaptation."**
  *Correction:* Short-term physiological adjustment within one individual's lifetime is **acclimatisation** (non-heritable). An evolutionary **adaptive feature** is **inherited in DNA** across generations (such as the inherited variants affecting oxygen responses in high-altitude populations).

callouts.title: **How school exams phrase 14.3 (Cambridge `0610` Topic `18.2`):**
callouts.body:
- **Definitions (`18.2.1` & `18.2.3`):** Memorise the exact phrases: *Adaptive feature = an inherited feature that helps an organism to survive and reproduce in its environment*; *Fitness = the probability of an organism surviving and reproducing in the environment in which it is found*.
- **Interpreting images (`18.2.2`):** When given a photograph or photomicrograph of an unfamiliar animal or plant leaf, always link **observable structure → physical/physiological mechanism → survival/reproduction benefit in that specific habitat** (e.g. *white fur → camouflage against snow → predators/prey cannot spot it → higher survival/feeding → reproduces and passes on alleles*).
- **Xerophytes & Hydrophytes (`18.2.4` Supplement):** Explain the adaptive features of hydrophytes and xerophytes to their environments using water potential gradient, diffusion distance, stomatal position, cuticle thickness, air spaces, and root/xylem structure.

callouts.title: 1. **Interpreting a transverse leaf photomicrograph:** In a practical exam, Kym looks down a light microscope at a stained transverse section (`TS`) of an unidentified leaf. She observes: (i) the leaf blade is curled into a hollow ring; (ii) the outer epidermis has a thick red-stained waxy cuticle (a chosen `8.5 µm` in this hypothetical image) and zero stomata; (iii) the inner epidermis has deep grooves containing stomata surrounded by fine hairs; and (iv) vascular bundles contain dense lignified xylem. Identify whether this leaf comes from a xerophyte or a hydrophyte, and explain how features (i), (ii), and (iii) adapt the plant to its habitat.
callouts.body:
2. **Explaining submerged pondweed anatomy:** A submerged freshwater plant (*Elodea*) has thin, simple leaves only two cell layers thick, no waxy cuticle, no stomata, and stems packed with large honeycomb air channels (`aerenchyma`) but almost no woody xylem tissue. Explain why *Elodea* needs no woody xylem and why large air channels are essential for its survival.
???

1. The leaf comes from a **xerophyte** (such as marram grass, *Ammophila arenaria*, adapted to dry, windy sand dunes). **(i) Curled leaf blade** encloses the inner surface away from external wind; **(ii) Thick waxy cuticle (a chosen `8.5 µm` in this hypothetical image) and zero outer stomata** prevent waterproof epidermal evaporation on the exposed outside surface; **(iii) Sunken stomata in grooves with hairs** trap a pocket of moist water vapour outside the stomatal pores, **reducing the water potential gradient (`ΔΨ`)** between the internal mesophyll air spaces and the trapped air, which greatly reduces water loss by transpiration.
2. *Elodea* needs **almost no woody xylem** because (1) the surrounding water provides **upthrust (buoyancy)** that physically supports the stems and leaves, and (2) water and mineral ions can diffuse directly into the thin leaves across the whole surface without needing long-distance xylem transpiration pull. The **large air channels (`aerenchyma`)** are essential because they provide **buoyancy** to help position the leaves toward light for photosynthesis and allow **oxygen (`O₂`)** produced by photosynthesis to diffuse rapidly down to the roots anchored in low-oxygen mud for aerobic respiration.

callouts.title: In an illustrative breeding programme, repeatedly choosing a small set of related high-yielding parents raises average milk yield but can reduce genetic diversity. The widget uses invented trajectories to explore this trade-off, not historical measurements from Gir cattle. Why does mating closely related high-yielding animals over many generations suddenly cause more calves to be born with rare genetic defects or weak immunity—and why is a genetically uniform crop field in danger if a new fungal pathogen arrives?
callouts.body:
- High milk yield uses up all the calcium in the cow's DNA, causing chromosomes to dissolve
- Repeatedly breeding closely related individuals narrows the gene pool and increases homozygosity, unmasking hidden harmful recessive alleles (`Aa × Aa → 25% aa`, **inbreeding depression**), while genetic uniformity means that if one plant or animal lacks a resistance allele to a new pathogen, the entire population is susceptible
- Selective breeding forces all alleles to mutate into dominant disease alleles
???
The second choice. Two related risks must be distinguished. Reduced vigour or fertility caused by mating relatives is ==inbreeding depression==; genetic uniformity can separately increase vulnerability to a shared threat:

- **Unmasking harmful recessive alleles:** Every organism carries a few rare, harmful recessive alleles (`a`) hidden harmlessly in the heterozygous state (`Aa`). When breeders repeatedly mate closely related top performers (inbreeding), the probability that both parents share the same hidden recessive allele rises sharply (`Aa × Aa → 25% aa`), increasing the risk of homozygous recessive disorders, reduced fertility and lower vigour.
- **Vulnerability to new pathogens or climate shifts:** In a genetically uniform crop monoculture or inbred herd, almost all individuals share the same alleles at immunity and stress loci. If a new strain of wheat stem rust (*Puccinia graminis*) or a severe drought hits the field, **no individual may carry a resistance allele**, so the entire crop can be wiped out at once. To prevent this, modern plant breeders preserve wild seed banks and periodically cross domesticated varieties back with hardy wild relatives—exactly as **E. K. Janaki Ammal** crossed sweet tropical *Saccharum officinarum* with wild Indian *Saccharum spontaneum*.

callouts.title: - **Misconception: "Selective breeding is the same thing as genetic engineering."**
callouts.body:
*Correction:* **Selective breeding** crosses whole organisms of the same (or closely related) species over **many generations** and selects offspring without directly editing DNA molecules. **Genetic engineering** (which we will study in Chapter 15) transfers or edits a specific gene directly at the molecular level (often between unrelated species, such as inserting the human insulin gene into a bacterial plasmid) in a single laboratory generation.
- **Misconception: "Humans evolved from chimpanzees, so chimpanzees are our ancestors."**
  *Correction:* Humans did not evolve from modern chimpanzees. Humans and chimpanzees are **evolutionary cousins** that diverged from a **shared common ancestor** roughly `6.5 million years ago`.
- **Misconception: "Selective breeding creates new alleles to make cows give more milk."**
  *Correction:* Human breeders cannot cause new alleles to appear; selective breeding **selects and combines pre-existing alleles** (and rare spontaneous mutations) across generations.

callouts.title: **How school exams phrase 14.4 (Cambridge `0610` Topics `18.3` & `1.2`):**
callouts.body:
- **Selective Breeding (`18.3.2` Core):** Always include all five points in order: *(1) selection by humans of individuals with desirable features; (2) crossing these individuals to produce the next generation; (3) selection of offspring showing the desirable features; (4) repetition over many generations* (plus naming the specific desirable feature in the question).
- **Natural vs Artificial Selection (`18.3.5` Supplement):** Outline the differences between natural and artificial selection (selective agent, traits selected, effect on wild survival fitness, rate, and genetic diversity).
- **Sequence Classification (`1.2.5` & `1.2.6` Supplement):** State that *sequences of bases in DNA and of amino acids in proteins are used as a more accurate means of classification*, and explain that *organisms which share a more recent ancestor (are more closely related) have base sequences in DNA that are more similar than those that share only a distant ancestor*.

callouts.title: 1. **Designing a selective breeding programme for drought-tolerant millet:** An agricultural institute in Rajasthan wants to breed a variety of pearl millet (*Pennisetum glaucum*) that produces heavy grain heads under low-rainfall conditions (`<250 mm yr⁻¹`). Describe step by step how the scientists should carry out this selective breeding programme.
callouts.body:
2. **Interpreting a DNA sequence alignment table:** Biologists sequence a `200-base` segment of a respiratory gene in a newly discovered forest mammal (**Species X**) and compare the percentage of identical DNA bases against four known mammals: **Species P (`96.5%`)**, **Species Q (`82.0%`)**, **Species R (`91.0%`)**, and **Species S (`78.5%`)**. State which species (`P, Q, R,` or `S`) is most closely related to Species X and which is most distantly related, and explain your reasoning using evolutionary principles.
???

1. (1) Grow a genetically varied population of pearl millet plants under controlled low-water (`<250 mm yr⁻¹`) conditions and **select parent plants** that produce the **heaviest grain heads despite the drought**. (2) **Cross-breed (cross-pollinate)** these selected drought-tolerant, high-yielding parent plants with one another (preventing pollination from unselected plants). (3) Collect the seeds, grow the **offspring under the same low-water conditions**, and measure their grain yield. (4) **Select only the best offspring** showing the highest grain mass under drought to be the parents of the next generation. (5) **Repeat this cross-breeding and selection cycle over many generations** until the entire millet variety breeds true for high grain yield under low rainfall.
2. Under the question's simplifying assumption that these homologous segments have comparable evolutionary rates, **Species P (`96.5%`)** provides the strongest evidence of close relationship to X, and **S (`78.5%`)** the most distant. More similar sequences generally reflect a more recent common ancestor. A real phylogenetic study compares more sequence and tests alternative explanations; this one `200-base` segment does not prove precise divergence dates.

callouts.title: Why the sickle-cell allele stays common in malaria belts
callouts.body:
We are now ready to solve the chapter's central mystery—and tie together the entire four-chapter arc of Volume IV (*Chapters 11, 12, 13, and 14*).

Consider two **hypothetical populations**, inspired by the malaria and sickle-cell studies of **Anthony Allison** in East Africa and **L. D. Sanghvi** and colleagues in India. Population H has no malaria exposure; Population M has persistent *P. falciparum* exposure. To isolate selection, assume random mating, a large population, no migration or new mutation, and constant relative reproductive contributions (`w`). The numbers below are **teaching assumptions**, not measured fitness values for named districts or modern patients. In M, let `wAA = 0.85`, `wAS = 1.00` and `wSS = 0.20`.

| Genotype (Chr `11`) | Anaemia & *P. falciparum* Malaria Effects | Relative Fitness (`w`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`HbᴬHbᴬ`** | predominantly HbA; usually biconcave cells; no sickle-cell anaemia; lacks the HbAS protection against severe malaria | **`w ≈ 0.85`** (selected against by malaria) |
| **`HbᴬHbˢ` (Carrier)** | `~60% HbA + ~40% HbS`; usually no sickle-cell anaemia; reduced risk of severe malaria, not complete protection | **`w = 1.00` (HIGHEST fitness)** |
| **`HbˢHbˢ`** | predominantly HbS (with variable HbF and HbA₂); HbS polymerises at low `O₂` into rigid crescents; **severe sickle-cell anaemia** | **`w ≈ 0.20`** (selected against by anaemia) |

In one of Allison's historical samples, parasites were detected in `113/247` children without sickle-cell trait (`45.7%`) and `12/43` with the trait (`27.9%`). **Detected parasites, severe disease and reproductive contribution are different measurements.** Those parasite percentages do not determine the fitness assumptions above.

Use all four sections of Chapter 14 (together with Chapters 11–13) to answer three synthesis questions:

1. **Molecular origin and non-directed mutation (`14.1` & Ch 11):** Explain how the `Hbˢ` allele originally arose on Chromosome `11`, and evaluate the claim that *"living in a malarial forest caused people's beta-globin genes to mutate into `Hbˢ` for protection."*
2. **Punnett inheritance and opposing selection pressures (`14.2–14.3` & Ch 13):** Construct the `2 × 2` Punnett square outcome when two heterozygous carriers (`HbᴬHbˢ × HbᴬHbˢ`) have children. Then explain why selection reduces `Hbˢ` in malaria-free Population H, whereas heterozygote advantage can maintain it in Population M. The model equilibrium is `q ≈ 15.8%`, giving approximately `26.6%` carriers among newborns under random mating.
3. **Heterozygote advantage and eradication prediction (`14.3–14.4`):** Suppose a public-health campaign removes malaria exposure immediately from Population M, after which you follow the next `20` generations while everything else stays constant. Predict and explain what will happen to the frequency of the `Hbˢ` allele in Population M over those `20` generations.
???

1. **Molecular origin (`14.1` & Ch 11):** `Hbˢ` differs from `Hbᴬ` by a base substitution in the `HBB` gene on Chromosome `11`: coding-strand `GAG → GTG`, corresponding to mRNA `GAG → GUG` and the traditional beta-chain substitution `Glu⁶ → Val⁶`. The altered surface favours haemoglobin polymerisation at low oxygen. Malaria does not specify that helpful mutation because it is needed; selection acts on inherited variants that occur. Mutation rates depend on the site and biological process, so the generic copying-error rate is not a measured historical origin rate for HbS.
2. **Punnett inheritance & balancing selection (`14.2–14.3` & Ch 13):**
    - **Cross (`HbᴬHbˢ × HbᴬHbˢ`):** Gametes `(Hbᴬ)` and `(Hbˢ)` combine in a `2 × 2` grid to yield **`25% HbᴬHbᴬ` : `50% HbᴬHbˢ` : `25% HbˢHbˢ`** (`1 : 2 : 1` genotype ratio).
    - **In malaria-free Population H:** There is no malaria mortality, so `HbᴬHbᴬ` and `HbᴬHbˢ` individuals have equal high fitness (`w = 1.00`), while the model gives HbSS a lower reproductive contribution (`w = 0.20`) because of sickle-cell disease. This disadvantage reduces transmission of HbS, reducing the HbS frequency, increasingly slowly as more copies remain in unaffected heterozygotes.
    - **In malarial Population M:** Two opposing selection pressures operate simultaneously. The model assigns HbAA a lower reproductive contribution because of malaria (`w = 0.85`), and HbSS a still lower contribution because of sickle-cell disease (`w = 0.20`). These are assumptions about the combined effect on descendants, not death rates for children today. **Heterozygous carriers (`HbᴬHbˢ`) have the highest fitness (`w = 1.00`, heterozygote advantage)** because `~60% HbA` prevents severe anaemia while several mechanisms, including altered parasite growth and clearance of infected cells, contribute to protection against severe malaria. Because `HbᴬHbˢ` survivors reproduce most successfully and pass `Hbˢ` to `50%` of their gametes, the allele is maintained at a stable equilibrium (**balancing selection**, `q* = 0.15/(0.15 + 0.80) ≈ 15.8%` under these assumptions).
3. **Prediction after malaria removal:** Set `wAA = wAS = 1.00` and retain `wSS = 0.20`. Selection continues against HbSS, but HbS copies in heterozygotes are sheltered from that recessive disadvantage. In this model the next generation's frequency is `q′ = (pq + 0.20q²)/(p² + 2pq + 0.20q²)`, where `p = 1 − q`. Starting at `q = 0.158`, twenty generations give about **`q = 0.0454`**, or **`8.66%` carriers** among newborns under random mating. The allele declines but does not vanish quickly; this is a model calculation, not a forecast for a district.

sections.heading: 15.1 Sunlit chains & an energy budget: food webs, ecological pyramids and population growth
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Sanjay Gandhi National Park (SGNP), Borivali & Oval Maidan, Mumbai

It is early October in **Sanjay Gandhi National Park (SGNP)** in Borivali, at the northern edge of Mumbai, just after the monsoon rains have triggered the once-in-eight-years mass flowering of the *Karvi* shrub (*Strobilanthes callosa*). Purple-blue blossoms carpet the basalt hillsides below the Kanheri Caves. Honeybees and carpenter bees hum from corolla to corolla; caterpillars chew the tender green leaves; a praying mantis waits motionless on a stem; a rufous treepie and a spotted owlet watch from a teak branch; and in the dappled shade below, a herd of spotted deer (*Axis axis*) grazes while an Indian leopard (*Panthera pardus fusca*) rests on a warm boulder overhead. Beneath their hooves, white threads of bracket fungi and billions of soil bacteria quietly digest fallen petals, shed antlers, and deer droppings back into dark forest humus. Across town at Oval Maidan, a single centuries-old **banyan tree** (*Ficus benghalensis*) spreads its aerial prop roots like a miniature forest of its own, feeding thousands of fig wasps, caterpillars, and fruit bats from one massive woody trunk.

:::scene Marine Drive Monsoon Promenade & Dadar Kitchen Sink, Mumbai

Stand on the promenade at Marine Drive as the June southwest monsoon rolls in off the Arabian Sea. Warm ocean water that evaporated under the May sun has cooled high in the sky into towering cumulonimbus clouds. Within minutes, sheets of rain drum onto the basalt ridges of Malabar Hill and Borivali; some flows down storm drains and the Mithi River back to the sea, while some soaks into the soil where banyan and mango roots drink it up by osmosis and send it skyward through xylem vessels to evaporate out of leaf stomata as water vapour. Now step into a kitchen in Dadar where Kym is helping wash a fresh bundle of *methi* (fenugreek, *Trigonella foenum-graecum*) pulled soil-and-all from a suburban farm. Clinging to the pale branching roots are dozens of tiny, rounded **root nodules** the size of mustard seeds. Slice one open with a fingernail and its inside gleams **pinkish-red**—coloured by an oxygen-binding protein called **leghaemoglobin**, cousin to the haemoglobin in Kym's own red blood cells, shielding millions of ***Rhizobium* bacteria** as they crack atmospheric nitrogen gas (`N₂`) into the amino acids that

sections.heading: 15.3 Footprints on the web: farming, deforestation, eutrophication and conservation
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Powai Lake Outfall, Carter Road Mangroves & Thane Creek Flamingo Sanctuary, Mumbai

Take a morning walk along the eastern shore of **Powai Lake** in central Mumbai where an urban storm-water drain empties nutrient-rich runoff into a sheltered cove. The water surface is choked with a thick emerald-green mat of floating algae and water hyacinth. Beneath that green blanket, the water is dark, murky, and foul-smelling; no submerged pondweed survives on the lake bed, and several silver tilapia fish float belly-up near the reeds, their gill covers flared in water that has been stripped of dissolved oxygen. An hour later, ride the train west to **Carter Road in Bandra** at low tide, where tangled shopping bags and polystyrene cups snag on the pencil-like breathing roots (`pneumatophores`) of *Avicennia marina* mangroves. Yet just across the harbour in the **Thane Creek Flamingo Sanctuary**, protected mudflats and treated wetland buffers host tens of thousands of lesser and greater flamingos—an important habitat where protection and monitoring can help conserve wildlife. sections.heading: 15.4 Living factories & rewritable code: fermenters, plasmids, recombinant insulin and CRISPR
sections.excerpt:
:::scene Irani Bakery at Dhobi Talao, Mumbai & Hindustan Antibiotics Fermenter Hall, Pimpri

It is five o'clock in the morning at a century-old Irani bakery near Dhobi Talao in south Mumbai. Inside the warm proofing trough, a baker punches down a pillowy mound of *brun-pav* bread dough that has doubled in volume overnight. Millions of microscopic **yeast** cells (*Saccharomyces cerevisiae*) have been respiring anaerobically through the flour sugars, blowing tiny bubbles of carbon dioxide (`CO₂`) into the stretchy gluten network; when the trays slide into the wood-fired brick oven at `220 °C`, gases expand and the loaf structure sets while much of the **ethanol** evaporates into the air; small amounts can remain in the bread. Two hours away along the Mumbai–Pune expressway at **Pimpri**, three-storey stainless-steel **industrial fermenters** gleam inside the halls of Hindustan Antibiotics—descendants of a plant incorporated in `1954` and commissioned in `1955–56` with international assistance—where sterile air bubbles through spargers, motorised paddles churn nutrient broth, and cold-water jackets carry away kilowatts of microbial heat. On the final Saturday of the school year, Kym and her biology class carry out a two-part capstone investigation that ties together every scale of *The Living World*—from molecules and cells to organs, inheritance, evolution, and the biosphere (Figure 15.9).

**Part 1 — Three Illustrative Mumbai Environments:**
The class compares **three fictional teaching datasets inspired by different Mumbai environments**. They are not field measurements and the sites are **not a single downstream transect**: the Mithi drains towards Mahim Creek, while Thane Creek is a different estuarine setting. Treat the numbers as evidence for hypotheses, not proof of a measured restoration or one site’s change through time. Light percentages mean transmission to a specified sampling depth in this model; `BOD` means oxygen demand measured over a standard

callouts.title: Imagine a simplified tree-centred food chain: **1 banyan tree → 8,000 caterpillars → 350 insect-eating birds → 6 bird-eating predators**. These are illustrative counts and masses for one defined study area, not an Oval Maidan census; the predators also depend on the surrounding habitat. Compare the shapes of the **pyramid of numbers**, the **pyramid of biomass** (`dry mass g m⁻²`), and the **pyramid of energy** (`kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹`) for this banyan food chain.
callouts.body:
- All three pyramids are inverted at the base because there is only `1` banyan tree
- The **pyramid of numbers is inverted at the base** (`1` tree `< 8,000` primary consumers), whereas both the pyramid of biomass (`4,500 kg → 120 kg → 12 kg → 1.2 kg` dry mass) and the pyramid of energy (`45,000 → 4,500 → 450 → 45 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹`) are **strictly upright**
- The pyramid of energy is inverted because eagles fly faster and burn more energy than trees
???
The second choice. If you plot the **number of individuals**, the bottom bar (`Level 1: 1 banyan tree`) is tiny while the second bar (`Level 2: 8,000 caterpillars`) is huge—producing an **inverted pyramid of numbers** at the base because counting individuals treats one `4,500 kg` tree and one `0.5 g` caterpillar as equal counts (`1 = 1`).

If you instead weigh the **dry mass of living material** at each level (`pyramid of biomass`), the single banyan tree (`4,500 kg` dry wood, roots, and leaves) vastly outweighs all `8,000` primary consumers (`120 kg`), which outweigh the `350` secondary consumers (`12 kg`) and the `6` predators (`1.2 kg`)—restoring an **upright pyramid**. And if you plot the **energy flowing through each trophic level per year** (`pyramid of energy`, in `kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹`), the diagram is **upright for the same area, period and food-source boundary** (`45,000 → 4,500 → 450 → 45 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹`), because this example assumes `10%` transfer of production at each step. In an energy budget using the same area, period and accounting boundary, energy incorporated into new biomass decreases up the chain.

callouts.title: - **Never draw food chain arrows pointing from predator to prey:** Writing `Leopard → Deer → Grass` to mean "the leopard eats the deer" is the single commonest ecological mistake. Arrows (`→`) **always** point in the direction of **energy flow** (`Grass → Deer → Leopard`).
callouts.body:
- **Energy is NEVER recycled:** Do not write that "decomposers recycle energy back to plants." Decomposers respire dead organic matter and release its remaining energy as **heat**, which escapes to the atmosphere. Decomposers recycle **mineral ions and carbon/nitrogen atoms**, never energy.
- **Pyramids of biomass vs pyramids of energy:** A pyramid of **biomass** shows the **dry mass** of organisms at each trophic level at a single moment (`g m⁻²`). A pyramid of energy shows the **annual rate of energy flow** (`kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹`) and **is upright when its area, period and food-source boundary match across levels**.

callouts.title: **How school exams phrase 15.1 (Cambridge `0610` Topics `19.1`, `19.2` & `19.4`):**
callouts.body:
- **Core definitions (`19.2` & `19.4`):** Memorise the exact wording for **food chain**, **food web**, **producer**, **consumer** (primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary), **herbivore**, **carnivore**, **decomposer**, **trophic level**, **population**, **community**, and **ecosystem**.
- **Energy efficiency questions (`19.2` Supplement):** When asked why energy transfer between trophic levels is inefficient (or why eating plants is more efficient than eating livestock), always name at least three specific losses: **heat lost in respiration**, **energy in egested faeces (indigestible cellulose/bone)**, **energy in excreted urine (urea)**, and **uneaten body parts** passing to decomposers.
- **Sigmoid curve questions (`19.4` Supplement):** Always link each phase to **both** the relative rates of birth and death (`B ≫ D` in exponential, `B = D` in stationary, `D > B` in death) **and** the specific limiting factors (`food supply`, `space`, `competition`, `predation`, `disease`, `toxic waste accumulation`).

callouts.title: 1. **SGNP trophic energy calculation:** In Sanjay Gandhi National Park, *Karvi* shrubs trap `20,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹` of solar energy into net plant biomass. Assuming a `10%` energy transfer efficiency at each step, calculate how much energy (`kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹`) is incorporated into the biomass of secondary consumers (such as Indian leopards feeding on spotted deer), and state four pathways by which the other `90%` is lost at each transfer.
callouts.body:
2. **Evaluating pyramid types:** Explain one advantage of using a pyramid of biomass rather than a pyramid of numbers, and one advantage of using a pyramid of energy rather than a pyramid of biomass.
3. **Food-web disturbance:** A bird eats caterpillars and beetles; a larger predator eats the bird. Predict two possible effects if the bird is overharvested. Why is the size of either effect uncertain?
???

1. **Level 1 (Producers — *Karvi* shrubs):** `20,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹` → **Level 2 (Primary consumers — Spotted deer):** `10%` of `20,000` = **`2,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹`** → **Level 3 (Secondary consumers — Indian leopards):** `10%` of `2,000` = **`200 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹`**. At each transfer step, the remaining `90%` is lost via: (1) **aerobic respiration and heat loss** during movement and body temperature regulation, (2) **indigestible egested faeces** (cellulose, hair, bone), (3) **excreted metabolic waste** (urea in urine), and (4) **uneaten body parts** passing to decomposers.
2. A pyramid of biomass accounts for the **size (dry mass)** of organisms, so it is not inverted when a single giant tree feeds thousands of small insects. A pyramid of energy measures the **rate of energy production and flow over a full year** (`kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹`) rather than a single snapshot standing crop, so it remains upright for a consistent production budget (even in fast-turnover plankton communities) and distinguishes a small, rapidly renewed producer standing crop from its much larger annual production. Energy estimates still require substantial sampling and measurements.
3. Caterpillars or beetles may increase and the larger predator may lose food. Alternative prey, competing consumers, reproduction and other limiting factors can change the response; a web does not supply a fixed numerical prediction.

callouts.title: During the July monsoon deluge in coastal Maharashtra, a farmer's low-lying tomato field becomes completely waterlogged for two weeks because its drainage ditch is blocked. Even though the farmer added ammonium fertiliser before the rains, the tomato plants turn pale yellow with stunted growth (`nitrogen deficiency`). Which combination of soil and root processes explains why waterlogging starves the plants of nitrate?
callouts.body:
- Waterlogging washes nitrogen gas (`N₂`) out of the leaves through the stomata
- Waterlogged soil lacks oxygen (`O₂`), which **(1) stimulates anaerobic denitrifying bacteria to convert soil `NO₃⁻ → N₂` gas**, **(2) stops aerobic nitrifying bacteria from oxidising `NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻`**, and **(3) starves root hair cells of `O₂` needed for aerobic respiration to make ATP for active transport of `NO₃⁻`**
- Excess water converts *Rhizobium* bacteria inside tomato roots into viruses
???
The second choice. Waterlogging fills all the air spaces between soil particles with water, driving out oxygen (`O₂`) and creating **anaerobic soil conditions**:

1. **Denitrification surges (`NO₃⁻ → N₂`):** Anaerobic **denitrifying bacteria** multiply in the oxygen-starved mud and convert existing soil nitrate ions (`NO₃⁻`) into `N₂` gas, which bubbles out into the atmosphere and is lost.
2. **Nitrification stops (`NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻` halts):** Aerobic **nitrifying bacteria** require oxygen to oxidise the ammonium fertiliser (`NH₄⁺`) into nitrite (`NO₂⁻`) and nitrate (`NO₃⁻`), so new nitrate production halts.
3. **Root hair active transport fails:** Tomato root hair cells absorb `NO₃⁻` against a concentration gradient by active transport, which requires ATP from aerobic respiration (`C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O`). Without soil `O₂`, root cells cannot make enough ATP to pump nitrate ions in. *(This is why farmers plough and drain fields to keep soil aerated.)*

callouts.title: **Inspecting legume root nodules at the kitchen sink (Mumbai Kitchen Investigation)**
callouts.body:
*Educational adaptation disclosure:* This safe household observation has been reviewed for safety and feasibility (using only market-fresh culinary herbs/legumes, tap water, a hand lens, and standard soap-and-water handwashing), though it has not been classroom-trialled for this edition.

Next time your family brings home a fresh, soil-dusted bunch of **fenugreek (*methi*)**, **groundnuts (*shengdana*)**, or green **chickpea (*hara chana*)** plants from the market, rinse the roots gently in a bowl of water instead of cutting them straight off:

1. **Locate the root nodules:** Look through a hand lens (`×10`) at the branching lateral roots. You may spot small, rounded root nodules (`1–3 mm` across) growing like tiny beads along the root surface.
If the roots have been removed, the plant is too young or nodules are not visible, this observation may not work. That does not show that legumes never fix nitrogen; try a mature, intact legume grown in suitable soil another time.

2. **Observe the leghaemoglobin pigment:** Press one nodule gently between two fingernails or the back of a spoon on a sheet of white paper (wash hands thoroughly with soap and water afterwards). Healthy, actively fixing nodules reveal a **pink or reddish-brown interior**—the colour of leghaemoglobin, an iron-containing oxygen-binding protein made by the legume host to keep free `O₂` away from the bacterial **nitrogenase** enzyme while delivering just enough oxygen for *Rhizobium* respiration.
3. **Connect to crop rotation:** This mutualistic partnership is why Indian farmers have rotated cereal crops (such as wheat, jowar, or rice, which deplete soil `NO₃⁻`) with leguminous pulses (*tur*, *moong*, *chana*, *groundnut*) in many farming systems: when the legume roots decompose after harvest, their fixed nitrogen is ammonified and nitrified into fresh `NO₃⁻` for the next cereal crop.

callouts.title: - **Plants do NOT absorb `N₂` through their stomata:** Never write that "plants take in nitrogen from the air through their leaves." In the biological examples here, nitrogen-fixing microbes convert `N₂` to ammonia/ammonium. Lightning makes nitrogen oxides that can become nitrate, and the industrial Haber process makes ammonia. These are different fixation routes. Plants absorb nitrate ions (`NO₃⁻`) (or `NH₄⁺`) from soil water through root hair cells.
callouts.body:
- **Do not confuse the three `-fication` terms:**
  - **Nitrogen fixation:** `N₂ (gas) → NH₄⁺ / amino acids` (*Rhizobium*, *Azotobacter*). **Lightning** instead forms nitrogen oxides that can become `NO₃⁻`; the **Haber process** makes `NH₃`.
  - **Nitrification:** `NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ (nitrite) → NO₃⁻ (nitrate)` (aerobic nitrifying bacteria in aerated soil).
  - **Denitrification:** `NO₃⁻ → N₂ (gas)` (anaerobic denitrifying bacteria in waterlogged soil; *harmful* to crop yield).
- **Plants respire 24 hours a day:** In carbon cycle questions, remember that plants carry out **aerobic respiration continuously day and night** (`releasing CO₂`), while carrying out **photosynthesis only in the light**.

callouts.title: **How school exams phrase 15.2 (Cambridge `0610` Topic `19.3`):**
callouts.body:
- **Carbon cycle (Core `19.3.1`) and water-cycle connection:** The water cycle is a useful linked model here: describe it in terms of **evaporation**, **transpiration**, **condensation**, and **precipitation**, and the carbon cycle in terms of **photosynthesis**, **respiration**, **feeding**, **decomposition**, **formation of fossil fuels**, and combustion.
- **Nitrogen cycle (`19.3.2–19.3.3` Supplement):** State the specific roles of microorganisms in decomposition, nitrification, **nitrogen fixation**, and **denitrification** alongside plant uptake of `NO₃⁻`, protein synthesis, feeding/digestion, and deamination. The named bacterial genera and the intermediate nitrite ion deepen our explanation; this syllabus does not require bacterial genus names.

callouts.title: 1. **Comparing aerated legume soil vs waterlogged soil:** A soil scientist analyses two adjacent agricultural plots in Maharashtra: **Plot A** is well-drained, ploughed, and planted with chickpea (*Cicer arietinum*, a legume); **Plot B** is compacted, waterlogged, and unploughed. Compare the rates of nitrogen fixation, nitrification, and denitrification in Plot A versus Plot B, and state which plot will have a higher soil nitrate (`NO₃⁻`) concentration.
callouts.body:
2. **Identifying bacterial guilds:** Name the specific type of bacteria that carries out each reaction: (a) `N₂ → NH₄⁺` inside pea root nodules; (b) `NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻` in aerated soil; (c) `NO₃⁻ → N₂` in waterlogged mud.
???

1. **Plot A (well-drained, ploughed chickpea legume field)** has **high nitrogen fixation** (mutualistic *Rhizobium* in chickpea root nodules converting `N₂ → NH₄⁺`), **high nitrification** (aerobic nitrifying bacteria using soil `O₂` to oxidise `NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻`), and **very low denitrification**, which tends to favour nitrate production. **If other conditions and losses are similar**, Plot A may have more nitrate. Fixation initially supplies the legume, however: nitrate concentration also depends on plant uptake, decomposition, fertiliser input and leaching, so the description alone cannot guarantee the measured concentration. **Plot B (compacted, waterlogged field)** has no crop specified, so we cannot infer its nodule abundance. Low soil `O₂` **inhibits aerobic nitrification** and strongly **promotes anaerobic denitrification** (`NO₃⁻ → N₂` gas escaping to the air), depleting soil nitrate.
2. (a) **Nitrogen-fixing bacteria** (specifically mutualistic *Rhizobium*); (b) **Nitrifying bacteria** (e.g. *Nitrosomonas* and *Nitrobacter*); (c) **Denitrifying bacteria** (e.g. *Pseudomonas*).

callouts.title: A student writes in an exam: *"When nitrate fertiliser washes into a river, the nitrates poison the fish and the algae on top use up all the oxygen during the day, so the fish die."* Identify the scientific errors in this statement and select the true mechanism that removes dissolved oxygen from the water.
callouts.body:
- The student is right: nitrate ions are a direct neurotoxin to fish gills
- In this example the main mechanism is nutrient enrichment and oxygen depletion, not direct nitrate poisoning. Algae respire day and night; in sufficient daylight their photosynthesis can release more oxygen than they consume. Meanwhile, the surface algal bloom **blocks sunlight** to submerged plants below, causing them to **die**, and **aerobic decomposer bacteria** multiplying on the dead organic matter consume the dissolved `O₂` via aerobic respiration
- Fish die because the algae eat all the fish eggs at night
???
The second choice. Follow the oxygen balance:

1. **Error 1:** The intended explanation here is **nutrient enrichment followed by oxygen depletion**. Nitrate toxicity depends on concentration, exposure and species, so “nitrate can never harm fish directly” would also be wrong.
2. **Error 2:** Algae **respire all the time**, using oxygen. In sufficient daylight, photosynthesis can release more oxygen than they consume; after dark, photosynthesis stops while respiration continues, sometimes causing a dangerous pre-dawn oxygen minimum.
3. **True mechanism:** Shading can kill submerged plants, while dead algae themselves also provide food for decomposers. Sewage organic matter can feed decomposers directly, without waiting for an algal bloom. **Aerobic decomposer bacteria** then multiply rapidly on the dead organic matter and carry out aerobic respiration, which consumes the dissolved `O₂` in the water and causes fish to suffocate.

callouts.title: - **Eutrophication mechanism (`0610 20.3`):** Explain the links rather than merely naming “pollution.” One possible pathway is: (1) nitrates/mineral ions cause **rapid growth of algae (`algal bloom`)**, (2) the surface algae **block light** to submerged plants below, (3) plants die, (4) **decomposer bacteria** increase in number on the dead organic matter, and (5) the bacteria carry out aerobic respiration, which uses up **dissolved oxygen (`O₂`)** so fish suffocate.
callouts.body: - **Greenhouse effect vs ozone hole (`0610 20.3`):** Do not confuse the enhanced greenhouse effect (`CO₂` and `CH₄` trapping outgoing **long-wave infrared heat radiation**, causing global warming) with ozone depletion (`CFCs` thinning stratospheric ozone `O₃`, which filters ultraviolet light). They are completely different physical processes.

callouts.title: **How school exams phrase 15.3 (Cambridge `0610` Topic `20`):**
callouts.body:
- **Deforestation (`20.2.4` Core):** Always cover all four syllabus dimensions: **extinction / loss of biodiversity**, soil erosion, **flooding**, and **increase of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere**.
- **Eutrophication (`20.3.4` Supplement):** The syllabus describes the causal links: *increased availability of nitrate and other ions → increased growth of producers → increased decomposition after death of producers → increased aerobic respiration by decomposers → reduction in dissolved oxygen → death of organisms requiring dissolved oxygen in water*.
- **Conservation & Sustainability (`20.4` Core & Supplement):** Give specific, actionable methods—for forests: **selective logging**, **coppicing**, **replanting/reforestation**, **quotas**, **education**, **protected reserves**; for fish stocks: **catch quotas**, **minimum net mesh size** (so young fish escape and breed), **closed breeding seasons**, **protected marine areas**, **monitoring**.

callouts.title: 1. **Restoring a collapsed coastal fishery:** A commercial fishing fleet uses fine-mesh bottom trawl nets year-round in a coastal bay. Within five years, the annual fish catch drops by `80%`. Explain why the fine-mesh nets caused the population crash, and describe three specific legal regulations that would restore the fishery as a **sustainable resource**.
callouts.body:
2. **Tracing downstream river pollution:** Raw sewage is discharged into a slow-flowing river at `Point X`. Explain why the concentration of dissolved oxygen (`O₂`) drops sharply `2 km` downstream of `Point X` and then gradually recovers `15 km` further downstream.
???

1. **Why the crash occurred:** Fine-mesh nets trap **small, juvenile (immature) fish** before they have reached reproductive age and bred even once, removing future breeding adults so the removal rate vastly exceeds the birth rate. **Three sustainable regulations:** (1) **Increase minimum net mesh size** (and fit escape panels) so juvenile fish slip through, survive to maturity, and reproduce; (2) **Enforce legal catch quotas** limiting the total mass of each species landed; (3) **Establish closed seasons and protected no-take marine reserves** over spawning grounds during breeding months.
2. At `Point X`, raw sewage introduces abundant organic matter (and mineral ions). `2 km` downstream, aerobic decomposer bacteria multiply rapidly as they digest the organic sewage and carry out intense aerobic respiration (`C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O`), consuming dissolved `O₂` faster than it can diffuse in from the air (`oxygen sag`). By `15 km` downstream, most of the organic sewage has been broken down, so decomposer bacterial numbers and respiration drop, while **diffusion of `O₂` from the air** (aided by riffles) and **photosynthesis by aquatic plants/algae** replenish dissolved `O₂`.

callouts.title: Suppose a molecular biologist accidentally cuts the human DNA containing the insulin gene with restriction enzyme **`EcoRI`** (which leaves sticky ends `-AATT-`), but cuts the bacterial plasmid vector with a different restriction enzyme, **`BamHI`** (which leaves sticky ends `-GATC-`), before adding **DNA ligase**. What will happen in Step 3, and how much human insulin will the bacteria produce?
callouts.body:
- DNA ligase will force any two DNA ends together regardless of base sequence, so normal human insulin is produced
- In this unmodified cloning setup, the EcoRI and BamHI sticky ends (`-AATT-` vs `-GATC-`) are **not complementary** and cannot base-pair (`A–T, C–G`); **the intended insulin insert does not ligate into the vector efficiently, so this model predicts no insulin-producing construct**
- The bacteria will make pig insulin instead of human insulin
???
The second choice. In this unmodified cloning setup, the EcoRI and BamHI sticky ends on the human insulin gene (`-AATT-`) and the sticky ends on the bacterial plasmid (`-GATC-`) are not complementary (`A` only pairs with `T`, and `C` only pairs with `G`). Without complementary base pairing between sticky ends, the human gene cannot anneal into the open plasmid, so DNA ligase cannot seal them together into a recombinant plasmid. The requirement in this example is **compatible ends**. The same enzyme is one route; some different enzymes also give compatible ends, and other cloning methods use other strategies.

callouts.title: - **Restriction enzymes vs DNA ligase (`0610 21.3`):** Never swap their jobs. **Restriction enzymes** *cut* DNA at specific base sequences; the enzymes in this cloning example produce **sticky ends**. DNA ligase *joins* two DNA fragments together by sealing bonds along the sugar-phosphate backbone after complementary sticky ends have base-paired, forming **recombinant DNA**.
callouts.body:
- **Plasmids vs bacterial chromosomes (`0610 21.1 & 21.3`):** The vector used to carry the human insulin gene into bacteria is a circular **plasmid**, not the main bacterial chromosome and not a ribosome.
- **Bread-making vs Bioethanol (`0610 21.2`):** In **bread-making**, it is **`CO₂` gas** that makes the dough rise (while ethanol evaporates during baking). In **biofuel production**, it is the ethanol that is collected and distilled as fuel.

callouts.title: **How school exams phrase 15.4 (Cambridge `0610` Topic `21`):**
callouts.body:
- **Why bacteria are useful (`21.1.1–21.1.2` Core & Supplement):** State: *(1) rapid reproduction rate, (2) ability to make complex molecules, (3) few ethical concerns over their manipulation and growth, and (4) the presence of plasmids*.
- **Cloning outline (`21.3.3` Supplement):** The syllabus asks for a simplified human-protein example. Describe these connected operations: *(1) isolate prepared DNA carrying the human coding sequence using a restriction enzyme, forming sticky ends; (2) cut a bacterial plasmid DNA with the same restriction enzyme, forming complementary sticky ends; (3) use DNA ligase to join the human insulin gene and plasmid DNA to form a recombinant plasmid; (4) insert the recombinant plasmid into bacteria; (5) grow the bacteria in a fermenter to replicate the plasmid and express the human protein*. This is the syllabus cloning outline; real insulin production additionally requires intron-free DNA, bacterial expression controls, selection, processing/folding and purification, as explained above.

callouts.title: 1. **Cooling-jacket failure in an antibiotic fermenter:** Inside an industrial fermenter producing penicillin from the fungus *Penicillium*, the cold water supply to the outer cooling jacket accidentally shuts off for three hours while the nutrient and oxygen supplies continue. Predict and explain what will happen to the temperature inside the fermenter and to the rate of penicillin production.
callouts.body:
2. **Washing powder enzyme temperature:** A parent washes a blood-stained cotton shirt in biological washing powder using boiling water at `90 °C` instead of warm water at `35 °C`, and finds the blood stain is still stuck to the fabric. Explain why the stain was removed at `35 °C` but not at `90 °C`.
???

1. **Temperature is likely to rise:** Respiring microbes release heat. Without the normal cooling-water supply, temperature rises if heat production exceeds remaining heat loss. Growth and penicillin production can slow as conditions move away from the optimum; sufficient overheating can denature proteins and kill cells. The vessel size, culture activity and remaining heat loss are unspecified, so we cannot calculate the temperature after three hours or guarantee that production becomes zero.
2. Blood stains contain proteins such as haemoglobin and fibrin; heat can coagulate proteins and make a stain harder to remove. Biological washing powder contains **protease enzymes** selected to work well at warm washing temperatures such as **`35–40 °C`** (the exact temperature depends on the enzyme and formulation), where they rapidly catalyse the hydrolysis of insoluble blood proteins into **soluble amino acids** that dissolve in the wash water. At **`90 °C`**, thermal agitation breaks internal bonds in the protease molecules, **denaturing their active sites** so they can no longer bind or digest the protein stain (while boiling heat also coagulates the blood protein onto the cotton fibres).

callouts.title: Mumbai environments & an insulin vial: closing the four-billion-year case file
callouts.body:
On the final Saturday of the school year, Kym and her biology class carry out a two-part capstone investigation that ties together every scale of *The Living World*—from molecules and cells to organs, inheritance, evolution, and the biosphere (Figure 15.9).

**Part 1 — Three Illustrative Mumbai Environments:**
The class compares **three fictional teaching datasets inspired by different Mumbai environments**. They are not field measurements and the sites are **not a single downstream transect**: the Mithi drains towards Mahim Creek, while Thane Creek is a different estuarine setting. Treat the numbers as evidence for hypotheses, not proof of a measured restoration or one site’s change through time. Light percentages mean transmission to a specified sampling depth in this model; `BOD` means oxygen demand measured over a standard test period, not a bacterial count.

| Illustrative Site | Nitrate `[NO₃⁻]`, Algal Cover & `DO` | Biological Community & Ecological State |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Station 1: SGNP Forest Headwaters** *(Borivali slope)* | Soil rich in `NO₃⁻`; stream `[NO₃⁻] = 1.1 mg L⁻¹`; `5%` algal cover; `92%` light; low `BOD = 1.3 mg L⁻¹`; **High `DO = 8.2 mg L⁻¹`** | Wild legumes with pink *Rhizobium* root nodules, submerged pondweed, mayfly nymphs, frogs, fish |
| **Station 2: Powai / Mithi Outfall Plume** *(sewage + runoff)* | Stream `[NO₃⁻] = 24.0 mg L⁻¹`; **`95%` surface algal bloom**; `8%` light; **High `BOD = 16.4 mg L⁻¹`**; **Hypoxic `DO = 1.4 mg L⁻¹`** | Submerged plants dead on bed; dense aerobic decomposer bacteria; **dead tilapia fish** |
| **Station 3: Thane Creek Mangrove Sanctuary** *(illustrative estuarine site)* | Stream `[NO₃⁻] = 3.2 mg L⁻¹`; `18%` algal cover; moderate `BOD = 2.8 mg L⁻¹`; **`DO = 6.8 mg L⁻¹` in this example** | *Avicennia marina* mangroves, fiddler crabs, mudskippers, flamingos |

**Part 2 — From Ecosystems to a Recombinant Insulin Vial:**
Back in the school laboratory, Kym's teacher places a `10 mL` vial of recombinant human insulin (`100 IU mL⁻¹`, a hypothetical bacterial-production example) beside a germinating **chickpea (*chana*) seed**—the very same kind of seed Kym placed on wet cotton wool on her monsoon window-ledge in **Chapter 0**.

Use all four sections of Chapter 15 (and the Five Big Ideas across *The Living World*) to answer three capstone questions:

1. **Trophic energy & population limits (`15.1`):** At Station 1, forest producers fix `30,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹` of solar energy into net plant biomass. Calculate how much energy (`kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹`) reaches tertiary consumers (`Level 4`) at `10%` transfer efficiency per step, explain why the calculation alone cannot tell us whether a `6th` feeding level exists in the park, and state why energy cannot be recycled by decomposers.
2. **Nitrogen cycle & eutrophication (`15.2–15.3`):** Explain how wild legumes and soil bacteria keep the aerated forest soil at Station 1 fertile without chemical fertiliser, and propose a plausible oxygen-depletion mechanism consistent with Station 2. Why do these three sites not establish a fall from Station 1’s `8.2 mg L⁻¹` to Station 2’s `1.4 mg L⁻¹`?
3. **Recombinant biotechnology (`15.4` & Chapters 10–11):** Describe the five-step process used to engineer *E. coli* bacteria to manufacture the human insulin inside the clinic vial, and explain why a prokaryotic bacterium can translate a human gene into the exact same amino acid sequence as a human pancreatic β-cell.
???

1. **Trophic energy & one-way flow (`15.1`):**
    - **Calculation:** `Level 1 (Producers) = 30,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹` → `Level 2 (Primary consumers) = 3,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹` → `Level 3 (Secondary consumers) = 300 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹` → **`Level 4 (Tertiary consumers) = 30 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹`**.
    - **What the calculation establishes:** A fifth level receives `3` and a sixth `0.3 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹` under the stated assumption. That is an energy density, not a complete population budget (`0.3 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹` equals `300,000 kJ km⁻² yr⁻¹`). Habitat area, feeding relationships and consumer needs are also required; these figures do not establish that SGNP has no sixth-level consumer.
    - **Why energy is never recycled:** Decomposers oxidise dead organic matter by respiration and release its remaining chemical energy as thermal energy (heat) to the atmosphere, which chloroplasts cannot trap; decomposers recycle mineral ions and carbon/nitrogen atoms, never energy.
2. **Nitrogen cycle at Station 1 & Eutrophication at Station 2 (`15.2–15.3`):**
    - **Evidence limit:** These are fictional values from separate environments, not repeat measurements of one parcel of water. They suggest a mechanism to investigate; repeated sampling, flow/light/temperature data and suitable controls would be needed to test a change through time or a treatment effect.
    - **Station 1 fertility:** Mutualistic **nitrogen-fixing *Rhizobium* bacteria** inside the pink root nodules of wild legumes (together with free-living soil *Azotobacter*) convert atmospheric **`N₂ → NH₄⁺` / amino acids**. When leaves and roots fall, decomposers break proteins down into **`NH₄⁺`** (**ammonification**), and because the hillside soil is well-drained and aerated with `O₂`, **aerobic nitrifying bacteria** oxidise **`NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻`** (nitrification) for root hair active transport.
    - **Station 2 eutrophication (one possible pathway):** (1) Leached **`NO₃⁻` fertiliser and sewage** (`24.0 mg L⁻¹`) enter the water; (2) they stimulate a dense surface **algal bloom** (`95%` cover); (3) the surface bloom blocks sunlight (`8%` transmission) to submerged aquatic plants below; (4) **submerged plants die** and sink as organic detritus; (5) aerobic decomposer bacteria multiply rapidly on the dead organic matter; (6) the bacteria carry out aerobic respiration (`BOD = 16.4 mg L⁻¹`), stripping **dissolved `O₂`** down to `1.4 mg L⁻¹`; (7) **tilapia fish suffocate and die** from lack of `O₂`.
3. **Recombinant human insulin & the universal code (`15.4` & Chapters 10–11):**
    - **Five-step pipeline:** Prepare intron-free insulin-coding DNA with bacterial expression controls; cut insert and plasmid to obtain compatible ends (the same restriction enzyme in this example); ligate and form recombinant plasmids; transform and select suitable bacteria; culture, recover, process/fold and purify the product. The first successful recombinant method made insulin’s A and B chains separately. Modern methods can use a precursor that is subsequently processed.
    - **Why the amino acid instructions can transfer:** The genetic code is nearly universal, so bacterial and human ribosomes generally assign the same amino acids to the same codons. Appropriate expression controls and intron-free coding DNA are also needed. Mature insulin contains **two chains totalling 51 amino acids**, and producing a correctly processed medicine requires more than translation alone.

explorers.subtitle: Logarithmic dial from 0.1 nm water molecules to the 10,000 km biosphere
explorers.summary: Sweep across eleven orders of magnitude to see why naked eyes, light microscopes, and electron microscopes each unlock a different layer of biology.

explorers.summary: Toggle between plant, animal, and prokaryotic cells to inspect how cell walls, chloroplasts, vacuoles, and mitochondria divide up the work of staying alive.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Redi’s Three-Jar Controlled Experiment
atlasLessons.question: Why do maggots appear only on meat that adult flies can physically touch, even when air circulates freely through fine gauze?
atlasLessons.explanation: Rotating Redi’s three glass jars in 3D shows that the gauze-covered jar admits scent and oxygen while blocking adult Sarcophaga flies, proving that maggots hatch from laid eggs rather than arising spontaneously from decaying meat.
atlasLessons.limits: Displayed fly trajectories and larval growth rates are scaled for visual clarity.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Hooke & Leeuwenhoek Optical Bench
atlasLessons.question: How did a tiny single glass bead lens outperform larger early compound microscopes to reveal living bacteria?
atlasLessons.explanation: Exploding the brass paddle and cork specimen stage in 3D shows how Leeuwenhoek’s short-focal-length spherical glass bead achieved 270× magnification with ~1.3 µm resolution, whereas Hooke’s two-lens compound tube magnified cork cell walls at ~30×.
atlasLessons.limits: Chromatic and spherical aberrations are summarised via the Rayleigh resolution limit.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Pasteur’s Swan-Neck Gravity Trap
atlasLessons.question: How does a curved glass neck allow oxygen in while keeping boiled nutrient broth sterile for years until tilted?
atlasLessons.explanation: In the 3D swan-neck flask, airborne dust and bacterial spores settle by gravity into the lowest U-bend of the glass tube. Only when you tilt the flask past 42° does sterile broth wash into the bend and carry trapped microbes back into the bulb.
atlasLessons.limits: Spore settling is modelled as deterministic trapping at the lowest bend.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Eleven Orders of Magnitude of Life
atlasLessons.question: Why must we switch from the naked eye to light microscopy and then electron microscopy as we zoom from a blue whale down to a DNA helix?
atlasLessons.explanation: Sweeping the logarithmic 3D scale dial across eleven orders of magnitude compares specimen dimensions against the wavelength of visible light (~400–700 nm), showing why viruses and ribosomes require electron beams.
atlasLessons.limits: Organism and macromolecule meshes are shown normalized inside the 3D comparison stage.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Seed Hydration and Development
atlasLessons.question: How does adding water change a viable seed, and what can a hydration model establish?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect a schematic chickpea cutaway. Chosen hydration parameters illustrate swelling and possible development; water enters permeable coat regions.
atlasLessons.limits: Illustrative rates and opening threshold, not measured seed data. Added-water percentage is relative to starting seed mass, unlike the chapter workbench water fraction.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Candle Combustion vs Seed Metabolism
atlasLessons.question: How do cellular pathways connect fuel reactions to ATP regeneration and construction?
