atlasLessons.explanation: Compare a conceptual flame account with coupled cellular reactions. Both involve reaction networks; only the cell has the coordinated machinery for cellular maintenance and inheritance.
atlasLessons.limits: The standard-state ATP allocation is a chosen account, not measured cellular efficiency or heat. Drawn steps do not count reactions.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: ATP Reactions and Cellular Work
atlasLessons.question: How can an ATP reaction be coupled to movement or chemical construction?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect the ATP schematic and rotary synthase. ATP reactions can support work when enzymes connect them to other changes; bond breaking alone requires energy.
atlasLessons.limits: Symbolic molecular representation. Whole-reaction free energy depends on conditions; an isolated bond does not contain the reaction free-energy change.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: ATP Supply and Cellular Work
atlasLessons.question: How does ATP connect energy transfers to cellular processes?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect the ATP carrier and rotary ATP synthase. Gradient-driven synthesis regenerates ATP; other enzyme systems couple ATP reactions to cellular work.
atlasLessons.limits: The rotor represents one ATP-synthesis mechanism, not all seven life processes or a literal gear connection between them.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Why Viruses Require a Host
atlasLessons.question: What cellular machinery does a virus lack for independent replication?
atlasLessons.explanation: Compare the viral capsid and bacterial host. Host ribosomes make viral proteins; enzymes copy the genome, using resources of the infected cell.
atlasLessons.limits: One schematic phage-host interaction. Other viruses enter differently; the capsid geometry is chosen, and absence of independent metabolism does not mean all chemistry stops.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Representative green plant cell
atlasLessons.question: How do the wall, vacuole, nucleus, mitochondria and chloroplasts fit together?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect the selected plant-cell structures in solid, X-ray and section views. A white onion bulb cell lacks developed chloroplasts while retaining mitochondria.
atlasLessons.limits: Schematic selected structures and counts; not every real plant cell has this equipment.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Organelle ancestry clues
atlasLessons.question: Which observations support bacterial ancestry for mitochondria and chloroplasts?
atlasLessons.explanation: Compare membrane folds and stacks with inherited DNA and bacterial-related ribosomes described in the chapter. Gene comparisons supply evidence beyond appearance.
atlasLessons.limits: Shapes alone do not establish ancestry; fold-area gain is a chosen geometry model.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Cell geometry and a chosen surface layer
atlasLessons.question: How does enlarging a cube change its surface area relative to volume?
atlasLessons.explanation: Change cube width and compare SA/V=6/L with the inner core remaining beneath a chosen 5 µm surface layer.
atlasLessons.limits: The coloured core is geometric, not measured oxygen penetration or a universal starvation limit. Assumed diffusion coefficient 2000 µm²/s; differs from chapter centimetre-block example.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Specialised cell shapes
atlasLessons.question: How do thin regions and extensions support different cell functions?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect a biconcave red blood cell, root hair and myelinated neurone. Relate their different shapes to exchange and communication.
atlasLessons.limits: Selected schematic shapes, not a vesicle-trafficking simulation or universal measured area gains.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Membrane diffusion and equilibrium
atlasLessons.question: Can opposing molecular crossings continue when net transfer is zero?
atlasLessons.explanation: Compare a lipid boundary and chosen equal-volume relaxation model; molecules continue moving near equilibrium.
atlasLessons.limits: Schematic particles and invented rate constant; not atomic dimensions or measured flux.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Water-selective channel
atlasLessons.question: How can a protein provide a faster water route without pumping it?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect a schematic hourglass channel and two-way exchange markers. Compare total water potentials for the direction of net transfer.
atlasLessons.limits: Not atomic coordinates, calibrated molecular throughput or a full map of selectivity chemistry.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Animal and plant water relations
atlasLessons.question: Why can a supporting wall change the outcome of water entry?
atlasLessons.explanation: Compare schematic red-blood-cell and walled-cell states as external solute conditions change. Pressure contributes to total water potential.
atlasLessons.limits: Chosen qualitative state thresholds and swelling scales, not universal cell-specific predictions.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Illustrative energy-coupled carrier
atlasLessons.question: How can an ATP-dependent carrier sustain transport that passive spreading would not?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect a generic carrier cycle and chosen ATP-response curve. The chapter separately explains root nitrate uptake through an ATP-built proton gradient and cotransporter.
atlasLessons.limits: Not Skou’s sodium–potassium pump or a real root nitrate pump. Chosen uncharged-solute ratio omits electrical forces; ATP loss need not instantly remove stored gradients.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Glucose and peptide connections
atlasLessons.question: How can molecular connections help explain different biological materials?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect schematic glucose and peptide models. Glucose has six carbons overall; its common six-membered ring includes one oxygen. Water interactions and carbon bonding are explained in the chapter.
atlasLessons.limits: Schematic teaching geometry; this scene does not show an ice lattice or simulate freezing.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Glucose-derived building units
atlasLessons.question: Why can polymers built from glucose-derived units have different properties?
atlasLessons.explanation: Compare the glucose building unit with the chapter’s starch, glycogen and cellulose plate. Link orientation and branching matter; the monomer model alone cannot establish polymer properties.
atlasLessons.limits: Schematic monomer and peptide models, not an interactive alpha/beta polymer conversion.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Backbone restrictions and protein folding
atlasLessons.question: Why can a protein sketch preserve the amino-acid sequence yet propose an impossible shape?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect a chosen two-basin backbone-angle surface and a schematic chain. Local crowding restricts arrangements; a local angle map does not predict every complete protein fold.
atlasLessons.limits: Invented illustrative surface, not measured atomic energies or the original Ramachandran map. Real maps vary with amino-acid type.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Enzyme binding and a chosen rate model
atlasLessons.question: Why does substrate binding alone not establish that a protein catalyses a reaction?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect an invented enzyme cleft and compare chosen Michaelis–Menten rate responses to substrate and inhibitor. The chapter explains the separate activation-barrier account.
atlasLessons.limits: Abstract shapes and chosen steady-state kinetics; no measured lactase rates, atomic docking or directly simulated transition state.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: An illustrative temperature response
atlasLessons.question: Why can warming first increase a reaction rate and later reduce it?
atlasLessons.explanation: Change the chosen temperature parameter and compare relative model activity. The picture changes shape at a declared model threshold; this is not a universal protein failure temperature.
atlasLessons.limits: No exposure-time history or pH slider here. Relative activity is not measured native-fold fraction; the model cannot establish irreversible damage or diagnose fever.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Five food-test examples
atlasLessons.question: What comparisons make a food-test result interpretable?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect five schematic positive examples: iodine, Benedict’s, biuret, ethanol emulsion and DCPIP. Compare their targets with the chapter’s table and keep known positives, blanks and untreated samples in a real investigation.
atlasLessons.limits: Schematic rack, not actual chemical measurements or a control experiment. All reagent procedures belong in a supervised school laboratory.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Photosynthetic material account
atlasLessons.question: How can atmospheric carbon become plant material?
atlasLessons.explanation: Compare the formal net-equation mass account with the chapter’s carbon journey from CO₂ to sugars and cell walls.
atlasLessons.limits: Formal net balance, not a dry-mass measurement of van Helmont’s tree or an atom-route simulation; water also supplies matter.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Aquatic plant gas observation
atlasLessons.question: Why does net oxygen release not measure gross photosynthesis?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect a modern schematic plant jar and chosen net-output markers. The chapter’s tracer evidence identifies water as the released oxygen source.
atlasLessons.limits: Not a reconstruction of Ingenhousz’s apparatus or calibrated bubbles; markers vanish at nonpositive chosen net output.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Chloroplast compartments
atlasLessons.question: How do light-supported reactions supply carbon-building reactions?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect thylakoid stacks and surrounding stroma. Light-supported machinery supplies ATP and NADPH; carbon fixation supplies small organic products.
atlasLessons.limits: The glucose model represents a later overall summary product, not the immediate product of the carbon-fixation cycle; no electron-transfer kinetics are simulated.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Invented limiting-factor surface
atlasLessons.question: Why can increasing one input sometimes leave the rate unchanged?
atlasLessons.explanation: Vary chosen light and CO₂ capacities and temperature to inspect a simple minimum-capacity model. Net output subtracts a chosen respiratory baseline 10.
atlasLessons.limits: Invented capacities and 25 °C peak, not a fitted Farquhar model, actual concentrations or universal plant optimum.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Representative leaf structure
atlasLessons.question: How do leaf structures support light capture, gas exchange and water balance?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect palisade columns, a guard-cell pair and adjacent vascular tubes. Connect the schematic to the chapter’s full leaf cross-section.
atlasLessons.limits: Selected representative structures, not a complete anatomical specimen or measured light-attenuation model.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Leaf water loss and xylem
atlasLessons.question: How does leaf evaporation contribute to water flow through connected xylem?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect the guard-cell and vascular schematic, then trace the chapter’s evaporation, tension and replacement-water chain.
atlasLessons.limits: Chosen aperture and transport-activity values are illustrative, not measured speeds or a universal response to light.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Phloem source–sink flow
atlasLessons.question: Why can phloem carry sugars upwards or downwards in different pathways?
atlasLessons.explanation: Compare the vascular tubes with the chapter’s loading, osmotic entry, pressure-driven flow and unloading account.
atlasLessons.limits: Tube schematic and invented relative activity; not a Poiseuille solver. Opposite bulk streams do not share one tube at the same moment; loading routes vary.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Compartments for Cellular Fuel Processing
atlasLessons.question: How do mitochondrial compartments help separate fuel-carbon processing from membrane energy transfer?
atlasLessons.explanation: The structural cutaway locates matrix and inner membrane. Glycolysis occurs outside the mitochondrion; its two net ATP and reusable carrier connect to the later carbon and electron routes. The 3D shape does not itself show every glycolytic reaction.
atlasLessons.limits: Manual structural and causal schematic; no calibrated oxygen-dose response, biochemical clock, total ATP yield or fixed aerobic-to-fermentation ratio.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Mitochondrial Cristae & Krebs Tricarboxylic Wheel
atlasLessons.question: How do the folded inner cristae and central matrix of the mitochondrion divide the work of the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation?
atlasLessons.explanation: Using Section cutaway mode on the 3D mitochondrion exposes the central matrix—where the 8-step Krebs cycle oxidises acetyl-CoA to CO₂ while loading NADH and FADH₂—surrounded by deeply folded cristae packed with electron-transport complexes.
atlasLessons.limits: Manual structural and causal schematic; no calibrated oxygen-dose response, biochemical clock, total ATP yield or fixed aerobic-to-fermentation ratio.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Rotary F₀F₁-ATP Synthase Molecular Turbine
atlasLessons.question: How does controlled H⁺ return couple a membrane gradient to ATP formation?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect rotor, shaft and catalytic head. Proton return drives motion linked to shape changes supporting ATP formation. Motion is schematic; no fixed rotation speed, coupling ratio or ATP yield is measured.
atlasLessons.limits: Manual structural and causal schematic; no calibrated oxygen-dose response, biochemical clock, total ATP yield or fixed aerobic-to-fermentation ratio.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Carbon Processing and Gas Measurements
atlasLessons.question: Why does an oxidation ledger have to include incoming oxygen?
atlasLessons.explanation: Use the main chapter mass ledger to balance fuel plus oxygen against total products. The 3D view locates carbon processing and controlled gas-measurement apparatus; it does not measure body-mass change or trace individual oxygen origins.
atlasLessons.limits: Manual structural and causal schematic; no calibrated oxygen-dose response, biochemical clock, total ATP yield or fixed aerobic-to-fermentation ratio.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Lactic & Alcoholic Fermentation NAD⁺ Rescue Fork
atlasLessons.question: How can carrier recycling support glycolysis, and why can waterlogged roots still lack oxygen?
atlasLessons.explanation: Compare the oxygen-linked relay with sustained oxygen absence. Fermentation restores NAD⁺; yeast and lactate routes have different products, and lactate can form with oxygen present. Rice internal gas spaces improve oxygen delivery to submerged tissues; they do not remove respiratory requirements.
atlasLessons.limits: Manual structural and causal schematic; no calibrated oxygen-dose response, biochemical clock, total ATP yield or fixed aerobic-to-fermentation ratio.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Waterlogged Root Hypoxia & ATP Starvation
atlasLessons.question: How can carrier recycling support glycolysis, and why can waterlogged roots still lack oxygen?
atlasLessons.explanation: Compare the oxygen-linked relay with sustained oxygen absence. Fermentation restores NAD⁺; yeast and lactate routes have different products, and lactate can form with oxygen present. Rice internal gas spaces improve oxygen delivery to submerged tissues; they do not remove respiratory requirements.
atlasLessons.limits: Manual structural and causal schematic; no calibrated oxygen-dose response, biochemical clock, total ATP yield or fixed aerobic-to-fermentation ratio.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Beaumont’s Gastric Window & the Alimentary Canal
atlasLessons.question: How did William Beaumont prove through Alexis St Martin’s gastric fistula that digestion is driven by coordinated muscular churning and chemical catalysis?
atlasLessons.explanation: Slicing the 3D muscular tube reveals inner circular muscle contracting behind the food bolus while outer longitudinal muscle shortens ahead of it, propelling chyme through pH-zoned compartments.
atlasLessons.limits: Travelling sinusoidal peristaltic wave along a cylindrical gut segment.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Ingestion, Digestion, Absorption & Egestion Across the Gut Wall
atlasLessons.question: Why is food in the intestinal lumen topology-wise still ‘outside’ the body’s internal cellular environment until it crosses the villus epithelium?
atlasLessons.explanation: Trace the meal along the lumen, then across the epithelial barrier. Glucose and amino acids use selective transport before entering capillaries; long-chain lipid products are rebuilt into chylomicrons before entering lymph. Water, ions and some other nutrients need no prior digestion.
atlasLessons.limits: Topological lumen-to-capillary boundary view.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Antagonistic Circular & Longitudinal Muscle Peristalsis
atlasLessons.question: Why can you swallow water even while hanging upside down?
atlasLessons.explanation: Exploding the 3D oesophageal wall shows that swallowing is not passive gravity fall: a reflex wave of circular-muscle constriction behind the bolus and relaxation ahead of it pushes food inexorably toward the stomach.
atlasLessons.limits: Single-bolus travelling constriction wave.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Regional pH Compartments for Amylase, Pepsin & Trypsin
atlasLessons.question: Why do digestive enzymes work under different conditions in different gut compartments?
atlasLessons.explanation: Compare illustrative activity curves as pH changes. Acid supports stomach pepsin activity; pancreatic bicarbonate is a major contributor to the different intestinal conditions. The curves are teaching shapes, not measured universal enzyme profiles.
atlasLessons.limits: Illustrative pH curves; values vary with enzyme and conditions.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Gastric Mucus–Bicarbonate Barrier & Pepsinogen Activation
atlasLessons.question: Why doesn’t the stomach’s own HCl (pH 1.8) and pepsin digest the living stomach wall itself?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect the protective mucus and bicarbonate layer, alongside the chapter explanation of epithelial joins, repair and inactive protease precursors. Surface mucus cells protect the stomach lining; no single layer guarantees complete protection.
atlasLessons.limits: Cross-sectional mucosal wall protection layer.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Amphipathic Bile Salts & 64-Droplet Lipid Emulsification
atlasLessons.question: How can smaller fat droplets provide four times the interface without proving a fourfold digestion rate?
atlasLessons.explanation: Choose a geometric division into 64 equal droplets of the same total volume. Their combined interface is four times larger. This is a droplet-geometry model, not a calibrated bile-concentration or enzyme-rate experiment; lipase supply and interfacial conditions still matter.
atlasLessons.limits: Equal-radius spherical subdivision model.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Lipase at the Fat-Droplet Interface
atlasLessons.question: Why does water-soluble pancreatic lipase act only at the oil–water surface of lipid droplets?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspecting the green pancreatic lipase enzymes docked around the 3D emulsified droplets shows how bile-salt emulsification multiplies accessible ester bonds for hydrolysis into fatty acids and monoglycerides.
atlasLessons.limits: Structural interface schematic; no calculated hydrolysis rate.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Intestinal Villus Capillary Cage vs Central Lacteal
atlasLessons.question: Why do absorbed glucose and amino acids enter the villus blood capillaries while long-chain fats enter the central lymphatic lacteal?
atlasLessons.explanation: Switching the 3D intestinal villus to X-ray or Section cutaway view reveals water-soluble sugars and amino acids crossing the single-cell brush-border epithelium into the capillary mesh, while bulky chylomicrons enter the porous central lacteal.
atlasLessons.limits: Single finger-like villus column with representative microvillus amplification.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Hepatic Portal Vein & First-Pass Liver Metabolic Checkpoint
atlasLessons.question: Why does venous blood from the small intestine detour through a second capillary bed in the liver before reaching the heart?
atlasLessons.explanation: The villus view identifies the capillary route. Blood leaving intestinal capillaries subsequently reaches the liver through the hepatic portal vein; that later organ route is explained in the chapter, rather than represented by a complete liver model here.
atlasLessons.limits: Villus and onward-route explanation; no modelled liver clearance or sinusoidal flow.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: C-Shaped Tracheal Cartilage Rings & Bronchial Tree
atlasLessons.question: Why is the trachea reinforced with incomplete C-shaped cartilage rings rather than rigid solid cylinders or soft muscle alone?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspecting the 3D trachea and bronchi above the expanding lungs shows how C-rings prevent airway collapse during negative-pressure inspiration while letting the oesophagus bulge forward during swallowing.
atlasLessons.limits: Upper bronchial tree and thoracic bellows model.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Rib Bucket-Handle Kinematics, Diaphragm Dome & Boyle’s Law
atlasLessons.question: How does chest expansion create the pressure difference that drives air into the lungs?
atlasLessons.explanation: The expanding ribcage and flattening diaphragm expand the lungs through pleural coupling. Alveolar pressure briefly falls below outside pressure, driving inward airflow. The displayed pressure swing is a chosen small schematic cycle.
atlasLessons.limits: Open-air breathing schematic; the pressure swing is not a closed-gas Boyle calculation.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Alveolar Cup, Capillary Mesh & Fick’s Law of Diffusion
atlasLessons.question: How does a 0.5 µm alveolar–capillary barrier transfer 250 mL of O₂ per minute at rest and up to 4,000 mL min⁻¹ during exercise?
atlasLessons.explanation: Exploding the 3D alveolar sac and its wrapping capillary basket shows red blood cells squeezing single-file past squamous Type I pneumocytes, maximising surface area A (~70 m²) and minimising barrier thickness Δx (~0.5 µm) in Fick’s law.
atlasLessons.limits: Steady-state alveolar–arterial partial pressure gradient.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Harvey’s One-Way Venous Valves & Quantitative Cardiac Output
atlasLessons.question: How did William Harvey use simple multiplication of stroke volume by heart rate—plus forearm vein valves—to refute Galen’s tidal blood theory?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspecting the 3D semilunar venous valve leaflets and cardiac output readout (Q = HR × SV ≈ 5 L min⁻¹) shows why blood must circulate in a closed one-way loop.
atlasLessons.limits: Coupled cardiac output and venous valve geometry.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Pulmonary & Systemic Figure-of-Eight Double Circulation
atlasLessons.question: Why do mammals and birds route blood through the heart twice on every complete circuit of the body?
atlasLessons.explanation: Tracing the blue pulmonary loop and red systemic loop in 3D shows why a double pump is essential: after blood loses pressure crossing the delicate pulmonary capillaries, the thick left ventricle re-pressurises oxygenated blood to 120 mmHg for systemic delivery.
atlasLessons.limits: Simplified figure-of-eight vascular loop coupled to the four-chamber heart.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Four-Chamber Heart Cutaway & One-Way Valve Cycle
atlasLessons.question: Why is the muscular wall of the left ventricle three times thicker than the right ventricle, and what makes the ‘lub-dub’ heart sounds?
atlasLessons.explanation: Slicing the 3D heart in Section mode reveals the 12 mm left ventricular myocardium versus the 4 mm right wall, plus the atrioventricular (‘lub’) and semilunar (‘dub’) valves snapping shut under reverse pressure gradients.
atlasLessons.limits: Synchronised cardiac cycle driven by heart-rate slider.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Artery Elastic Wall, Vein Semilunar Valve & Capillary Pore
atlasLessons.question: How do the wall layers and lumen diameters of arteries, veins, and capillaries match their local blood pressures and flow velocities?
atlasLessons.explanation: Comparing the three 3D vessel cylinders side-by-side shows thick elastic/smooth-muscle tunica media in high-pressure arteries, wide lumens with pocket valves in low-pressure veins, and a single-cell endothelium in exchange capillaries.
atlasLessons.limits: Cross-sectional segments normalized for direct wall-thickness comparison.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Single-File Biconcave Erythrocytes & Capillary Tissue Exchange
atlasLessons.question: Why does a human red blood cell eject its nucleus and squeeze single-file through a 7 µm capillary lumen?
atlasLessons.explanation: Biconcave red cells have a short diffusion distance and flex through narrow capillaries. Loss of the nucleus leaves room for haemoglobin. Oxygen diffusion and net fluid filtration are separate processes; lymphatics return net filtered fluid.
atlasLessons.limits: Focuses on erythrocytes and plasma flow inside the vessel trio.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Interventricular Septum & Left-to-Right Shunt Mechanics
atlasLessons.question: Why does a hole in the muscular interventricular septum (VSD) force oxygenated blood from the left ventricle into the right ventricle rather than the reverse?
atlasLessons.explanation: Slicing the 3D heart to inspect the interventricular septum shows that left ventricular systolic pressure (120 mmHg) is nearly five times right ventricular pressure (25 mmHg), driving a left-to-right shunt that overloads pulmonary capillaries.
atlasLessons.limits: Assumed uncomplicated postnatal left-to-right shunt; pulmonary flow increases without an assumed fall in systemic oxygen saturation.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Point-to-Point Synaptic Signalling vs Broadcast Hormones
atlasLessons.question: How does a 0.5 ms neurotransmitter pulse across a 20 nm synaptic cleft compare with blood-borne hormone signalling?
atlasLessons.explanation: Compare signals routed through neural connections with blood-borne hormones acting on cells with suitable receptors. Neural and hormonal onset and duration vary, and both systems can work together.
atlasLessons.limits: Focused on the 20 nm cleft geometry and receptor specificity. The relay is an excitatory chemical example; presynaptic regulation and inhibitory synapses also exist.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Sensory, Relay & Motor Neurone Architecture in the Reflex Arc
atlasLessons.question: How does a spinal reflex arc trigger muscle withdrawal before the conscious cortex even registers pain?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspecting the 3D myelinated neurone and synaptic relay shows how routing a nociceptive spike directly from sensory neurone → spinal relay interneurone → motor neurone cuts conduction path length and synaptic delay.
atlasLessons.limits: 3D myelinated motor neurone and synaptic junction. Waveforms are schematic, not an integration of Hodgkin–Huxley equations.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Myelinated Axon, Nodes of Ranvier & Saltatory Conduction
atlasLessons.question: How does wrapping an axon in insulating Schwann-cell myelin speed action potentials from 2 m s⁻¹ up to 90 m s⁻¹ while saving metabolic energy?
atlasLessons.explanation: Exploding the 3D motor neurone shows Schwann myelin sheaths preventing transmembrane current leak across internodes so the depolarising wave leaps node-to-node across voltage-gated Na⁺ channels studied by Obaid Siddiqi.
atlasLessons.limits: Hodgkin–Huxley style travelling wave along discrete nodal segments. Waveforms are schematic, not an integration of Hodgkin–Huxley equations.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Ca²⁺-Triggered Synaptic Vesicle Exocytosis across the 20 nm Cleft
atlasLessons.question: Why can nerve impulses cross a chemical synapse in only one direction, and how is the electrical signal converted to chemical and back?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect presynaptic release and postsynaptic reception in this excitatory chemical relay. Presynaptic regulatory receptors and inhibitory synapses also exist; this drawing isolates one forward route.
atlasLessons.limits: Quantal vesicle release scaled to stimulus threshold. The relay is an excitatory chemical example; presynaptic regulation and inhibitory synapses also exist.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Axonal Conduction Velocity vs Synaptic Delay Budget
atlasLessons.question: Which stages contribute delay between a receptor signal and muscle activation?
atlasLessons.explanation: Trace axonal propagation separately from chemical release, diffusion and postsynaptic responses. The drawn withdrawal circuit has two central junctions plus a neuromuscular junction. A chosen time budget does not measure hot-pan withdrawal.
atlasLessons.limits: Illustrative timing depends on chosen inputs; no universal reflex latency.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Sectioned Human Eyeball, Fovea Cone Pit & Optic Disc
atlasLessons.question: Why is colour acuity sharpest dead-centre on the fovea while the optic disc creates a complete blind spot?
atlasLessons.explanation: Slicing the 3D eyeball in Section cutaway mode reveals the cornea, iris, crystalline lens, and posterior retina with the high-cone-density foveal pit and axon-packed optic nerve head.
atlasLessons.limits: Thin-lens optical ray bundle to the fovea.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Ciliary Muscle Ring, Suspensory Ligaments & Lens Accommodation
atlasLessons.question: Why does contracting the ciliary muscle make the suspensory ligaments go slack and the crystalline lens bulge thicker for near reading?
atlasLessons.explanation: At near viewing distance the ciliary muscle contracts, ligament tension falls and the lens becomes more convex. At 25 cm the chosen 17 mm reduced-eye model needs about 62.82 D total eye power; this is not the lens power alone.
atlasLessons.limits: Thin-lens vergence model (1/f = 1/u + 1/v) with 17 mm retinal distance.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: PIN3 Auxin Redistribution, Acid Growth & Phototropic Curvature
atlasLessons.question: How does a plant coleoptile bend toward unilateral blue light without a single muscle or neurone?
atlasLessons.explanation: Shining directional light on the 3D coleoptile tip redistributes indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) to the shaded flank; proton pumps acidify the shaded cell walls, activating expansins so turgor elongates the shaded side faster and bends the shoot toward the light.
atlasLessons.limits: Cholodny–Went differential elongation beam model.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Voltage-Gated Na⁺ Channel Blockade at Nodes of Ranvier
atlasLessons.question: How does pufferfish tetrodotoxin (TTX) or Siddiqi’s para mutation silence nerve conduction without altering resting K⁺ leak?
atlasLessons.explanation: Dropping stimulus efficacy below threshold at the 3D Nodes of Ranvier demonstrates how plugging voltage-gated Na⁺ channels prevents the regenerative depolarising upstroke while leaving the −70 mV resting potential intact.
atlasLessons.limits: Threshold-gated nodal Na⁺ current model. Waveforms are schematic, not an integration of Hodgkin–Huxley equations.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Pancreatic Islet β/α Cells & GLUT4 Vesicle Translocation
atlasLessons.question: How does insulin secreted by pancreatic β-cells open the glucose door on muscle and liver membranes after a carbohydrate meal?
atlasLessons.explanation: Raising blood glucose above 90 mg dL⁻¹ in the 3D islet station triggers β-cell insulin exocytosis; insulin binding to its tyrosine-kinase receptor translocates intracellular GLUT4 vesicles into the plasma membrane, accelerating glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis.
atlasLessons.limits: Steady-state insulin/glucagon ratio and GLUT4 membrane insertion fraction. Illustrative assumptions; rates and volumes are not individual clinical predictions.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Cutaneous Arteriolar Vasomotion, Eccrine Sweat & Piloerection
atlasLessons.question: How does a 2 mm layer of human skin switch between a heat radiator in summer and a thermal insulator in winter?
atlasLessons.explanation: Slicing the 3D dermis while sweeping ambient temperature shows hypothalamic sympathetic control dilating superficial arteriolar loops and activating coiled eccrine sweat glands in heat, or constricting arterioles and contracting arrector pili muscles in cold.
atlasLessons.limits: Coupled radiative/convective and evaporative dermal heat flux model. Illustrative assumptions; rates and volumes are not individual clinical predictions.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Evaporative Sweat Cooling vs High-Humidity Heat Balance
atlasLessons.question: Why is a 38 °C day when dry heat evaporates sweat instantly far safer than a humid coastal afternoon when sweat drips off unevaporated?
atlasLessons.explanation: Driving ambient temperature above 37 °C in the 3D skin block shows radiative heat transfer reversing inward, leaving latent heat of sweat evaporation (2,420 kJ L⁻¹) from eccrine ducts as the body’s sole cooling channel.
atlasLessons.limits: Dermal heat balance model. Illustrative assumptions; rates and volumes are not individual clinical predictions.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Hepatic Deamination & Renal Clearance of Urea
atlasLessons.question: Why must excess amino acids be deaminated in the liver and converted into urea before the kidneys filter them out?
atlasLessons.explanation: Following urea through the 3D glomerulus and nephron tubule shows how the liver converts toxic ammonia (NH₃) into neutral, highly water-soluble urea that passes freely through Bowman’s capsule for urinary excretion.
atlasLessons.limits: Glomerular and tubular urea clearance view. Illustrative assumptions; rates and volumes are not individual clinical predictions.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Glomerular Ultrafiltration, Loop of Henle & Aquaporin-2
atlasLessons.question: Why do human kidneys filter 180 L of plasma every day only to reabsorb 99% of it along the nephron tubule?
atlasLessons.explanation: Following the 3D nephron from Bowman’s capsule through the proximal tubule, countercurrent Loop of Henle (300 → 1,200 mOsm L⁻¹), and ADH-regulated collecting duct shows how high filtration plus selective reabsorption purges urea while normally recovering nearly all glucose and ~99% of water.
atlasLessons.limits: Steady-state GFR (125 mL min⁻¹) and ADH-dependent collecting-duct water reabsorption. Illustrative assumptions; rates and volumes are not individual clinical predictions.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Cholera Toxin Cl⁻ Efflux & Mahalanabis’s SGLT1 ORS Rescue
atlasLessons.question: Why does adding equimolar glucose to salt water allow a cholera-stricken gut to absorb water when plain saline fails?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspecting the 3D tubular cotransport and antibody defence stages shows how SGLT1 Na⁺–glucose symporters remain intact during cholera toxin secretion, pulling Na⁺, glucose, and osmotic water back into the bloodstream.
atlasLessons.limits: Represented via tubular Na⁺/glucose cotransport and mucosal immunity. Illustrative assumptions; rates and volumes are not individual clinical predictions.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Y-Shaped IgG Antibody Hinge, Fab Paratopes & Vaccine Memory
atlasLessons.question: How can one class of Y-shaped IgG protein both lock onto millions of distinct pathogen epitopes and flag them for macrophages?
atlasLessons.explanation: Exploding the 3D IgG heterotetramer reveals two heavy and two light chains linked by disulphide bridges: hypervariable Fab tips clamp complementary pathogen epitopes while the conserved Fc stem recruits phagocytes and complement.
atlasLessons.limits: Flexible hinge angle shown locking onto a spherical viral capsid. Illustrative assumptions; rates and volumes are not individual clinical predictions.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Pre-Formed Antivenom IgG vs Clonal Memory B-Cell Immunity
atlasLessons.question: Why does a snakebite victim need immediate passive IgG antivenom infusion rather than an active vaccine?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspecting the 3D IgG Fab–antigen lock shows that passive immunity supplies pre-made antibodies immediately (0-day lag) to neutralise circulating toxin, though without generating memory B cells.
atlasLessons.limits: Direct 3D IgG neutralisation complex. Illustrative assumptions; rates and volumes are not individual clinical predictions.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Hyperglycaemia, PCT SGLT Saturation & Osmotic Diuresis
atlasLessons.question: Why does untreated diabetes mellitus (>180 mg dL⁻¹ blood glucose) cause glucose to spill into urine (glycosuria) and pull excess water with it?
atlasLessons.explanation: Sliding blood glucose up to 240 mg dL⁻¹ in the 3D Islet and Nephron stations saturates the proximal convoluted tubule’s SGLT symporters, leaving un-reabsorbed glucose in the filtrate where it opposes osmotic water reabsorption in the collecting duct.
atlasLessons.limits: Coupled islet GLUT4 and nephron tubular transport threshold model. Illustrative assumptions; rates and volumes are not individual clinical predictions.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Avery–MacLeod–McCarty DNase Proof & the DNA Information Polymer
atlasLessons.question: Why did destroying protein or RNA leave Griffith’s transforming principle intact, whereas DNase abolished bacterial transformation completely?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspecting the 3D B-DNA double helix shows how genetic information is physically stored in the linear sequence of A, T, G, and C nitrogenous bases shielded inside the sugar–phosphate backbone.
atlasLessons.limits: Historical fibre model ≈10 bp/turn; relaxed B-DNA commonly ≈10.5. Geometry schematic. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Franklin’s Photo 51, B-DNA Pitch (3.4 nm) & Antiparallel Strands
atlasLessons.question: How did diffraction measurements, chemical evidence and model-building together reveal complementary DNA strands and an approximately 2 nm double helix?
atlasLessons.explanation: Rotating and exploding the 3D B-DNA double helix from the top and side shows the 2.0 nm constant diameter enforced by purine–pyrimidine Watson–Crick base steps stacked 0.34 nm apart inside antiparallel 5′→3′ and 3′→5′ phosphodiester ribbons.
atlasLessons.limits: Historical fibre model ≈10 bp/turn; relaxed B-DNA commonly ≈10.5. Geometry schematic. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Khorana’s Synthetic Triplets & the 64-Codon Genetic Cipher
atlasLessons.question: Why are 3-base codons the minimum word length needed for a 4-letter nucleotide alphabet to specify 20 amino acids, and how did Har Gobind Khorana crack the table?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect the ribosome, tRNA adaptors and emerging chain; the adjoining cipher investigation tests synthetic RNA sequences explicitly.
atlasLessons.limits: Standard nuclear genetic code. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: RNA Polymerase Transcription Bubble & 80S Ribosome Translation
atlasLessons.question: How does RNA polymerase transcribe a 3′→5′ DNA template into 5′→3′ mRNA, and how do the A, P, and E sites of the ribosome translate it?
atlasLessons.explanation: Stepping from the 3D RNA polymerase transcription bubble to the 80S ribosome A–P–E tRNA bench traces a gene from unwound DNA template to growing polypeptide chain.
atlasLessons.limits: Coupled transcription bubble and 3-slot ribosomal translation. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: From Primary Amino-Acid Chain to 3D Active Protein Machines
atlasLessons.question: How does the linear sequence of amino acids emerging from the ribosome’s exit tunnel dictate the 3D shape of an enzyme, antibody, or ion channel?
atlasLessons.explanation: Exploding the 3D 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits exposes the nascent polypeptide chain folding as polar, non-polar, and charged side chains interact.
atlasLessons.limits: Nascent chain emergence from the 60S ribosomal subunit. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Structural Comparison of Duplex DNA vs Single-Stranded mRNA
atlasLessons.question: Why is double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (with thymine) built for permanent archival storage while single-stranded ribonucleic acid (with uracil) serves as a transient messenger?
atlasLessons.explanation: Comparing the 3D B-DNA double helix against the single-stranded mRNA ribbon emerging from RNA polymerase highlights the 2′-OH ribose group, uracil base pairing, and single-stranded flexibility.
atlasLessons.limits: Side-by-side duplex DNA and single-stranded mRNA comparison. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Sickle-Cell GAG→GTG Point Mutation & HbS Fibre Polymerisation
atlasLessons.question: How can mutating a single adenine to thymine out of 3 billion base pairs alter haemoglobin interactions at low oxygen and potentially distort red blood cells into a rigid sickle?
atlasLessons.explanation: Switching the β-globin codon 6 slider from GAG (hydrophilic glutamate) to GUG (hydrophobic valine) in 3D exposes a sticky surface patch on deoxygenated HbS tetramers, causing them to polymerise into 14-stranded stiff rods that warp the erythrocyte.
atlasLessons.limits: Single-fibre axial polymerisation inside a deformable erythrocyte mesh. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Silent, Missense, Nonsense & Frameshift Mutation Consequences
atlasLessons.question: Why does a base substitution in the third ‘wobble’ position of a codon often leave the amino-acid sequence unchanged, whereas a single base deletion changes the downstream reading frame?
atlasLessons.explanation: Comparing the 3D ribosome reading frame with the β-globin point mutation station illustrates how triplet reading frames respond to substitutions versus insertions/deletions.
atlasLessons.limits: Same amino-acid sequence does not guarantee no RNA-processing or production effects; these are held fixed here. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Codon Degeneracy & Wobble Base Pairing on the Ribosome
atlasLessons.question: Why do six different mRNA codons (UUA, UUG, CUU, CUC, CUA, CUG) all specify the same leucine residue into a growing protein?
atlasLessons.explanation: Select the synonymous HBB example: changed DNA and RNA still specify leucine. RNA processing and production are held fixed here.
atlasLessons.limits: A-site tRNA anticodon geometry. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Meselson–Stahl Semiconservative Replication Fork & Okazaki Fragments
atlasLessons.question: How do heavy and light DNA strands distinguish competing copying models over two generations?
atlasLessons.explanation: Compare heavy, hybrid and light fractions in the Meselson–Stahl station. This follows duplex ancestry, not primers or Okazaki-fragment chemistry.
atlasLessons.limits: Unwound Y-fork geometry without trombone loop folding. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Sister Chromatids, Centromere Kinetochores & Chromosome Counting
atlasLessons.question: Why does an S-phase replicated chromosome with two sister chromatids still count as one chromosome until protein links are released and sisters separate?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspecting the 3D X-shaped metaphase chromosomes and separating anaphase chromatids clarifies how chromosome count follows centromere number while DNA mass doubles in S-phase and halves in anaphase/telophase.
atlasLessons.limits: Representative metacentric chromosome pairs. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Flemming’s Mitotic Spindle, Metaphase Plate & Anaphase Separation
atlasLessons.question: How does the bipolar microtubule spindle normally distribute one copy of every chromosome?
atlasLessons.explanation: Dragging the mitotic phase slider through Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, and Telophase in 3D shows kinetochore microtubules aligning X-shaped chromosomes on the equatorial metaphase plate before cohesin cleavage lets motor proteins pull sister chromatids to opposite poles.
atlasLessons.limits: Two representative homologous chromosome pairs shown for visual clarity. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Clonal Mitotic Propagation vs Meiotic Recombination in Crops
atlasLessons.question: Why does vegetative stem cutting preserve an elite sugarcane or mango genotype intact, whereas growing from seed shuffles parental traits?
atlasLessons.explanation: Comparing the 3D Mitosis spindle (genetically identical 2n clones) with the Meiosis I crossing-over tetrad explains the trade-off between clonal uniformity and sexual genetic diversity.
atlasLessons.limits: Comparative mitotic vs meiotic division mechanics. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Stem Cell Niche & Waddington Epigenetic Differentiation Landscape
atlasLessons.question: If a neuron, an immature red-cell precursor, and a smooth muscle cell carry the exact same DNA genome, how do they become so different?
atlasLessons.explanation: Watching pluripotent stem cells roll down the branching valleys of Waddington’s 3D epigenetic landscape illustrates how transcription factors and chromatin marks selectively express lineage-specific genes without deleting DNA.
atlasLessons.limits: Three-valley bifurcating potential surface. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Gurdon’s Nuclear Transfer & Yamanaka’s iPSC Reprogramming
atlasLessons.question: How did nuclear transfer and cell reprogramming show that specialised cells can retain instructions for other cell types?
atlasLessons.explanation: In the 3D Waddington epigenetic landscape, reprogramming pushes a differentiated somatic nucleus back uphill to the pluripotent summit, restoring its capacity to roll down any developmental valley.
atlasLessons.limits: Potential-energy landscape representation of epigenetic state. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Meiosis I Homologous Bivalent, Chiasma & Crossing Over
atlasLessons.question: How do prophase I crossing over and metaphase I independent assortment generate genetically unique haploid gametes?
atlasLessons.explanation: Rotating the 3D homologous bivalent tetrad in Prophase I reveals non-sister chromatids breaking and rejoining at the X-shaped chiasma, swapping maternal and paternal allele segments before Meiosis I and II halve ploidy from 2n to n.
atlasLessons.limits: Single chiasma exchange shown on a homologous chromosome pair. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Side-by-Side Mitosis (2n → 2n) vs Meiosis (2n → n) Mechanics
atlasLessons.question: What is the key mechanical difference at Metaphase I that makes meiosis halve chromosome number while mitosis preserves it?
atlasLessons.explanation: Switching between the 3D Mitosis and Meiosis stations shows individual chromosomes lining up single-file in mitotic metaphase versus paired homologous bivalents lining up side-by-side in meiotic Metaphase I.
atlasLessons.limits: Comparative 3D spindle and bivalent views. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Triploid (3n = 33) Bivalent Pairing Failure in Seedless Bananas
atlasLessons.question: Why are triploid (3n) Cavendish bananas poorly fertile, while parthenocarpy permits seedless fruit, yet able to grow huge fruit clusters when propagated by suckers?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspecting homologous synapsis in the 3D Meiosis I station shows why three copies of each chromosome cannot pair cleanly two-by-two at Metaphase I, causing unbalanced anaphase segregation and inviable gametes while mitotic sucker growth (2n/3n → 3n) proceeds normally.
atlasLessons.limits: Chromosome-sorting schematic: irregular segregation reduces fertility; parthenocarpy separately permits fruit without fertilisation. The 3D station is schematic; use adjoining text and 2D investigations for detailed mechanisms.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Mendel’s Monohybrid Probabilities and Sampling Uncertainty
atlasLessons.question: Why do Tt × Tt parents give an expected 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt genotype ratio and a 3 : 1 phenotype ratio?
atlasLessons.explanation: Compare the expected genotype columns with the four-cell Punnett grid. The cross selector changes between Tt × Tt, Tt × tt and TT × tt. Increasing N reduces the displayed standard error; the columns are expected probabilities, not a fresh random sample.
atlasLessons.limits: One locus with complete dominance and equal gamete probabilities. No dihybrid tower, random tosses or guaranteed convergence on every run is shown.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Homologous Chromosome Pair, Gene Loci & Allelic Variants
atlasLessons.question: How can two chromosomes carry matching gene loci but different versions of a gene?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect the maternal and paternal chromosome rods and their matching locus bands. Homozygotes have matching alleles at a locus; heterozygotes have different alleles. The adjacent family symbols illustrate two carrier parents and an affected child.
atlasLessons.limits: Schematic marker bands, not measured chromosome geometry or enzyme concentrations. The family example assumes one autosomal gene, complete expression and no new mutation.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Diagnostic Test Cross (Dominant Phenotype × Homozygous Recessive)
atlasLessons.question: Why does a recessive offspring reveal a hidden allele, while an all-dominant sample cannot prove a parent is homozygous?
atlasLessons.explanation: Compare the Tt × tt model (expected 1:1 tall:dwarf) with the known TT × tt model (all tall). A dwarf offspring establishes that the tall parent carried t. A finite all-tall sample supports TT but can occur by chance from Tt; the atlas does not simulate an actual breeding trial.
atlasLessons.limits: One locus with complete dominance, equal gamete probabilities and no new mutation. Known parental genotypes generate probabilities; observing finite offspring is a separate inference.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Autosomal Pedigree Clues and Their Assumptions
atlasLessons.question: Within a fully expressed single-gene model, what can an affected child of two unaffected parents reveal?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect the fixed carrier-parent family Aa × Aa and its affected aa child at the chromosome-and-pedigree station. The Punnett probabilities are 25% AA, 50% Aa and 25% aa for each pregnancy. The chapter’s separate pedigree figure compares dominant and recessive deductions.
atlasLessons.limits: One autosomal locus, complete penetrance, no new mutation and reliable relationships. Real clinical pedigrees may include reduced penetrance or new variants; the atlas has no pedigree-mode toggle.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: ABO Alleles and Two Cell-Surface Antigens
atlasLessons.question: Why does an AB red blood cell display both A and B antigens rather than a blended intermediate?
atlasLessons.explanation: Use the ABO selector (0=A, 1=B, 2=AB, 3=O) to inspect schematic surface antigens. A and B transferases attach different terminal sugars to H-antigen chains. In AB, both products occur on the same cell; a common non-functional O allele adds neither terminal sugar.
atlasLessons.limits: Standard ABO model with H-antigen present. Sugar markers are schematic shapes, not molecular scale or antigen-density measurements; rare variants and Bombay phenotype can alter typing.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Complete Dominance vs Codominance on the Cell Surface
atlasLessons.question: Why can one working A allele give Group A, whereas A and B together give Group AB?
atlasLessons.explanation: Compare A (selector 0), B (1), AB (2) and O (3) on the cell-surface station. One working A allele supplies sufficient transferase for Group A; A and B together supply both antigen-producing activities. A count of working alleles does not measure an exact enzyme percentage.
atlasLessons.limits: Representative surface markers, not measured antigen coating or enzyme doses. The atlas selects one representative genotype per group; standard ABO inheritance is assumed.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: X and Y Chromosomes and an Expected Sex Ratio
atlasLessons.question: In the typical XX/XY model, which parent supplies the chromosome that makes a zygote XX or XY?
atlasLessons.explanation: Compare the schematic X and Y chromosomes. An egg supplies X, while sperm have expected X and Y proportions of one half each. The chromosome grid in the chapter therefore assigns 50% XX and 50% XY probabilities to each fertilisation; observed birth ratios need not be exactly equal.
atlasLessons.limits: Typical XX/XY model and equal fertilisation probabilities; chromosome size is schematic, and variations in sex chromosomes or development are not simulated.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: X-Linked Alleles from Mother to Son
atlasLessons.question: Why does the fixed carrier-mother × normal-father model give 50% affected sons but 25% affected children overall?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect the X/Y station and its fixed offspring bars. Sons receive their X from their mother and Y from their father; half of sons inherit the altered X in this cross. Half of daughters inherit it too and are carriers in the simple recessive model. Use the chapter’s separate cross lab to change parent genotypes.
atlasLessons.limits: The atlas bars show one fixed cross, not a rotatable three-generation X-linked pedigree. Some women heterozygous for haemophilia variants have bleeding symptoms; F8 and F9 are separate genes and X-inactivation affects expression.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: The ABO Mechanism Behind the Mumbai Ward Puzzle
atlasLessons.question: How do A, B and non-functional O alleles help explain the standard ABO grids in the ward puzzle?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect the A, B, AB and O antigen patterns, then return to the chapter’s parental Punnett grids. Under the stated two-family standard-ABO assumptions, AB × O excludes an ordinary O child. The separate colour-vision pedigree explains a different clinic puzzle and does not identify the newborns.
atlasLessons.limits: The atlas illustrates antigen expression, not clinical identity testing or a full parental-cross search. Records and DNA identity testing would confirm a real assignment; rare ABO variants and H-antigen deficiency require further investigation.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Variation Before Selection
atlasLessons.question: How can inherited differences change which cells contribute to later populations?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect susceptible and pre-existing resistant cells in an illustrative Petri dish, then compare how a chosen survival pressure changes their fractions.
atlasLessons.limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Mutation Supply and Selection
atlasLessons.question: What shows that a resistant variant can exist before exposure?
atlasLessons.explanation: The dish represents pre-existing variation. Historical fluctuation tests and replica plating support that possibility; some antibiotics can also increase mutation rates without specifying a useful mutation.
atlasLessons.limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Reproductive Success in a Changing Environment
atlasLessons.question: Why can the same inherited variant have different reproductive success when conditions change?
atlasLessons.explanation: A chosen two-peak landscape changes with drug pressure. It represents relative reproductive contribution, not a measured moth allele trajectory or an inevitable path toward perfection.
atlasLessons.limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Differential Survival in an Illustrative Culture
atlasLessons.question: Can the resistant fraction rise without any new mutation?
atlasLessons.explanation: The model starts with990 susceptible and10 resistant cells. A chosen exposure removes susceptible cells more readily; displayed fractions are calculated from survivors, not clinical cure or relapse.
atlasLessons.limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Floating and Dry-Habitat Leaves
atlasLessons.question: How do rolled hairy leaves and floating leaves solve different physical problems?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect a sheltered stomatal pocket and a floating leaf with gas spaces. Floating water-lily leaves have upper stomata and can carry water-repellent wax; fully submerged leaves exchange dissolved gases without stomata.
atlasLessons.limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Structure, Mechanism and Reproductive Benefit
atlasLessons.question: How can an inherited structure help under particular environmental conditions?
atlasLessons.explanation: Use the leaf cutaways to connect sheltered humid air with lower water loss, and internal gas spaces with buoyancy and gas transport. Other plants and animals have different suites of features.
atlasLessons.limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Choosing Which Variants Reproduce
atlasLessons.question: How does choosing breeding parents differ from environmental differences in reproductive contribution?
atlasLessons.explanation: The illustrative fitness surface helps distinguish a desirable trait from reproductive success in a specified environment. It does not calculate a historical crop yield or the breeder equation.
atlasLessons.limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Fossils and Uncertain Evolutionary History
atlasLessons.question: What evidence do fossils preserve, and what requires further inference?
atlasLessons.explanation: Compare schematic fossil strata. Sahni described Pentoxyleae in1948 as Jurassic; the relevant Rajmahal deposits were later dated Early Cretaceous. This scene does not infer a DNA clock or prove direct ancestry.
atlasLessons.limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates. Relative genotype contributions are assumed; not measurements for modern patients.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: An Assumed Heterozygote Advantage
atlasLessons.question: How can selection maintain a variant harmful in homozygotes?
atlasLessons.explanation: Change the assumed AA disadvantage while AS fitness is1 and SS fitness is0.20. The mean-fitness curve and equilibrium illustrate balancing selection in a hypothetical random-mating population.
atlasLessons.limits: Illustrative geometry and chosen model parameters; no clinical days, historical breeding measurements or exact divergence dates. Relative genotype contributions are assumed; not measurements for modern patients.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Illustrative Trophic Production Pyramid
atlasLessons.question: Why can a tree invert a numbers pyramid while a consistently bounded production pyramid remains upright?
atlasLessons.explanation: Adjust transfer efficiency to compare new biomass production at successive levels. At the stated 10%, tertiary consumers have 0.1% of starting production; other efficiencies give different results. Heat and chemical energy in detritus are distinct outputs.
atlasLessons.limits: Tier widths are displayed for inspection. Counts and production are illustrative; use the same area/period and include imported food. This does not prove a maximum food-chain length.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Energy Accounting and Food-Supply Routes
atlasLessons.question: Why can an intermediate livestock conversion reduce food energy supplied from the same harvested crop?
atlasLessons.explanation: The chapter’s food-supply example follows harvested edible energy before human digestion: 10,000 kJ directly, or 1,000 kJ after a stated 10% livestock conversion. The atlas pyramid separately follows new biomass production.
atlasLessons.limits: The atlas does not calculate actual people per hectare. Crop choice, livestock, feed digestibility, grass/by-products and farming system change the comparison.

atlasLessons.title: Linked Model: Carbon Reservoirs and Reused Atoms
atlasLessons.question: How do photosynthesis, respiration, burial and combustion move carbon between reservoirs?
atlasLessons.explanation: Use the chapter’s carbon-cycle figure to trace carbon forms and reservoirs. The atlas nodule/lake station connects the broader idea of matter movement to microbial nutrient transformations.
atlasLessons.limits: The atlas is a nodule/lake schematic, not an interactive global four-box carbon model. Photosynthesis is the main sunlit entry route; chemoautotrophs also fix carbon.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Root Nodules and Nitrogen Transformations
atlasLessons.question: How do fixation, nitrification and denitrification change nitrogen into different usable or gaseous forms?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect the nodule and its microbes: biological fixation produces ammonia/ammonium. Aerobic nitrification produces nitrite then nitrate; denitrification can reduce nitrate towards N₂. Lightning follows a separate nitrogen-oxide/nitrate route.
atlasLessons.limits: A schematic, not a calibrated soil forecast. Fixation initially supplies the legume; uptake, leaching, harvesting and residue return also affect soil nitrate.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Nutrient Enrichment and Low Oxygen
atlasLessons.question: Why can a bloom contribute to low oxygen even though algae photosynthesise?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect one possible nutrient-enrichment pathway. Producer growth supplies organic matter for decomposers; respiration uses dissolved oxygen. Shading can contribute, sewage organic matter can act directly, and living algae respire by day and night.
atlasLessons.limits: Illustrative high/low state, not a compulsory seven-stage sequence or numerical oxygen forecast. Mixing, flow, temperature and night-time respiration matter.

atlasLessons.title: Linked Model: Forest Carbon Stocks and Conservation
atlasLessons.question: How can clearing a forest change stored carbon and future carbon uptake?
atlasLessons.explanation: The chapter’s conservation figure links biomass removal, burning/decay, photosynthetic uptake, habitats and nutrient cycling. Compare these mechanisms with the atlas’s nutrient and ecosystem views.
atlasLessons.limits: The atlas has no global-carbon or forest-clearing slider. A local effect depends on subsequent land use, regrowth and the time period.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Fermenter Conditions and Waste Handling
atlasLessons.question: Why must a fermenter control oxygen, nutrients, temperature, pH and waste products?
atlasLessons.explanation: Inspect the sparger, impellers, probes and cooling jacket. They support culture conditions while respiratory heat and wastes must be managed; product recovery/processing follows growth.
atlasLessons.limits: An illustrative E. coli response near 37 °C, not every microbe’s optimum or a prediction of temperature after a cooling failure.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Recombinant DNA and Guided Cutting
atlasLessons.question: What does compatible-end cloning achieve, and what still has to happen after a Cas9 cut?
atlasLessons.explanation: Prepare intron-free insulin coding DNA with bacterial controls; pair compatible ends, seal with ligase and select transformed cells. Recover, process/fold and purify the product; mature insulin has two chains. Cas9 targets suitable DNA near a PAM, and cell repair creates the edit.
atlasLessons.limits: Stylised plasmid/Cas9 models, not atomic structures or a promise of exact repair. Different enzymes can make compatible ends, and unintended outcomes require checking.

atlasLessons.title: 3D Atlas: Mumbai Environments and a Hypothetical Insulin Vial
atlasLessons.question: What explanations fit the fictional site comparisons, and what additional evidence would test them?
atlasLessons.explanation: Connect trophic budgets, reused atoms, nutrient enrichment and recombinant protein production. The chapter’s three Mumbai-inspired datasets are illustrative comparisons of separate environments.
atlasLessons.limits: Not a single downstream watershed or a measured restoration. Mithi drains to Mahim Creek; Thane Creek is separate. One snapshot cannot establish a time trend or treatment effect.

widgets.title: Redi Jars
widgets.challengePrompt: Inspect Jar 3 (Fine gauze) at Day 5 or later to see where the flies lay their eggs when smell escapes but flies cannot enter.
widgets.cutaway: Inside the rotting meat: bacteria and blowfly larvae secrete digestive enzymes that break muscle proteins into volatile amines (putrescine and cadaverine) that drift through Jar 3’s gauze and attract adult female Sarcophaga flies.
widgets.idealised: The simulation tracks macroscopic blowfly eggs and larvae; microscopic bacteria already on the meat continue decomposing all three samples until Pasteur’s later swan-neck flask experiment.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: Redi places identical pieces of meat into three jars—open, parchment-sealed, and gauze-covered.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up
watchSteps.caption: 2/5 Close-up: By Day 2.5, blowflies smell the meat and lay microscopic clutches of eggs directly on Jar 1’s meat and atop Jar 3’s gauze.

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away
watchSteps.caption: 3/5 Cut-away: Rising scent molecules pass easily through the fine gauze mesh, refuting the claim that sealed jars only failed for lack of fresh air.

watchSteps.title: 4. Side-on trend
watchSteps.caption: 4/5 Trend: By Day 6, larvae crawl over Jar 1’s meat and atop Jar 3’s netting, while the meat inside Jar 3 stays 100% maggot-free.

watchSteps.title: 5. Your turn
watchSteps.caption: 5/5 Your turn: Scrub through all 8 days or switch jars to compare the open, sealed, and gauze controls.

widgets.title: Leeuwenhoek Scope
widgets.challengePrompt: Switch to the "2.0 mm (70×)" or "0.7 mm (275×)" lens and adjust Focus within 4 µm of 0 to bring the swimming animalcules into sharp view.
widgets.cutaway: Inside the single soda-lime glass bead: the tiny radius of curvature (r = 0.7 mm) bends light steeply at both surfaces, giving focal length f ≈ r / 2(n − 1) ≈ 0.9 mm and 275× magnification when held close to the cornea.
widgets.idealised: Real spherical glass beads suffer from chromatic fringes and edge curvature outside the central 30% of the field of view.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: At 70× (a 2.0 mm glass sphere), pond water reveals filamentous Spirogyra algae spirals and fast Paramecia.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up
watchSteps.caption: 2/5 Close-up: Switching to Leeuwenhoek’s smallest 0.7 mm sphere jumps to 275× magnification—enough to resolve tumbling rod bacteria (2–3 µm).

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away
watchSteps.caption: 3/5 Cut-away: A single spherical bead avoids the compound lens reflections that blurred Hooke’s multi-lens tubes.

watchSteps.title: 4. Side-on trend
watchSteps.caption: 4/5 Trend: Turning the brass focus screw even 20 µm away from the focal plane blurs the microscopic swimmers into soft haloes.

watchSteps.title: 5. Your turn
watchSteps.caption: 5/5 Your turn: Pull Focus back to 0 µm and compare all three glass bead sizes.

widgets.title: Monsoon Imbibition
widgets.challengePrompt: Select "Monsoon soak (28 °C + water)" and advance Time to at least 24 hours to watch the radicle root break through the seed coat.
widgets.cutaway: Inside the cotyledon cells: incoming H₂O molecules dissolve the sucrose-raffinose glass matrix, reducing cytoplasmic viscosity by >10,000× so respiratory enzymes and substrates can diffuse and collide.
widgets.idealised: Respiration curves show representative Vigna radiata (moong bean) laboratory rates at 28 °C; individual seeds vary by coat thickness and age.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: In a dry cupboard jar (10% water), the moong bean’s cytoplasm is locked in a solid sugar-glass state.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up
watchSteps.caption: 2/5 Close-up: Within 6 hours of monsoon rain soaking into the seed, water content rises past 45% and oxygen uptake leaps >500-fold.

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away
watchSteps.caption: 3/5 Cut-away: Inside the hydrated cell, dissolved enzymes collide rapidly with glucose to recharge ADP into ATP.

watchSteps.title: 4. Side-on trend
watchSteps.caption: 4/5 Trend: A boiled seed absorbs the exact same physical water early on, but its heat-unfolded enzymes produce zero O₂ uptake and zero ATP.

watchSteps.title: 5. Your turn
watchSteps.caption: 5/5 Your turn: Switch back to the living soaked seed at 36 hours to see the radicle root emerge.

widgets.title: Seed Flame3D
widgets.challengePrompt: Switch to "Living Seed Cell (ATP Engine)" and increase Metabolic rate above 1.2× to watch ATP packets shuttle energy from the enzyme hub to build the growing polymer chain.
widgets.cutaway: Inside the mitochondrial enzyme complex: instead of letting oxygen slam directly into carbon at 1,000 °C, enzymes pass electrons down a stepped chain at 28 °C, using each small energy drop to cock the negatively charged triphosphate spring of ATP.
widgets.idealised: Each glowing golden sphere represents a pool of thousands of ATP molecules diffusing across nanometre distances inside the cell.

watchSteps.title: 1. Wide view
watchSteps.caption: 1/5 Wide shot: Left, a candle flame shatters hydrocarbon fuel into hot, disordered gas; right, a seed cell channels fuel energy into ordered polymers.

watchSteps.title: 2. Close-up
watchSteps.caption: 2/5 Close-up: Zooming into the candle flame shows 100% of the chemical energy escaping as random kinetic motion.

watchSteps.title: 3. Cut-away
watchSteps.caption: 3/5 Cut-away: Inside the living cell, green catalytic enzymes step fuel energy into golden ATP springs without burning the cell.

watchSteps.title: 4. Side-on trend
watchSteps.caption: 4/5 Trend: Speeding up metabolism dispatches more ATP packets per second to the blue DNA-guided assembly site.

watchSteps.title: 5. Your turn
watchSteps.caption: 5/5 Your turn: Rotate the 3D stage or switch between side-by-side, cell, and flame views.

widgets.title: Cell Inventory
widgets.challengePrompt: Find a plant cell with mitochondria and no developed chloroplasts.
widgets.cutaway: A plant wall lies outside its cell membrane. Inside, ribosomes build proteins and mitochondria support ATP supply; neither job depends on the cell being green.
widgets.idealised: Each schematic is enlarged separately; membranes and ribosomes are oversized, and most molecular crowding is omitted.

watchSteps.title: 1. Shared machinery
watchSteps.caption: Animal cells have a membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, a nucleus and mitochondria.

watchSteps.title: 2. Add the green parts
watchSteps.caption: A leaf cell also has a wall, a sap-filled vacuole and chloroplasts.

watchSteps.title: 3. Inside an onion
watchSteps.caption: The white bulb cell keeps mitochondria despite having no developed chloroplasts.

watchSteps.title: 4. DNA without a nucleus
watchSteps.caption: A bacterium keeps DNA in its cytoplasm and still builds proteins at ribosomes.

watchSteps.title: 5. Explain the difference
watchSteps.caption: Compare the onion with the green leaf. Which job changes?

widgets.title: Organelle Clues
widgets.challengePrompt: Reveal all four groups of clues for a chloroplast and explain why shape alone is insufficient.
widgets.cutaway: The DNA shown is the organelle’s own inherited DNA. Many proteins it uses are encoded by genes now in the host nucleus, so present-day organelles depend on the cell around them.
widgets.idealised: The four clue groups organise evidence; they are not four equally weighted experiments or a replay of ancient engulfment.

watchSteps.title: 1. A suggestive outline
watchSteps.caption: Two surrounding membranes are one clue, not proof.

watchSteps.title: 2. A second recipe
watchSteps.caption: Add DNA inside the compartment.

watchSteps.title: 3. Internal machinery
watchSteps.caption: Add bacterial-related ribosomes; these enlarged dots stand for real molecular structures.

watchSteps.title: 4. Compare inheritance
watchSteps.caption: Division and comparative gene sequences strengthen the ancestry inference.

watchSteps.title: 5. Another bacterial branch
watchSteps.caption: Chloroplast genes trace their ancestry to cyanobacteria.

widgets.title: Sav Cubes3D
widgets.challengePrompt: Choose a 10 cm side and a 2 mm reached layer: how much of the volume remains untouched?
widgets.cutaway: The centre slice shows a square untouched core. Its full three-dimensional volume is max(side − 2 × depth, 0)³; the fraction reached uses that volume, not the coloured area of this slice.
widgets.idealised: A uniform sharp-front layer is a geometric assumption; real diffusion makes concentration gradients, and potato dye is not oxygen crossing a cell membrane.

watchSteps.title: 1. The smaller cube
watchSteps.caption: A 1 cm cube has 6 cm² of surface for 1 cm³ of interior.

watchSteps.title: 2. Double the side
watchSteps.caption: A 2 cm cube has four times the surface and eight times the volume.

watchSteps.title: 3. Slice through it
watchSteps.caption: A chosen 2 mm layer leaves an untouched core; depth is not elapsed time.

watchSteps.title: 4. Tenfold side
watchSteps.caption: The 10 cm cube has SA/V 0.6 cm⁻¹ and only 11.5% reached volume at the same depth.

watchSteps.title: 5. Test another depth
watchSteps.caption: Change depth and side independently. The 2D drawing keeps a fixed scale; the 3D view fills its frame.

widgets.title: Diffusion Membrane
widgets.challengePrompt: Start with 50 particles per side, keep the divider permeable, then step the model. Explain why counts can change despite equal starting concentrations.
widgets.cutaway: The divider permits a crossing in either direction. Each step draws a new direction independently of concentration; no particle can inspect which side has more space.
widgets.idealised: 100 tokens follow a two-dimensional fixed-step random walk; solvent collisions are implicit, distances and steps are uncalibrated, and equilibrium fluctuates.

watchSteps.title: 1. Unequal start
watchSteps.caption: 80 left and 20 right in equal volumes make different concentrations.

watchSteps.title: 2. Block passage
watchSteps.caption: A closed divider prevents transfer even though particles can still wander on their own side.

watchSteps.title: 3. Open both directions
watchSteps.caption: The same opening permits both rightward and leftward crossings. Use Step 20 bounces to count them.

watchSteps.title: 4. Equal start
watchSteps.caption: 50 on each side does not freeze the particles; each trial can fluctuate.

watchSteps.title: 5. Your count
watchSteps.caption: Press Step 20 bounces several times. Compare total crossings with their signed difference.

widgets.title: Water Potential
widgets.challengePrompt: Balance inside and outside water potential while their solute contributions remain different.
widgets.cutaway: Positive internal pressure raises water potential. At +0.50 MPa it exactly balances this chosen solute difference; water still crosses both ways.
widgets.idealised: Chosen potentials are held fixed as pressure is varied independently; the model predicts direction, not evolving cell volume, concentration or time.

watchSteps.title: 1. No added pressure
watchSteps.caption: At zero pressure the inside has lower water potential, so net water entry is favoured.

watchSteps.title: 2. Add pressure
watchSteps.caption: Raising inside pressure reduces the difference driving net entry.

watchSteps.title: 3. Balance
watchSteps.caption: −0.80 + 0.50 = −0.30 MPa: no net water transfer, without equal solutes.

watchSteps.title: 4. Reverse
watchSteps.caption: An imposed pressure above the balance can favour net water exit.

watchSteps.title: 5. Find the balance
watchSteps.caption: Move the control yourself and explain what changes the direction.

widgets.title: Osmosis Cells
widgets.challengePrompt: Choose concentrated surroundings and show the plant membrane separating from its wall.
widgets.cutaway: The cellulose wall stays outside the cell membrane. The vacuole can lose water and shrink; sufficient water loss pulls the membrane-bound contents away from the wall.
widgets.idealised: Shapes and stages are qualitative; no salt permeability, membrane mechanics, time course or measured volume is calculated, and the 3D solid denotes the membrane envelope.

watchSteps.title: 1. Starting cells
watchSteps.caption: Two cell envelopes are shown at different enlargements.

watchSteps.title: 2. Water enters
watchSteps.caption: In dilute surroundings the animal swells; the plant presses against its wall.

watchSteps.title: 3. A wall changes the outcome
watchSteps.caption: The schematic animal endpoint is rupture; the plant builds opposing turgor pressure.

watchSteps.title: 4. Water leaves
watchSteps.caption: Concentrated surroundings can shrink animal cells and plasmolyse plant cells.

watchSteps.title: 5. Compare
watchSteps.caption: Change surroundings at the same selected stage; explain which boundary supports pressure.

widgets.title: Root Transport
widgets.challengePrompt: Follow the proton pump and cotransporter through the whole energy relay.
widgets.cutaway: The ATP-driven proton pump and the nitrate cotransporter are different proteins. Stored proton electrochemical energy connects their actions.
widgets.idealised: This is a manually stepped pathway diagram; it calculates neither ionic charge balance nor kinetic rates or fixed transport stoichiometry.

watchSteps.title: 1. Separate routes
watchSteps.caption: A proton pump and cotransporter span the root hair membrane.

watchSteps.title: 2. Spend chemical energy
