watchSteps.caption: ATP hydrolysis couples to proton export through the pump.

watchSteps.title: 3. Store a gradient
watchSteps.caption: Export establishes a proton electrochemical gradient across the membrane.

watchSteps.title: 4. Couple the return
watchSteps.caption: Protons moving down that gradient can drive nitrate entry against its concentration gradient.

watchSteps.title: 5. Explain the relay
watchSteps.caption: Nitrate accumulation uses energy indirectly; water enters through its own water-potential gradient.

widgets.title: Enzyme Barrier
widgets.challengePrompt: Use matched chemistry, lower both hurdles by 35 chosen units, and reach stage 4 to regenerate the enzyme.
widgets.cutaway: Complementary chemical groups position reactants and stabilise difficult arrangements. The contact symbols stand for interactions, not a rigid outline lock or atomic coordinates.
widgets.idealised: Energies and geometry are chosen; progress is not time. No reaction rate, equilibrium shift or universal speed multiplier is calculated.

watchSteps.title: 1. Same endpoints
watchSteps.caption: Both routes start at 20 and finish at 10. The net change is −10 chosen units.

watchSteps.title: 2. A lower route
watchSteps.caption: Lowering the peak by 35 reduces forward and reverse barriers by the same amount.

watchSteps.title: 3. Temporary complex
watchSteps.caption: Binding brings the substrate into a useful chemical environment.

watchSteps.title: 4. Change the chemistry
watchSteps.caption: A similar outline with the wrong group need not support catalysis.

watchSteps.title: 5. Release and reuse
watchSteps.caption: Return to matched chemistry, then release products and regenerate the enzyme.

widgets.title: Enzyme Conditions
widgets.challengePrompt: Compare the heat-exposed sample at assay temperature 60 °C and pH 7.0. Explain why its rate is lower than the fresh comparison at the same settings.
widgets.cutaway: Warming increases encounters while loss of functional structure can remove active enzyme. The pH factor describes activity, not a measured denatured fraction.
widgets.idealised: No named enzyme is fitted. Parameters, fixed exposure and surviving share are invented; every setting is a new sample, not reversible damage or a human fever model.

watchSteps.title: 1. Cooler comparison
watchSteps.caption: At 20 °C and pH 7, inspect a separately prepared fresh sample.

watchSteps.title: 2. More encounters
watchSteps.caption: At 40 °C more encounters increase the model rate while most enzyme remains active.

watchSteps.title: 3. Shape loss matters
watchSteps.caption: At 60 °C encounters are faster, but the chosen active fraction is much smaller.

watchSteps.title: 4. Compare pH
watchSteps.caption: At the same temperature, altered pH reduces the chosen chemistry factor.

watchSteps.title: 5. Fair residual-activity test
watchSteps.caption: Compare a previously heat-exposed sample at the same assay pH and temperature. This is no recovery trajectory.

widgets.title: Food Detective
widgets.challengePrompt: Choose iodine and valid controls, then actually run the comparison. What does U reveal?
widgets.cutaway: A positive control checks that the reagent and method can detect the target; the blank checks for a misleading background. An invalid comparison leaves the unknown inconclusive.
widgets.idealised: Unknown U and all outcomes are invented. Written observations replace colour measurement; extraction, sensitivity and matrix interference require real laboratory controls.

watchSteps.title: 1. Reducing sugar
watchSteps.caption: Run Benedict’s with valid controls. This invented unknown stays blue.

watchSteps.title: 2. Starch
watchSteps.caption: Run iodine: the unknown gives blue-black while the blank does not.

watchSteps.title: 3. Peptide bonds
watchSteps.caption: Run biuret: purple supports protein, without showing whether it is folded or active.

watchSteps.title: 4. Extractable oil
watchSteps.caption: Run the emulsion test. Compare cloudiness with the clear reagent blank.

watchSteps.title: 5. Vitamin C
watchSteps.caption: Run DCPIP, then deliberately fail the positive control and rerun. A negative unknown is then uninterpretable.

widgets.title: Carbon Account
widgets.challengePrompt: Choose two accounting batches and reach stage 4. Check each element on both sides.
widgets.cutaway: Thylakoid reactions release oxygen from water and supply ATP and an electron carrier. Enzymes in the stroma incorporate carbon dioxide into small carbon products.
widgets.idealised: Formal glucose summaries, not single reactions or literal atom paths. No photon number, efficiency, measured yield or elapsed time is calculated.

watchSteps.title: 1. Absorb energy
watchSteps.caption: Light transfers energy; it supplies no carbon atoms.

watchSteps.title: 2. Water oxygen
watchSteps.caption: Isotope evidence links released O₂ to water.

watchSteps.title: 3. Carbon source
watchSteps.caption: Carbon dioxide supplies carbohydrate carbon.

watchSteps.title: 4. Smaller products
watchSteps.caption: Small three-carbon products supply larger carbohydrates.

watchSteps.title: 5. Conserve atoms
watchSteps.caption: Double the fuller summary: double every material term, with water still on both sides.

widgets.title: Limiting Lab
widgets.challengePrompt: Clear trials. Capture L=20, CO₂=80, T=25 °C, then L=60 with the other two unchanged. Moving controls alone is not a trial.
widgets.cutaway: The smallest of three invented capacities caps gross photosynthesis. The chosen oxygen-use baseline is subtracted to obtain net exchange. Real plants have interacting, smoother responses.
widgets.idealised: R=min(L,C,max(0,100−((T−25)/2)²)); net=R−10, all invented relative units. Each setting is a new sample, not recovery; no calibrated bubbles, gas volume or universal optimum.

watchSteps.title: 1. Capture a baseline
watchSteps.caption: Record light capacity 20 with carbon capacity 80 at 25 °C.

watchSteps.title: 2. Change light only
watchSteps.caption: Run the requested comparison: gross rises from 20 to 60.

watchSteps.title: 3. Carbon becomes limiting
watchSteps.caption: At carbon capacity 20, more light cannot lift gross rate above 20.

watchSteps.title: 4. A third cap
watchSteps.caption: At the chosen model temperature 45 °C the thermal capacity is zero. This is not a plant damage threshold.

watchSteps.title: 5. Respiration continues
watchSteps.caption: In darkness gross oxygen production is zero; net exchange is negative because respiration continues.

widgets.title: Sap Routes
widgets.challengePrompt: Follow stored carbohydrate upwards: choose Store → shoot phloem and reach stage 4.
widgets.cutaway: Xylem liquid is pulled under tension. Phloem sap flows down a pressure difference set up by loading, osmotic water entry and unloading. These are different mechanisms.
widgets.idealised: Enlarged separate pathways; stages focus attention, not calibrated sap motion. Passive and active loading occur; no opposing bulk streams in a single sieve tube.

watchSteps.title: 1. Evaporation first
watchSteps.caption: Start at the moist leaf surfaces.

watchSteps.title: 2. Transmit tension
watchSteps.caption: Cohesion connects the pulled liquid to the xylem column.

watchSteps.title: 3. Replace water
watchSteps.caption: Roots supply water along a decreasing total water-potential gradient.

watchSteps.title: 4. Load a different tissue
watchSteps.caption: In phloem, osmotic water entry raises source pressure.

watchSteps.title: 5. Send sugars upwards
watchSteps.caption: A storage organ can supply a growing shoot: source to sink is not always downward.

widgets.title: Respiration Relay
widgets.challengePrompt: Inspect stage 4 with O₂ available, then stage 4 under sustained O₂ absence. Explain what stops and why this does not mean all cellular ATP vanishes instantly.
widgets.cutaway: The inner membrane separates matrix from intermembrane space. Electron transfer powers H⁺ export; return through a different protein drives rotor/shaft motion and shape changes in its stationary ATP-forming head. The head faces the matrix.
widgets.idealised: Manual causal-focus snapshots overlap in life; enlarged geometry and H⁺ tokens do not encode counts. The absent-O₂ comparison is settled after residual gradient loss, with no kinetic clock, speed, fixed coupling ratio or yield.

watchSteps.title: 1. Collect electrons
watchSteps.caption: Fuel reactions load carriers; carbon and electron routes are different.

watchSteps.title: 2. Pump outwards
watchSteps.caption: With O₂ available, electron transfer drives H⁺ from matrix to intermembrane space.

watchSteps.title: 3. Keep a difference
watchSteps.caption: Concentration and electric potential both contribute; the membrane must hold the difference.

watchSteps.title: 4. Couple return to ATP
watchSteps.caption: H⁺ returns towards the matrix through synthase; its rotor turns while catalytic shapes in its stationary head change.

watchSteps.title: 5. Remove the terminal acceptor
watchSteps.caption: Compare sustained O₂ absence after residual gradients dissipate. This aerobic relay stalls; glycolysis can still supply ATP if NAD⁺ is regenerated.

widgets.title: Oxidation Ledger
widgets.challengePrompt: At 1.0 kg, inspect Total inputs and products. Identify the incoming oxygen and explain why the combined products exceed the starting fuel mass while all inputs still balance all outputs. The original-fat allocation tab is optional deeper work.
widgets.cutaway: The full ledger includes incoming molecular oxygen. Separately, the paper assigns the original fat’s carbon and four of its six oxygen atoms to CO₂, and its hydrogen plus two oxygen atoms to water. Oxygen exchange with body water makes this an approximate accounting convention, not uniquely traced atom paths.
widgets.idealised: Complete oxidation of representative C₅₅H₁₀₄O₆ uses nominal C12/H1/O16 masses. The approximately 84%/16% original-fat allocation assumes oxygen exchange; it is not the total product ratio, an isotope trace or a human mass-change model.

watchSteps.title: 1. Include oxygen
watchSteps.caption: One kilogram of representative fat combines with about 2.9023 kg O₂; total products are about 3.9023 kg.

watchSteps.title: 2. Scale the whole ledger
watchSteps.caption: Two kilograms doubles every mass term, including incoming oxygen.

watchSteps.title: 3. Go deeper: original fuel
watchSteps.caption: Return to one kilogram and allocate only the ORIGINAL fat: about 842 g to CO₂ and 158 g to water, usually rounded 840/160.

watchSteps.title: 4. Test zero sample
watchSteps.caption: At zero fuel, oxygen input and both product masses are zero. Per-reaction atom coefficients describe the formal equation, not atoms in this empty sample.

watchSteps.title: 5. Go deeper: compare accounts
watchSteps.caption: At one kilogram, total CO₂ is about 2.814 kg; only about 0.842 kg is assigned to the original fat in the separate convention.

widgets.title: Carrier Routes
widgets.challengePrompt: Inspect carrier stage 4 in all three routes. Identify the electron recipient and explain why fermentation adds no ATP beyond glycolysis’s two net ATP.
widgets.cutaway: NAD⁺ accepts electrons during glycolysis and becomes NADH. Passing those electrons onwards restores NAD⁺: the aerobic chain ultimately passes electrons to oxygen; fermentation passes them to organic recipients. Recycling permits glycolysis to continue and is a separate matter from ATP yield.
widgets.idealised: Three manually selected route accounts compress compartments and omit proton-balanced NAD chemistry. No clock, gas volume, rate or total aerobic ATP yield is calculated; mixed idli communities are outside this comparison.

watchSteps.title: 1. Supply an empty carrier
watchSteps.caption: Glycolysis requires oxidised NAD⁺ to accept electrons from fuel.

watchSteps.title: 2. Load the carrier
watchSteps.caption: Glucose becomes two pyruvates; NAD⁺ becomes NADH. Four ATP formed minus two invested is two net ATP.

watchSteps.title: 3. Aerobic recycling
watchSteps.caption: The oxygen-linked electron chain restores NAD⁺ and supports additional ATP through the membrane relay, without a universal total.

watchSteps.title: 4. Yeast recycling
watchSteps.caption: Electrons reach an organic recipient on the ethanol route. Two ethanol and two CO₂ per glucose; recycling adds no extra ATP.

watchSteps.title: 5. Lactate recycling
watchSteps.caption: Pyruvate receives electrons to form lactate and restores NAD⁺. This route releases no CO₂; lactate can also form when O₂ is present.

widgets.title: Digestive Steps
widgets.challengePrompt: At stage 4, capture a product endpoint for each food. Compare the recorded products, then explain their different routes. The stamp records captures, not explanation accuracy.
widgets.cutaway: The lumen-facing intestinal cell membrane carries final digestive enzymes and transport proteins. Making a product in the lumen and moving it across a membrane are different events. These stages select explanatory focus; real digestion overlaps.
widgets.idealised: Three selected food routes, five manual focus states. Unit symbols omit atoms/end groups and are not a chemical mass ledger. No digestion clock, residence time or rate is calculated.

watchSteps.title: 1. Start starch
watchSteps.caption: Salivary amylase begins producing maltose and shorter chains. It does not turn all starch straight into glucose.

watchSteps.title: 2. Change compartments
watchSteps.caption: Stomach acid limits salivary amylase; it is not the same condition for every digestive enzyme.

watchSteps.title: 3. Start protein
watchSteps.caption: Pepsin begins hydrolysing protein into peptides under acidic conditions. Later enzymes continue the work.

watchSteps.title: 4. Separate two fat changes
watchSteps.caption: Bile stabilises droplets; pancreatic lipase and water change covalent connections.

watchSteps.title: 5. Reach an absorbable sugar
watchSteps.caption: Brush-border enzymes include maltase, which turns maltose plus water into glucose. Capture endpoints yourself to compare foods.

widgets.title: Emulsification
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture two positive-volume geometry trials with the same reference radius and different division. Compare saved areas; the stamp records this controlled comparison, not the accuracy of an explanation.
widgets.cutaway: Each drawn circle projects a sphere. With fixed total fat volume, k³ equal droplets each have radius R/k. Total area becomes k times the reference area, not k³ times. Dispersing molecules among droplets does not hydrolyse those molecules.
widgets.idealised: All equal spheres are shown as a spread-out projection, with chosen millimetre dimensions and conserved 3D volume. Real droplets vary in size/shape. No molecular hydrolysis, enzyme kinetics or digestion-rate multiplier is inferred.

watchSteps.title: 1. Set a reference
watchSteps.caption: A chosen 3 mm sphere has volume 36π mm³ and surface area 36π mm². These are invented model dimensions.

watchSteps.title: 2. Make eight spheres
watchSteps.caption: Linear division 2 gives eight equal droplets, radius 1.5 mm. Total area doubles; volume is unchanged.

watchSteps.title: 3. Go deeper: sixty-four
watchSteps.caption: Linear division 4 gives 64 spheres, radius 0.75 mm and four times the original area. It does not establish four times the biological rate.

watchSteps.title: 4. Test no fat
watchSteps.caption: Zero reference radius gives no droplets, zero volume and zero area; an area ratio would divide by zero, so it is not applicable.

watchSteps.title: 5. Change the amount
watchSteps.caption: A 2 mm reference with division 2 is a different fat volume from the 3 mm reference. Do not call that a controlled fixed-volume comparison.

widgets.title: Absorption Routes
widgets.challengePrompt: At stage 4 with positive supply, capture glucose and long-chain lipid endpoints. Compare their saved destinations. The stamp records endpoint captures, not explanation accuracy.
widgets.cutaway: Crossing the epithelium requires entry through the lumen-facing membrane, processing where needed, and exit through the tissue-facing side. Glucose entry can use the sodium gradient maintained by an ATP-driven pump. Long-chain lipid products are rebuilt and packaged before lymph transport. Bulk flow in vessels follows these membrane events.
widgets.idealised: Manual focus states track abstract marked material, not unchanged molecules or a timed transport process. No permeability, tissue damage, absorption efficiency or transit time is modelled. Zero supply gives zero marked portions in every compartment.

watchSteps.title: 1. Arrive at a barrier
watchSteps.caption: The glucose is still in the lumen. Small size alone does not explain its movement across a lipid membrane.

watchSteps.title: 2. Use an ion gradient
watchSteps.caption: Sodium-coupled glucose entry depends indirectly on ATP used by the tissue-facing ion pump. Glucose exits through a separate transporter.

watchSteps.title: 3. Carry glucose onwards
watchSteps.caption: After epithelial exit and capillary entry, portal blood carries glucose to the liver. A vessel flow arrow is not a membrane pump.

watchSteps.title: 4. Compare long-chain material
watchSteps.caption: Cells rebuild fat and make chylomicrons. These packages travel through lacteals and lymph to blood near the heart; original droplets and micelles do not.

watchSteps.title: 5. Keep an exception
watchSteps.caption: Some shorter-chain fatty acids take the portal blood route. The route diagram remains meaningful at zero supply, but all material compartments are empty.

widgets.title: Breathing Gradients
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture one shallow rapid trial (250 mL × 24 breaths/min) and one quiet resting trial (500 mL × 12 breaths/min). Explain why both move 6.0 L/min in total yet deliver different fresh alveolar ventilation.
widgets.cutaway: During inhalation, diaphragm and external intercostal contraction expands thoracic volume, lowering alveolar pressure slightly below atmospheric pressure (−1 mmHg) so outside air pushes in. In the chosen adult example, about 150 mL stays in the conducting airway dead space (trachea, bronchi, bronchioles) where no gas exchange occurs.
widgets.idealised: Representative sea-level gauge pressures and a chosen adult 150 mL anatomical dead space illustrate Boyle’s-law bulk flow and partial-pressure diffusion. Adult two-lung alveolar counts (~300–500 million, Ochs et al. 2004 mean 480 million) vary widely with lung size and age.

watchSteps.title: 1. Quiet inhalation
watchSteps.caption: External intercostals lift the ribs up and out while the diaphragm flattens downward. Alveolar pressure dips to −1 mmHg and outside air pushes in.

watchSteps.title: 2. Quiet exhalation
watchSteps.caption: Muscles relax and elastic recoil shrinks lung volume, raising alveolar pressure to +1 mmHg while pleural pressure stays negative (−4 mmHg).

watchSteps.title: 3. Test shallow rapid breathing
watchSteps.caption: At 250 mL × 24 breaths/min, total ventilation is still 6.0 L/min, but 150 mL dead space per breath leaves only 2.4 L/min of fresh alveolar air.

watchSteps.title: 4. Exercise and coordinated control
watchSteps.caption: Movement signals and working-muscle feedback help increase breathing. Chemical regulation contributes; arterial CO₂ usually stays near resting during moderate steady exercise.

watchSteps.title: 5. Bell-jar model honesty check
watchSteps.caption: Pulling the bottom rubber sheet lowers internal pressure like the diaphragm, but rigid jar walls cannot swing like ribs and the wide air gap is not a thin fluid-coupled pleural cavity.

widgets.title: Double Pump
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture one Intact double pump state (tab 0) and one Post-natal VSD case state (tab 2). Explain why a hole in the post-natal ventricular septum pushes oxygenated blood left-to-right back into the lungs rather than sending deoxygenated blood into the aorta.
widgets.cutaway: Both ventricles pump the same volume per minute in series when the septum is intact, but the left ventricular wall is about three times thicker than the right so it can generate ~120 mmHg for the long systemic circuit while the right ventricle generates ~25 mmHg to protect thin alveolar capillaries. Because LV pressure far exceeds RV pressure after birth, an uncomplicated ventricular septal defect shunts oxygenated blood left-to-right.
widgets.idealised: Steady-state series flow and representative ventricular peak pressures; pressure falls along vessels before capillaries. Route stages select explanatory views while both sides of the heart operate together. The chosen postnatal VSD ratio is not a prediction for every defect. Harvey’s 1628 Troy/apothecaries’ lower-bound arithmetic is kept distinct from the chosen modern metric calculation (HR × SV).

watchSteps.title: 1. Enter the right heart
watchSteps.caption: Deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae enters the thin-walled right atrium and passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

watchSteps.title: 2. Gentle lung loop vs high-pressure body loop
watchSteps.caption: The right ventricle pumps through the pulmonary artery at ~25 mmHg; oxygenated blood returns via pulmonary veins to the left atrium, then enters the thick-walled left ventricle (~120 mmHg peak).

watchSteps.title: 3. Harvey 1628 vs modern cardiac output
watchSteps.caption: In Frankfurt (1628), Harvey showed even 1 drachm per beat over 1,000 beats in 30 min equals 10 lb 5 oz; our modern 70 bpm × 60 mL example gives 4.20 L/min.

watchSteps.title: 4. Post-natal VSD left-to-right shunt
watchSteps.caption: Because LV systolic pressure (~115 mmHg) far exceeds RV pressure (~35 mmHg), oxygenated blood jets left-to-right into the RV and recycles through the lungs (Qp > Qs).

watchSteps.title: 5. Fish single circulation comparison
watchSteps.caption: In a fish, blood passes from the heart through gill capillaries directly to body capillaries without a second pump, so systemic pressure is much lower.

widgets.title: Vessel Exchange
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture Aorta (segment 0) and Capillary bed (segment 3). Explain why blood slows down ~1,000-fold in capillaries even though each individual capillary is microscopic.
widgets.cutaway: A single capillary is only ~8 µm wide, but billions of capillaries arranged in parallel have a combined cross-sectional area of ~4,500 cm²—roughly 1,000 times the aorta’s 4.5 cm². By continuity (v = Q / A_total), blood crawls at ~0.2 mm/s, giving time for oxygen and nutrient exchange across the one-cell-thick wall.
widgets.idealised: Continuity velocity v = Q / A_total uses representative adult total cross-sectional areas ; the fluid account shows net filtration and lymphatic return without fixed return fractions. Individual vessels and capillary beds vary dynamically with arteriole smooth-muscle tone.

watchSteps.title: 1. High-pressure elastic aorta
watchSteps.caption: Thick muscular and elastic walls withstand ~120/80 mmHg surges and recoil to keep blood moving fast (~181 mm/s at 4.9 L/min) through a 4.5 cm² lumen.

watchSteps.title: 2. Billions of parallel capillaries
watchSteps.caption: Total cross-sectional area balloons to ~4,500 cm², dropping speed to ~0.18 mm/s across a one-cell-thick endothelial wall.

watchSteps.title: 3. Tissue fluid and lymphatic return
watchSteps.caption: Pressure and barrier properties govern net filtration in ordinary steady tissue beds. Gases diffuse separately; lymphatics return net filtered fluid and escaped proteins.

watchSteps.title: 4. Low-pressure veins with valves
watchSteps.caption: Veins have thinner walls, wide lumens and semilunar valves that prevent low-pressure blood from flowing backward.

watchSteps.title: 5. Platelets and the fibrin mesh
watchSteps.caption: At a wound, platelets trigger the conversion of soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads that trap red blood cells to stop bleeding and block pathogens.

widgets.title: Reflex Action Potential
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture one Myelinated reflex arc trial (tab 0) and one Unmyelinated axon loop (tab 1), Voluntary ruler catch (tab 2), or Siddiqi para^ts blocked trial at ≥30 °C (tab 3). Explain why myelination or a spinal reflex loop cuts total response latency.
widgets.cutaway: A neurone is not a copper wire: no free electrons flow down the axon. Instead, Skou’s Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump uses ATP to keep Na⁺ high outside and K⁺ high inside (−70 mV rest). When depolarised to threshold (−55 mV), voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open so Na⁺ rushes in (+30 mV peak), followed by K⁺ channels opening to repolarise the membrane. In Obaid Siddiqi’s para^ts Drosophila mutant, warming above 30 °C reversibly silences the voltage-gated Na⁺ channels.
widgets.idealised: Chosen conduction scaling and delays illustrate a defined pathway. They do not measure thermal withdrawal or Drosophila physiology. The para tab illustrates reversible channel failure; it is not a fly-speed prediction.

watchSteps.title: 1. Fast myelinated spinal reflex
watchSteps.caption: This chosen 1.3 m pathway uses 72 m/s and counts three chemical junctions. Its 36.8 ms sum is an illustrative calculation, not a measured hot-pan reflex.

watchSteps.title: 2. Remove the myelin sheath
watchSteps.caption: Compare chosen conduction scaling with and without insulation. Actual demyelination may slow or block propagation; this is not a patient prediction.

watchSteps.title: 3. Compare voluntary ruler-drop reaction
watchSteps.caption: The model adds a chosen processing delay. A real ruler catch is measured from fall distance and includes visual processing and finger movement.

watchSteps.title: 4. Siddiqi’s para^ts fly at 22 °C
watchSteps.caption: At a permissive 22 °C, the temperature-sensitive para^ts sodium channels fold and open normally, firing full +30 mV action potentials.

watchSteps.title: 5. Reversible thermal block at 32 °C
watchSteps.caption: Warming the para^ts mutant to 32 °C disables its voltage-gated Na⁺ channels: the spike vanishes while the resting potential stays at −70 mV.

widgets.title: Synapse Transmission
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture one Forward (Pre → Post) trial that stimulates a postsynaptic impulse and one Reverse test (Post → Pre) trial. Explain how the location of vesicles and receptor proteins enforces one-way conduction.
widgets.cutaway: Cambridge 0610 Supplement four-step synapse sequence: (1) an arriving electrical impulse stimulates presynaptic vesicles to release neurotransmitter molecules into the synaptic gap, (2) neurotransmitter diffuses across the ~20 nm gap down its concentration gradient, (3) neurotransmitter binds with complementary receptor proteins on the postsynaptic membrane, and (4) an electrical impulse is stimulated in the next neurone. The release-and-receive arrangement gives this excitatory relay its forward direction; presynaptic regulatory receptors and inhibitory synapses also exist.
widgets.idealised: A chosen excitatory relay: vesicle counts, receptor fractions and delays illustrate stage relationships rather than calibrated physiological rates. Inhibition and presynaptic regulation are not simulated.

watchSteps.title: 1. Normal forward synaptic relay
watchSteps.caption: At 40 Hz across a 20 nm cleft, 5 vesicles release neurotransmitter, binding 55% of postsynaptic receptors and depolarising the next neurone past −55 mV threshold.

watchSteps.title: 2. Inside the four-step chemical relay
watchSteps.caption: Neurotransmitter crosses the 20 nm cleft by diffusion in less than a microsecond; the ~0.7 ms synaptic delay comes mainly from Ca²⁺ entry, vesicle fusion and receptor gating.

watchSteps.title: 3. Test reverse stimulation (Post → Pre)
watchSteps.caption: Stimulating the receiving side does not reverse the release machinery of this drawn relay. This model omits other synapses and regulatory receptors.

watchSteps.title: 4. Competitive receptor blockade (curare)
watchSteps.caption: When curare occupies 85% of postsynaptic receptors, vesicles still release neurotransmitter across the gap, but receptor binding stays below the −55 mV threshold.

watchSteps.title: 5. Breakdown enzyme inhibition
watchSteps.caption: Blocking acetylcholinesterase leaves neurotransmitter trapped in the cleft, keeping postsynaptic receptors bound and preventing the synapse from resetting.

widgets.title: Eye Accommodation Tropism
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture one Near object focus (≤60 cm) and one Distant object focus (≥200 cm) in tab 0 (or two contrasting light/tropism states). Explain why contracting the circular ciliary muscle slackens the suspensory ligaments instead of pulling them tight.
widgets.cutaway: For near focus, ciliary contraction reduces tension on the suspensory ligaments and the elastic lens becomes more convex. Relaxation restores ligament tension and flattens the lens for distant focus. Iris muscles control aperture rather than lens focus.
widgets.idealised: A chosen reduced eye uses 17 mm effective image distance. Component powers and plant auxin fractions, rates and bending are schematic, not measurements or individual predictions.

watchSteps.title: 1. Near focus on a book (25 cm)
watchSteps.caption: At 25 cm the chosen 17 mm reduced eye requires about 62.82 D. Ciliary contraction slackens the ligaments and the schematic lens becomes more convex.

watchSteps.title: 2. Distant focus across the sea (400 cm)
watchSteps.caption: At 400 cm the chosen reduced eye requires about 59.07 D. Relaxed ciliary muscle restores ligament tension and the schematic lens flattens.

watchSteps.title: 3. Antagonistic iris muscles in bright light
watchSteps.caption: At 90% light intensity, circular iris muscles contract and radial muscles relax, constricting the pupil to 2.55 mm to protect the retina while foveal cones resolve colour.

watchSteps.title: 4. Shoot phototropism and shaded-side auxin
watchSteps.caption: Under unilateral light (80%), auxin made in the shoot tip accumulates on the shaded side (68% vs 32% lit), stimulating shaded cells to elongate faster and bending the shoot +32.4° towards light.

watchSteps.title: 5. Horizontal seedling gravitropism
watchSteps.caption: Gravity concentrates auxin on the lower side (68%): in the shoot, high auxin stimulates elongation (+32.4° upward); in the root, high auxin inhibits elongation (−27.0° downward).

widgets.title: Glucose Thermoregulation
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture one hot or high-humidity state and one cold or contrasting glucose state (e.g. Dadar May 38 °C vs Cold room 15 °C, or Mango meal vs Fasting). Explain why arterioles vasodilate or vasoconstrict while capillaries stay fixed in position, or how insulin and glucagon oppose drifts from 5.0 mmol/L.
widgets.cutaway: Cambridge 0610 negative feedback around a set point: the brain (hypothalamus at 37.0 °C) coordinates sweat glands, skeletal muscle shivering, hair erector muscles and smooth muscle in the arterioles supplying skin surface capillaries (capillaries themselves never move toward or away from the surface). In blood glucose control (set point ~5.0 mmol/L), pancreatic islet beta cells secrete insulin to stimulate liver glucose-to-glycogen storage, whereas alpha cells secrete glucagon to stimulate liver glycogen-to-glucose breakdown.
widgets.idealised: Illustrative scenarios, not individual predictions: thermal energy balance (metabolic generation, dry transfer and evaporative latent heat at 2,420 J/g) and two-hormone pancreatic negative feedback around a 5.0 mmol/L plasma glucose set point.

watchSteps.title: 1. Dadar afternoon heat (38 °C, 65% RH)
watchSteps.caption: Arterioles supplying skin surface capillaries vasodilate (145.5% diameter) while sweat glands secrete 420 g/h; evaporation removes latent heat (2,420 J/g) to hold core temperature near 37 °C.

watchSteps.title: 2. Cold room (15 °C) heat conservation
watchSteps.caption: Skin arterioles vasoconstrict (64% diameter) so less warm blood enters fixed surface capillaries, hairs stand upright, sweat stops, and skeletal muscle shivering generates +96 W of heat.

watchSteps.title: 3. High Mumbai humidity (38 °C, 85% RH)
watchSteps.caption: Damp air slows sweat evaporation so most secreted sweat drips off without removing latent heat, causing net core heat storage.

watchSteps.title: 4. Pancreatic insulin & glucagon loop
watchSteps.caption: After a sweet mango meal (85% load), pancreatic beta cells secrete insulin so the liver converts glucose into insoluble glycogen; during fasting (15% load), alpha cells secrete glucagon.

watchSteps.title: 5. Type 1 diabetes and insulin injection rescue
watchSteps.caption: Without insulin (30% slider), higher plasma glucose raises the filtered load beyond the chosen recovery capacity (330 mg/min) and spills into urine; injected insulin (75% slider) restores normal liver storage.

widgets.title: Nephron Filtration
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture one Normal hydration state (5 mmol/L plasma glucose) and one Untreated hyperglycaemia state (16 mmol/L) or Dehydrated afternoon state. Explain why glucose appears in urine at 16 mmol/L even though the model stipulates an intact glomerular protein barrier.
widgets.cutaway: This model follows two main stages across the cortex and medulla; all daily totals and capacity rates sum both kidneys: (1) High blood pressure in the glomerulus filters water, glucose, urea and ions into the renal capsule (~180 L/day) while retaining red blood cells and plasma proteins (0.0 g/100mL in filtrate); (2) The renal tubule selectively reabsorbs 100% of glucose (up to T_m ≈ 330 mg/min), most water (via aquaporins) and needed ions back into blood, leaving urea, excess water and excess ions to form urine in the collecting duct.
widgets.idealised: Two-kidney adult mass balance (GFR 80–140 mL/min, proximal glucose transport maximum T_m = 330 mg/min, 44% passive medullary urea recycling) chosen for teaching; the 1924 experiments support filtering and recovery, not these numerical parameters.

watchSteps.title: 1. Glomerular ultrafiltration (125 mL/min)
watchSteps.caption: At normal hydration (5 mmol/L plasma glucose), two kidneys filter 180 L/day into renal capsules while retaining cells and most large proteins; displayed protein zeros are rounded.

watchSteps.title: 2. Selective reabsorption of 100% glucose
watchSteps.caption: In the proximal renal tubule, ATP-supported sodium–glucose carriers rescue 100% of filtered glucose (162 g/day) and ~99.2% of water, leaving 0.0 g/100mL glucose in 1.5 L/day urine.

watchSteps.title: 3. Hot Mumbai afternoon water rescue
watchSteps.caption: During sweating and dehydration, collecting-duct aquaporin channels increase water reabsorption to 99.55%, cutting urine volume to ~0.75 L/day and concentrating urea ~128-fold.

watchSteps.title: 4. High-protein meal and liver deamination
watchSteps.caption: Liver deamination of excess amino acids doubles plasma urea (0.06 g/100mL); the nephron excretes 60.5 g/day of urea while still rescuing 100% of filtered glucose.

watchSteps.title: 5. Hyperglycaemia above renal T_m (16 mmol/L)
watchSteps.caption: When untreated Type 1 diabetes raises filtrate glucose to 16 mmol/L, proximal tubule carriers saturate at 330 mg/min; the un-reabsorbed 30 mg/min spills into urine and pulls water with it by osmosis (3.8 L/day).

widgets.title: Immunity Vaccine Memory
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture one Primary response or Passive state and one Vaccinated secondary memory state (or Matching vs Mismatched antigen state). Explain how memory cells or complementary antigen shape change the speed, height and duration of protection.
widgets.cutaway: Specific active immunity depends on complementary 3D shape: lymphocytes carry receptors matching a pathogen’s specific antigen, divide, and secrete protein antibodies that either destroy pathogens directly or mark them for phagocytes, while leaving long-lived memory cells. Passive immunity (placenta, breast milk, antivenom) supplies borrowed antibodies for immediate short-term cover but produces zero memory cells.
widgets.idealised: Deterministic primary/secondary lymphocyte kinetics, exponential passive IgG catabolism (t₁/₂ = 21 days), and small-intestinal Na⁺–glucose cotransport vs cholera-toxin Cl⁻ secretion.

watchSteps.title: 1. Primary response on first exposure (0% memory)
watchSteps.caption: In this chosen illustration without prior memory, naive lymphocytes respond after a lag and antibody level reaches 28 AU at Day 14—below the 40 AU illustrative reference line.

watchSteps.title: 2. Post-vaccine secondary response (90% memory)
watchSteps.caption: After vaccination with weakened pathogen or antigen, memory cells respond within 1 day and surge to 220.2 AU by Day 7, illustrating a faster response that can reduce illness; protection varies.

watchSteps.title: 3. Antigen–antibody lock-and-key specificity
watchSteps.caption: Antibodies made against Antigen A have a complementary binding site for the chosen A features; model B (20% slider) is assumed unrecognised, though real antigens can cross-react and a new primary response is needed.

watchSteps.title: 4. Passive immunity decay (no memory cells)
watchSteps.caption: The borrowed IgG example begins at 80 AU and uses a chosen 21-day half-life. Placental IgG and local breast-milk protection differ; transfer itself creates no specific memory.

watchSteps.title: 5. Cholera Cl⁻ toxin vs Oral Rehydration Solution
watchSteps.caption: Cholera toxin drives Cl⁻ secretion into the small intestine so water leaves blood by osmosis; ORS supplies glucose and electrolytes; the chosen 80% support control uses intact Na⁺–glucose cotransport to support net absorption in this illustrative water ledger.

widgets.title: DNA Base Pairing
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture two contrasting DNA double-helix or Chargaff states (e.g. Human 30% A vs GC-rich 15% A, or a Complementary rung vs a Purine bulge test). Explain how complementary pairing (A=T, C≡G) enforces Chargaff’s rules and keeps the double helix a uniform 2.0 nm wide.
widgets.cutaway: Cambridge 0610 Topic 4.1 DNA structure: two sugar–phosphate strands coil into a double helix (2.0 nm wide, 3.4 nm per 10-base-pair turn, 0.34 nm step in Rosalind Franklin’s Photo 51). Cross-links are formed by pairs of bases that always pair A with T (2 hydrogen bonds) and C with G (3 hydrogen bonds). Because a two-ring purine (A or G) always pairs with a one-ring pyrimidine (T or C), standard pairing maintains an approximately 2 nm overall helix diameter and %A = %T, %G = %C.
widgets.idealised: B-form DNA helical geometry (3.4 nm pitch, 0.34 nm rise, 10 bp/turn, 2.0 nm diameter) and exact Watson–Crick base equivalence (%A = %T, %G = %C).

watchSteps.title: 1. Human beta-globin HBB double helix (30% A)
watchSteps.caption: Two antiparallel strands coil around a central axis with complementary A=T (2 H-bonds) and C≡G (3 H-bonds) pairing within an approximately 2 nm helix.

watchSteps.title: 2. Erwin Chargaff’s base-ratio equivalence (30% A)
watchSteps.caption: When Adenine is 30.0%, complementary Thymine must also be 30.0% (60% A+T), leaving 40.0% split equally between Guanine (20.0%) and Cytosine (20.0%).

watchSteps.title: 3. GC-rich bacterial DNA (15% A, 70% GC)
watchSteps.caption: Lowering Adenine to 15.0% raises Guanine and Cytosine to 35.0% each; three hydrogen bonds per C–G pair increase total H-bonds to 33 and raise thermal stability.

watchSteps.title: 4. Rosalind Franklin’s Photo 51 geometry
watchSteps.caption: At Rung 10, the vertical rise reaches 3.40 nm and the helix completes a full 360° turn (0.34 nm and 36° per base pair), matching the X-cross and 10th layer line of Photo 51.

watchSteps.title: 5. Purine–purine mismatch bulge (>2.0 nm)
watchSteps.caption: Forcing two 2-ring purines opposite each other at Rung 6 produces an exaggerated schematic bulge (not a measured mismatch width), showing why only purine–pyrimidine pairs fit.

widgets.title: Codon Cipher Khorana
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture two contrasting synthetic RNA or reading-frame trials (e.g. Nirenberg poly-U vs Khorana (UC)n, or Frameshift +1 vs +3). Explain why 4 bases must be read in triplets (4³ = 64) and how +3 restores the reading frame.
widgets.cutaway: Four bases read 1 at a time give 4¹ = 4 words; 2 at a time give 4² = 16 words (still fewer than 20 amino acids); 3 at a time give 4³ = 64 triplet codons (61 sense codons + 3 stop codons UAA, UAG, UGA). Crick and Brenner (1961) proved ribosomes read non-overlapping triplets without commas: +1 or +2 insertions scramble every downstream codon, whereas +3 restores the reading frame. Nirenberg (poly-U → Phe) and Har Gobind Khorana (repeating copolymers such as (UC)ₙ → Ser–Leu) deciphered all 64 triplets.
widgets.idealised: Cell-free translation of 18-nucleotide synthetic mRNA templates using the standard 64-codon genetic code (61 sense codons + 3 stop codons).

watchSteps.title: 1. Nirenberg & Matthaei poly-U (1961)
watchSteps.caption: Synthetic polyuridylic acid (UUU·UUU·UUU...) directs cell-free E. coli ribosomes to assemble pure polyphenylalanine (Phe–Phe–Phe), cracking the first codon.

watchSteps.title: 2. Har Gobind Khorana’s (UC)ₙ copolymer
watchSteps.caption: Repeating dinucleotide UCUCUCUCUCUC splits into alternating triplets UCU (Serine) and CUC (Leucine), producing strictly alternating Ser–Leu–Ser–Leu.

watchSteps.title: 3. Khorana’s (UG)ₙ and (AG)ₙ copolymers
watchSteps.caption: Switching to Template #2 ((UG)ₙ = UGU·GUG) yields alternating Cys–Val–Cys–Val, proving the exact letter order inside mixed triplets.

watchSteps.title: 4. Amber nonsense stop codon (UAG)
watchSteps.caption: When UAG appears at Codon 5 (Template #2 in tab 2), no tRNA matches; release factors halt translation and release a 4-residue fragment, matching Obaid Siddiqi’s nonsense mutants.

watchSteps.title: 5. Crick & Brenner +1 vs +3 reading-frame proof
watchSteps.caption: Inserting +3 bases (+1 full triplet) into the phage message restores the downstream CAU (His) reading frame, whereas +1 or +2 scrambles every subsequent triplet.

widgets.title: Transcription Translation Ribosome
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture two contrasting transcription-translation states (e.g. Child X Silent Codon 3 CTG→CTT vs Child Y Missense Codon 6 GAG→GTG, or Reference HbA vs Nonsense Stop). Explain why Child X encodes the usual beta-globin amino-acid sequence under this model’s assumptions while Child Y builds sticky HbS.
widgets.cutaway: Cambridge 0610 Topic 17.1 Supplement protein synthesis: (1) the gene coding for the protein remains in the nucleus; (2) messenger RNA (mRNA) is a copy of a gene; (3) mRNA is made in the nucleus and moves to the cytoplasm; (4) mRNA passes through ribosomes; (5) the ribosome assembles amino acids into protein molecules; and (6) the specific sequence of amino acids is determined by the sequence of bases in the mRNA. DNA controls cell function by encoding enzymes, membrane carriers, neurotransmitter receptors and antibodies.
widgets.idealised: Other protein-family pictures are analogies, not HBB mutation predictions for those genes. Models codons 1–7 of human beta-globin (HBB) after initiator methionine cleavage, following Vernon Ingram (1956–1957) and Cambridge IGCSE 0610 Topic 17.1.

watchSteps.title: 1. Reference adult beta-globin (HbA) at Codon 6
watchSteps.caption: In the nucleus, coding DNA (GTG CAC CTG ACT CCT GAG GAG) is copied into mRNA (GUG CAC CUG ACU CCU GAG GAG); at Codon 6 (GAG), the ribosome inserts hydrophilic Glutamic acid (Glu⁶).

watchSteps.title: 2. Child X silent substitution (Codon 3 CTG → CTT)
watchSteps.caption: At Codon 3, DNA CTG becomes CTT so mRNA CUG becomes CUU; because the 64-codon code is degenerate, CUU still codes for Leucine (Leu³) and the amino-acid sequence is unchanged; RNA processing and function are assumed unaffected here.

watchSteps.title: 3. Child Y missense substitution (Codon 6 GAG → GTG)
watchSteps.caption: At Codon 6, DNA GAG becomes GTG so mRNA GAG becomes GUG, replacing hydrophilic Glu⁶ with hydrophobic Valine (Val⁶) and creating a sticky surface patch on deoxygenated HbS.

watchSteps.title: 4. Nonsense stop substitution (Codon 6 GAG → TAG)
watchSteps.caption: Changing DNA GAG to TAG turns mRNA Codon 6 into the amber stop codon UAG, halting the ribosome prematurely and releasing a non-functional 5-residue fragment.

watchSteps.title: 5. DNA control of membrane carriers & receptors
watchSteps.caption: Switching to Protein Family #3 (Na⁺–glucose carrier) or #4 (synaptic neurotransmitter receptor) shows how the same sequence-to-folding pipeline governs every cell machine.

widgets.title: DNA Replication Meselson
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture two contrasting density-gradient trials. Explain which predicted bands distinguish semi-conservative copying from the alternatives.
widgets.cutaway: In semi-conservative replication, each original DNA strand templates a new complementary strand. The idealised isotope model starts with heavy DNA, then follows copying in light medium: one generation gives hybrid duplexes; two generations give hybrid and light duplexes. The first result distinguishes conservative copying, and the second distinguishes the dispersive alternative. The eukaryotic fork and proofreading view is a separate teaching comparison, not the same bacterial experiment.
widgets.idealised: Idealised isotope fractions and density bands; generation timing is chosen. The human nuclear-fork comparison is separate from the bacterial isotope experiment. High copying accuracy does not mean every cell preserves an exact unchanged genome.

watchSteps.title: 1. Heavy baseline
watchSteps.caption: The model starts with two heavy strands per duplex, producing the heavy-density band.

watchSteps.title: 2. One copying generation
watchSteps.caption: The idealised first generation has hybrid duplexes: one original heavy strand plus one new light strand.

watchSteps.title: 3. Test the conservative prediction
watchSteps.caption: Conservative copying predicts separate heavy and light bands after one generation, unlike the observed intermediate band.

watchSteps.title: 4. A second generation distinguishes alternatives
watchSteps.caption: Semi-conservative copying gives hybrid and light bands. The dispersive model predicts one progressively lighter band.

watchSteps.title: 5. Copying accuracy
watchSteps.caption: Proofreading and repair reduce errors. Rates and origin counts in this separate fork view are illustrative approximations; mutations can remain.

widgets.title: Mitosis Meiosis Stepper
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture two contrasting division states. Compare chromosome number, DNA-molecule number and ploidy separately.
widgets.cutaway: The chosen diploid human example has46 chromosomes. S phase copies them into46 linked sister pairs containing92 DNA molecules, while ploidy remains2n. Mitosis separates copies into two daughter cells; mutations are excluded from this counting model. Meiosis separates homologous pairs and then sister chromatids; four haploid products describe the sperm-production model, not four functional eggs or direct gamete production in every plant.
widgets.idealised: Chromosome bookkeeping for chosen human and plant presets. Four meiotic products follow the sperm model. Mutation, unusual ploidy and incomplete segregation are not represented in normal mitosis; triploid products are schematic, not a prediction that every product is inviable.

watchSteps.title: 1. Count copies after S phase
watchSteps.caption: In the chosen human model,46 chromosomes now comprise92 sister chromatids. Copying DNA does not add another homologous chromosome set.

watchSteps.title: 2. Separate copied chromosomes
watchSteps.caption: The idealised mitotic endpoint gives two daughter nuclei with46 chromosomes each. New mutations and unusual chromosome counts are not represented.

watchSteps.title: 3. Separate homologous pairs
watchSteps.caption: Meiosis I reduces the chosen diploid count from46 to23 per daughter nucleus; chromosomes still have sister chromatids.

watchSteps.title: 4. Separate sister chromatids
watchSteps.caption: The illustrated sperm model produces four haploid sorting products. Fertilisation can restore the diploid count; egg formation has unequal products.

watchSteps.title: 5. Triploid segregation is often unbalanced
watchSteps.caption: Three homologous copies cannot divide into equal paired sets. Poor fertility and parthenocarpy help explain seedless Cavendish fruit; clonal propagation retains low diversity, with possible new mutations.

widgets.title: Stem Cell Expression Lab
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture two contrasting expression profiles. Explain how the ON entries change while the six displayed entries remain in this illustrative panel.
widgets.cutaway: Most body cells share most inherited DNA; selective expression helps produce different functions. This comparison chooses a diploid human nucleus with46 chromosomes and retains six displayed entries, including a grouped OCT4/SOX2 entry. ATP5F1A and GAPDH stay ON as housekeeping examples in this panel. INS illustrates beta-cell expression, HBB erythroblast expression, and CHAT motor-neurone acetylcholine synthesis. Mutations, immune-cell DNA rearrangements, polyploidy and loss of the nucleus prevent an exact-genome rule for every body cell.
widgets.idealised: Six-entry on/off panel with invented transcript counts, regulator overrides and progress percentages. Retaining6/6 displayed entries is a model assumption, not a whole-genome measurement. Housekeeping examples remain ON in the illustrated states; real expression is graded and context-dependent.

watchSteps.title: 1. A stem-cell programme
watchSteps.caption: The illustrative starting panel keeps housekeeping examples and OCT4/SOX2 ON. Real stem cells differ in potency; the panel is not a full catalogue of genes or cell types.

watchSteps.title: 2. A beta-cell example
watchSteps.caption: The model opens INS while HBB and CHAT are OFF. Regulator settings and transcript counts are invented teaching values, not sufficient experimental recipes.

watchSteps.title: 3. An erythroblast example
watchSteps.caption: The chosen nucleated erythroblast expresses HBB. A mature mammalian red blood cell later loses its nucleus; it is not another intact46-chromosome state.

watchSteps.title: 4. A cholinergic motor-neurone example
watchSteps.caption: CHAT produces choline acetyltransferase, helping cholinergic motor neurones synthesise the acetylcholine that signals to skeletal muscle.

watchSteps.title: 5. Reprogramming retained information
watchSteps.caption: Gurdon nuclear transfer and Yamanaka reprogramming show that many specialised nuclei retain developmental information. They do not prove that every DNA sequence remains unchanged or that every cell reprogrammes.

widgets.title: Mendel Punnett Simulator
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture two contrasting Mendel crosses or sample sizes (e.g. 3:1 Hybrid Rr × Rr vs 1:1 Test Cross Rr × rr, or Small Pod N = 16 vs Mendel 1866 limit) to explain how gamete alleles produce 1:2:1 genotypes, 3:1 phenotypes, and 1:1 test crosses.
widgets.cutaway: Cambridge 0893 & 0610 Topic 17.4: A gene is a length of DNA at a specific locus on a chromosome that codes for a protein; an allele is an alternative form of a gene. In a diploid organism (2n), homologous chromosomes carry two copies of each gene—either homozygous (RR or rr) or heterozygous (Rr). Because a single functional allele (R) synthesises enough active enzyme (such as starch-branching enzyme SBEI in round peas) to produce the full trait, R is dominant and r is recessive. Meiosis separates homologous chromosomes so each haploid gamete (n) receives 1 allele; random fertilisation in Rr × Rr produces a 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr genotype ratio and a 3 : 1 phenotype ratio, whereas a test cross (Rr × rr) produces a 1 : 1 ratio.
widgets.idealised: Models monohybrid Punnett probabilities, haplosufficient enzyme dosage (100% RR, 50% Rr, 0% rr), and sample-size convergence against Johann Gregor Mendel’s 1866 Brno pea ledger.

watchSteps.title: 1. Parental pure cross (RR × rr → 100% Rr F₁ hybrids)
watchSteps.caption: Crossing a homozygous dominant round-seed parent (RR) with a homozygous recessive wrinkled-seed parent (rr) yields 100% heterozygous Rr F₁ seeds; the recessive r allele is unexpressed but preserved intact.

watchSteps.title: 2. Monohybrid F₁ self-cross (Rr × Rr → 1:2:1 & 3:1)
watchSteps.caption: When two Rr hybrids self-pollinate, 50% R and 50% r gametes combine in a 2×2 Punnett grid to give 25% RR, 50% Rr, and 25% rr genotypes (1:2:1) and 75% round : 25% wrinkled phenotypes (3:1).

watchSteps.title: 3. Diagnostic test cross (Rr × rr → 1:1)
watchSteps.caption: Crossing a dominant-phenotype plant of unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive tester (rr) yields 50% Rr and 50% rr offspring (1:1) if the parent is heterozygous, unmasking the hidden recessive allele.

watchSteps.title: 4. Small-sample bounce (N = 16) vs large-sample convergence
watchSteps.caption: At N = 16 (a single pea pod batch), random fertilisation bounce shifts the observed percentage away from 75%; increasing N from 16 to 64, 400, and 7,324 converges on 3:1.

watchSteps.title: 5. Brno 1866 ledger across 19,959 pea outcomes (2.98 : 1)
watchSteps.caption: Across all seven pea characters in his 1866 Brno monograph, Johann Gregor Mendel counted 14,949 dominant and 5,010 recessive F₂ outcomes (2.98 : 1) and verified the hidden 1 RR : 2 Rr split in F₃.

widgets.title: Abo Codominance Pedigree
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture two contrasting ABO parental crosses (e.g. IᴬIᴼ × IᴮIᴼ 4-Group Cross vs IᴬIᴮ × IᴼIᴼ Swap Check, or IᴬIᴮ × IᴬIᴮ Codominance) to compare possible and excluded offspring blood groups.
widgets.cutaway: Cambridge 0610 Topic 17.4 (Extended): Codominance occurs when both alleles in a heterozygote are expressed independently and simultaneously in the phenotype. The human ABO blood group gene on Chromosome 9 has three common alleles in the population (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, Iᴼ), though any diploid person inherits only two. Iᴬ codes for GTA enzyme (attaching GalNAc = Antigen A), Iᴮ codes for GTB enzyme (attaching D-Gal = Antigen B), and Iᴼ carries a ΔG261 frameshift loss-of-function deletion (leaving unmodified H-antigen). Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant (IᴬIᴮ = Group AB with both antigens), while both Iᴬ and Iᴮ are dominant to recessive Iᴼ (IᴬIᴼ = Group A; IᴮIᴼ = Group B; IᴼIᴼ = Group O).
widgets.idealised: Models diploid 2×2 Punnett inheritance across all 36 (6×6) parental combinations of ABO genotypes (IᴬIᴬ, IᴬIᴼ, IᴮIᴮ, IᴮIᴼ, IᴬIᴮ, IᴼIᴼ) and autosomal pedigree deduction rules.

watchSteps.title: 1. Four-blood-group cross (IᴬIᴼ × IᴮIᴼ → AB, A, B, O)
watchSteps.caption: When a heterozygous Group A mother (IᴬIᴼ) and heterozygous Group B father (IᴮIᴼ) have children, the 2×2 Punnett grid gives 25% IᴬIᴮ (AB), 25% IᴬIᴼ (A), 25% IᴮIᴼ (B), and 25% IᴼIᴼ (O).

watchSteps.title: 2. Hospital swap check (IᴬIᴮ × IᴼIᴼ → 50% A, 50% B, 0% O)
watchSteps.caption: A Group AB parent (IᴬIᴮ) passes either Iᴬ or Iᴮ (never Iᴼ), and a Group O parent (IᴼIᴼ) passes only Iᴼ, so biological children can only be Group A (IᴬIᴼ) or Group B (IᴮIᴼ)—never AB or O.

watchSteps.title: 3. Codominance 1:2:1 phenotype ratio (IᴬIᴮ × IᴬIᴮ)
watchSteps.caption: Crossing two Group AB parents (IᴬIᴮ × IᴬIᴮ) produces 25% Group A (IᴬIᴬ), 50% Group AB (IᴬIᴮ), and 25% Group B (IᴮIᴮ)—a 1:2:1 phenotype ratio that directly mirrors the 1:2:1 genotype ratio.

watchSteps.title: 4. Two Group A carriers producing a Group O child (IᴬIᴼ × IᴬIᴼ)
watchSteps.caption: Two Group A parents who both carry a hidden Iᴼ allele (IᴬIᴼ × IᴬIᴼ) have a 25% chance of a Group O child (IᴼIᴼ) and a 75% chance of a Group A child (25% IᴬIᴬ + 50% IᴬIᴼ).

watchSteps.title: 5. Pedigree Detective Rule 1 vs Rule 2
watchSteps.caption: In family pedigrees, two unaffected parents having an affected child proves a recessive allele (Aa × Aa → aa); conversely, two affected parents having an unaffected child proves a dominant allele.

widgets.title: Sex Linked Cross Lab
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture two contrasting X-linked crosses (e.g. Carrier Mum × Normal Dad vs Normal Mum × Affected Dad, or Carrier Mum × Affected Dad) to explain why sons inherit X-linked traits from their mother and why fathers cannot pass X-linked traits to sons.
widgets.cutaway: Cambridge 0610 Topics 17.1 & 17.4 (Extended): Human females are XX (producing 100% X ova) and males are XY (producing 50% X sperm and 50% Y sperm), giving a 1:1 sex ratio at fertilisation. A sex-linked characteristic is one in which the gene responsible is located on a sex chromosome (usually the non-homologous region of the X chromosome, ~156 Mb and ~850 genes vs ~57 Mb and <100 genes on Y), making it more common in one sex than in the other. Because an XY male has only one X chromosome (hemizygous), a single recessive allele (Xᵇ or Xʰ) causes the condition, and males cannot be unaffected carriers.
widgets.idealised: Models 2×2 X/Y gamete Punnett segregation and separate probabilities among daughters (XX), among sons (XY), and among all children for X-linked loci.

watchSteps.title: 1. Carrier mother × Normal father (XᴮXᵇ × XᴮY)
watchSteps.caption: A carrier mother passes Xᵇ to 50% of her children: 0% of daughters are affected (50% XᴮXᴮ normal, 50% XᴮXᵇ carriers), while 50% of sons are affected (XᵇY) because sons have no second X chromosome.

watchSteps.title: 2. Normal mother × Affected father (XᴮXᴮ × XᵇY → 0% affected sons)
watchSteps.caption: An affected father gives every son his Y chromosome (never his X), so 0% of sons inherit the father’s Xᵇ allele; instead, 100% of daughters inherit his Xᵇ and become unaffected carriers (XᴮXᵇ).

watchSteps.title: 3. Carrier mother × Affected father (XᴮXᵇ × XᵇY → affected daughters)
watchSteps.caption: An X-linked recessive condition appears in a daughter (XᵇXᵇ) only when she inherits a recessive allele from both her carrier/affected mother and her affected father (50% of daughters here).

watchSteps.title: 4. Haemophilia clotting cascade bridge (Xᴴ/Xʰ)
watchSteps.caption: Switching to the Haemophilia locus (Xᴴ/Xʰ) shows how Xʰ leaves clotting Factor VIII/IX non-functional in XʰY sons, preventing soluble fibrinogen from forming a fibrin mesh in wounds.

watchSteps.title: 5. Morgan 1910 Drosophila white-eye chromosome proof (X⁺/Xʷ)
watchSteps.caption: Switching to Fly eye colour models Thomas Hunt Morgan’s 1910 Columbia Fly Room discovery: F₂ white eyes appeared exclusively in males (XʷY), proving genes sit physically on chromosomes.

widgets.title: Variation Mutation Lab
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture two contrasting variation or mutation trials. Explain which differences are inherited and which values are assumptions.
widgets.cutaway: Continuous and discontinuous describe observed patterns, not universal causes. The height example reflects genes and environment; the ABO example uses inherited categories. Replica plating shows resistance can pre-exist exposure. Mutations are not specified by need; their probabilities vary among sites, and some antibiotics can increase mutation rates.
widgets.idealised: All distributions, plate coordinates, rate multipliers and mutation-effect fractions are illustrative. Continuous/categorical patterns do not guarantee particular genetic causes.

watchSteps.title: 1. Continuous variation
watchSteps.caption: The invented height distribution shifts with a chosen nutrition offset; bell shape is an assumption, not a defining rule.

watchSteps.title: 2. ABO categories
watchSteps.caption: Nutrition does not change inherited ABO alleles. This does not mean every categorical trait is independent of environment.

watchSteps.title: 3. Recover pre-existing resistance
watchSteps.caption: Illustrative matching colony positions let you locate resistant cells in the unexposed source. They are not historical plate coordinates.

watchSteps.title: 4. Change an assumed mutation rate
watchSteps.caption: The 1× to 50× factors are invented examples, not measured effects of unspecified chemical or radiation doses.

watchSteps.title: 5. New variants and new combinations
watchSteps.caption: Mutation changes DNA; meiosis and fertilisation reshuffle inherited variation. Neither predicts which change would help.

widgets.title: Natural Selection Simulator
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture two contrasting culture or population trials. Compare both the number and the fraction of the favoured variant.
widgets.cutaway: Selection changes the contribution of inherited variants to descendants. Greater survival, mating success or fertility can matter. The culture model applies differential survival, then density-limited reproduction. It has no patient or immune system. Sickle-cell balancing selection uses constant relative reproductive contributions and random mating; historical parasite prevalence is a different measurement.
widgets.idealised: Culture steps are not clinical days or antibiotic-course advice. Moth curves are constructed; HbS follows an explicit large-population recurrence with no mutation or migration. Genotype fractions describe newborns before selection.

watchSteps.title: 1. Continuous culture exposure
watchSteps.caption: The invented culture starts with 990 susceptible and 10 resistant cells. Continued exposure can increase the resistant fraction; no clinical cure is predicted.

watchSteps.title: 2. Remove drug after step 3
watchSteps.caption: Now remove exposure from the same model. Density limits growth and resistance has a modest reproductive cost; removal does not automatically create resistant relapse.

watchSteps.title: 3. Camouflage and bird predation
watchSteps.caption: The moth curves are illustrative morph frequencies inspired by field evidence, not dated measurements or allele counts.

watchSteps.title: 4. Follow many generations
watchSteps.caption: Changing reproductive contribution can change a population without an individual moth choosing its wing colour.

watchSteps.title: 5. Heterozygote advantage
watchSteps.caption: The model recurrence uses wAS=1 and wSS=0.20. Higher malaria pressure lowers wAA, changing the balancing equilibrium; these are assumed fitness values.

widgets.title: Adaptive Features Selective Breeding
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture two contrasting plant, breeding or sequence comparisons. Explain a mechanism and identify the model assumptions.
widgets.cutaway: Rolled hairy leaves shelter humid air and reduce water-vapour loss. Floating water-lily leaves have upper stomata and may have water-repellent wax; fully submerged leaves exchange dissolved gases without stomata. Breeding gains and diversity changes depend on the programme. Homologous sequence similarity supports relationships, but dates need rate models and independent calibration.
widgets.idealised: Plant dimensions and performance, breeding trajectories and homologous alignments are invented teaching examples. No universal hydrophyte cuticle rule, historical crop yield or exact molecular stopwatch is asserted.

watchSteps.title: 1. A sheltered stomatal surface
watchSteps.caption: Marram grass shelters humid air. Dimensions and water-saving percentages in this comparison are invented, not species constants.

watchSteps.title: 2. A floating leaf is not a submerged leaf
watchSteps.caption: The water-lily upper surface faces air and can carry wax. Internal gas spaces support buoyancy and gas movement; numerical performance is assumed.

watchSteps.title: 3. An illustrative breeding programme
watchSteps.caption: These crop trajectories are constructed to explore selection and diversity. They are not Janaki Ammal’s measured historical results.

watchSteps.title: 4. Compare a livestock scenario
watchSteps.caption: The milk-yield values are invented. Related-parent mating can expose harmful recessives; genetic uniformity can separately increase shared vulnerability.

watchSteps.title: 5. Count synthetic sequence differences
watchSteps.caption: Compare X with invented species. Identity is counted from aligned bases; neither a tree root nor a divergence date is supplied by percentage alone.

widgets.title: Ecosystem Trophic Lab
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture two contrasting ecosystem, pyramid, diet efficiency, or sigmoid growth trials (e.g. Direct Crop Diet vs Livestock Meat Diet, or Banyan Tree Pyramid vs SGNP Web) to compare trophic energy retention and carrying capacity.
widgets.cutaway: Energy flows from light to chemical energy and eventually heat; atoms move between reservoirs and can be reused. Trophic transfer compares new biomass production at adjacent levels for the same area and period; 10% is an example, not a universal law. Food supplied directly or through livestock is a separate budget before human digestion. Energy per area alone cannot decide predator viability. The batch-culture curve illustrates lag, growth, stationary and death phases.

widgets.title: Nutrient Cycles Eutrophication
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture two contrasting nitrogen cycle, eutrophication, carbon cycle, or deforestation trials (e.g. Aerated Legumes vs Waterlogged Paddy, or Low vs High Nitrate Runoff in Powai Lake) to compare soil nitrate or dissolved oxygen.
widgets.cutaway: Biological fixation converts N₂ to ammonia/ammonium. Lightning instead forms nitrogen oxides that can become nitrate; the Haber process makes ammonia. Decomposition, aerobic nitrification and low-oxygen denitrification move nitrogen between forms. Nutrient enrichment can increase producer growth and decomposer respiration, reducing dissolved oxygen. Shading is one possible route; sewage organic matter and living algae also consume oxygen. Model outputs are illustrative, not Mumbai measurements.

widgets.title: Biotech Fermenter Plasmid Lab
widgets.challengePrompt: Capture two contrasting recombinant plasmid, industrial fermenter, enzyme biotech, or GM crop trials (e.g. Optimum 37 °C vs Overheated 55 °C Fermenter, or Compatible vs Incompatible DNA Ends) to compare product yields.
widgets.cutaway: Prepare intron-free insulin coding DNA with bacterial expression controls, obtain compatible insert/vector ends, join with ligase, transform and select cells, then culture, recover, process/fold and purify the product. The shared code supplies matching codon meanings; mature insulin has two chains. Same-enzyme cutting is one compatible-end method. Fermenters require waste control as well as suitable nutrients, oxygen, pH and temperature. Baking removes much ethanol; temperature alone does not predict what remains.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Why diffusion needs no pump: thermal kinetic energy
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: Alveolar oxygen and dissolved glucose do not 'want' to enter blood; random thermal collisions at 37 °C drive net movement down a concentration gradient (Fick's First Law: J = -D dC/dx).
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: Why does pulmonary oedema (fluid thickening the alveolar wall from 0.5 µm to 5 µm) starve the blood of oxygen even when the lungs are full of fresh air?
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckAnswer: By Fick's law, rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to barrier thickness Δx; increasing Δx tenfold cuts the oxygen diffusion rate tenfold.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Boyle's Law in the thorax: how volume change drives airflow
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: Lungs have no skeletal muscle of their own. Contracting the diaphragm and external intercostals increases thoracic volume V, dropping alveolar pressure P below atmospheric pressure (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂) so air rushes in.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: During inhalation, thoracic volume increases by 12% while temperature stays constant at 310 K. Does intra-alveolar pressure rise or fall relative to atmospheric pressure?
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckAnswer: It falls below atmospheric pressure (by ~1–2 mmHg), creating a pressure gradient that pushes outside air into the alveoli.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Why cellular respiration doesn't set the cell on fire
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: Combusting 1 mole of glucose releases ΔG°' = -2,870 kJ all at once as heat and light. Mitochondria harvest the exact same reaction across enzyme-catalysed steps, capturing ~30–32 ATP molecules (~30.5 kJ/mol each).
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: Both a burning marshmallow and a respiring muscle cell react glucose with oxygen to form CO₂ and H₂O. Why is respiration classified as exothermic in Unit 8.1, and how does the cell survive it?
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckAnswer: It is exothermic because the products (CO₂ + H₂O) have stronger bonds and lower chemical potential energy than glucose + O₂; enzymes lower activation energy at 37 °C and couple the released energy into ATP rather than pure heat.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Leaf pigment chromatography: chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, carotene & xanthophyll
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: Spinach leaves look uniformly green, but paper chromatography separates four distinct photosynthetic pigments by their relative solubility in the mobile solvent vs hydrogen-bonding to cellulose paper.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.keyEquation: Rf = distance travelled by pigment spot ÷ distance travelled by solvent front
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: On a chromatogram of spinach extract, carotene travels 7.2 cm while the solvent front travels 8.0 cm. Calculate Rf and explain why carotene travels higher than chlorophyll b (Rf = 0.42).
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckAnswer: Rf = 7.2 ÷ 8.0 = 0.90. Carotene is non-polar and much more soluble in the non-polar mobile solvent (and less strongly adsorbed to polar cellulose paper) than chlorophyll b.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Skeletal joints as third-class levers: trading force for speed
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: The biceps inserts just ~4 cm from the elbow pivot (fulcrum), while a ball in the hand sits ~32 cm away. By the principle of moments (F_biceps × d_in = F_load × d_out), the biceps must pull with 8× the load's weight — trading force advantage for rapid, wide-arc hand motion.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.keyEquation: M = F × d⊥   (Clockwise moment = Anticlockwise moment)
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: You hold a 15 N textbook in your hand 30 cm from your elbow pivot. Your biceps tendon attaches 3.0 cm from the elbow pivot. What upward force must your biceps muscle exert to keep your forearm horizontal?
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckAnswer: F_biceps × 3.0 cm = 15 N × 30 cm ⇒ F_biceps = 450 ÷ 3.0 = 150 N.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: Refraction in the microscope & eye lens, and why leaves reflect green light
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: Convex lenses in microscopes and the human eye bend rays toward a focal point on the retina (1/f = 1/u + 1/v). Meanwhile, chlorophyll absorbs red (~660 nm) and blue (~450 nm) wavelengths to drive photosynthesis, reflecting green (~530 nm) into our cone cells.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.keyEquation: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂   and   M = I ÷ A
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: What happens to the rate of oxygen bubble production in pondweed (Elodea) when illuminated with pure green light (530 nm) compared with red (660 nm) or blue (450 nm) light of the same intensity?
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckAnswer: Oxygen bubble production drops sharply under green light because chlorophyll a and b reflect/transmit green wavelengths rather than absorbing them to excite electrons.

crossDisciplinaryBridges.sourceRef: Ch 8 · Earth's Carbon Reservoirs & Greenhouse IR Absorption
crossDisciplinaryBridges.title: How photosynthesis, cellular respiration & combustion govern Earth's carbon cycle
crossDisciplinaryBridges.summary: Every year, terrestrial and marine photosynthesis fixes ~120 Gt of carbon from atmospheric CO₂ into organic biomass, while respiration and decomposition return ~120 Gt. Burning fossilised Carboniferous biomass adds an uncompensated ~10 Gt C/yr.
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckQuestion: Why does atmospheric CO₂ concentration at Mauna Loa dip every northern-hemisphere summer and peak every winter?
crossDisciplinaryBridges.microCheckAnswer: In northern summer, vastboreal and temperate forests photosynthesise faster than ecosystems respire, drawing down atmospheric CO₂; in winter, photosynthesis slows while respiration and decomposition continue releasing CO₂.

schoolTextbook.title: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 (Second Edition)
schoolTextbook.authors: Mary Jones, Diane Fellowes-Freeman & Michael Smyth

units.title: Respiration
twsStrands: Scientific enquiry: analysis, evaluation and conclusions
units.scienceInContext: Discuss how scientific knowledge develops over time by shared understanding and investigation. Describe how science is used in different societies and industries, and how it is used in research. Evaluate topics using scientific understanding.

topics.title: The human respiratory system
topics.summary: Trace the pathway of air from nose and mouth through larynx (voicebox), trachea (supported by C-shaped cartilage rings), bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli, plus ciliated epithelial and goblet cells that sweep mucus upward.
cambridgeWatchouts: Always write 'trachea' (not just windpipe) and distinguish 'bronchus' (singular) from 'bronchi' (plural).
Do not confuse the trachea (airway with cartilage rings) with the oesophagus (food tube behind it).

topics.title: Gas exchange
topics.summary: How oxygen diffuses from alveolar air spaces across the one-cell-thick alveolar and capillary walls into red blood cells, while carbon dioxide diffuses in the opposite direction down its concentration gradient.
cambridgeWatchouts: State that alveolar and capillary walls are 'one cell thick' — never write 'cell walls are thin' (animal cells have no cell wall!).
Always name 'diffusion down a concentration gradient' and mention the rich blood capillary network that maintains a steep gradient.

topics.title: Breathing
topics.summary: Mechanical ventilation of the lungs: how contraction and relaxation of the external intercostal muscles and diaphragm change thoracic volume and pressure to cause inspiration (breathing in) and expiration (breathing out).
cambridgeWatchouts: Never write 'breathing is respiration'. Breathing is mechanical ventilation of the lungs; respiration is a chemical reaction in all living cells.
In the bell-jar model, note its limitations: the glass jar cannot move like the ribcage, and the rubber sheet pulls down from a point rather than flattening from a dome.

topics.title: Respiration
topics.summary: Aerobic respiration inside mitochondria of living cells: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, releasing useful energy for movement, active transport, growth, and keeping body temperature constant.
cambridgeWatchouts: Cambridge mark schemes strictly forbid 'energy is produced/made/created'. Always write 'energy is released from glucose'.
Know the word equation by heart: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.

topics.title: Blood
topics.summary: Structure and function of the four components of blood: plasma (transports dissolved glucose, amino acids, CO₂, urea, hormones, and heat), red blood cells (biconcave discs packed with haemoglobin, no nucleus, carry O₂ as oxyhaemoglobin), white blood cells (have a nucleus, phagocytes and lymphocytes that defend against pathogens by phagocytosis and producing antibodies), and platelets (clotting).
cambridgeWatchouts: Explain HOW each adaptation helps: 'no nucleus leaves more space for haemoglobin so each red blood cell can carry more oxygen'; 'biconcave shape gives a large surface area to volume ratio for rapid diffusion of oxygen in and out'.

units.title: Properties of materials
twsStrands: Scientific enquiry: analysis, evaluation and conclusions
units.scienceInContext: Describe how science is used in different societies and industries, and how it is used in research.

topics.title: Dissolving
topics.summary: Solutes, solvents, and conservation of mass when substances dissolve — the chemical basis of blood plasma and cytoplasm as aqueous solutions.
cambridgeWatchouts: Mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent (particles are conserved when glucose or salt dissolves in water or plasma).

topics.title: Solutions and solubility
topics.summary: Concentrated, dilute, and saturated solutions, and how temperature affects the solubility of solids vs gases (such as dissolved oxygen in warm vs cold river water).
cambridgeWatchouts: While most solid solutes become MORE soluble as temperature rises, gases like oxygen become LESS soluble in warmer water — crucial for fish respiration in heated rivers.

topics.title: Planning a solubility investigation
topics.summary: Identifying independent, dependent, and control variables, choosing intervals, and recording repeatable results.
cambridgeWatchouts: Always state the exact volume of water (e.g., 100 cm³) as a control variable when comparing solubility.

topics.title: Paper chromatography
topics.summary: Separating mixtures of dissolved pigments (such as chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, xanthophyll, and carotene in plant leaves) using a pencil baseline and solvent front.
cambridgeWatchouts: Draw the baseline in pencil, never ink, because ink dyes dissolve in the solvent and contaminate the chromatogram.
Keep the solvent level BELOW the sample spots so the spots do not wash directly into the solvent reservoir.

units.title: Forces and energy
twsStrands: Scientific enquiry: analysis, evaluation and conclusions

topics.title: Forces and motion
topics.summary: Balanced and unbalanced forces and resultant force on moving organisms and objects.
cambridgeWatchouts: Balanced forces mean constant velocity (including stationary), not necessarily at rest.

topics.title: Speed
topics.summary: Calculating speed = distance ÷ time, nerve impulse conduction speeds (~100 m/s), and cheetah vs human locomotion.
cambridgeWatchouts: Always check units (m/s vs km/h) before substituting into speed = distance ÷ time.

topics.title: Describing movement
topics.summary: Interpreting distance–time graphs: gradient equals speed, horizontal flat line means stationary.
cambridgeWatchouts: A steeper slope on a distance–time graph means higher speed, not climbing a hill.

topics.title: Turning forces
topics.summary: Moments of a force (moment = force × perpendicular distance from pivot) and the principle of moments — the physical foundation for Unit 7.4 Moving the body (bones, joints as pivots, and antagonistic biceps/triceps muscles).
cambridgeWatchouts: Always measure distance perpendicular to the line of action of the force from the pivot (joint).
State the unit of moment as N m or N cm (never J).

topics.title: Pressure between solids
topics.summary: Pressure = force ÷ area (N/m² or N/cm²), comparing camel footpads (large area, low pressure on desert sand in Unit 4.1) vs sharp predator claws and teeth.
cambridgeWatchouts: When explaining camel feet or snowshoes, always follow the 3-step chain: larger area → force spread out → smaller pressure → does not sink.

topics.title: Pressure in liquids and gases
topics.summary: How particle collisions with container walls create gas pressure, how volume changes affect pressure, and why blood pressure and thoracic pressure drive circulation and breathing (Unit 1.3).
cambridgeWatchouts: Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls of the container, not particles colliding with each other.

topics.title: Particles on the move
topics.summary: Diffusion in liquids and gases driven by random kinetic motion of particles from higher concentration to lower concentration, and how temperature and concentration gradient control the rate of diffusion across cell membranes and alveoli.
