cambridgeWatchouts: Individual particles move randomly in all directions; only the NET (overall) movement is from higher concentration to lower concentration.

units.title: Ecosystems
units.scienceInContext: Discuss how scientific knowledge develops over time by shared understanding and investigation. Evaluate topics using scientific understanding. Discuss the impact science can have on the environment world-wide.

topics.title: The Sonoran Desert
topics.summary: Interactions between organisms and abiotic factors in the Sonoran Desert: saguaro cacti (wide shallow roots, pleated water-storing stem, spines instead of leaves), Gila woodpeckers, bats as nocturnal pollinators, Kangaroo rats, and desert food webs/habitats.
cambridgeWatchouts: Distinguish carefully between 'ecosystem' (all living organisms + non-living environment interacting in an area), 'habitat' (the place where an organism lives), and 'niche' (the role an organism plays in its ecosystem).

topics.title: Different ecosystems
topics.summary: Comparing mangrove forests (aerial breathing roots/pneumatophores, salt excretion, nursery habitat for young fish), sea ice in the Arctic Ocean (algae growing on the underside of sea ice feeding krill → arctic cod → seals → polar bears), and tropical rice paddies.
cambridgeWatchouts: Arrows in a food chain or food web ALWAYS point in the direction of energy transfer (from eaten to eater), never 'who eats whom'.

topics.title: Intruders in an ecosystem
topics.summary: How introduced/invasive species (such as buffelgrass in the Sonoran Desert, prickly pear, cane toads, or stoats in New Zealand) outcompete native species for light, water, minerals, and nesting sites because they lack natural predators or pathogens in the new habitat.
cambridgeWatchouts: When asked why an invasive species spreads rapidly, give TWO linked reasons: (1) no natural predators/herbivores/diseases in the new ecosystem, and (2) outcompetes native species for named resources (water, light, space, food).

topics.title: Bioaccumulation
topics.summary: How persistent, non-biodegradable toxins (DDT, mercury, PCBs, microplastics) accumulate inside an organism over time (bioaccumulation) and increase in concentration at each higher trophic level along a food chain (biomagnification), causing thin eggshells in ospreys and eagles.
cambridgeWatchouts: Always state that the toxin is 'persistent / does not break down (non-biodegradable) and is not excreted'.

Explain biomagnification quantitatively: one primary consumer eats many contaminated producers, one secondary consumer eats many primary consumers, so the top predator ingests the combined toxin dose of thousands of organisms below it.

units.title: Materials and cycles on Earth
scienceStrands: Earth and Space: Cycles on Earth
twsStrands: Scientific enquiry: analysis, evaluation and conclusions
units.scienceInContext: Discuss how scientific understanding is used and developed by people working on their own and working together, such as the peer-review process. Discuss the impact science can have on the environment world-wide.

topics.title: The structure of the atom
topics.summary: Protons (+1), neutrons (0), and electrons (-1), electrostatic attraction, and Rutherford's gold-foil model.
cambridgeWatchouts: An atom has no overall charge because number of protons (+1) equals number of electrons (-1).

topics.title: Purity
topics.summary: Calculating percentage purity of salts, diamonds, gold alloys, and seawater components.
cambridgeWatchouts: Percentage purity = (mass of pure substance ÷ total mass of sample) × 100%.

topics.title: Weather and climate
topics.summary: Distinguishing short-term atmospheric weather from long-term climate averages and global climate zones that determine terrestrial biomes.
cambridgeWatchouts: Weather is day-to-day atmospheric conditions; climate is the average weather pattern over 30+ years.

topics.title: Climate and ice ages
topics.summary: Glacial and interglacial periods, ice-core trapped air bubbles, peat bog pollen records, and glacial boulders as evidence of past climate and plant evolution.
cambridgeWatchouts: Pollen grains have tough outer coats that resist decay in anaerobic acidic peat bogs, showing which plant species lived at each depth/age.

topics.title: Atmosphere and climate
topics.summary: How early photosynthetic cyanobacteria oxygenated Earth's atmosphere, locked carbon into limestone and fossil fuels, and how modern combustion and deforestation perturb the greenhouse effect.
cambridgeWatchouts: Photosynthesis evolved ~2.4–3.5 billion years ago, removing CO₂ and releasing O₂ into the atmosphere.

units.title: Light
scienceStrands: Earth and Space: Earth in space
twsStrands: Scientific enquiry: analysis, evaluation and conclusions

topics.title: Reflection
topics.summary: Law of reflection (angle of incidence i = angle of reflection r, measured from the normal).
cambridgeWatchouts: Always measure angles of incidence and reflection from the NORMAL (90° dashed line), never from the mirror surface.

topics.title: Refraction
topics.summary: Bending of light as it changes speed across air/water/glass/cornea boundaries — the optical principle behind microscope objective lenses (Ch 0) and eye cornea/lens focusing onto the retina (Ch 9).
cambridgeWatchouts: Light slowing down (air → glass/water) bends TOWARD the normal; light speeding up (glass/water → air) bends AWAY from the normal.

topics.title: Making rainbows
topics.summary: Dispersion of white light through a prism into the continuous spectrum (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet) because violet refracts more than red.
cambridgeWatchouts: Violet light slows down the most in glass and refracts through the largest angle; red light refracts the least.

topics.title: Colours of light
topics.summary: Primary colours of light (red, green, blue — matching the 3 cone photoreceptors in the human retina!), colour filters, and why plant leaves look green (chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green light).
cambridgeWatchouts: Primary colours of LIGHT are Red, Green, and Blue (RGB), which add to make white light — corresponding directly to human S, M, and L retinal cone cells.

topics.title: Galaxies
topics.summary: Spiral, elliptical, and irregular galaxies, the Milky Way, and stellar dust clouds.
cambridgeWatchouts: Galaxies are held together by gravity.

topics.title: Rocks in space
topics.summary: Asteroids, the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, and how the Chicxulub asteroid impact 66 million years ago triggered mass extinction and mammalian adaptive radiation.
cambridgeWatchouts: Most asteroids orbit the Sun in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.

topics.title: Nutrients
topics.summary: The six groups of nutrients and water: proteins (growth and repair of cells, antibodies, enzymes, haemoglobin), carbohydrates (starch and sugars for energy release in respiration), fats and oils (energy store, cell membranes, thermal insulation), vitamins (Vitamin A for night vision/rod cells, Vitamin C for healthy skin/gums and preventing scurvy, Vitamin D for calcium absorption and preventing rickets), minerals (calcium for strong bones/teeth, iron for making haemoglobin and preventing anaemia), fibre (cellulose to stimulate peristalsis and prevent constipation), plus iodine test for starch and Benedict's test for reducing sugars.
cambridgeWatchouts: Fibre (roughage) is NOT digested or absorbed into the blood, so Cambridge treats it separately from nutrients that enter cells, though it is essential in a balanced diet to keep the alimentary canal moving.

Memorise each specific deficiency pairing: Vitamin D / Calcium → rickets; Vitamin C → scurvy; Vitamin A → night blindness; Iron → anaemia (fewer red blood cells / less haemoglobin → less oxygen transported → less aerobic respiration → tiredness).

topics.title: A balanced diet
topics.summary: How daily energy requirements (in MJ or kJ) depend on age, sex, activity level, and pregnancy/lactation; consequences of energy imbalance (malnutrition, starvation, obesity, type 2 diabetes, and coronary heart disease from excess saturated fat).
cambridgeWatchouts: 1 MJ = 1,000 kJ = 1,000,000 J. Always check whether a bar chart uses kJ or MJ!

When explaining why excess carbohydrate or fat intake causes mass gain, state: energy intake in food exceeds energy used in respiration/activity, so excess glucose is converted to fat and stored in adipose tissue.

topics.title: Growth, development and health
topics.summary: Growth by cell division (mitosis) and cell enlargement, adolescent growth spurts, and how lifestyle choices and drugs affect health — specifically how components of tobacco smoke damage gas exchange and circulation: nicotine (addictive, narrows blood vessels, raises blood pressure and heart rate), carbon monoxide (binds irreversibly to haemoglobin in red blood cells to form carboxyhaemoglobin so blood carries less oxygen, forcing the heart to work harder and starving a developing fetus of oxygen), tar (carcinogen that causes lung cancer, paralyses cilia in the trachea/bronchi so mucus accumulates, leading to chronic bronchitis and emphysema where alveolar walls break down), and particulates.
cambridgeWatchouts: Never mix up the three components of cigarette smoke: NICOTINE = addictive + constricts blood vessels; CARBON MONOXIDE = replaces oxygen on haemoglobin; TAR = causes cancer + paralyses cilia + leads to bronchitis/emphysema.

topics.title: Moving the body
topics.summary: The human skeleton, hinge joints (elbow, knee) vs ball-and-socket joints (shoulder, hip), cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments vs tendons, and why skeletal muscles work in antagonistic pairs (biceps and triceps): muscles can only exert force by pulling when they contract, never by pushing.
cambridgeWatchouts: Always state the fundamental rule: 'Muscles can only pull (when they contract); they cannot push. Therefore two muscles arranged as an antagonistic pair are needed to pull a bone in opposite directions across a joint.'
To bend (flex) the arm at the elbow: biceps contracts AND triceps relaxes. To straighten (extend) the arm: triceps contracts AND biceps relaxes.

units.title: Chemical reactions
twsStrands: Scientific enquiry: analysis, evaluation and conclusions
units.scienceInContext: Describe how science is used in different societies and industries, and how it is used in research. Evaluate topics using scientific understanding.

topics.title: Exothermic reactions
topics.summary: Chemical reactions that transfer thermal energy to the surroundings (temperature rises), including combustion, oxidation of glucose in cellular respiration (Unit 1.4), and self-heating cans.
cambridgeWatchouts: Respiration is an exothermic process that occurs continuously inside all living cells.

topics.title: Endothermic reactions
topics.summary: Chemical reactions and processes that absorb energy from the surroundings (such as citric acid + sodium hydrogencarbonate sherbet, instant cold packs, and photosynthesis absorbing light energy in chloroplasts).
cambridgeWatchouts: In an endothermic reaction in solution, energy is taken in from the solution, so the thermometer reading falls.

topics.title: Reactions of metals with oxygen
topics.summary: Metal + oxygen → metal oxide, comparing reactivity of magnesium, iron (including reversible O₂ binding to iron(II) in haemoglobin!), copper, and gold.
cambridgeWatchouts: Haemoglobin uses an iron ion at the centre of each haem group to bind oxygen reversibly without permanently rusting.

topics.title: Reactions of metals with water
topics.summary: Metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen (sodium, potassium, calcium) and why Na⁺ and K⁺ ions are the charge carriers of nerve impulses.
cambridgeWatchouts: Test for hydrogen gas: a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.

topics.title: Reactions of metals with dilute acids
topics.summary: Metal + dilute acid → salt + hydrogen (hydrochloric acid → chlorides, sulfuric acid → sulfates, nitric acid → nitrates) — linking to hydrochloric acid (pH ~1.5–2.0) in the human stomach.
cambridgeWatchouts: Hydrochloric acidalways forms a chloride salt; sulfuric acid forms a sulfate salt.

units.title: Magnetism
twsStrands: Scientific enquiry: analysis, evaluation and conclusions
units.scienceInContext: Discuss how scientific knowledge develops over time by shared understanding and investigation. Evaluate topics using scientific understanding.

topics.title: Magnetic fields
topics.summary: Magnetic field lines from north pole to south pole, attraction and repulsion.
cambridgeWatchouts: Magnetic field lines always point AWAY from North and TOWARD South, and never cross.

topics.title: The Earth as a giant magnet
topics.summary: Earth's magnetic field generated by its liquid iron outer core, compass navigation, and magnetoreception in migratory birds and sea turtles.
cambridgeWatchouts: Geographic North is near a magnetic south pole, which is why the north-seeking pole of a compass needle points north.

topics.title: Electromagnets
topics.summary: Building an electromagnet with a coil of wire, electric current, and a soft iron core.
cambridgeWatchouts: Soft iron is used for the core because it magnetises and demagnetises easily when the current is switched on and off.

topics.title: Investigating electromagnets
topics.summary: How number of turns on the coil, current, and core material affect electromagnet strength.
cambridgeWatchouts: Increasing the number of turns or increasing the current increases the strength of the electromagnet.

schoolQuestions.prompt: Trace the path of an oxygen molecule from the air outside the nose until it reaches an alveolus, and explain how the rings of cartilage in the trachea and the ciliated cells lining the bronchi help keep the lungs working.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
Pathway: nose → pharynx → larynx (voicebox) → trachea → bronchus → bronchiole → alveolus.
1. C-shaped rings of cartilage support the trachea and bronchi so the airway does not collapse when air pressure drops during inhalation.
2. Goblet cells secrete sticky mucus that traps dust and bacteria, and cilia on ciliated epithelial cells beat rhythmically to sweep the mucus up to the throat to be swallowed.
schoolQuestions.fadedPrompt: Complete the mark-scheme explanation: Rings of ________ prevent the trachea from collapsing when pressure drops during breathing in. Sticky ________ traps dust and bacteria, and beating ________ sweep it up and out of the airways.
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: Air travels nose → larynx → trachea → bronchus → bronchiole → alveolus. Cartilage rings hold the trachea open against low pressure during inhalation; goblet cells make mucus to trap dust/microbes and ciliated cells beat to sweep mucus up to the throat.

schoolQuestions.prompt: Explain three ways in which the structure of an alveolus and its blood supply are adapted to maximise the rate of gas exchange by diffusion.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
By Fick's law, diffusion rate increases with surface area and concentration gradient, and decreases with barrier thickness:
1. Millions of alveoli provide a huge total surface area (~70 m² in adults) so many O₂ and CO₂ molecules diffuse simultaneously.
2. Both the alveolus wall and the capillary wall are only ONE CELL THICK, giving a tiny diffusion distance (~0.5 µm).
3. Continuous blood flow in the dense capillary network and continuous ventilation maintain a steep concentration gradient for O₂ (higher in alveolus than blood) and CO₂ (higher in blood than alveolus).
schoolQuestions.fadedPrompt: The alveolus wall and capillary wall are each only ________ cell thick, which makes the diffusion ________ very short. Continuous blood flow maintains a steep ________ gradient.
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: 1. Large surface area from millions of alveoli. 2. Alveolar and capillary walls are one cell thick so the diffusion distance is very short. 3. Good blood supply in capillaries and breathing keep a steep concentration gradient for oxygen and carbon dioxide.

schoolQuestions.prompt: Describe and explain the sequence of events in the ribcage, intercostal muscles, and diaphragm that causes air to enter the lungs when you breathe in (inspire).
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
Step 1 (Muscles): External intercostal muscles contract (pulling the ribcage upwards and outwards) AND the diaphragm muscle contracts (flattening downwards).
Step 2 (Volume): The volume inside the thorax (chest cavity) increases.
Step 3 (Pressure): Because volume increases, pressure inside the thorax and lungs decreases below atmospheric pressure (Boyle's law).
Step 4 (Airflow): Air flows down the pressure gradient from outside the body through the trachea into the lungs.
schoolQuestions.fadedPrompt: When breathing in, the intercostal muscles and diaphragm ________. This causes the volume inside the thorax to ________, so the pressure inside the lungs ________ below atmospheric pressure, drawing air in.
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: The external intercostal muscles contract to move the ribcage up and out, and the diaphragm contracts and flattens. This increases the volume of the thorax, which decreases the pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure, so air flows into the lungs.

schoolQuestions.prompt: Two thermos flasks are set up: Flask A contains live germinating pea seeds in surface steriliser; Flask B contains dead boiled pea seeds in surface steriliser. Write the word equation for aerobic respiration and explain why the thermometer in Flask A reads 6 °C higher after 48 hours than Flask B.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
Word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
In Flask A, the living germinating pea cells carry out aerobic respiration inside their mitochondria to release energy for cell division and radicle growth. Because respiration is an exothermic reaction, some of the energy released from glucose is transferred as thermal energy (heat), raising the temperature. In Flask B, boiling killed the cells and denatured their respiratory enzymes, so no respiration occurs.
schoolQuestions.fadedPrompt: Word equation: ________ + oxygen → ________ + water. Live peas in Flask A carry out aerobic ________ inside their ________, which is an exothermic reaction that ________ thermal energy.
schoolQuestions.fadedAnswer: glucose; carbon dioxide; respiration; mitochondria; releases
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. The live germinating peas in Flask A respire aerobically, releasing energy from glucose; some energy is released as heat so temperature rises. Boiled peas in Flask B are dead (enzymes denatured) and cannot respire.

schoolQuestions.prompt: State two structural differences between a red blood cell and a white blood cell as seen under a light microscope, and explain how each adaptation of a red blood cell helps it transport oxygen efficiently to respiring tissues.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
Differences under microscope: (1) Red blood cells have no nucleus, whereas white blood cells have a prominent (often lobed) nucleus; (2) Red blood cells are smaller biconcave discs, whereas white blood cells are larger and can change shape.
Adaptations of red blood cells:
1. Cytoplasm is packed with haemoglobin, which binds reversibly with oxygen in the lungs to form oxyhaemoglobin and releases oxygen at respiring cells.
2. Having no nucleus (and no mitochondria) leaves more internal volume for haemoglobin molecules.
3. Biconcave disc shape gives a large surface area to volume ratio so oxygen diffuses in and out rapidly; flexibility lets them squeeze through narrow capillaries.
schoolQuestions.fadedPrompt: Red blood cells contain the red pigment ________ which binds oxygen. Unlike white blood cells, mature red blood cells have no ________, leaving more space for haemoglobin, and have a ________ disc shape for a large surface area.
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: Red blood cells have no nucleus and are biconcave discs, while white blood cells have a nucleus. Having no nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin to carry oxygen; the biconcave shape provides a large surface area to volume ratio for rapid oxygen diffusion.

schoolQuestions.bookSection: Workbook 2.4 Paper chromatography of leaf pigments (pp. 33–36)
schoolQuestions.prompt: A student crushes green spinach leaves in propanone and spots the extract onto chromatography paper to separate the photosynthetic pigments. Explain (a) why the baseline must be drawn in pencil rather than ink, and (b) why the solvent level in the beaker must start below the pencil line.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
(a) Pencil lead is graphite, which is insoluble in the solvent and stays in place. Ink contains dyes that would dissolve in the rising solvent and travel up the paper, mixing with the leaf pigments.
(b) If the solvent level started above the baseline, the spinach pigment spot would dissolve directly into the pool of solvent in the beaker instead of travelling up the paper fibres.
schoolQuestions.fadedPrompt: Pencil graphite is ________ in the solvent, whereas ink dyes would dissolve and move up the paper. Keeping the solvent below the baseline stops the pigment spot from ________ into the beaker liquid.
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: (a) Pencil is insoluble in the solvent, whereas ink would dissolve and run up the chromatogram. (b) If the solvent were above the line, the leaf pigment spot would dissolve into the pool of solvent in the beaker instead of separating up the paper.

schoolQuestions.prompt: Consider the human forearm as a lever with the elbow joint as the pivot. A student holds a 12 N stone in her hand at a perpendicular distance of 0.30 m from her elbow pivot. Her biceps muscle attaches to the radius bone 0.04 m from the elbow pivot. Calculate the upward force the biceps must exert to keep the forearm horizontal.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
1. Clockwise moment of stone about elbow = force × distance = 12 N × 0.30 m = 3.6 N m.
2. For equilibrium (forearm stationary horizontal), anticlockwise moment of biceps = clockwise moment = 3.6 N m.
3. F_biceps × 0.04 m = 3.6 N m ⇒ F_biceps = 3.6 ÷ 0.04 = 90 N.
schoolQuestions.fadedPrompt: Clockwise moment = 12 N × 0.30 m = ________ N m. For balance, F_biceps × 0.04 m = 3.6 N m, so F_biceps = ________ N.
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: Clockwise moment = 12 × 0.30 = 3.6 N m. Anticlockwise moment = F × 0.04 = 3.6 N m, so F = 3.6 ÷ 0.04 = 90 N.

schoolQuestions.prompt: Explain how three structural adaptations of the saguaro cactus help it survive and photosynthesise in the hot, dry Sonoran Desert ecosystem.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
1. Wide, shallow root system spreads far just beneath the soil surface to absorb rainwater rapidly after brief desert showers before it evaporates.
2. Thick, pleated green stem stores tonnes of water in swollen cells and contains chloroplasts to carry out photosynthesis.
3. Leaves are reduced to sharp spines with a thick waxy cuticle, which greatly reduces surface area for water loss by transpiration and protects the stored water from thirsty herbivores.
schoolQuestions.fadedPrompt: The saguaro has wide shallow ________ to absorb rain quickly, a thick pleated green ________ that stores water and photosynthesises, and ________ instead of broad leaves to reduce water evaporation and deter herbivores.
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: 1. Wide, shallow roots absorb water quickly over a large area when it rains. 2. Thick pleated stem stores large volumes of water and photosynthesises. 3. Spines instead of leaves reduce surface area for water loss and stop animals eating the cactus.

schoolQuestions.prompt: In an Arctic Ocean food chain, photosynthetic algae grow on the underside of sea ice: ice algae → krill → Arctic cod → ringed seal → polar bear. Explain what the arrows in the food chain represent, and predict how melting of Arctic sea ice affects the polar bear population.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
1. The arrows represent the direction of energy transfer (chemical energy in food passing from one trophic level to the next).
2. If sea ice melts, ice algae lose their habitat on the underside of the ice, so the producer population falls → less food for krill → fewer Arctic cod → fewer ringed seals → polar bears have less prey AND less sea-ice platform from which to hunt seals, causing the polar bear population to decrease.
schoolQuestions.fadedPrompt: Arrows in a food chain show the direction of ________ transfer. Melting sea ice destroys the habitat of ________ (the producers), reducing food for krill, cod, and seals, so the polar bear population ________.
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: Arrows show the direction of energy transfer. Melting sea ice reduces the habitat for photosynthetic ice algae, leaving less food for krill, cod, and seals, and removes the ice platform polar bears need to hunt seals, so polar bear numbers fall.

schoolQuestions.bookSection: Topic 4.3 Intruders in an ecosystem (pp. 139–141) & WB 4.3 (p. 76)
schoolQuestions.prompt: Buffelgrass is an invasive grass introduced to the Sonoran Desert from Africa. Explain why buffelgrass spreads rapidly in the Sonoran Desert and how it reduces the population of native saguaro cacti.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
1. Buffelgrass spreads rapidly because in the Sonoran Desert it has few or no natural herbivores, pests, or pathogens that controlled it in its native African habitat.
2. It grows in dense clumps and outcompetes native desert plants (including young saguaro seedlings) for scarce water, mineral ions, and space.
3. Dry buffelgrass fuels frequent, hot wildfires; buffelgrass regrows quickly after fire, whereas native saguaro cacti are not adapted to fire and are killed.
schoolQuestions.fadedPrompt: Invasive buffelgrass has no natural ________ in the Sonoran Desert, ________ native saguaro seedlings for water and minerals, and fuels frequent ________ that kill native cacti.
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: Buffelgrass has no natural herbivores or diseases in the Sonoran Desert. It grows densely and outcompetes native saguaro seedlings for water, minerals, and space, and causes frequent wildfires that kill saguaro cacti.

schoolQuestions.bookSection: Workbook 4.4 Bioaccumulation & Unit 4 Check your progress (pp. 82–87)
schoolQuestions.prompt: A lake is sprayed with a very low concentration (0.000003 ppm) of the persistent insecticide DDT to kill mosquito larvae. Years later, fish-eating grebes and ospreys at the top of the food chain die or lay eggs with shells so thin they break. Using the terms bioaccumulation and biomagnification, explain why top predators suffer poison levels millions of times higher than the water.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
1. Persistence: DDT is non-biodegradable (does not break down) and fat-soluble, so organisms cannot excrete it; it builds up inside an organism's tissues over its lifetime (bioaccumulation).
2. Food chain transfer: Microscopic plankton absorb DDT from water → each small fish eats thousands of plankton → each large fish eats many small fish → each osprey/grebe eats many large fish.
3. Biomagnification: Because biomass is lost to respiration at each trophic level while all the DDT is retained, the concentration of DDT increases at each higher step of the food chain until it reaches a toxic dose in the top predator.
schoolQuestions.fadedPrompt: DDT does not ________ down and cannot be excreted, so it builds up in tissues (________). Each predator eats many prey from the level below, so the toxin concentration ________ along the food chain (biomagnification).
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: DDT is persistent (does not break down) and is not excreted, so it builds up in an organism over time (bioaccumulation). Because each consumer eats many organisms from the trophic level below, the concentration of DDT increases up the food chain (biomagnification) to reach toxic levels in top predators.

schoolQuestions.prompt: (a) Describe how you would test a sample of food for (i) starch and (ii) reducing sugar (glucose), stating the positive colour change for each. (b) Explain why a person whose diet lacks iron feels tired and short of breath.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
(a)(i) Starch test: Add a few drops of iodine solution; a positive result changes from orange-brown to blue-black.
(a)(ii) Reducing sugar test: Add Benedict's solution and heat in a water bath at 80 °C; a positive result changes from blue to green/yellow/orange/brick-red precipitate.
(b) Iron is needed to make haemoglobin in red blood cells. Without enough iron (anaemia), red blood cells contain less haemoglobin and carry less oxygen to respiring cells. Cells carry out less aerobic respiration and release less energy, causing tiredness and breathlessness.
schoolQuestions.fadedPrompt: (a) Iodine turns from brown to ________ with starch; heated Benedict's turns from blue to ________ with glucose. (b) Iron is needed to make ________, which carries oxygen for aerobic ________.
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: (a)(i) Add iodine solution; turns blue-black if starch is present. (a)(ii) Add Benedict's solution and heat; turns brick-red/orange if sugar is present. (b) Iron is needed to make haemoglobin in red blood cells; a shortage causes anaemia so less oxygen is transported to cells for aerobic respiration, releasing less energy.

schoolQuestions.prompt: A 13-year-old student needs 10.0 MJ of energy per day, while a pregnant woman needs 10.9 MJ and a woman who is breastfeeding needs 11.7 MJ. Explain (a) why active teenagers need a high proportion of protein and calcium in their diet, and (b) why energy requirements increase during pregnancy.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
(a) Teenagers are undergoing rapid growth by cell division (mitosis): protein is required to synthesise new cell structures, cytoplasm, and muscle fibres, while calcium (with Vitamin D) is required to mineralise growing bones.
(b) During pregnancy, extra energy is required for respiration in the growing fetus's dividing cells and placenta, plus the mother uses more energy moving a larger body mass.
schoolQuestions.fadedPrompt: Teenagers need ________ to build new cells for growth and ________ to build strong bones. A pregnant woman needs extra energy for ________ in the growing fetus and to carry extra body mass.
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: (a) Protein is needed to make new cells and muscle tissue during growth; calcium is needed to build strong growing bones. (b) Extra energy is needed for respiration and cell division in the developing fetus and to move the mother's increased body mass.

schoolQuestions.bookSection: Topic 7.3 Growth, development and health — Smoking (pp. 248–251) & WB 7.3 (p. 144)
schoolQuestions.prompt: Tobacco smoke contains nicotine, carbon monoxide, and tar. Explain specifically how (a) carbon monoxide reduces the birth mass of babies born to mothers who smoke, and (b) tar leads to chronic bronchitis and emphysema.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
(a) Carbon monoxide diffuses into the mother's blood and binds irreversibly to haemoglobin in red blood cells (forming carboxyhaemoglobin), so each red blood cell carries less oxygen. Less oxygen diffuses across the placenta to the fetus, so fetal cells carry out less aerobic respiration, release less energy for cell division and protein synthesis, and the baby grows more slowly.
(b) Tar paralyses and destroys the cilia on ciliated epithelial cells lining the trachea and bronchi. Mucus and trapped bacteria are no longer swept up, triggering persistent coughing (chronic bronchitis) that damages and ruptures the thin walls of the alveoli (emphysema), greatly reducing the surface area for gas exchange.
schoolQuestions.fadedPrompt: Carbon monoxide binds to ________ in place of oxygen, so fetal cells respire less and grow slower. Tar paralyses ________ so mucus builds up, and coughing breaks down ________ walls, reducing surface area for gas exchange.
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: (a) Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin so the mother's blood carries less oxygen to the fetus; fetal cells respire less and have less energy for growth. (b) Tar paralyses cilia in the airways so mucus and bacteria accumulate (bronchitis); persistent coughing breaks down alveolus walls (emphysema), reducing the surface area for gas exchange.

schoolQuestions.bookSection: Topic 7.4 Moving the body & Unit 7 Check your progress (pp. 252–262, WB p. 153)
schoolQuestions.prompt: Explain why two muscles — the biceps and the triceps — are needed at the elbow hinge joint to bend and straighten the forearm, and state the role of tendons, ligaments, and synovial fluid at the joint.
schoolQuestions.workedExample:
1. Antagonistic pair rule: Muscles can only exert a pulling force when they contract; a muscle cannot push a bone when it relaxes. Therefore two antagonistic muscles pulling in opposite directions across the joint are required.
2. Bending (flexing) the arm: the biceps contracts (pulling the radius upwards) while the triceps relaxes. Straightening (extending) the arm: the triceps contracts (pulling the ulna downwards) while the biceps relaxes.
3. Tendons (tough, non-elastic cords) attach muscle to bone to transmit the pulling force; ligaments (slightly elastic) hold bone to bone to stabilise the joint; cartilage and synovial fluid reduce friction and absorb shock where bones meet.
schoolQuestions.fadedPrompt: Muscles can only ________ when they contract; they cannot push. To bend the arm, the biceps ________ and the triceps ________. ________ attach muscle to bone, while ligaments attach bone to bone.
schoolQuestions.modelAnswer: Muscles can only pull when they contract and cannot push, so an antagonistic pair is needed to pull the forearm bones in opposite directions. To bend the arm, biceps contracts and triceps relaxes; to straighten it, triceps contracts and biceps relaxes. Tendons attach muscle to bone, ligaments hold bone to bone, and synovial fluid lubricates the joint to reduce friction.

misconceptions.topic: Living vs. Non-Living, Dormancy & Spontaneous Generation (Ch 0 & Ch 1)
misconceptions.details: - Misconceptions: - "Fire, clouds, or rivers are alive because they move, grow, and consume fuel; a dry seed or unhatched cyst is dead because it does not move or use measurable oxygen." (Driver et al. 1994; Carey 1985: over 50% of 10–12-year-olds misclassify either fire/sun/clouds or dormant seeds/spores when pushed on criteria). - "Weevils in a sealed tin of rice or maggots in rotting meat appear by themselves out of the food." (Spontaneous generation intuition). - Decisive evidence: - *Dry moong seeds vs. candle flame: Weigh dry moong (mung bean) seeds before and after soaking in water, and compare a sealed jar of sprouting moong* (which fogs up, warms slightly, and turns limewater milky from cellular respiration while building ordered root/shoot tissue) against a candle flame under a jar (which breaks wax down into $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and snuffs out, leaving zero c

misconceptions.topic: Cells & Scale: Size, Interior & Why Cells Are Small (Ch 1 & Ch 2)
misconceptions.details: - Misconceptions: - "Atoms, molecules, viruses, bacteria, and human cells are all roughly the same 'microscopic' size." (Tretter et al. 2006; AAAS Project 2061: 54% of middle-schoolers think molecules are larger than or the same size as cells). - "A cell is a flat 2D fried-egg drawing filled with empty water around a few floating organelles." (In reality, the cytoplasm is a crowded 3D molecular city—roughly $20\text{–}30\%$ protein/RNA by volume). - "An elephant is bigger than a mouse because an elephant's cells are bigger than a mouse's cells." (48% of middle-school students on AAAS items). - Decisive evidence: - Surface-Area-to-Volume Ratio ($SA/V$) cube calculation & kitchen test: Cut three cubes of firm paneer or raw potato ($0.5\text{ cm}$, $1\text{ cm}$, $2\text{ cm}$ on a side) and soak them in beetroot juice or turmeric water for 15 minutes, then slice them in half. The dye penet

- Misconceptions: - "Molecules move from high to low concentration because they 'want' more space or 'try' to reach equilibrium." (62% of students, Odom & Barrow 1995 Osmosis and Diffusion Conceptual Assessment). - "Once equilibrium is reached, molecules stop moving." (58% of students, Odom & Barrow 1995). - "In salt water, salt rushes into a plant cell and bursts it / water moves because salt 'sucks' it." - Decisive evidence: - 3D random-walk particle simulation: Every molecule moves in a blind, random thermal bounce (`:::recall` The Invisible World Ch 3). More molecules on the left simply means more random bounces crossing left-to-right than right-to-left every millisecond. At equilibrium, equal numbers cross both ways—zero net change, nonstop motion. - Kitchen Forensics: Soak two identical raw potato strips (measured to the nearest millimetre, $60\text{ mm}$) for 30 minutes—one in pla

- Misconceptions: - "High temperatures 'kill' enzymes." (Enzymes are single folded protein molecules, not living organisms; they cannot die—thermal jiggling breaks the weak hydrogen/ionic bonds holding their 3D active site in shape, which is denaturation). - "Enzymes are used up in the reaction they catalyse." (46% of students, AAAS Project 2061). - Decisive evidence: - Raw vs. boiled potato/liver with $6\%$ pharmacy hydrogen peroxide ($\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$) or *fresh raw papaya/pineapple juice vs. boiled juice on set dahi (curd)/gelatin*: raw catalase froths $\text{O}_2$ violently and can froth a second batch of $\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$ (proving the enzyme was not used up); boiled potato produces zero bubbles because catalase is denatured.

misconceptions.topic: Photosynthesis & Where Plant Mass Comes From (Ch 5)
misconceptions.details: - Misconceptions: - "Plants get their food and almost all of their solid weight from the soil through their roots." (85%+ of students, Harvard Minds of Our Own / AAAS Project 2061 item `ME029`: 73% of middle-schoolers reject the claim that a tree's dry mass comes mainly from carbon dioxide gas in the air). - "Sunlight is a substance/ingredient that gets baked into sugar." (Light provides energy to split water and lift electrons, not atoms of matter). - Decisive evidence: - Jan Baptista van Helmont's 5-year willow tree experiment (published 1648): A $2.27\text{ kg}$ ($5\text{ lb}$) willow sapling grew to $76.8\text{ kg}$ ($169\text{ lb } 3\text{ oz}$) in a covered pot of oven-dried soil, while the dry soil lost only $57\text{ g}$ ($2\text{ oz}$)! Combined with Ingenhousz (1779) and Saussure (1804): the carbon atoms that make wood cellulose ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_5$)$_n$ come fr

- Misconceptions: - "Respiration means breathing in and out with your lungs." (67% of 12–14-year-olds, Driver et al. 1994). - "Plants photosynthesise during the day and respire only at night." (64% of students, Haslam & Treagust 1987). - "When you exercise and lose 1 kg of fat, that mass turns into heat/energy or sweat." (Meerman & Brown 2014 BMJ: over $84\%$ of lost fat mass is exhaled into the air as $\text{CO}_2$ gas; the remaining $16\%$ becomes $\text{H}_2\text{O}$). - Decisive evidence: - Stoichiometric atom-tracking of glucose ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2 \to 6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$) and fat oxidation, plus fermenting idli batter or yeast + sugar in a warm Mumbai kitchen inflating a balloon with $\text{CO}_2$.

- Misconceptions: - "Deoxygenated blood in your veins is bright blue, like the lines on your wrist or textbook diagrams." (52% of students; venous blood is dark maroon-red, never blue—your skin scatters red and blue light differently). - "Your stomach is a big bag taking up your whole belly, and food goes straight from the stomach into the bloodstream or out as faeces." (In reality, the small intestine does $>90\%$ of chemical digestion and absorption, and faeces are mostly undigested plant fibre, water, and dead gut bacteria, not metabolic 'excretion').

- Misconceptions: - "Only certain cells have DNA (e.g., brain cells have brain DNA, skin cells have skin DNA, and plants have no DNA because they aren't animals)." (51% of middle-schoolers think plants lack DNA or that different body cells carry different DNA; AAAS Project 2061). - "A dominant allele is stronger, healthier, and more common in the population than a recessive allele." (e.g., polydactyly—having six fingers—is caused by a dominant allele, yet $>99.8\%$ of people have five fingers). - Decisive evidence: - Kitchen DNA extraction from mashed banana or papaya using dish soap, table salt, and chilled surgical spirit (isopropyl alcohol) to spool visible white threads of plant DNA onto a toothpick.

- Misconceptions: - "When exposed to an antibiotic or a new climate, individual organisms mutate or adapt on purpose in order to survive, and pass that acquired change to their offspring." (79% of students, Bishop & Anderson 1990; Gregory 2009). - "Antibiotic resistance means your human body becomes resistant/immune to the antibiotic." (WHO 2015 multi-country survey: 76% of respondents believed the human body, rather than the bacteria, becomes resistant to antibiotics!). - Decisive evidence: - Luria & Delbrück (1943) / Lederberg replica plating (1952) and the Harvard Mega-Plate experiment: mutations happen randomly before the bacterium ever meets the antibiotic; the antibiotic simply kills the susceptible majority and leaves the pre-existing mutant with the whole plate to itself.

schoolWordingEntries.firstPrinciples: Living systems are self-maintaining, cellular machines that use external free energy (coupled via ATP) to maintain low internal entropy and replicate digital instructions (DNA).
schoolWordingEntries.cambridgeWording: MRS GREN (Topic 1.1): Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion, Nutrition. Every IGCSE paper expects exact definitions (e.g., Excretion = removal of waste products of metabolism and substances in excess; Nutrition = taking in materials for energy, growth and development).
schoolWordingEntries.examinerTrap: Trap 1: Calling egestion (passing undigested fibre as faeces) excretion. Faeces never entered your body cells' chemical reactions! Excretion is $\text{CO}_2$ from lungs and urea/water/salts from kidneys/sweat. Trap 2: Defining respiration as "breathing". In IGCSE, respiration is strictly "the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy for metabolism".

schoolWordingEntries.firstPrinciples: Viruses are acellular genetic packages (RNA or DNA inside a protein capsid, sometimes with a lipid envelope) that have zero ribosomes or ATP synthesis of their own and execute only inside a host cell.
schoolWordingEntries.cambridgeWording: Topic 1.2 & 1.3: Five Kingdoms (Prokaryote, Protoctist, Fungus, Plant, Animal); Viruses are explicitly classified as non-living on the grounds that they do not carry out the seven MRS GREN processes on their own and consist only of a protein coat and genetic material.
schoolWordingEntries.examinerTrap: Trap: Calling a virus a "cell" or a "bacterium", or saying it has a cell membrane or cytoplasm.

schoolWordingEntries.firstPrinciples: Cells are bounded 3D lipid-bilayer compartments packed with macromolecular machinery; eukaryotic organelles partition incompatible chemical reactions.
schoolWordingEntries.cambridgeWording: Topic 2.1 & 2.2: Animal vs. Plant vs. Bacterial cells (cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, vacuoles, mitochondria, chloroplasts, ribosomes, circular DNA + plasmids in bacteria). Formula: $\text{Magnification} = \text{image size} \div \text{actual size}$ ($M = I / A$, using $1\text{ mm} = 1000\text{ }\mu\text{m}$).
schoolWordingEntries.examinerTrap: Trap: Saying plant cells have chloroplasts and lack mitochondria! Root hair cells and onion bulb cells have zero chloroplasts (they are underground in the dark), and all living plant cells have mitochondria to respire 24 hours a day.

schoolWordingEntries.firstPrinciples: Random thermal motion ($k_B T$) of particles causes net flux down a concentration or chemical potential gradient; membranes with aquaporins pass small water molecules while blocking hydrated ions/sucrose.
schoolWordingEntries.cambridgeWording: Topic 3.1–3.3: Extended IGCSE defines osmosis using water potential: "the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential (dilute solution) to a region of lower water potential (concentrated solution), through a partially permeable membrane". Terms: turgid, turgor pressure, flaccid, plasmolysis.
schoolWordingEntries.examinerTrap: Trap: Saying "water moves from a high concentration of solution to a low concentration". A concentrated sugar solution has a low concentration of free water molecules (low water potential)! Always say water potential or dilute to concentrated solution.

schoolWordingEntries.firstPrinciples: Enzymes are folded polypeptide chains whose 3D active-site pocket stabilises the transition state and lowers activation energy ($E_a$). Thermal agitation above $T_{\text{opt}}$ breaks weak intramolecular bonds, unfolding the pocket.
schoolWordingEntries.cambridgeWording: Topic 4.1 & 5.1: Food tests (Benedict's for reducing sugars, iodine for starch, biuret for protein, ethanol emulsion for fats, DCPIP for vitamin C). Enzymes: substrate, active site, enzyme-substrate complex, complementary shape, optimum temperature/pH, denaturation.
schoolWordingEntries.examinerTrap: Trap: Never write "high temperature kills the enzyme". Examiners deduct the mark immediately. Enzymes were never alive; write: "kinetic energy increases, bonds holding the enzyme's 3D shape break, the active site changes shape and is no longer complementary to the substrate—the enzyme is denatured."

schoolWordingEntries.firstPrinciples: Light-driven oxidation of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ in thylakoid membranes generates ATP and NADPH, which the Calvin cycle uses to fix $\text{CO}_2$ into triose phosphate / glucose.
schoolWordingEntries.cambridgeWording: Topic 6.1: "Photosynthesis is the process by which plants synthesise carbohydrates from raw materials using energy from light". Balanced equation: $6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2$ in the presence of light and chlorophyll (which transfers light energy into chemical energy).
schoolWordingEntries.examinerTrap: Trap: Writing that plants "make energy" during photosynthesis. Energy cannot be created or destroyed (The Moving World Ch 7); chlorophyll transfers light energy into chemical energy stored in carbohydrates.

schoolWordingEntries.firstPrinciples: Stepwise oxidation of carbon fuels coupled to proton pumping across the inner mitochondrial membrane to spin ATP synthase.
schoolWordingEntries.cambridgeWording: Topic 12.1–12.3: Aerobic respiration ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2 \to 6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$) vs. Anaerobic respiration in yeast ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 \to 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 2\text{CO}_2$) and in human muscle ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 \to 2\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_3$, lactic acid), plus oxygen debt removed in the liver.
schoolWordingEntries.examinerTrap: Trap: Writing "respiration produces energy". IGCSE mark schemes insist on "respiration releases energy" (from chemical stores in glucose).

schoolWordingEntries.firstPrinciples: DNA is a double-stranded antiparallel polymer of four nucleotides whose sequence of triplets specifies the amino-acid sequence of polypeptides folded at ribosomes.
schoolWordingEntries.cambridgeWording: Topic 17 & 18: Chromosome, gene, allele, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, genotype, phenotype, mitosis (genetically identical diploid cells for growth/repair), meiosis (reduction division producing genetically different haploid gametes).
schoolWordingEntries.examinerTrap: Trap: Confusing gene (a length of DNA that codes for a protein) with allele (an alternative version of a gene).

schoolWordingEntries.firstPrinciples: Random mutations generate heritable variation; differential survival and reproduction shifts allele frequencies across generations.
schoolWordingEntries.cambridgeWording: Topic 18.3: IGCSE 6-step mark-scheme recipe for natural selection: (1) genetic variation within populations, (2) production of many offspring, (3) struggle for survival / competition for resources, (4) better-adapted individuals survive, (5) reproduce and (6) pass on their alleles to the next generation.
schoolWordingEntries.examinerTrap: Trap: Writing "bacteria mutate in order to become resistant to the antibiotic". Mutation is random and happens before/independently of the antibiotic; the antibiotic is the selection pressure.
